Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have the same effect on everyone?
Answer: They have the same actions, but the result depends on the person. Drugs defined by a specific formula will have the same basic actions universally, since those actions arise from the makeup of the chemicals. But, the experienced effects of a drug like an SSRI depends on all the personal and situational factors involved as well: how someone metabolizes it, what their health is like, how their nervous system is functioning, how high their dose is and how long they take it for, and so on. Most mechanisms of SSRIs will always be in action, such as the eponymous serotonin reuptake inhibition. What that causes to happen in someone’s mind, body, or behavior is much more complex because more than just the drug action is involved. Some effects are so common that the majority of patients will experience them, even if we choose patients at random or give the drugs to random people who aren’t patients and have no reason to take them. Some effects are common but only developing in a minority of patients, often due to differences between people that only become relevant to their everyday lives in certain kinds of situations. Some effects are common but easily prevented, resulting from things like poor drug management. Many effects are less common, or outright rare, and we don’t always know why they occur. Context, management, and personal traits all play a part in drug reactions. So, SSRIs have the same fundamental effects in everyone on the pharmacological level, but what this means for someone’s experiences is more complicated and personal. Some drug effects are pretty much universal, like attenuating certain kinds of signaling and sensation, though the intensity of those effects will still vary. Some drug effects are so rare they only occur once in every 1,000 to 10,000 patients. Most effects fall between those two extremes of incidence. The most relevant thing to understand is how the mechanisms of SSRIs carry particular risks and that even if we can’t predict every outcome, we can know that there are dangers to use which must be addressed.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do SSRIs/SNRIs work if serotonin hypothesis seems to be untrue?
Answer: There are two simple possibilities: Most people don’t find SSRIs/SNRIs to “work” for depression. There is no hypothesis needed for a mechanism of efficacy when efficacy is no better than placebo. But, there are still the exceptions — the patients whose experiences diverge far from the average. Some people experience very significant relief, sometimes even overnight, and there is a pharmacological reason for this. It won’t be the same reason from one person to the next, though, since each person is looking for their own particular alterations and the mechanisms behind each alteration can potentially differ between cases as well. In all cases, people are altered. What that means to them will depend on their reactions, their goals, their priorities, and their level of understanding.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do SSRIs work in increasing serotonin levels in the brain? Why don't we experience extreme happiness when consuming foods high in tryptophan?
Answer: Q1. How do SSRIs work in increasing serotonin levels in the brain? They don’t. The primary serotonergic effect of SSRIs is in the name: serotonin reuptake inhibition. They prevent the brain from putting serotonin back into storage for later reuse, instead stranding it between synapses where it doesn’t belong and has no business being at the time. This is bad for the brain and the brain works hard over the next weeks and months to do what it can to mitigate the harmfulness of this brain-hacking through neuroplastic processes like downregulation. So, SSRIs don’t increase how much serotonin is in the brain. They impact how much serotonin is available for use insofar as they prevent the normal recouping and reuse of serotonin, and some research suggests they even lead to a reduced production of serotonin, but they don’t supply extra serotonin. Their acute effect is to impair the normal regulation of serotonin so that receptors are being inundated by serotonin the brain didn’t want to be there, which you might be considering “increasing serotonin levels”. This may or may not relate to why any given patient finds SSRIs useful. Most depression patients find such drugs more harmful than helpful or simply unhelpful, so clearly most patients don’t find this or any drug mechanism all that useful. For patients who do find SSRI use preferable, the reasons will vary as will the mechanisms behind those experiences. Generally, the only people experiencing “extreme happiness” when starting an SSRI are people the SSRI caused mania, hypomania, or euphoria in, which is a minority reaction and usually a serious one. Q2. Why don't we experience extreme happiness when consuming foods high in tryptophan? Because serotonin isn’t happiness. Serotonin is to happiness what words are to great poetry: one of the tools involved in the experience, but a tool which must be used judiciously and in systematically applicable ways in order to produce the desired result. Most use of words is not great poetry, and throwing judiciousness and systemization out the window by listing all the words you know in any order is quite unlikely to create a poem generations look back on as great. Even if we assumed for the sake of the question that this hypothetical diet high in tryptophan significantly increased serotonin production, only people experiencing a health problem would be severely underproducing serotonin or improperly using serotonin. Unless the reason was a poor diet in the first place, eg a nutritional deficiency, eating foods higher in tryptophan wouldn’t fix the problem. And even if a diet somehow did fix any underlying problem, the result would be “euthymia”: a normal mood, not “extreme happiness”. Most depressions aren’t a symptom of illness, and most illnesses causing depression aren’t nutritional deficiencies. A good diet can contribute to good health and to good mental wellbeing, as can avoiding psychotropic drugs or using them only judiciously. If someone’s diet causes “extreme happiness” because of a higher-than-average tryptophan content, that would itself be a sign of illness or a genetic vulnerability to potentially serious medical complications.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it common to experience increased anxiety after starting an SSRI? Should I discontinue use?
Answer: It is very common. It may or may not go away. “Anxiety” is a somewhat broad concept. There can be many drug effects a patient might consider included, like nervousness, agitation, panic attacks, dissociation. There can also be drug effects that seem very similar to it at times, like akathisia, tachycardia, temperature dysregulation, hypomania. Anxiety in the somewhat narrower sense, not lumping in things like akathisia, is one of the most common effects for people to experience when starting a new drug or dose. It is typical with beginning a drug, with upping the dose, and with trying to quit. This is the result of the drug actions themselves, so it is an expected effect which many, many people will experience. Does it mean you should stop using the drug? Not necessarily, but sometimes. How intense the anxiety is, whether it is getting worse or getting better over the course of the first few days, and whether other symptoms are also occurring must be considered. For some people, this will be a time-limited effect that fades as drug tolerance sets in. For others, it stays around or becomes worse or more complex over time. In some instances, it is a symptom of something more serious that may require intervention or immediate drug discontinuation, like a toxidrome. By itself, anxiety doesn’t tell us whether someone should keep using the drug, or what the specific cause is. Someone needs to do some research and get professional consultation. In any case, though, anxiety should be taken as an indication that someone is trying to titrate too quickly. These effects can occur even at a very gradual pace of introducing or reducing the drug, but most people are instructed to move more quickly than is ideal for keeping anxiety at a minimum. Some people will find a drug more tolerable (or a discontinuation more workable) if they move the dose much more slowly. Many prescribers prefer to start too fast and only slow down if a patient experiences major problems as a result, but that isn’t necessarily responsible or preferable and it also contributes to the dangerous trend of SSRI drug effects being misdiagnosed and mistreated.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do any antidepressants, such as Lexapro, treat both anxiety and depression?
Answer: “Treat” is defined arbitrarily. All drugs marketed as “antidepressants” are psychotropics, which means all of these drugs can affect our mental experiences, our emotions, our behaviors. These drugs don’t treat causes of anxiety or depression, so there is no medical line to draw here. What is relevant is the psychotropic effects — what changes we consider desirable, and how likely a drug is to cause those changes. This is more complex because we aren’t talking about objective health or brain functioning and we aren’t even talking about the same set of goals across all patients or situations of use. It is defined personally, individually, and subjectively. Any of these drugs can potentially affect someone’s experience of anxiety, or depression, or both. Whether the alterations experienced are considered helpful, or worth all the downsides, is where the complications arise.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do some people judge the mentally ill for not wanting to take their medications? Do they know they're not perfect and don't fix everything? Finally, do they know how bad the side effects are?
Answer: Probably three main reasons: 1. People often feel inconvenienced by others if their behavior or thoughts or attitudes are less predictable, more abrasive, harder to understand, or harder to control. This has an aspect of self preservation, not wanting to potentially be subjected to difficult or dangerous situations. It also has an aspect of ignorance and laziness, not wanting to learn about and accommodate the needs and experiences of others. If someone is judging a person for not wanting to use toxic, disabling drugs, there is some sort of reasoning behind it. It might be misguided, it might be poorly expressed, but they are making some sort of association between drug use and their personal goals in the matter. It is something which must be addressed on an individual basis. 2. Marketing is the key to psychiatry’s industrial success. Marketing the drugs and other products, marketing the psychiatric beliefs, marketing the social applications of psychiatry (to everyday consumers, to administrative bodies, to government). The trouble with marketing being such an integral part of psychiatry’s popularity and profitability is that we are basing most of our decisions on unearned faith instead of outcomes. Many people have expectations about so-called “mental illness” and psychiatric inventions which have no basis in reality, and these baseless ideas are pushed onto people targeted as ‘patients’. Mainstream culture, the most powerful world governments, and most industry are strongly pro-psychiatry. Conversely, criticism of psychiatry is stigmatized. A harmful perspective about psychiatry is the cultural norm. 3. They have little idea what other people are really going through. Some are just dangerously naive and haven’t put in the work to better understand what psychiatric drugs do, how they affect people, what we are labeling as “mental illness”, and what people need in life to feel and function better. Those are pretty huge topics and it takes a lot of work to have a more grounded and insightful understanding of them. Most people simply aren’t informed enough to make great decisions about these matters. On the other hand, some people are just willfully uneducated and prefer judging, controlling, and ostracizing to connecting with the humanity behind what others are going through and why they are making the decisions they make. The disinterest in connecting can be a serious practical barrier to understanding. As with any of these concerns, the behavior revolves around the person doing the judging, not anyone else. So, do most people know that psychiatric drugs usually fail or cause more harm than good? No. Though many people are at least a little skeptical, and it is common to feel like drug overuse is occurring, the people pushing psychiatry on others are fundamentally lacking evidence that what they are doing will accomplish what is best for someone. Do most people know how bad psychiatric drug effects can be, and how often they are severe? No. If they looked into the data about how drug use turns out, they’d probably have a radically different approach to things. Some scary risks are very uncommon drug outcomes and aren’t an everyday thing people need to worry about. However, some of the most concerning drug effects are extremely common and wreaking major havoc in society. Marketing, an avoidance of responsibility, and profits obscure or steer us away from the path to better outcomes.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why don’t my antidepressants help my apathy?
Answer: One of three reasons: There are some basic steps to take. The cause of the apathy needs to be investigated and addressed. The drug regimen needs to be evaluated and modified. Education about drug effects, risks, and management should be pursued. All of this should be undertaken with proper communication with a responsible and effective professional.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are there any potential withdrawal symptoms when switching from Lexapro to Prozac, similar to those experienced when abruptly stopping antidepressants?
Answer: Switching IS stopping. The same withdrawal symptoms can be experienced whether someone is reducing their dose, quitting their drug, switching their drug, or changing their schedule of drugging to be less frequent (like missing a dose, or going to once a day from twice a day). Physical dependence relates to several factors involved in the use of a given drug. This includes the actions of that drug on the nervous system, but also things like the release design of the drug, how long it takes our body to process the drug on average, what other drugs are being taken which might slow our metabolizing of the drug, whether we are keeping a consistent schedule in dosing, and so forth. Since there are many variables and they can differ between patients and situations, outcomes also differ. Switching between drugs is discontinuing the drug we have become physically dependent upon, by definition. Whether the drug being switched to will prevent some or all withdrawal symptoms will depend on that array of factors and someone’s ability to cope in the moment (so things like health, drug history, and lifestyle management can play a role in outcomes). Some drugs are more similar than others when it comes to each factor involved in physical dependence. Some patients are also more flexible in what kinds of changes they can tolerate before their nervous system is overwhelmed. Withdrawal is typical but not universal when switching between drugs in the same broad marketing class (such as SSRIs, in the question’s example). Withdrawal is to be expected when switching between classes, like swapping an SSRI for an NaSSA. With respect to the actions of a drug, there is a higher risk of symptoms developing when some key actions differ or one drug has a much higher potency (affinity) than the other. Even within the group of SSRIs, to continue using the same example, some drugs have more potent DRI or NRI effects than the others, or more potent histaminic effects or opioidergic effects than the others. The greater the difference, the more likely symptoms are to result when trying to switch to a less potent drug option. But even drugs sharing a very potent action, like SRI, aren’t necessarily interchangeable due to the other factors mentioned above. If a drug is metabolized at a different rate, for instance, that can potentially make a big difference in how someone tolerates a swap.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do antidepressants have a period where they make you feel worse before they start working? If so, why would someone choose to take them?
Answer: Q1. Do antidepressants have a period where they make you feel worse before they start working? It isn’t usually that simple. There are three basic types of effects: ones that come on pretty much right away but eventually fade, ones that come on pretty much right away and stick around rather than fading, and ones that come on after a while of continuous use (whether days, weeks, or months) instead of right away. Any of these effects might be considered desirable or undesirable by a specific patient or clinician. So, both ‘good’ and ‘bad’ reactions can happen right away, both ‘good’ and ‘bad’ reactions can happen later on. Because the vast majority of drug effects are usually considered undesirable by most people, most effects in each of these three categories will be adverse and something people want to avoid. Some drug effects most often occur as temporary symptoms following dose changes, like when first starting a drug, increasing the dose, or decreasing the dose. When these are uncomfortable, substantially impairing, or dangerous, they can make it harder to start a drug and stay on it. In a modest minority of cases, they are so serious as to make drug use impossible. In addition to these kinds of effects, drug tolerance sets in after a while of daily use, and that can reduce some adverse reactions, depending on the symptom and the patient. However, if someone was relying on those reactions to consider a drug useful, drug tolerance can be counterproductive as well. But, for context, most patients never find these drugs to do what they were wanting them to do. That is to say, it would be inaccurate to suggest the problem is that these drugs are hard to start but usually pay off in the end, because they don’t usually pay off regardless of whether someone found them easy or difficult to tolerate. While it is true that a certain subset of effects most commonly occur in the earliest days or weeks of use but then fall away or at least get milder, most adverse effects are not in that smallish group of effects. Most don’t either go away, get worse instead of better, or come on later instead of right after a new dose is started. So, it is usual to have a rocky start when initiating a drug, but the burden more often increases rather than decreasing with ongoing drug use. Especially when we consider that people tend to find quitting more difficult that starting due to withdrawal and other reduction-related drug effects. Unimpressive average drug effectiveness coupled with the high rate of adverse effects and the significant rate of serious effects makes it so that most patients find any given drug more helpful than harmful in net. This speaks to the prescribing situation as well, since it is prescribers who mediate which patients are given a drug in the first place and how that drug is managed. If we prescribed these drugs more selectively, or managed them differently, it would change the rate at which certain outcomes happened. We could change how often the drugs are given or who they are given to so that more patients found them meaningfully useful. We could change how they are manged so that some drug effects happened a lot less often. Unfortunately, current market pressures promote unnecessary prescribing and poor management — the opposite of what we should aim for. Q2. If so, why would someone choose to take them? This is an easier and simpler thing to answer. It mostly comes down to just two possibilities:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What are the possible reasons for feeling worse after starting an antidepressant like Lexapro?
Answer: The most likely reason is that these drugs make people feel bad. These drugs are fundamentally bad for the body, and a consequence of their adverse actions is adverse effects. It is typical to feel worse instead of better when taking these drugs, and some people who do feel better still experience significant adverse reactions. If someone feeling worse after starting or staying on a drug like escitalopram (aka Lexapro) is feeling worse because of the drug and not because of other unrelated factors, there are three main reasons why that could be: Tapering up or down more slowly and reducing the total number of drugs being taken at any given time can reduce some of the risks of feeling worse. Making sure to calibrate the dose for someone’s body and situation is also useful. But, even using a low dose carefully and by itself is still usually going to make someone feel worse. These aren’t feel-good drugs. They can induce euphoria or outright mania, but most adverse effects feel bad or cause problems with everyday functioning or wellbeing.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Due to emotional numbing, I made a reduction of my antidepressant Nortriptyline from 160mg to 155mg (under the care of my doctor). How long will it take for my brain to register the reduction?
Answer: Your brain is registering the reduction immediately. There are three concerns here, though. So, if you made the reduction, your brain is already registering that difference. Whether that will significantly change how it feels to be on the drug is a more complex and personal question. It can take days, weeks, or longer to more fully adjust to large dose changes, but this was not a large dose change and maybe easier to adjust to.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do antidepressants have delayed onset of action although they increase monoamines instantly? Also, I don't think this is the real mechanism.
Answer: They don’t have a delayed onset of action, but our experiences can change over time. Drugs marketed as “antidepressants” are a whole clusterfuck of actions and effects and these are changing the nervous system as early as the first dose we take. None of them are delayed onset. But just like with other psychotropic drugs, from caffeine to opiates to alcohol to corticosteroids, our body is continuously changed during ongoing use. Our nervous system and other parts of our body are adapting to the presence of the drug and the disruptions it is causing. This is not a single, one-time change, it is an ongoing change which is influenced both by the acute actions of the drug and by the changes which have already been produced though exposure to that drug. Antidepressants also cause damages and other harms which can accumulate and become more noticeable over time. How we experience a drug will be affected by these various kinds of cumulative changes or damages. The rate of many drug effects will increase with continuous use of antidepressants, for instance apathy syndrome, withdrawal syndrome, sexual impairment. We don’t always know all of the mechanisms involved, but we can see that the gradual and progressive alterations caused by drug exposure change someone’s experiences and level of functioning. So, the concern here is whether effects which are increasingly experienced with continuous use are desired by the patient or prescriber. Most will be undesirable, just as most drug effects in general are undesirable, but sometimes someone will find particular ones useful. Sometimes the very same effect one patient finds useful is an intolerable adverse effect to another, as well.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can some people not experience any effects from taking antidepressants?
Answer: All people are affected by antidepressants, but what they notice can vary. By their very nature, these are alterants which change and poison our bodies. There is no way to take them and avoid experiencing any effects as a result. However, not all effects will be equally noticeable, equally harmful, or equally significant to each patient. Someone may or may not feel all whacked out when taking an antidepressant, regardless of what is going on in their body as a result of drug use. Someone may feel drug use is pretty neutral overall, just as they may feel drug use is helpful in ways or impairing in ways. It is impossible to experience no effects at all, but someone may not consciously notice effects that they consider important. Also note that these drugs interfere with our mental ability to self-assess, so sometimes people will feel unaltered and feel just fine even if they are feeling or acting bizarrely and very much unlike themselves.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Would it hurt to take anti psychotic pills even if you don't have psychosis? I want to try taking some in the case I do have psychosis but scared it may cause side effects if I maybe don't have it. Is there any harm in doing this?
Answer: Yes, these drugs hurt all people who take them. The question with psychiatric drugs isn’t whether or not they can be harmful, it is whether the risks of the harms involved are outweighed by the potential upsides and someone has exhausted all more appropriate strategies first. You don’t have to be experiencing ‘psychosis’ for drug use to be considered more helpful than harmful, and drug use won’t necessarily be justifiable even if you are experiencing ‘psychosis’. Diagnosis or clinical terminology isn’t what determines whether the upsides outweigh the downsides. These drugs are harmful to all people who take them. 100% of patients. Some people are more harmed than others, some people notice more harms than others or are more incapacitated by harms than others, but the bottom line is that these are fundamentally toxic, disruptive, harmful drugs and using them is harmful no matter our reasons for use or whether use seems justifiable to us. So your question doesn’t come down to whether this would harm you, but rather whether the risk of harm seems worth taking on. If you aren’t sure whether or not you are experiencing things that clinicians would label as psychosis, a drug won’t help you with that. These drugs don’t provide diagnostic information — any experiences you are concerned about may or may not be diminished by drug use, and this has nothing to do with whether a professional would label them as psychosis or slap on a psychiatric diagnosis circumscribing psychosis. These drugs are not made any more helpful or any less harmful by someone’s diagnosis.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible to develop an addiction to antidepressants such as SSRIs? If so, what are the factors that contribute to dependence on them?
Answer: Addiction to drugs like SSRIs works the same as addiction to other drugs. Neurofunctional, psychological, and lifestyle factors can all contribute to addiction. Some drugs are more liable to produce addiction due to their actions, but most cases of addiction come down to something other than drug mechanism. Conventionally, physical dependence is also required for addiction, and all psychiatric psychotropics do cause physical dependence — even in patients who do not become addicted in the sense you seem to be asking about. But, exactly what we mean by “addiction” is probably important to unpack here. Many or perhaps even most long-term patients meet key criteria for addiction, like difficulty quitting even in the absence of benefits, adverse effects interfering with life goals, and continued use despite harms. However, in most of these cases, it is not the stereotypical picture of someone jonesing for their next hit, craving the drug and losing track of their social or moral center in a desperate attempt to score. So, some people feel that meeting the general criteria without looking like a crackhead caricature should still be referred to as addiction because people have lost control of their use and their lives are suffering significantly as a result. Others feel the term should be reserved for situations where use has no clinical endorsement, people are taking higher-than-prescribed doses or unintended methods of delivery, and jonesing is likely. These are social distinctions more than pharmacological or biofunctional ones.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I took some antidepressants (Zoloft) due to my depression, then I had a maniac episode. Am I now a bipolar person?
Answer: This tells us nothing new about you as a person. Drugs like sertraline (aka Zoloft) are pro-manic. That is, they promote mania as a general influence — not just in patients with a history of mania, not just in patients with a special vulnerability to mania. The rate of hypomania/mania being caused by drugs like SSRIs is surprisingly high, both in use and as a discontinuation effect. Experiencing mania in response to sertraline does not tell us anything about you other than that you experienced mania in response to sertraline, and that is assuming you are referring to a causal connection here instead of saying that mania happened but may or may not be related. It is not really clear what a “bipolar person” would be. “Bipolar depression” refers to a pattern of depression alternating with mania, generally as part of a single psychological system of experiences. If this is a drug effect, it isn’t bipolar depression in that sense. “Bipolar disorder” refers to a range of diagnoses which have a variety of criteria including the excluding of all medical disorders and drug effects, so that idea is also inapplicable here if this was a drug effect. So far as we know from the information provided, you’re simply a person who has experienced depression and experienced a bad reaction to Zoloft. This is a red flag, though. Mania being caused by one stimulus makes it more likely there will be other stimuli which may also cause mania for us. Someone should evaluate what variables involved in the situation contributed to the mania and then consider how to minimize the risks involved in interacting with those variables in the future. For instance, it may be important to avoid similar drugs in the future, or perhaps there was a specific drug combination or set of lifestyle factors needing to be adjusted so that this is not as likely to happen again. Maybe it was the sertraline all by itself, maybe there is more to address.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it beneficial to continue seeing a psychiatrist who is not helping us, or should we switch to a different one?
Answer: Your question basically answers itself. If someone is not helping you, they are not benefiting you. If you want help, obviously something has to change. Maybe the current psychiatrist is doing a bad job but could do a better job, or maybe there are mistakes being made or a misunderstanding going on. Or, maybe their beliefs, knowledge, or approach will never be compatible and it is important to move on. Those are details you will have to assess yourself. There is one consideration beyond just whether the doctor is helpful though, which is whether being on the books with them is beneficial to you in some way. For instance, if you are receiving aid from a government or community program and leaving that doctor would put your position in jeopardy, that might make this decision more complicated even if the psychiatrist is totally useless as a practitioner. If your current psychiatrist is not helpful, does that mean you should switch to a different one? Maybe, or maybe psychiatry itself is a bad fit in the first place. Alternatives to an ineffectual practitioner aren’t limited to just other psychiatrists. There is a whole world of options out there, both professional and otherwise, which people have found helpful. Figuring out what works best for you is ultimately a very personal journey.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: When do withdrawal symptoms typically start after stopping an SSRI?
Answer: Probably within the first week off, on average. Individual experiences vary a lot. Some people start experiencing withdrawal even before their daily dose is due, and some people are on the other extreme end and go several months before withdrawal symptoms hit them. Most experiences seem to fall within the range of a couple weeks. Some people will notice symptoms beginning within the first 1–3 days, others experience a longer delay. The specific drug being discontinued can also play a part. The shortest half-life drugs may be more likely to cause issues within the first day of cessation while fluoxetine (especially due to its longer-lived metabolite, norfluoxetine) can delay onset by days or weeks. The more systems a drug potently acts on directly, the more likely withdrawal seems to be, and this may also affect average onset a bit. For people stopping an SSRI with a proper taper, symptoms would likely have already been occurring long before the final dose was discontinued. A taper aims to keep symptoms minimal and manageable, but symptoms are still typical. Going off slowly enough should mean that the full cessation does not produce much more disruption than the incremental reductions done along the way, though.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If I took a QT prolonging medication before (40 mg fluoxetine) and turned out fine, could a different one cause serious complications (clarithromycin 500mg)?
Answer: Yes, there is always the risk of a worse reaction. There are three main concerns here. Firstly, as another answer highlights, serious rhythm problems can be caused by a drug alone but there are often risk factors playing a role in who experiences a severe reaction and who does not. Those other risk factors are subject to change, so where things stand for you today is not necessarily where they stood back when you took fluoxetine. The drug being taken is not the only variable. Secondly, the specific mechanisms by which drugs disrupt or threaten to disrupt heart rhythm are not all the same, and someone can be more vulnerable to one than to another. While an untroubled experience with fluoxetine may suggest you are less likely to experience serious rhythm problems if you used fluoxetine again in the future, all other things being equal, they don’t necessarily speak to how you will react to dissimilar drugs. Thirdly, your previous use of fluoxetine may actually pose an issue itself. Changes to your body and its functioning occur with the use of drugs like SSRIs and there can be long-term repercussions even for people who have been off the drug for a while. What doses you took, for how long, how you tapered off, what other stressors were going on, and how you felt during use and recovery can be assessed to weigh the relevance of past fluoxetine use in managing the risks of new QT-prolonging drugs. Basically, we can’t know for sure how someone will react to these drugs, even if we have their entire medical and drug history in hand. But, there are some risk factors to look out for, and some risk-reducing strategies for drug prescribing and management which can make it less likely someone will have a serious rhythm issue. Still, the potential for more serious reactions following from drugs that mess with QT will always be there.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can a psychiatrist prescribe antidepressants, such as SSRIs, without diagnosing someone with depression? How can someone request to be prescribed an SSRI from their doctor?
Answer: Q1. Can a psychiatrist prescribe antidepressants, such as SSRIs, without diagnosing someone with depression? In places like America, drugs such as SSRIs can be prescribed for any reason by any doctor (and some additional kinds of practitioners, as well). What is legal or accepted may differ in some parts of the world. No diagnosis is necessary for prescribing, and most prescriptions of “antidepressants” aren’t for depression so a depression diagnosis is even less necessary. Diagnosis is irrelevant in most respects, and if you’re paying out of pocket there is no reason to get a psychiatric diagnosis at all. However, what a healthcare or drug plan will cover can sometimes depend on administrative factors of this sort. Sometimes what kind of paperwork a clinician fills out, and what they put down on it, can affect what your care plan will cover. The average patient relies on coverage to be seeing doctors and using drugs, though generic SSRIs are among the cheapest drugs for patients stuck without help. In situations where putting true information keeps a patient from being covered, some clinicians might put whatever the administrative rules require for coverage. Q2. How can someone request to be prescribed an SSRI from their doctor? That can depend on what your relationship is like with that doctor, but usually it is reasonable to simply say that you have concerns A, B, C and think an SSRI will help for reasons X, Y, Z. They can agree or disagree with your conclusion, but the important thing is that you communicate what is going on and what you would consider helpful. The stakes are not high here, though, as it is almost impossible to find a prescribing psychiatrist who refuses a patient an SSRI. You can get an SSRI prescription more easily than you can get a bottle of water from the average psychiatrist. The vast majority of prescriptions aren’t even in the best interest of the patient, but prescribing is expanding, not shrinking.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I took so many sertraline but nothing happened to me. Why? I am 17 years old.
Answer: Why not? If you mean you took an overdose, you may not notice a huge difference from the effects of a normal dose. Standard dosing is already making use of most of sertraline’s potency potential, so scaling up the dose won’t likely make someone feel totally different. Higher doses will produce more adverse effects and more severe adverse effects than lower doses, but some patients don’t find SSRI overdoses to be greatly troubling and it is more likely to experience a really bad reaction with ultra-high chronic dosing versus a single overdose. Overdosing is still dangerous and not recommended, and many people feel really bad when overdosing, but it is not something that basically guarantees a serious reaction, unlike many other kinds of psychotropic drugs. If you mean you’ve been taking sertraline every day as directed but haven’t noticed any upsides, that is sadly typical. Though these are powerful drugs, their ability to produce desirable alterations is limited and unreliable. Most patients find them inadequate or plain unhelpful. It could be that longer use or a higher dose would make a difference for you, but usually the changes people are hoping for never come. These drugs are powerful tools but have a pretty narrow range of usefulness and are more often misapplied than appropriately applied. I would reassess your goals, intervention options, and drug management to see if something can be adjusted to facilitate better results. That you are asking this question on here also suggests you are not receiving sufficient professional support and education, so doing extra research is important.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can someone be diagnosed with bipolar disorder based on a short period of knowing them?
Answer: Psychiatric diagnoses are tautologies, not identifications. Unmarried men are bachelors. That is a tautology. It does not identify why the men are unmarried, it does not explain how people can marry or not marry, it is just a statement which labels unmarried men as being “bachelors”. It isn’t about evidence, it isn’t about reality, it is just a term of convenience. Psychiatric diagnoses, such as “bipolar disorder”, function the same way. An industry-sponsored body comes up with how they want to define the idea as a diagnosis — the diagnostic criteria — and then it becomes a term of convenience hypothetically meant to convey those criteria. It does not explain anything about the experiences being labeled, like why they happened or if or when they might happen again, or how to respond to them, or what a patient needs. No knowledge is required, it is simply about whether a clinician wants to say that the information they are provided meets the diagnostic criteria that was voted into popular use. It is a label which refers specifically to the information they were provided. If more information is provided later, the label may no longer apply. If new experiences occur which violate the diagnostic criteria, the label may no longer apply. It isn’t an identifying of something in the body of a patient, or the cause of their experiences, it is just a term of convenience to basically say “that stuff over there (which the patient told me or I observed or assumed)”. A clinician can be as slapdash and ignorant as they’d like when assigning a diagnosis. It has no scientific legitimacy, it is just a made-up tautology. So, a patient can be diagnosed based on a five second interaction or based on the accounts of others but no personal interaction at all or based on medical records. The less time spent interviewing and digging for more information and context, the more likely a diagnosis is to be ditched or adjusted later on, but in any case the diagnosis has no physical reality. The experiences are the same no matter what label we give them, and no matter what labeling system we decide to use any given day or year. Because the diagnosis adds no new information to someone’s experiences, it is not something which can be ‘right’ or ‘wrong’ in the traditional sense, or in the sense of other medical diagnoses. The only thing to evaluate is whether or not it followed the diagnostic rules for using the term.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why is psychotherapy offered to adults if the brain stops developing at age 25? For example, if you've spent your childhood and adolescence being depressed, won't your brain have deleted the pathways for non-depressive ways of thinking?
Answer: That’s not really how any of that works. First off, the brain does not stop developing at age 25. That is an urban myth like saying we only use 10% of our brains. Though it is true that a lot of milestone development will happen by age 25, some important aspects of brain development continue well beyond 25, and our brain will be maturing in ways throughout our entire lives. We never have a static, finished product — our brain is always being altered, adjusted, reshaped to some degree. Continuing, maturation and neuroplastic change are overlapping but mostly separate categories. Development is about the brain’s age-related changes which we assign value to because of social utility. Much of this development will involve neuroplasticity, however most neuroplastic changes aren’t about brain development. The brain is constantly changing itself even after it is matured. This plasticity is an essential capacity which is used every second of every day. I’m not sure why you think people can still learn the names of new friends or still learn things at their jobs or still learn better communication or still learn new hobbies after age 25 but think psychotherapy would not be effective after age 25. Things like mood, memory, habit, and learned skills all rely on the brain being changed, and the brain is always changeable no matter how old we become. There are ages and situations in which some kinds of learning are easier, but change is a given. This speaks to your more specific query about “pathways for non-depressive ways of thinking”. “Pathways” in this loose sense are not pathways which we start off with and then lose over time, they are things we can create or alter at any phase of our lives. The brain, at any age, can be changed to cause or alleviate, increase or decrease depression. Note that not all depressions are about our thinking, either, and those which are rooted in it will not necessarily be helped by psychotherapy or specific psychotherapies.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Have there been cases where individuals did not experience any benefits from SSRI/SNRI medication for major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, or social phobia?
Answer: Of course. Whether someone finds alcohol, meth, tobacco, SSRIs, or other drugs beneficial depends a lot on what they are considering a benefit and how likely particular substances are to produce the alterations someone prefers. It is typical for someone to feel that SSRIs/SNRIs don’t pull their weight — that they have no major benefits, that they cause more bad than good, or that any upsides are clinically negligible and don’t lead to the life outcomes someone is hoping for. These drugs have no special value in unipolar depression, bipolar depression, or social anxiety and there is no reason to expect someone would find them more helpful than harmful.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can SSRI withdrawal symptoms be permanent?
Answer: That depends on how we define “withdrawal symptoms”. Not all symptoms that occur with a dose reduction or drug discontinuation are withdrawal. Where we draw the line between withdrawal and all the other kinds of symptoms is not something medicine has concretized into globally accepted boundaries. The simplest thing to say is that these symptoms can last indefinitely, and some people will have permanent symptoms or lifelong symptoms. Which of them are considered “withdrawal” is the trickier part. By its nature, withdrawal is supposed to be a temporary collection of symptoms that relate to the body shifting to a new homeostasis after physical dependence upon a drug is no longer being met. So, while this can take months or years in some cases, withdrawal theoretically does end sooner or later. But, it is messier than that because the destabilization producing symptoms can last long after the unmet physical dependence is no longer a problem. As part of recovery, many patients will also find themselves more sensitive to a variety of stressors and determine that they need to make some lifestyle adjustments to reduce their symptoms. When management is inadequate, symptoms can be prolonged or even worsened. I bring this up because it highlights how the length of symptoms is not just about their natural course, it is also about how somebody responds to them.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is there a higher likelihood for children of parents with severe mental illnesses, such as schizophrenia, to develop the same conditions?
Answer: Broadly speaking, sure. Specifically speaking, it is not a coherent thing to say. “Mental illnesses” are just bullshit, not objectively separate “conditions” which can be compared and then concluded as being ‘the same’ or ‘not the same’. So, the entire premise of the question is incoherent if we are being literal. If we are more generous and assume the bot question is just spouting off marketing dogma, we can ignore the diagnoses themselves and just talk about experiences — the things commonly referred to as depression, mania, psychosis, panic, and so on. While these are things anyone can experience, it is true that some people are more likely to experience some of them. Everything from genes to latitude to diet to parenting style to income can affect what people experience, directly and indirectly. There are many risk factors which are more likely to be present when someone has a parent said to be “severely mentally ill”, meaning we can anticipate an average increase in some of these experiences because of those variables. Sometimes this is because the same factors led to similar experiences in both the parents and the children, sometimes the impairments experienced by parents disadvantage their children, sometimes poor social infrastructure and support simply fails all of them whatever their personally unique needs may be. But, importantly, a parent’s diagnosis doesn’t lay out any of those variables. Statistics relying on diagnostic labels instead of actual influences will be nonsense at best, willfully and exploitatively dishonest at worst.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: It’s been over a month since I stopped taking sertraline but why do I still feel side effects like brain zaps and anxiety mood changes? The root cause of anxiety it’s your thinking and I perfectly master that better than before so it’s hard lately.
Answer: Basically, it takes longer than a month to recover. Most people will have more than just one short month of symptoms like this after quitting continuous use of an SSRI, and the fading of symptoms is only the initial stage of recovery from drug changes. These are potent drugs and the alterations they cause in the nervous system are deep and longer-lasting. Since our bodies retain the ability to change in response to new circumstances, many of the same mechanisms that led to physical dependence will also help you adapt away from drug alterations. However, some drug changes or damages involve other mechanisms and recovery from them may look different, when recovery is possible. In any case, it is not just very normal but outright typical to be experiencing things like brain zaps, anxiety, and mood changes after quitting sertraline, whether it has been a day, a week, a month, or a few months. A long adjustment period is needed, and most people will experience symptoms like this as a result of that transition. Neglecting to properly taper off after long-term use can make these experiences even more intense. You don’t mention whether or not you tapered, or what gradualness of taper you used if you did taper, but these symptoms indicate you discontinued more quickly than your body could handle. As for anxiety, anxiety is not just the result of thinking. Your hormones can cause anxiety no matter what you are thinking. It is true that our thought life can influence anxiety, most especially in the sense of increasing anxiety, decreasing anxiety, or perpetuating patterns of anxiety. But, even a well-maintained approach to mental wellbeing won’t necessarily diminish or prevent anxiety caused by drugs. Some patients struggle with health anxiety and panicking about drug symptoms during recovery, but even more people experience anxiety that comes on and leaves independent of our thought-life. It is part of our bodies adjusting away from the dysfunction induced by SSRIs. The good news is that most people do experience a substantial amount of recovery. Whether it will take a few months more, over a year, or many years is not predictable, but these should not be permanent symptoms. In the meantime, reducing stressors can be an important part of self-care that might reduce symptom intensity. Carving out time and space to rehabilitate is recommendable. Some patients should also consider reinstating a low dose of the drug to stabilize and reduce symptoms before more gradually tapering off again later. It is an option to consider the appropriateness of and talk to your prescriber about. Experiencing anxiety again does not mean your previous efforts have failed. There is just a new variable now that your previous practices may not be able to overcome. It should resolve on its own within months to years, though. Doing extra things to cope with or work through anxiety in the present can be helpful, though. Treating yourself more gently and remembering that these drug disruptions are temporary may be useful. Some patients also tolerate milder interventions for symptoms like anxiety, from salt baths to magnesium, and some find management strategies that help, like sensory deprivation or biofeedback. I suggest reading up on what other patients have found helpful and seeing what might be useful to you personally. Below are some links to resources about tapering, symptom management, and recovery that can help you better understand your situation, your options, and how to work out a recovery plan with any professionals on your side. You may also wish to join at least one recovery community so that you can get ongoing and personalized feedback and interact with other people who can relate to your experiences.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What are the potential benefits of stopping an SSRI medication abruptly compared to gradually reducing the dosage before discontinuation?
Answer: Less of a toxic drug means less drug toxicity. Continuous use always involves the risk of things going worse to discontinue abruptly instead of tapering. However, that does not mean there can be no upsides whatsoever to quitting more quickly than many patients can tolerate. Being off the drug sooner is an upside unto itself, since these are harmful drugs and lessening exposure is an inherently positive thing for our overall health. Sometimes being on a much lower dose or off the drug entirely right away is actually essential, if there is an emergency caused or worsened by ongoing use of it. Simplifying management of other interventions, or decreasing the wait time between the SSRI and another drug, can be an upside as well. Avoiding the potential complexities, cost, and suffering of tapering is worth a mention. But, as I opened with saying, these tradeoffs that people make to taper appropriately are made because they are much preferable to the alternative — severe adverse reactions, disability, or occasionally even death.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How much time do side effects pass after stopping antipsychotics?
Answer: There is no guaranteed timeframe. Each individual experience is different and will depend on variables like someone’s health, genes, drug history, and method of cessation. Each symptom can be different as well, since some may disappear in days or weeks while others take months or years. Some drug effects may last the rest of someone’s life, particularly if the drug caused serious injury or someone was using it for many years and caused changes that will never fully reverse. In short, it isn’t unusual for someone to still be struggling a year or more after short-term use of antipsychotics, and long-term use tends to require even more recovery. A key concern here is that a drug does not have to still be in your system to still be causing effects, just like someone doesn’t have to still be punching you in the face for their previous punches to still be hurting a lot. These drugs cause profound and harmful interference in the body and it can take time for the body to work through or work around any issues that had been caused by drug exposure. How quickly or effectively the nervous system or other systems are able to recover is complex and situational. While some symptoms are more likely to be long-term than other symptoms are, each person’s recovery is unique. To make things even more complicated, people will usually experience new symptoms before they experience recovery if they had been using the antipsychotic for more than a month or so. Physical dependence and other changes in the nervous system are the natural result of continual drug use and someone will usually have to make it through an adjustment period featuring withdrawal syndrome and other potential symptoms. It is still possible to see a reduction in some drug symptoms even while these transitional symptoms increase, though. For instance, someone may feel less sedated but more anxious.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is there a medication that activate serotonin receptors in the brain similar to the way dopamine agonists like pramipexole do? Why can't I find any serotonin analogues?
Answer: Are there serotonin agonists? Yes. There aren’t a ton of uses for serotonin agonists, though. There is not usually much upside to agonizing serotonin directly like that, and some of the most popular serotonin agonizing drugs are drugs which use that mechanism to produce recreational psychedelic effects. The specific kinds of serotonin receptors being agonized will be integral to what kinds of effects are produced as a result, and fucking with monoamine systems so aggressively is usually a recipe for disaster. The possibility of undesired effects usually outpaces the possibility of desired ones when agonizing serotonin, both in terms of scope and commonness. Direct agonists of dopamine are pretty problematic, too, and that is why the drug example you mention is best known for its use in neurodegenerative conditions where people are suffering from reduced dopamine activity. ‘Indirect agonists’ of serotonin (and of dopamine) are more widely used and are less aggressive.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why isn't MDMA prescribed as an antidepressant?
Answer: It is. This is a complex issue, though, so simply pointing out that prescribing has happened historically and is happening in the present doesn’t cover everything important to know. Especially since prescribing is still atypical and was never the norm even many decades ago. There are some factors affecting when and how MDMA is prescribed which treat MDMA different from drugs like SSRIs or NaSSAs, and it would not be very suitable to use MDMA in the same way drugs marketed as “antidepressants” are typically used anyhow. In many countries, many popular psychedelics and amphetamines are restricted or outright banned. This isn’t based on whether a drug has legitimate therapeutic uses, or how dangerous a drug can be, it is primarily a politically motivated decision which is not accountable to the facts about drug use or policy outcomes. Not only does this largely prevent prescribing, it can also stunt research and the developing of prescribing expertise and programs. As a consequence, there is a lot more research into ‘antidepressant’ management and outcomes than there is MDMA management and outcomes. Without funding, marketing, and clinical protocols, MDMA is a lot less likely to be used by prescribers even in places where it might be legal. The more industry parties can profit off the mainstream acceptance and use of MDMA, the more it will filter into mainstream psychiatric prescribing, though patentable analogues and combo drugs are what we will likely end up with. The upsides of MDMA also differ somewhat from those of typical antidepressants like reuptake inhibitors and antagonists, and it is more useful as a tool of rapid revolutionary change than as a lifestyle drug for daily doping. Usually, antidepressants are used to stimulate, sedate, cognitively impair, etc and while MDMA can also provide those influences, it has a more profound and unusual effect on our perceptions and mental associations. The primary value of MDMA is psychological, not chemical.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is Wellbutrin an antidepressant that helps with fatigue?
Answer: It is more stimulating than most common antidepressants. Any of the drugs marketed as “antidepressants” can make someone more fatigued or less fatigued, but how often they cause one reaction as compared to the other varies by drug and dose. It can depend on a range of things, like why the fatigue is happening in the first place, someone’s genes and health, and the drug regimen itself — what dose is taken, for what period of time, and sometimes even whether a dose is taken in the morning versus the evening. Drugs can both stimulate and promote fatigue, so the two influences are not mutually exclusive, but many drugs will be either more potently stimulating or more potently sedating in a noticeable way. The personal reactions of patients can vary based on many factors other than just the drug itself, but each drug will have traits that can make it more likely to significantly sedate or more likely to significantly stimulate. Bupropion (aka Wellbutrin) is one of the more stimulating drugs and so it is more likely than most antidepressants to reduce fatigue and to make it harder to sleep. Because individual reactions still vary, someone may or may not find bupropion to reduce fatigue, or at least to not make tiredness even worse. But, it is one of the drugs prescribers will most often look to if a patient wants one of these kinds of drugs and wants a more stimulating one.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do herbal supplements work as well as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for treating mild/moderate depression in adults who have never taken antidepressants before?
Answer: There can’t be a singular answer to that question. There are literally innumerable drugs which can be categorized as “herbal supplements”, and they obviously would not all have equal value in situations of depression. We would have to compare specific regimens: particular doses of particular drugs prepared and taken in particular ways for particular lengths of time under particular conditions. Millions of plant drugs can’t be appropriately summarized here, we require a focus on individual comparisons. Some of these drugs can be just as helpful or even more helpful than SSRIs, some surely wouldn’t be. And like SSRIs themselves, herbal drugs can be counterproductive or even dangerous, as well. The complication is not exclusive to the drug side of the equation, either. How we define “mild/moderate depression” and “work” will be key. If we used the same standards which were used in the regulatory approval of SSRIs back in their time, we would still face some problems. Firstly, SSRIs didn’t even outperform placebo using those standards, so “work as well” means “work as well as not using the drug at all”. Secondly, what actually helps a patient, especially in the long term, will be more personal and variable and doesn’t match up to those standard clinical criteria and study rubrics anyhow. That kind of drug research is only marginally useful to people who want good outcomes. So, we have three necessary variables which shape outcomes: “Herbal supplements” can be more useful, less useful, and just as useful as SSRIs. There are even herbal supplements which share the same actions as SSRIs. Since SSRIs usually fail, and drugging for mild to moderate depression should be a last resort, this question is not as practical as it may appear to be on the surface. And additional concerns are important to address if we want to properly apply drug information. For instance, we need to be able to ensure that drug products are and contain what they claim to, which many will not, and patients will require appropriate drug management and may not receive it.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can an antidepressant work if others haven't?
Answer: Sure, with caveats. There are a few caveats to get out of the way here in order to understand what your question could mean. The first is that “antidepressants” aren’t a specific type of drug — any drug could be an “antidepressant” if it was marketed as one, and there is no pharmacological difference between drugs currently considered “antidepressants” and all the other psychotropic drugs people use. Each individual drug has its own traits and collection of actions and nothing makes something an antidepressant or not an antidepressant. We don’t know anything about a drug marketed as an “antidepressant” other than that it will be a powerful psychotropic. The second caveat is that “working” is whatever you want it to be. These drugs have no special “antidepressing” mechanism or influence which sets them apart or provides something patients are needing. These drugs are simply alterants and each person has their own idea of what kind of alterations would be helpful. Someone extremely fatigued might find a strongly stimulant drug helpful whereas someone suffering from insomnia might prefer a strongly sedating drug, for instance. Antidepressants are taken for any number of concerns, like anxiety, depression, pain, headaches, trouble sleeping, etc. This wide variety of effects and preferences is in addition to how each person can have a unique reaction to any given drug. What a drug does, how a person wants to feel, and how a drug interacts with someone’s body, mind, and expectations present a multi-variable equation. We can’t know how someone will react beforehand, though data can help us make a decent prediction. There is always the possibility of someone reacting in an unexpected way, now or in the future. Given these limitations, there are three main factors to look at when trying to figure out if trialing more drugs might lead to different outcomes: If we don’t pay attention to these influences, we can end up trialing drugs in ways far less likely to be helpful. There is not actually a huge variety of types of antidepressants, so most drugs people find helpful in situations of depression, anxiety, pain, headaches, insomnia, etc will not actually be marketed as “antidepressants”. Antidepressants usually fail to provide the benefits people were looking for, or to do so at an acceptable prices. That is also partly to say, they usually cause more harm than good, especially in the long-term. Proper management can sometimes change whether someone finds a drug helpful or whether they find it more useful than harmful, so that should be as big of a focus as drug selection when someone is trying to promote better outcomes.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I have horrible anxiety switching from Lyrica to gabapentin. What should I do?
Answer: Research and self-advocate. There are three basic steps to take: Maybe this is pregabalin withdrawal, maybe this is a bad reaction to starting gabapentin, maybe it is some combination of both drugs’ effects on you, maybe it is something else. You might from withdrawal and tapering resources like this one helpful in building an understanding of gabapentinoid dependence and discontinuation problems: Important topics in the Tapering forum and FAQ

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do people who take antipsychotic medications experience more cognitive impairment than those with untreated schizophrenia?
Answer: Those aren’t comparable categories. There are two problems with your categorizing. The first is that “cognitive impairment” covers a wide range of problems. Someone can experience a severe impairment but still be functional in society, but someone can also experience only a moderate impairment and have trouble with everyday tasks, jobs, and relationships. How we grade an impaired state clinically or socially is only one facet of the impact of that impairment. And since we are talking about dozens of kinds of impairments, and experiences which can involve any number of concurrent impairments, severity isn’t the key consideration and doesn’t communicate something uniform. The second problem is that “people who take antipsychotic medications” and “those with untreated schizophrenia” are not uniform groups, either, and are not particularly related to one another. Most people who take antipsychotics aren’t taking it for psychosis, much less a “schizophrenia” diagnosis. They may be on one antipsychotic, two, or even three. They may be on three or five or seven other psychotropic drugs or none at all. They may be on a lower dose, a medium dose, or a high dose. It would not make sense to categorize all their experiences together and brand it “the antipsychotic experience”. We miss out on almost all the details that matter when doing so. Likewise, “untreated schizophrenia” is not a coherent idea. First off, it is literally not even a thing. “Schizophrenia” is a retrospective diagnosis, not a pathology or cause of someone’s experiences, not a categorization of what someone’s impairments are. “Untreated” is incoherent as well, as there are no medical treatments for “schizophrenia” — it has no medical validity. What someone considers “treatment” is arbitrary. We could consider drugs treatment, or jelly donuts, or holding someone hostage, or giving someone a hug. “Untreated schizophrenia” draws no verifiable boundaries and the diagnosis is applied to many different experiences with different levels of impairment, sometimes without cognitive impairment at all. There is no way to answer your question in a logical and fair manner because it is not asking something coherent. Neuroleptic drugs are impairing. Psychological crises are impairing. How this plays out for cognition will depend on many factors which are not specified by calling something a drug effect or “psychiatric disorder”. The categories do not provide use a specific population to look at, or a way to exclude active variables which may change our results in ways we did not intend. And the idea of “impairment” or “more cognitive impairment” is not specific enough for us to create an objective comparison. Subjectively, people will provide their own perspective which can completely contradict the perspectives of anyone else. Aside from pointing out the inability for the question to be answered as currently formulated, there is one useful fact I can provide. Helping people labeled as “schizophrenic” doesn’t require us to cognitively impair them. The choice is not between someone receiving no help and someone being drugged. The choice is also not between “treating” and “not treating” if our focus is the needs and concerns of the individual instead of the needs and concerns of a self-interested industrial model. Whether or not someone is impaired beforehand, there are things we can do to support them without cognition-impairing drugs. That doesn’t mean cognition-impairing drugs are automatically always wrong and bad, I’m just reminding us that “drug use”, “treatment”, and “progess”/“rehabilitaiton” are in no way interchangeable concepts.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are you worried about the risks of developing psychotic symptoms from cannabis use?
Answer: I’m worried about society’s firm disinterest in responsible drug use. In America, we have a very heavy investment in harmful drug attitudes. In the mainstream discourse, we prefer lies and withholding to education and accountability. Governmentally and industrially, we prefer lifestyle drug use only if it is controllably profitable, with no relation to whether that use turns out well for people. Institutionally and in local communities, we don’t want people to know the risks of drugs or how to properly manage them, even and especially when they are using them daily. We are largely against harm mitigation strategies. None of this is specific to cannabis, but all of it can cause problems in cannabis use. Everyone should be concerned about the adverse neuropsychological effects of commonly used drugs, including cannabis. They should be concerned because we are in a dire state of inadequate research, deliberate miseducation, and rampant profiteering at the expense of consumers. They should be concerned because harmful drug philosophies affect more than just cannabis use or cannabis users. They should be concerned because the crises caused by these philosophies are paid for in part by our taxes, and can also take clinical support away from people experiencing medical problems that weren’t so preventable.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If someone asked you 'why are we still using Quora if we have AI chatbots?' How would you respond?
Answer: Trick question! Quora is filled with chatbot questions and answers. Quora is pushing fake questions and answers pretty hard, and even before it was doing so, spambots made a very comfortable permanent home on Quora. Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How can a person who has been taking antidepressants for a long time then get an episode of depression?
Answer: All the same causes of depression apply whether or not someone is using antidepressants. In most cases, for most patients, most causes of depression won’t be alleviated or blocked by the use of drugs marketed as “antidepressants”. They aren’t a magical potion that wards off depression, they are just psychotropic drugs which alter our mental states by disrupting brain functioning and our body’s hormones. They don’t usually put an end to an episode of depression, and there is no evidence-based expectation that they would reliably prevent future episodes either. Antidepressants aren’t medical treatments, antidotes, or vaccines, they are just alterants. There are exceptional patients who find drug use very helpful, whether in the short-term or also for maintaining freedom from depression that had previously dogged them. Most people are not in that small minority of patients, and even those patients can still face depression from other causes (medical or psychological). Problematically, one of the more common causes of depression is psychiatric drugs themselves, including antidepressants. Many patients experience new episodes of depression because of drug effects, whether as part of an acute change, a gradual change, or physical dependence.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What are the reasons that people with severe mental illnesses, such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, are unable to fully recover despite advancements in medication and treatment?
Answer: Some causes won’t be resolved, and most people are not provided the best tools and support we have. So-called “mental illness” is not something physically inherent, like some medical problem which may or may not be treatable. But, the origin or trigger of these experiences being in some way psychological does not mean everything is reversible or avoidable after changes have been made or harms have been done. Sometimes there are traumas, harms, deprivations, or developmental impairments that still have a deep and lasting impact on someone’s daily experiences decades later even if someone makes progress in rehabilitating. Prospects for improvement are superb, but there is by no stretch any guarantee of full recovery. We have not changed that fact in the entire history of psychiatry or psychology. The good news is that plenty of people do have the potential to experience a full recovery, though not everyone defines that in the same way and there is no universal clinical standard either. Many people do reach that goal, sometimes within the system and often in spite of it. This is largely independent of whatever advancements you are referring to, as the basic needs of people in rehabilitating aren’t things we were only recently able to understand and meet. Newly minted psychotherapies and newly approved drugs don’t seem to have moved the needle much. The successes people experience are usually relying on strategies which could have been used hundreds or thousands of years ago, and some actually were. This brings us to the bad news, which is that most patients never have the institutional education and support that would best help them succeed. Despite full recovery being a realistic goal for countless people, the mainstream psychiatric and psychological systems are not designed to help people meet that realistic goal. In many cases, mainstream intervention actually worsens outcomes or prevents vital progress, and typical interventions can even be outright deadly. The more informed, variegated, personalized support that would best serve the majority of patients is absent from most care settings and is deprioritized by most government and by industry itself. We are basically choosing not to do better for patients. The mainstream psychiatric and psychological system are not based on the principles that would promote better outcomes. Things like accountability to patient outcomes, a focus on personal goals instead of standardized clinical rubrics, evidence shaping policy and procedure more than money and marketing do, and an emphasis on what works rather than what is most profitable or convenient. While it is true that sometimes people are not willing to put in the work that it may require to recover fully, the much more common problem is that patients are prevented from receiving the support they need by the conflicts of interest built into industry, government, and society. Industrial advancements won’t help with that; industrial advancements tend to accelerate the systematic disregarding of what patients actually need, prefer, and do best with. No new drugs or psychotherapies and no clinical research will fix the fact that we are not prioritizing individuals and what will work best for them. That is very firmly a social problem and one we need to address on the social level. Though clinical evidences can be a part of fighting the failed philosophies dominating our social and industrial institutions, they obviously haven’t turned the tide yet. We have the information we need to know that we are being fucked instead of being properly helped, so there is some other missing ingredient to doing better. In review:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do most antidepressants (SSRIs) not work for severe depression? Are there any that have been proven effective?
Answer: Antidepressants don’t literally ‘anti-depress’. Calling a drug an “antidepressant” does not magically imbue it with the ability to eliminate depression. Of course, the objective in the marketing name is to trick people into thinking these drugs have a special power in depression or that they can reliably counter depression. But, that is just marketing, that isn’t reality. Capn’ Crunch is not a real captain with a real boat sailing around the world really giving kids breakfast cereal. There are no ‘antidepressing’ mechanisms to these drugs, there is nothing which sets them apart from all other psychotropic drugs, and there is no reason to expect depressions to typically vanish just because someone takes some drugs. For depressions that aren’t the result of a medical disorder (so, all psychiatric diagnoses), drugs have limited relevance. And for depressions which are the result of medical disorders, antidepressants don’t treat the underlying causes, though sometimes other kinds of drugs might. In either case, the causes of depression and what someone’s needs and goals are can all differ between patients and situations. “Depression” is a category containing many, many different kinds of experiences and concerns. Drugs like antidepressants are prescribed in depression because they cause altered states, and the hope is for the altered state to be somehow more advantageous or bearable than an unaltered state. This is true regardless of the cause of the depression or what the drug mechanisms are. There are drug influences which can offer clear incentives for use, like stimulation, sedation, numbing, cognitive disruption. For some patients, these may be desirable influences even if the depression itself is still occurring. For a few patients, these kinds of alterations may be the difference between getting out of bed at all and not. In severe depression, even modest effects are more likely to have a meaningful impact on quality of life — patients have less to lose to adverse effects even if they happen and patients have more to gain from practical effects which help them work through impairments. The luckiest of patients may feel full relief from depression when using certain drugs, or be helped in resolving a depression through other means with the aid of drug alterations. The rest of patients are stuck with the prospect of drug use that is either unhelpful or inadequately helpful. Does that mean the drugs ‘don’t work’? I’d contend no — a drug working for at least one person is a drug working. It becomes a problem to suggest that a drug working for just one person or just a few people should mean it works for most people, or everyone. It becomes a problem to prescribe the drug as if it is someone’s best or only hope just because they are experiencing depression and the drug has been branded as “an antidepressant”. But, there can be clinical and personal value to drug use. That said, no antidepressant or type of antidepressant has ever proven more helpful or effective than all the others in broader use, particularly when we look at long-term outcomes instead of short-term snapshots. Some drugs are more likely to cause particular alterations, whether those alterations are considered desirable or adverse, but how individuals respond still varies even when we increase the odds of particular reactions.
