Likewise, what alterations someone feels helpful or preferable is individual. What “works” means is personal. There are many kinds of drugs marketed as antidepressants, and each drug has many different actions on the nervous system and on the body more widely. There can be tangible differences in the actions or affinities or other pharmacological traits of these drugs which matter to patients and to how useful they find a particular drug or dose. Like all groups of drugs, SSRIs feature upsides and downsides compared to other antidepressants. For instance, they are more likely to cause apathy syndrome and a variety of sexual problems than many other drugs but are less likely to be deadly in overdose than TCAs or to cause hypertensive crisis like MAOIs. Differences will exist between drugs grouped together, too, like fluoxetine being more likely to cause insomnia than most other SSRIs but providing the best chance of a smooth downtaper during discontinuation compared to all other reuptake inhibitors. None of these drugs will be great for most patients, but each one might be great for at least a few. Why are most patients not finding any given drug extremely helpful? It does not offer what they need or prefer or does not do so at a workable cost to their health and functioning.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What’s the point of psychotherapy if the therapist does absolutely nothing to help resolve the issue and instead reminds you of all the things you already know you’re doing wrong, which you already heard from other people who you weren’t even paying?
Answer: Yes, what’s the point? Either a practitioner is providing services you find useful or they aren’t. If they aren’t, either their approach needs to change or yours does. Maybe they aren’t utilizing the right strategies or therapies for you, maybe the communication isn’t good, maybe you aren’t sure how to make use of what they provide, maybe this is just the wrong person or even the wrong kind of professional to be seeing, maybe professionals aren’t the way forward for you. You shouldn’t have to justify bothering to see a therapist — either they are delivering support or insights or information or tools you need or they aren’t. Whatever the deficit here, if something is missing, something will have to be changed to move things in a better direction.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why can't emotional blunting be treated by atypical antipsychotics unlike other negative symptoms?
Answer: Because the “positive/negative symptom” concept is bullshit. There is no special relationship between experiences just because they are marketed as “positive symptoms” or “negative symptoms”. Consequently, we can’t expect drug use to impact all symptoms similarly based on their grouping. Neuroleptics can both newly cause or mitigate pretty much any of the experiences which are part of the diagnostic criteria for labels like “schizophrenia”: hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, social withdrawal, apathy, anhedonia, cognitive impairment, sleep problems, etc. Since these kinds of experiences do not function in the same way in all situations, and thus in all patients who might be prescribed drugs, there would be no reason for everyone to experience the same changes in their experiences as a result of drug use. Added to this is how responses vary even in cases where underlying causes might be similar, and there are many personal, medical, drug, and social factors which can impact drug outcomes. However, some drug mechanisms are more central or potent or reliable than others, meaning some drug effects are more likely to happen than others, when looking at the same drugs and the same doses and the same periods of use. Emotional blunting is going to be far more common than improved emotional range with continuous use of these drugs because their mechanisms causing blunting are universal whereas the relevance of drug mechanisms for acting on any pre-existing blunting will be limited and situational.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Throughout April and early May, I tapered my escitalopram dose from 5mg to nothing by eliminating 1 dose per week. It went well, but one week ago, I started feeling kind of funny again. How much longer should I expect this to last?
Answer: It is not predictable, but hopefully just a few months. While the main period of symptoms is estimated to average 2–3 months in a lot of SSRI research, individual experiences vary a lot. Some people don’t suffer for that long, others have years of symptoms instead. While withdrawal symptoms and other adjustment symptoms can begin during the taper, being totally off the drug is something you will require many months to adapt to more appreciably. In the meantime you might notice strange feelings or differences in how your body is responding. If you were on escitalopram for more than a couple months before this taper, it is very likely the taper was too rapid and that you may see an escalation in symptoms as your body is overwhelmed for a while. Proper tapering takes a lot longer, and this kind of more rapid reduction is most appropriate after only short-term use. It is also bad to skip doses instead of reducing the daily amount taken, as what you did can make it harder for the nervous system to adjust and make discontinuation problems more likely. Reinstating a very low daily dose may potentially help you stabilize and is something to read about and discuss with your prescriber if symptoms continue or start worsening. If you aren’t sure how to make lower doses, which seems likely if you were skipping days of use instead of smoothly reducing dose amounts, you can check out the resources linked below to learn more about dose management, tapering, and withdrawal recovery:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do anti-psychotics lose their efficacy over time like SSRIs?
Answer: “Efficacy” is arbitrary, but these drugs do involve tolerance and progressive changes. Like all psychiatric drugs, neuroleptics do produce drug tolerance and do cause progressive alterations in the nervous system and other parts of the body. Our experience of being on the drug can change as a result. This can mean that certain effects which began with drug initiation fade away somewhat (like nausea or even sedation), or that new effects appear or become more intense over time with continued drugging (like apathy or memory loss). Whether it is a useful or harmful thing depends partly on someone’s goals and priorities, but the ultimate course of long-term use is typically for someone to become increasingly debilitated. These drugs prevent normal functioning and there are medical consequences which can aggregate or intensify with ongoing use, regardless of how someone feels about the mental alterations they are experiencing. The name “antipsychotic” is just a marketing term, not a pharmacological description or a therapeutic assurance. These drugs have no specifically ‘antipsychosing’ mechanisms and are not liable to prevent future psychoses, either. Someone experiencing a disruption of hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, or other experiences with the initiation of an antipsychotic does not suggest the drug has lost efficacy if it does not prevent those experiences from recurring. To make things even messier, these drugs can cause new instances of psychosis, whether in patients with a history of psychosis or patients without. Continuous use can potentially make future psychosis more likely instead of less likely, as will poor drug management (like needlessly high doses, or neglecting to taper properly). How we are defining and measuring for “efficacy” can shape what we say happens with drug use, but the bottom line is they cause progressive and cumulative changes in patients.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the purpose of prescribing antidepressants by psychiatrists?
Answer: Whatever. On the most basic level, these drugs are used to stop the nervous system from working correctly. This is done to produce altered states — different ways of thinking, feeling, perceiving, behaving. But, the specific goals of prescribing will depend on the people and situation involved. Not everyone has the same objectives, same goals, same interests. Sometimes a prescriber is working on behalf of a patient, sometimes they are working against a patient. These drugs have a wide variety of influences which can selectively be used to our advantage. For example, effects like cognitive impairment can reduce rumination or hyperawareness, effects like sedation can help someone fall asleep more readily or cloud anxiety, effects like emotional numbing can reduce dysphoria or grief, effects like stimulation can punch through fatigue or brain fog. There can also be advantages for physical symptoms, like numbing reducing neuropathic pain or disrupting the brain interfering with headaches. But, use is aspirational. People hope for certain effects or results, but they are not guaranteed. What level of influence we are willing to settle for, and what we are willing to trade away in terms of our health and safety and quality of life, will vary just as responses to particular drugs and doses and lengths of use can vary. Usually, these drugs don’t provide the changes people were wanting, and they are usually more harmful than helpful in the end (even sometimes if they were very helpful for someone).

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can antipsychotics cause feelings of depression and anxiety, despite being used to treat psychosis?
Answer: Yes, those facts are unrelated. Antipsychotics prevent the brain from working normally and this can carry a wide variety of neuropsychological consequences. Apathy, dysphoria, anxiety, dissociation, sedation, mania, psychosis, loss of libido, compulsive behavior, cognitive impairment, and other drug effects are always a possibility, and people are nearly guaranteed to experience at least one — typically several. Some drugs, doses, management styles, and situations of use can be riskier than others with respect to particular effects, but these are blanket risks which apply to all patients and all circumstances of use. The fact that many people are given antipsychotics if they have a history or episode of psychosis is irrelevant to what the risks of these drugs can be, aside from how drugs which disrupt brain functioning will always involve neuropsychological risks. So, it is true that neuroleptics are prescribed because they break the brain and breaking the brain can sometimes interfere with the processes expressing in ways clinicians might call “psychosis”. But, such drugs have no special focus on psychosis and their use in psychosis is not specifically why they have these kinds of risks. Sometimes both the desired and undesired mental alterations stem from the same drug actions, but sometimes not. These drugs are doing dozens of things in the nervous system and in the body more generally so the causes of particular alterations can be complex and plural. Sometimes a patient’s medical and drug history can shape their drug reactions to an extent, but psychosis doesn’t specify any of that. “Psychosis” is a broad term for many kinds of experiences which don’t all work or look the same and doesn’t provide us a physical understanding of someone’s risk factors or drug reactions.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can antidepressants potentially cause or worsen mania in patients with depression? Is there any evidence to support this in both unipolar and bipolar depression?
Answer: Yes, and sure. Drugs marketed as “antidepressants” are basically fundamentally pro-manic. That is, they have mechanisms which promote mania. It isn’t an unusual or unexpected reaction, it follows from the actions of the drugs. This pro-manic influence applies to all patients, not just psychiatric patients, not just depression patients, not just patients with a history of mania. These drugs have no special effects in any particular population, as their actions are the same across all patients. How the body reacts to the actions of drugs is more variable, though, and each drug and dose will carry a unique signature of influences for people to be reacting to. Drugs causing mania in patients who have a history of mania will not necessarily be causing mania for the same reasons as the patient had already experienced mania in the past. However, many patients with recurring mania will have stress triggers and a lot of people will find some or all psychotropic drugs to be one of those stress triggers, especially stimulant drugs like “antidepressants” tend to be. Put colloquially, psychotropics poke at the nervous system and can provoke a manic reaction. Patients may find starting or quitting a dose provocative, and some will find ongoing use to increase the frequency of manias.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Under what circumstances would a psychiatrist prescribe an antipsychotic like Abilify to someone who does not show symptoms of psychosis or schizophrenia, but only depression or anxiety?
Answer: Any. Neuroleptics are prescribed very freely and no special justification or circumstances are required for the average prescriber to use them in depression, anxiety, or both. These are serious drugs, but are seldom actually prescribed with serious consideration or accountability. Most prescribing is not for psychosis. The marketing name “antipsychotics” is just a way to popularize products and certain applications, it does not describe anything about the drugs pharmacologically or what they are best for or appropriate for. The same goes for other marketing labels, like “antidepressants”, “mood stabilizers”.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible for Prozac to induce mania in someone who has never experienced it before? Is this a common occurrence?
Answer: Yes, and it is relatively uncommon. SSRIs, including Prozac (fluoxetine), are pro-manic drugs and so it is very common for patients to be made manic by their use or discontinuation. Most cases will be patients with no previous history of mania. However, drug-induced hypomania is more common than drug-induced mania — the more extreme form. Especially when drug management is undertaken responsibly, hypomania appears to occur several times more often than full blown mania, or psychosis. Some research suggests hypomania/mania is caused often enough to be considered a “very common” drug effect — 10% or more of patients having it as an effect sooner or later. Management quality can impact this to a degree. More careful uptapering and downtapering can reduce the likelihood of manic reactions, and screening patients to reduce prescribing in higher-risk situations can prevent some instances as well. The converse is also true, with mismanagement making manic reactions more likely.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the purpose of prescribing SSRI's if they do not cure depression?
Answer: Alterants are prescribed to alter. The basis of prescribing is that either the patient or people in society will hopefully prefer an altered state to an unaltered one. It isn’t about medical health, it isn’t about mental wellbeing, it is about changing how someone is thinking, feeling, and acting. The actual goals and priorities involved will depend on the people and circumstances involved. Not everyone is prescribing or using SSRIs for the same reasons, and they are prescribed for dozens of different physical and psychological concerns. Most uses, to note, are not for depression despite the marketing namesake “antidepressants”. Why is alteration desirable to people? Physical and emotional suffering or debilitation, social judgements, control, or even punishment. People are hurting, people are desperate, people are confused, people are different from what society pressures them to be. Drugging can potentially be a way to escape or to mitigate experiences, to conform or to limit individuals. Drugs are seldom the best tool for patients to reach for, but they are the best marketed tool and most available and accessible tool in most cases. Most patients are also unaware of the full risks involved and out drugging usually turns out, so use is often about being scammed. In depression in particular, some people will also find partial changes better than no changes at all. Most depressions are psychological in origin and thus cannot be medically ‘treated’ or ‘cured’, but even if we took ‘cure’ to mean resolving a depression long-term, drugs are not usually going to provide what patients are looking for. In less common cases, though, people will settle for incomplete relief because they have found no better options and may have no way to actually kick the depression no matter what they try. This can be especially in medical depressions where the causes is undetermined or untreatable.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible to give depressed individuals the same dose of an antidepressant until it works instead of trying different ones?
Answer: Not usually. In most cases, no dose of any particular drug will “work”, so it doesn’t matter how high or low it is, whether it is taken once or twice a day, or how long it is trialed for. These are not magic pills, they are just alterants like other psychotropics which have no special value in depression. You wouldn’t tell someone to keep drinking different amounts of beer each day until their depression disappears, and doing the same thing with drugs like SSRIs should sound just as ridiculous to us. There are upsides and downsides to any psychotropic, and drugs marketed as “antidepressants” are usually more harmful than helpful. This deficit is not a matter of dosing, it is a matter of benefits. There are three basic steps to trialing a drug, following evaluation meant to determine if drugging might be appropriate and which drug to experiment with. First, the drug is (or should be) uptapered slowly so the body has time to adjust to the dysfunction-inducing mechanisms of the drug (aka tolerance). It is not usually wise to start on the target dose right away. Second, a particular dose is held for a few weeks to a month to see what medium-term alterations are caused. Someone might feel different at day 20 than at day 1 because these drugs cause progressive alterations in the brain. And third, a patient can explore higher doses if lower doses were not adequate. To more fully exhaust the potential usefulness of a drug, escalating the dose is usually necessary. Drug failure is the norm, not the exception, so being careful and being efficient with dosing will still not greatly boost how often drugs “work”. Steps like those mentioned above can give someone the best chance of optimizing drug benefits, but antidepressants usually don’t sufficiently “work” in depression. There is no reason to expect that they would, especially since depression is a broad category with experiences whose underlying causes and expressions can vary a lot and the goals and priorities of each patient can differ as well. The only alternative for the majority of patients will be to try something else, whether a different drug or different therapeutic strategy.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is prescribing anti-psychotics more for damage control than optimal mental health?
Answer: That depends on who is doing the prescribing. There are many ways the prescribing of antipsychotics can be performed. Sometimes it is to keep a patient socially or physically manageable to staff, sometimes it is to calm them or sedate them so they don’t appear bothered even if they still are, sometimes it is to quiet them or subdue them so they don’t stand out, sometimes it is an acute intervention to change the course of experiences like depression, mania, insomnia, or psychosis, sometimes it is because other psychiatric drugs are failing, etc. The goals and priorities will differ from one prescriber to another, and sometimes from one prescribing situation to another. While we can speak about net trends, like how these drugs are used on average, that is not an absolute which will describe all instances of prescribing. In the vast majority of cases, these drugs are not prescribed to facilitate “optimal mental health”, whatever we consider that to be, since most people can do better and feel better without them when receiving appropriate support. Just what is meant by “damage control” can also be ambiguous though. Damage control like reducing ER visits, or damage control like reducing job changes, or damage control like reducing relationships, or damage control like reducing criminal charges? Damage to what or who? Put basically, in psychiatry these drugs are being prescribed for social purposes rather than medical purposes. Sometimes the social purpose is one originated by the patient, sometimes it is about the judgements and biases of the prescriber or their host society. Generally, these drugs are prescribed to change someone’s thoughts, feelings, or behavior to be considered more socially acceptable. This shapes the mainstream guidelines about prescribing and management and may be in conflict with the health or desires of patients themselves. But, individual patients may have their own interests in using drugs, sometimes regardless of what is more socially accepted. Given the many factors shaping prescribing, the question you ask must be addressed to each instance of prescribing if we want to get an accurate answer.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why does Zoloft make me feel like I’m not myself? I have been dealing with this for days where I have memory problems and I question reality and get agitated.
Answer: Alterants alter. Drugs like sertraline (aka Zoloft) stop the brain from working correctly and cause altered states through the disruptions they cause in the nervous system. This will often impact our sense of self and reality, our mood, or cognition, our behavior. Sometimes the changes are minor, other times they are quite radical. Some people feel normalish, others feel very off. Whatever the case is, it comes down to how psychiatric drugs produce abnormal functioning in the brain. We call people high on cannabis ‘stoned’ and people high on alcohol ‘drunk’ but there is no parallel word for how drugs like SSRIs change people. All patients are altered by the use of these drugs, but whether those alterations are considered desirable or undesirable by the patient is more variable. Most drug effects will generally be considered undesirable, but some can go either way, like sedation, stimulation, cognitive impairment, emotional numbing. If you are experiencing effects you don’t like, they should be reported to the prescriber and you need to decide if the upsides of drug use outweigh these downsides — particularly while also considering if other options may involve less of a tradeoff. It is unlikely you have to accept these effects just to make progress. Note that some effects can be more concerning than others in terms of the risks to our health. It could be that the drug symptoms you describe are part of edging into a hypomania or a toxidrome, for example, so it may be important to reconsider the dose or drug before anything worsens. Or, perhaps these are just how this particular drug makes you feel regardless. They sound unlikely to be worth enduring long-term, and the drug as well as your drug management should be reviewed to make sure you are given the best options for addressing whatever led to drug use in the first place.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do Antipsychotic medications make you worse before they start to make you better, only that’s what my husbands psychiatrist said?
Answer: The psychiatrist probably means that psychotropic drugs involve drug tolerance. There is no expectation that antipsychotics would make someone feel better, so the most common pattern is feeling worse and then…still feeling worse. With months or years of use tends to come feeling worse yet, or feeling nothing at all. A few patients are quite resilient to the incapacitating influences of these drugs, but the general trend is for someone to be in a worse state the longer they use the drug for. There aren’t ‘good’ and ‘bad’ effects of the drug on the body itself, the effects are all bad. Whether someone feels better or worse is a more complicated thing, since reactions vary and the very same drug reactions might be ‘better’ for one patient but ‘worse’ for another based on their preferences and goals. Since responses can change over time, whether a patient feels helped can change over time, too. A key concern here is that psychotropic drugs usually produce drug tolerance. The body changes itself in response to the continuous disruptions caused by drug use, and this can reduce some of the drug symptoms people felt in the earliest days or weeks of use. For example, some people feel less sedated in the daytime after a while of use. This doesn’t mean the drug itself has become less potent, or less sedating as in the example, it just means that the body has altered itself to try and maintain internal balance better. The body is always changing itself in response to psychotropic drug use because if it did not, the drugs would kill us. However, some things should not get worse with drug initiation, like mania or delusions, and a drug worsening them likely means discontinuation is best or necessary. Psychiatrists usually say that people starting a psychiatric drug can expect to feel worse before they feel better for two main reasons. The first reason is that starting a drug, or a new higher/lower dose of a drug, often feels rough. People are commonly hit with many symptoms all at once and can feel overwhelmed or discouraged and want to quit in the earliest few days before drug tolerance has more fully set in and they have a clearer picture of what drug effects will stay intense and what drug effects might fade away some as the body changes itself. There is no guarantee any effects beginning after drug initiation will dissipate, but many people see at least a few changing as part of drug tolerance. Some will deepen or worsen instead, so, the option is not just for the effects to lessen or stay the same. The second reason is that positive results are typically held out in front of patients like a carrot on a stick to convince them to do whatever the doctor says — use higher doses, use more drugs, spend years on drugs instead of months, etc. People are taught to trust doctors and people are often desperate so this kind of tactic works most of the time, but it is just a mirage in the sense that most patients never experience the benefits they were using psychiatric drugs to find. Psychiatrists encouraging patients to just keep drugging because good things are up ahead are usually lying and wanting to keep people coming back even if they aren’t helping their patients in the ways they say they will. The mantra “the right drug/dose for you is out there” is a marketing ploy, not an evidence-based statement. So, in summary, there are two core things to emphasize:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Has anyone felt better with psychiatric medications? Do they work?
Answer: Some people find them useful in some ways some of the time. The very inclusive “has anyone” is easy to answer. There are absolutely some people who have found drug use helpful. This is true whether we are asking about SSRIs, neuroleptics, caffeine, methamphetamine, cannabis, khat, or fish oil supplements. It is only when you start asking about percentages that we need to more strongly define “felt better” or “work”. Not everyone defines those terms similarly, and not everyone has the same needs or same goals when it comes to drug use. It is simple and typical for psychiatric drugs to make us feel differently. They are, after all, psychotropics. It is more exceptional for those changes to be positive or helpful, as most will be undesirable or problematic. Most people end up finding psychiatric drugs more harmful than helpful overall, whether that is apparent right away or something which takes months or years to find out. That emphasizes how we aren’t just having to look at drug upsides but also drug downsides. There is no scientific measurement of psychiatric drugs ‘working’. Psychiatric diagnoses are totally unscientific and are just cultural in nature — popular psychosocial criteria are voted on and adjusted over time to reflect the pressures and biases of society. There is no objective measurement of “mental disorder” or of “drug efficacy”. It is all up to those pressures and biases. So, the very same data could be claimed to show drug efficacy or drug inefficacy because it all depends on how we are choosing to interpret and frame things. This is why I began my answer focusing on patients instead of social standards. What each specific individual finds useful and finds more helpful than harmful is what we should care most about. Whether that is 1% of people or 10% of people or 70% of people should inform our institutional investment in drugs, but that is not how the world really works. These drugs are primarily marketed or prescribed for uses they usually fail at but are continually prescribed for because prescribing dogma is not accountable to outcomes. One final piece of the puzzle is the comparing of drugs to everything else people can do to meet their goals. It is obvious that drug alterations can be helpful or harmful in particular contexts, but we also need to look at the broader range of strategies for rehabilitation. Most of what people find helpful is not going to be psychotropic drugs, and drugs represent some of the most dangerous options available for changing how we feel and experience. An understanding of when and how drug use might be responsible will require us to also understand the upsides, downsides, and usefulness of other ways of meeting our goals.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What are the good effects of Effexor RX?
Answer: “Good” is arbitrary. In terms of the body’s health, drugs like venlafaxine (aka Effexor) are innately bad. The impair and toxify the body. Aside from fringe benefits like harming certain cancer cells just like they harm many other kinds of cells in the body or impairing the immune system so that it does not go overboard into autoimmunity, there aren’t really “good effects” in the literal, physical sense. But, “good effects” with these kinds of drugs aren’t measured by what’s going on in the body. Rather, someone’s perceptions, feelings, and behavior are what is being commented on. This is much more open-ended and subjective, since what we consider “good thinking” or “good feeling” or “good behaving” is personal and cultural instead of scientific. Not only can “good” be anything someone wants it to be, the very same drug effect that one person considers “good” can be “bad” to another person. Our values, goals, and priorities are individual instead of universal. Some of the drug influences people are most commonly interested in include sedation (making someone tired or sleepy), stimulant effects, physical and psychological numbing, cognitive impairment. Such effects can appeal to people experiencing insomnia, fatigue, anxiety, rumination, emotional pain, or even physical pain. Drug use can also just worsen what was already happening, or newly cause these things, but many patients are desperate and many prescribers will misrepresent the upsides and downsides involved. Unfortunately, these drugs are much more likely to cause effects people don’t want than effects people do want. The most widely experienced and most reliable effects are ones most patients are not considering good. However, the most common desired and most common undesired effects are so common because of what the drugs do in the body. There is a logical reason for them to happen, so we can try to use strategies to maximize upsides or minimize downsides.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If you take a mixture of anti-psychotic drugs and stop taking them does your brain ever go back to pre-med state?
Answer: Probably not. Not fully. These are extremely potent and disruptive drugs and it is unavoidable that they will have a long-term influence when someone has been using them continuously, especially multiple drugs. On one hand, some of the changes caused by drug use work through the very same mechanisms which allow the brain to adapt away from drug effects after we discontinue the drugs. So, there is an innate capacity to at least partially recover. On the other hand, there are harms caused by these drugs which are more about their toxicity than our neuroplastic adaptation to their impairing actions. Those changes are sometimes things we can heal from, but it is not a guarantee. An important thing to understand, however, is that our brain isn’t staying in one state and arrangement from year to year. Throughout our whole lives, our brains are changing. If someone takes drugs for a while and then quits them, there will be changes in their brain which reflect that. If someone does not take drugs, their brain will still differ from how it was months or years earlier. We are always moving forward, to a new state and new arrangement which responds both to our past influences and current experiences. Drug use will involve changes, and sometimes a depth of changes, which differ from those we would experience otherwise. But, with or without drug use we are still moving on to a new brain to some extent. The central problem is when drug changes are adverse — when they cause health issues, psychological difficulties, impairments, a loss of quality of life. It is typical for people to have long-lasting adverse effects after use of these drugs, whether “long-lasting” means months, years, or a lifetime. Sometimes these long-lasting effects will result in health conditions, disability, or serious losses (hobbies, relationships, careers, joy). Sometimes they are more bearable. Everyone will be changed by these drugs, but the impact of those changes will differ between patients and situations, as well the intensity and nature of those changes. Does anyone ever truly “go back to their pre-med state”? Only to a degree. It isn’t like turning off a lightswitch and then turning it back on. The good news is that everyone has some level of ability to rehabilitate after the use of neuroleptics (aka ‘antipsychotics’). The bad news is that some drug harms may last a long time, and some people will have serious or even permanent consequences. Individual reactions and cases will vary, and some people may be more sensitive or reactive. What steps we take in order to recover can potentially make a difference in our prognosis, and factors related to drug use and management can also play a part in outcomes. For example, poor drug management, polydrugging, and ultra-long-term use tend to produce worse outcomes on average. Conversely, reducing stressors, maintaining a healthy lifestyle, and avoiding medical mismanagement of symptoms can promote better outcomes.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it true that antipsychotics do not produce a high? How do individuals with schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders function on these medications if they do not feel any effects from them?
Answer: Q1. “Is it true that antipsychotics do not produce a high?” That depends on what you mean by “a high”. Some people think that only a euphoric, energetic altered state is “a high”, for example. Others include things like sedation, numbing effects, psychedelia, etc. Fewer people consider any psychotropic effect at all “a high”, which seems to be your implication in the second question here. Put simply, these drugs produce obvious functional and mental alterations in people, whatever you choose to characterize those effects as. Individual reactions vary, but feeling no different at all is exceptional and people are being altered even if they report feeling nothing. Neuroleptics are occasionally used recreationally for those purposes, especially by people with less access to more traditional recreational drugs. Because they are typically pretty awful feeling to take, most people avoid them, whether as recreation or after trialing them as a patient. Their recreational uses are pretty limited and the bottom line is that there are less dangerous, less disruptive drugs to take to experience key alterations people sometimes use antipsychotics to feel — sedation, euphoria, dissociation, numbness, etc. The mainstream perception is that they have no recreational value whatsoever. Q2. “How do individuals with schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders function on these medications if they do not feel any effects from them?” There are two misconceptions here. The first is that these drugs have some sort of innate or reliable actions which reverse disability associated with psychosis. Generally, these drugs are more likely to create or perpetuate disability than to lift it, especially when used continuously instead of as an acute intervention over the course of a day or three. Of course, the situation is complex — there are many things which can be disabling and drug use can affect them differentially. The second misconception is that feeling an effect is required for alterations to be occurring. Though most people will easily distinguish between a daily neuroleptic dose and a placebo pill because of how potent and impairing or otherwise unpleasant the neuroleptics are, we can experience alterations even if we don’t consciously feel different. That said, these drugs also impair our self-awareness, so sometimes they are causing significant effects we are only unaware of because our awareness has itself been altered. Many people can’t fully function in society and in their private lives while using these kinds of drugs. They are pretty bad for the brain and can be deeply impairing. Higher doses and longer periods of use tend to be even more challenging to remain functioning through. Usually, people will be able to cite specific differences they see in their experiences which are holding them back. For people who find these drugs to diminish things like psychosis or insomnia, such upsides will often be noticeable as well.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do placebo effects work?
Answer: Technically, they don’t. “Placebo” is the term used for an intervention which is meant to have no relevant mechanism of action. If we consistently get a positive result with placebo instead of a neutral result, we discover that whatever we are calling “placebo” actually has a relevant mechanism of action. We find out we were wrong and that there is something active instead of neutral. That realization can lead to new protocols for helping people. Because there are many variables involved in any intervention, sorting out what specific aspect or collection of aspects is relevant is often more complicated. Figuring out the mechanisms involved is even more complicated, and we usually can only get so far. We often don’t even understand the mechanisms behind interventions we already knew were effective. The human body is more of a mystery than not still. If you want to know how placebo effects work — how a placebo is causing effects which are effective instead of just being neutral — it will depend entirely upon what placebo you’re talking about and how it was being used. We can be wrong about interventions in a nearly endless number of ways, and many different things can be wrongly labeled as “placebo”. But, a good start is to remember that some of what goes on in an intervention using a drug or device is not involving the drug or device.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: After 1 month of taking antidepressants, I feel much better. Maybe the best days of my adulthood life. Will this feeling continue?
Answer: It might. These drugs are complicated because we can’t predict who will find them helpful or how long helpful alterations will last for. It is possible that this good feeling will last indefinitely, maybe even as long as you stay on the drug or maybe even if you later discontinue the drug. Lifelong usefulness may be even more likely in patients who respond very positively right away, within the first day or three. What will likely happen here depends partly on why you feel so much better and whether there are any underlying things which can be adjusted to prevent you from feeling bad again in the future. How much of this positive change revolves just around pharmacology hasn’t been specified. There are several different scenarios that can play out if the good feeling doesn’t last, assuming you aren’t just talking about a hypomanic drug reaction. Two of the most common ones are discussed below. Some people feel greatly helped in the early weeks or months of use, but experience these upsides waning as use continues. Drug tolerance or other changes in the body caused by chronic use can mean that good feelings or relief are short-lived for some patients. Research suggests a large minority of patients experience tolerance reactions that very significantly reduce how useful they feel an antidepressant is. How this is measured can vary, and what effects matter to patients in the first place can also vary, so the takeaway here is simply that sometimes upsides fade. Some patients bump the dose up and feel another temporary wave of intensified relief, others try to add on other drugs or therapies or settle for the long-term level of relief they already experience. Some people find drug use really helpful and the helpfulness continues more or less on the same level for months or even years, but then all of the sudden disappears. Sometimes over a period of days, other times literally overnight. This is colloquially called “poop-out” and is most popularly associated with SRI drugs in the mainstream dialogue. It has not been settled exactly why this happens, but many theories revolve around the nervous system being overstressed by the adverse mechanisms of the drugs. It seems especially likely to occur in people who are already carrying a history of serious drug stresses, like quitting a drug cold turkey in the past, or who encounter additional stressors in the time leading up to the ‘tachyphylaxis’. Some people switch drugs or cycle drugs in response to this, others become reverse tolerant to drugs and have to stay away from them. Feeling “maybe the best…of my adulthood life” is an exceptional drug reaction. Most patients never feel that great from taking antidepressants, so you are already winning a sort of lottery. Where things go from here is not predictable, so whether this is a sustained change or an altered state that won’t remain is unclear. We can only find out by living. But, there may be steps you can take to promote the upsides staying around. For some examples, be sure to take the drug on a very consistent schedule, be sure to get enough sleep, seek help with addressing any underlying causes of whatever led to drug use in the first place. Ideally, psychiatric drugs are short-term use drugs which help people stabilize in a crisis. Their risks increase with chronic use, and they cause progressive alterations in the nervous system which can change how we react to them as time goes on.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How long do antidepressant discontinuation symptoms last?
Answer: A few months is standard, but shorter or longer periods are also common. Withdrawal syndrome and other reduction-related drug symptoms last a variable amount of time. Though research suggests the average is probably 2–3 months on average after continuous use of a drug, not all experiences are average and sometimes individual symptoms caused by quitting last much longer than the onset of withdrawal (for instance anxiety or sexual problems). A few patients may not notice much withdrawal at all, at least their first time quitting, but on the other extreme, a minority of patients experience discontinuation symptoms for years or even decades. Many factors can influence which symptoms occur, when they start, how long they last, and how severe they become. Some factors are known, others are not. Some revolve around the regimen or its management, others around the patient or their history. Many different kinds of medical issues get lumped into “withdrawal” and the average course and severity of them will differ. Basically, we are talking about a wide range of medical concerns, even if we were just looking at one specific drug instead of the large group of differently acting drugs all marketed under the “antidepressant” banner. No matter the drug or the discontinuation plan, individual experiences will vary. There is no duration limit to speak of, so we can’t guarantee that particular symptoms will certainly stop within a particular amount of time. Patients reducing, discontinuing, or switching antidepressants need to be aware of the risks and how to manage them appropriately. Proper management, most notably tapering slowly, can potentially reduce or even prevent withdrawal problems for many patients. However, long-term use, higher doses, and shorter half-life drugs tend to entail greater difficulties on average. Because reactions are not predictable and can be disabling or even life-threatening at times, taking the necessary steps to facilitate drug recovery is imperative. Below are some resources discussing tapering and discontinuation, withdrawal symptoms and their management, and drug recovery more broadly. The first four are off-site resources many patients have found helpful, the last two are additional Quora posts which delve deeper into antidepressant withdrawal symptoms and syndromes and the general process of seeking the appropriate support for going off antidepressants.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do you think psychiatrists are too quick to label people without making sure the patient meets the criteria for specific mental conditions?
Answer: I think it is more accurate to say that psychiatrists are often too quick to judge people. Anyone who really knows psychiatry knows the diagnoses are bullshit, and that the entire concept of “mental illness” is bullshit. This is the explicitly stated starting place of psychiatry, not something we conclude after researching psychiatric claims. In theory, the label shouldn’t matter one way or another because it is nonsense with no real-world application for patients in the clinical sense. But, that is just in theory. In reality, many people pretend or are deluded into thinking these diagnoses aren’t bullshit and that they somehow provide vital information about patients and their needs. Many clinicians will make serious assumptions about patients based on psychiatric labels and psychiatric label history which can impact the quality of care and kinds of resources patients receive. As a consequence, there are some very significant real-world ramifications to diagnoses and which are chosen, even if the diagnoses are just bullshit. How labels are perceived in society can dramatically change the experience a patient has with psychiatry, with the government, or with their local community. Since the problem is the assuming instead of the labels in isolation from that assuming, I would propose that the biggest problem here isn’t how slow or quick labels are applied, or what rules they follow, but rather how so many people are acting as if the labels mean something they don’t and can’t mean. Without bad, baseless assumptions, we could use any labels we wanted and not be putting people in extra danger. If we all acknowledged the labels are just bullshit, that would remove much of their harmful influence. There is another facet to this question which also needs to be covered. The primary drive behind the use of psychiatric labels isn’t clinical at all, it is administrative. In many places, patients get a label every time they see a psychiatrist because it is part of the paperwork involved in the industry. Practitioners could provide the same services and support even if labels didn’t exist at all, but labels are integral to the industries involved in psychiatry — academia, pharmaceuticals, clinical services, etc. Labels are also integrated into research and regulation. In the end, mainstream psychiatry depends on the abuse of diagnoses because mainstream psychiatry only has the current level of popularity and power as a result of intersecting with those industries and being the government-sponsored expression of them in the clinical space. What this means for your question is that following the criteria created for labels is less important to the daily functioning of psychiatry than simply putting labels on paper no matter what they are, what they might mean, or how they work out for a patient. Since these labels are bullshit but are liable to have very significant real-world impact because of the assumptions made by professionals and by society, it is obvious that the pressure to prioritize paperwork over coherent or factual content is dangerous and problematic. But, only psychiatrists who work outside the standard reimbursement systems — those who only take out-of-pocket payment — can ignore all this (if they choose to). Most patients are stuck relying on some form of reimbursement to make use of psychiatry, so most patients are stuck dealing with the backwards world of hasty labels and harmful assumptions.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do antidepressants reverse the effects of depression-induced memory loss?
Answer: Sometimes, in some ways. For example, stimulant drugs can sometimes reduce brain fog or other experiences contributing to difficulty with memory. For another example, sedating drugs may promote sleep in people with chronic insomnia that was contributing to memory difficulties. Or, if drug use alleviates depression or numbs anxiety, that will also naturally reduce or eliminate any memory problems which were being caused by an ongoing depression or by chronic anxiety. All of these drugs are stimulating and sedating to some degree, and people occasionally find them to alleviate depression or other pre-existing causes of memory problems. However, these drugs are also cognitively disruptive drugs and can cause memory problems that weren’t already going on, regardless of whether they are helping with memory problems already present. When all the effects of these drugs are evaluated together, they typically have a net negative effect on thinking and memory. But, there can be exceptions — not everyone has the more average kind of reaction, and the level of impairment being experienced before drug use began can play a big role in whether someone notices a positive difference from drugging. The simplest thing to say is that a drug being marketed as an “antidepressant” doesn’t imply it will help improve memory.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I have been taking Lexapro for two weeks and I don't feel any different. Is this normal?
Answer: Sure. It is common enough for people to not feel greatly different on an SSRI, especially in the earliest days or weeks of use or when someone is on a lower dose. Sometimes people are less vulnerable to the disruptive influences of the drug, sometimes they metabolize a drug extra quickly and are experiencing a lower dose than was expected, sometimes the drug effects are interfering with someone’s ability to perceive them, sometimes the actual dose is itself so low that someone doesn’t feel particularly drugged, sometimes the drug effects aren’t being properly recognized as being caused by the drug, sometimes people only care about particular effects and don’t bother to count any other drug changes that were going on. It is likely but not quite guaranteed that you will feel different after months of use than you feel after just two weeks. Though these kinds of drugs are causing pretty radical changes in the brain within just hours of your very first dose, the alterations caused by drug use are also progressive and will continue to deepen and broaden with continued exposure. Some drug effects are more likely to occur before drug tolerance happens, like nausea, while others are more likely to occur as ongoing use changes the nervous system, like apathy. Either way, not all changes will be noticeable to a patient, even if they might be objectively demonstrated through medical testing or people around the patient notice them.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do people commonly experience withdrawal symptoms from antidepressants like SSRIs or SNRIs? If so, when do these symptoms typically occur?
Answer: Yes, withdrawal symptoms are the norm after continuous use of these drugs. The majority of patients will experience noticeable withdrawal symptoms when trying to quit serotonin reuptake inhibitor drugs like those marketed as SSRIs, SNRIs, and TCAs after a month or two of use. Higher doses, longer periods of use before cessation, untapered discontinuation, and other factors (like a rocky drug history, metabolizing drugs more quickly than the average patient, certain medical conditions) can increase the likelihood of withdrawal symptoms, and symptoms being more numerous, more severe, more lasting. The good news is that tapering gradually can help most people reduce the severity of their withdrawal reaction, and potentially avoid many of the more serious symptoms that would otherwise occur. Like with other drug reactions, withdrawal has some common patterns but individual reactions still occupy a wide range. So, for instance, symptoms often begin within the first 3 days, but some patients will not see problems for a week, or even a month. Fluoxetine is the SRI drug which (along with its main metabolite of note) stays around in the body the longest, far longest than all the others. This makes fluoxetine withdrawal syndrome more likely to have a much later onset compared to the rest of the drugs. Conversely, drugs with the shortest stay in the body, like venlafaxine, are notorious for causing withdrawal so quickly some patients can’t even make it 24 hours between doses without symptoms starting even if they aren’t reducing or quitting at all. For the majority of patients, symptoms will begin within the first month or so of quitting, and the average duration of withdrawal is reported to be around 2–3 months in recent literature aggregating withdrawal information from decades of research and patient reporting. For a minority of patients, withdrawal symptoms mysteriously start later than that, sometimes much later. Aside from how ultra-long-lasting drugs like fluoxetine can delay the onset of withdrawal, this might sometimes be because symptoms are the result of the nervous system being unable to compensate adequately and some patients will be able to deal with the stresses of discontinuation for a while before their nervous system is ultimately overwhelmed. For a minority of patients, symptoms will last much longer than just a few months, and can continue for years or longer. Where to draw the line between withdrawal syndrome and other reduction-emergent drug effects is not firmly established, and withdrawal itself is a grouping of many different kinds of symptoms whose underlying dynamics are not all shared. Some symptoms are more likely to be lasting years while others are more likely to be lasting just weeks. Still, outcomes vary, based on the factors involved. It is not clear if some drugs are much more likely than others to cause years-long symptoms, but some drugs are more likely to cause specific kinds of symptoms as a result of their mechanisms.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can psychosis occur without having schizophrenia or bipolar disorder?
Answer: Of course. “Schizophrenia or bipolar disorder” have never caused a single instance of psychosis. They are labels which are applied to experiences which sometimes include psychosis but have causes that are not specified by the diagnoses. The diagnoses aren’t referring to some sort of disorder in the brain which causes someone’s experiences, they are just a shorthand way to talk about those experiences, like how calling an unmarried man a “bachelor” doesn’t tell us why he is unmarried. In marketing narratives and in psychiatric dogma, diagnoses are also a fairy tale told about the experiences. Most causes of psychosis aren’t eligible for psychiatric diagnosis because they are caused by a medical problem, like an injury, illness, or drug. “Schizophrenia”, “bipolar”, and other psychiatric diagnoses exclude all medical problems and are supposed to only be referring to psychological causes (like stress, trauma, developmental differences). So, there is a narrower range of things which can cause psychosis said to be eligible for psychiatric diagnosis, though that range still includes an incredible variety of circumstances and experiences. But, a confusing catch here is that the reality of psychiatric practice differs. Countless patients are given psychiatric diagnoses even though their experiences are part of a medical problem. The official criteria for using these diagnoses will often go ignored, in part or in full. Anyone experiencing psychosis is at risk of a psychiatric diagnosis being applied to their experiences, no matter what the cause is and no matter what the diagnostic criteria say. Psychiatrists are even more likely to misdiagnose such cases, but other fields can do it too.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What should you do if you are taking antidepressants that are not effective? Should you stop taking them or try different medications until you find one that works?
Answer: Learn, experiment, self-advocate. For most people, the experience is that “antidepressants are not effective”. It is not universal, it is just the standard, average, most common experience. Sometimes trying a different dose, dose timing, drug, or drug combination helps someone break out of that more average, standard experience, but usually not. No matter how many drugs or doses are tried, these drugs simply don’t usually do what prescribers and patients are hoping. They don’t have the mechanisms or ability to do what most people are wanting, and are typically prescribed inappropriately. They have a greater capacity to harm than to help and standard prescribing does not provide patients the best shot at success. Understanding drug limitations, responsible drug management, and how to make the most of whatever they can do is important. But, there is no safe assumption that switching between drugs until one “works” is best. This is for two reasons. Firstly, because these are dangerous drugs and the period of starting and stopping drugs will involve further elevated risks in many respects. It can be like playing Russian Roulette where eventually someone experiences a catastrophically bad reaction because they were trying drug after drug. This is risky both because reactions can vary dramatically between drugs and because our history of use can make us more vulnerable to future drug harms. Secondly, because most people will never find a drug or combination of drugs which is adequate and preferable. Most people find drug use more harmful than helpful, because the upsides tend to be modest if present at all and because the downsides are very often pronounced and can be serious. The dogmatic plan to just keep cycling through drugs until something works out is a dangerously bad plan for most people and is not based in clinical evidence. It is alluring to many, but is more of a religious faith than a grounded plan we can rely on usually paying off for patients. Where does that leave most people, then? So-called “antidepressants” are only one of numerous tools we have to try and help people, whether they were looking to use drugs for anxiety, depression, insomnia, neuropathic pains, headaches, or other concerns. But, most options will not be offered by the prescribers of these drugs, so people have to research and discover their own options to try out, ideally with the support of a knowledgeable community or professional. Properly excluding any medical disorders that may require treatment is also an integral part of moving forward, and something many psychiatric patients aren’t provided outright. Standing up for yourself and taking direct actions to learn more about your needs and what other people have found helpful will sometimes be an essential step in the process of recovery or management. Lucky people will find success with the most mainstream, industrialized options, but millions upon millions of people aren’t so lucky. There is not necessarily an easy, fast, or one-step fix. And Sometimes there is no real ‘fix’ at all. In any case, an active effort to find approaches that might be helpful is part of being an effective patient. This can take months or even years of personal growth and experimentation, and the best path will be as unique as the individual walking it.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can antipsychotics be stopped without the risk of psychosis returning and causing permanent damage if they are not taken again?
Answer: Psychosis is always a risk of antipsychotics. All patients are at risk of experiencing psychosis from reducing or stopping a neuroleptic drug, aka “antipsychotic”. This applies to patients with no history of psychosis as well as patients with one or more previous instances. It is an unavoidable drug risk which results from its pharmacological actions and how the nervous system adapts to them. This risks exists regardless of why someone was taking a neuroleptic drug, and higher doses as well as longer periods of use can make drug-induced psychosis more likely. Some patients will be more vulnerable to this kind of drug effect than others, and some patients with previous experiences of psychosis may be more susceptible to destabilization from the difficulties of drug cessation. It can very commonly be a painful, confusing, exhausting process to try and quit an antipsychotic, which stresses both the body and the mind. Going at an appropriate pace, plus having the education and support in place to tackle the struggle effectively, can reduce the likelihood or severity of most reduction-emergent drug effects, or a general emotional ‘decompensation’. Preparation and proper management of drug tapering can sometimes make or break stable, successful discontinuation. However, most patients are not given the information, resources, or correct clinical advice they need in order to quit more safely, and bad discontinuation reactions are very often misconstrued as “relapse” even in formal research settings. Speaking more broadly, experiences regarded by clinicians as “psychosis” are always a risk, regardless of someone’s psychological or drug history. Even if someone never used or quit an antipsychotic, they are still at risk of psychosis. The human nervous system is innately capable of producing these experiences, and we sort of practice them every night when we dream. It would be misleading to say there is no baseline risk of psychosis, because everyone is at some level of risk and there are a lot of things which can contribute to psychosis. Many, many factors can raise or lower the likelihood of these experiences occurring, and plenty can be done to help patients with a history of psychosis prevent or mitigate future instances. The personal, clinical, and social objectives here should not be to guarantee an absence of psychosis. That wouldn’t be realistic and also wouldn’t be in the best interest of patients. The goals should be to improve the kinds of functioning and quality of daily life valued by the individual patient, to accountably protect and support people who are needing help or are more vulnerable, and to facilitate the ability for individuals and communities to respond constructively to present and future stressors, including the potential outcomes of stressors. It does everyone a disservice to orient social and institutional policy around the demonization of “psychosis” instead of the failures which leave people unhelped or actively harmed.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I recently started taking 15 mg Flouxetine about a month ago. Since then I've been having lucid dreams and occasionally depersonalization and derealization anxiety. At this point it only feels like my dreams are real. Should I switch medications?
Answer: Probably, yes. Research, talk to your prescriber, and talk to your pharmacist. You mention that there are concerning drug symptoms which can potentially interfere with quality of life, daily functioning, or even your safety in extreme circumstances. You seem to suggest that these have either been staying about as strong or have worsened over time instead of improving. It is likely things will only be like this or be worse in the future, so taking action now may be important to preventing even worse drug experiences later on. You are saying that fluoxetine is changing your sense of reality so much that everyday waking life doesn’t feel real, and that is probably the most concerning symptom of all. This warrants an immediate conversation with your prescriber, and reducing or quitting is almost certainly the best step to take. I’m not suggesting to quit without consultation, just pointing out it is usually what works out best for people in general. This alone is not enough information to decide about drug switching, though. You may simply be on too high of a dose. You might be experiencing serotonin toxicity or other kinds of drug effects that might be less problematic for you if you were taking only a lower dose. Patients should be gradually tapered onto and off of drugs like SSRIs, including fluoxetine. This can help prevent someone from being overwhelmed by the potency of a drug, or from escalating needlessly and dangerously high on the dose. Additionally, some people are less able to metabolize these drugs and might experience a dose which is higher than what the prescriber intended. Getting evaluated for factors (diet, genes, other drugs, medical conditions, etc) that can impair your metabolism of fluoxetine might be helpful here. Of course, some people will react badly to fluoxetine even at lower doses, and most people find SSRIs more harmful than helpful regardless of which drug they are taking or what dose they are using. It is very possible you will have to switch drugs or stay away from these kinds of drugs in the future. Because there are other details to the situation which might be integral to your experiences and to how to address them, we on Quora can’t tell you what will work out best or even provide an educated guess. Your reasons for using drugs, your medical history and drug history, and other details might be just as important as your mentioning fluoxetine at 15mg/day. It could be the fluoxetine isn’t even the culprit here if you discontinued a different drug when starting it.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I'm on antipsychotic, antidepressant, and benzodiazepines at the same time. Is this good or bad?
Answer: “Good or bad” in what sense? These drugs are inherently bad for your health, and will be more bad than good for most patients even if taken one at a time instead of all together. They carry many serious risks and can easily make someone’s situation worse instead of better. Someone on this kind of regimen is likely going to end up regretting it, whether that takes weeks, months, or years. But, that doesn’t mean there is no possibility of upsides. We have to weigh the possibility of upsides against the risks involved, and we have to weigh the value of alternatives as well. There are at least three things each person needs to be concerned with: If you’ve already done everything you can outside of drug use and it wasn’t enough, and you have found a regimen which provides an optimal balancing of upsides and downsides, and you have adequate or even superior professional support, maybe your drug use is a “good” thing for your life overall. There are many, many factors to be accounting for here and without knowing those factors we can’t tell you what should work out best for you. What you prioritize and what your goals are will ultimately be pretty personal, so it is also up to you to decide whether the risks being taken on (including the risks of bad effects and outcomes later on) are worth it for you.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can psychiatric medications permanently damage/change the brain? I have taken antipsychotics for several years for anxiety. It has been three months since I stopped all the medications, but I am still experiencing emotional numbness. Do I have hope?
Answer: Those are somewhat separate questions. It is scientifically established without any room for doubt that these drugs can permanently damage or otherwise change the brain. This is true for babies, children, adults, and is true of both humans and other animals. Neuroleptics are fundamentally toxic drugs with a profoundly deleterious effect on the brain. The drug manufacturers themselves admit to these risks. However, the damages and other changes come in degrees, and we seldom understand exactly how they work or what they mean for a patient. We also seldom know what patients are most affected or least affected by particular damages and changes. Most of our characterizing drug reactions comes down to the experiences patients report, or what can be observed externally. This won’t necessarily correspond to clear physical alterations in the brain we can use to monitor someone’s health or symptoms. The first and most important detail is what someone actually feels — how they are thinking, what is going on with their emotions, what their body feels like, how someone is behaving, etc. That is the best window we have into what is going on in the brain except for a limited subset of drug effects which can create very obvious physical changes in the brain very quickly, like strokes or brain bleeds. Whether a patient is on drugs or has quit them, standard methods of assessing the brain for damage or largescale changes will not be very useful for discerning most of the kinds of damages and alterations drugs have caused. A patient can quit antipsychotics and have lifelong drug impairments but still look ‘normal’ to doctors using typical brain imaging techniques. So, we know for sure these drugs can and do cause harms, and we know that patients may experience long-term or even permanent symptoms as a result. But, this does not mean patients experiencing drug symptoms months after discontinuation must therefore be permanently damaged or that there is no hope for improvement even years after discontinuation. Unfortunately, we do know that some patients will struggle with some harms for the rest of their lives. Some drug effects can also be deadly, or can lead to premature death from other causes. The good news is that we know even more patients are able to partially or fully recover from many kinds of drug symptoms, even severe ones. The nervous system has an innate ability to repair or rewire around many kinds of drug harms. This can take weeks, months, years, or decades, but there is always an ability for improvements to be experienced in a variety of areas. Neuroplasticity doesn’t simply negate the influences of drug use, and an absence of symptoms doesn’t mean we are fully healthy again in our brains. But, this ability to restore and adapt can often help patients overcome the adverse impact of drugs on their everyday experiences. There will always be a lasting mark left on the brain after long-term psychiatric drug use, but many people experience a significant reduction of drug symptoms when given enough time to recover, and a supportive lifestyle for doing so. When we quit these drugs, we are creating a new brain situation. We aren’t reverting back to how we were before the drugs, but we also aren’t stuck with all the changes made by drugs. We have an ability to repair some things, and to plastically change in response to many others. This won’t be enough to overcome some drug harms, and it is typical for patients to have years or a lifetime of noticeable changes in their experiences after long-term use of neuroleptic drugs like you mention. But, I think that the ability for the brain to heal and to rewire is very much a reason to have hope. Especially since three months is a very short period after so many years of drug use. It is pretty common to experience a year or more of numbness carrying on after quitting neuroleptics even for patients who recover much of their emotional functioning. Three months will often feel like a very long time, but you are looking at a recovery which is more in the scope of years or even longer, so still being numb doesn’t mean that you will feel that way forever. You have to first get through any withdrawal after quitting, as well, which can delay greater recovery for months on average, or years for less fortunate patients.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can taking an SSRI like Zoloft cause mania and psychosis in individuals with bipolar disorder? Is this statement accurate?
Answer: Mania and psychosis are SSRI risks for everyone. There are no drug effects which are a risk specifically to patients given a “bipolar disorder” diagnosis. Psychiatric drugs carry the same fundamental risks for all patients, so reactions like mania or psychosis can be experienced by anyone. It is true that some patients are at higher risk of some drug problems, like sudden cardiac death or seizures or allergic reactions or alopecia. This can apply to neuropsychological effects, like apathy, akathisia, mania, panic attacks, psychosis, dissociation. We don’t know all the factors which go into determining how someone reacts to a drug, but it is clear that some patients are more vulnerable than others in various ways. However, the factors which affect someone’s risk levels aren’t determined by psychiatric diagnoses. Indeed, psychiatric diagnoses tell us nothing about someone’s body or brain other than that no medical disorder is suspected to be behind whatever experiences were being labeled. They don’t contain information about how a patient will react to particular stressors, including specific drugs or classes of drugs. This is the case whether we are talking about “bipolar disorder”, “schizophrenia”, “major depressive disorder”, or other everyday diagnoses. It is by design, and these diagnoses are always being applied to a range of differing experiences that can work and express differently from one person to the next. Some patients given a “bipolar disorder” diagnoses are more susceptible to many triggers for mania or psychosis than the average person would be. Some aren’t. Sometimes patients will be more vulnerable to disruptive effects of certain drugs, like SSRIs, but not all psychotropic drugs. Sometimes it can even depend on the drug, like sertraline (Zoloft) versus another SSRI like fluoxetine (Prozac). The diagnosis isn’t what determines whether someone will be more susceptible than average. That said, there are many factors which often accompany a “bipolar” diagnosis which can increase risks of bad drug reactions. Things like professional drug mismanagement, polydrugging, or adverse lifestyle influences like inadequate sleep. Still, these are practical and statistical considerations which won’t be guaranteed by the diagnosis itself.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: On average, how long does it take for antidepressants to work? How can you tell if they are working if there are no changes after a few weeks of taking them regularly and without missing any doses?
Answer: Q1. “On average, how long does it take for antidepressants to work?” On average, they never work. That isn’t the most useful answer in general, but it is the only way to answer the question as you phrased it. For most patients, it isn’t about how long they wait, it is about how drugging isn’t going to produce the results they are wanting. Drugs marketed as “antidepressants” are most successful at causing things we don’t want them to cause, like physical dependence, sexual dysfunction, GI problems. Good outcomes are less common and less reliable. For most uses, both on-label and off-label, these drugs are only as good as placebo on average or even worse than placebo on average. No matter what dose is used, no matter how long someone takes a drug for consistently, most people find them either more harmful than helpful or just plain unhelpful. For people who do see upsides to use, the onset of those upsides will depend on what the upsides are. People will typically find these drugs sedating or stimulating within the first dose or three, with cognitive impairment, emotional numbing, and various other effects usually arising within the first couple weeks. Some people see drug symptoms come on strong at first but then fade back some, others see the same effects just getting worse and worse or staying strong, and sometimes symptoms only begin several weeks or months into use. It is not wholly predictable, and what kinds of alterations a patient is desiring will vary as well. Sometimes the exact same drug reaction can be undesirable to one person but the whole point of taking the drug for another. Whether we are talking about noticing initial changes or experiencing near-full relief, drugs can “work” as fast as overnight or take up to 2–3 months to assess the value of. This is partly because the changes caused by drug use are cumulative and progressive, so they are acting immediately but how someone feels as a result may differ at 1 week, or 1 month, or 1 year as compared to just 1 day. Because responsible drug management involves tapering drugs up and down to start drugs, switch drugs, or discontinue them, there is also going to be a period during which a patient is not on what might be the optimal dose for them. A proper drug trial of a new dose will have to involve a tapering period as well as a period of stabilizing on the new dose and seeing how it makes them feel. Some patients don’t find lower doses helpful but find higher doses worthwhile. Q2. How can you tell if they are working if there are no changes after a few weeks of taking them regularly and without missing any doses? “Working” is whatever you want it to be. If your prescriber has told you that these drugs fix medical problems in your body or have a special ability to reduce depression or anxiety or other concerns, they lied to you. Drugs sold as “antidepressants” have nothing special about them to set them apart from other psychotropics. They don’t have any fundamentally ‘anti-depressing’ mechanisms. They are prescribed to cause altered states — altered brain states which can also then produce altered mental states. An altered state means we are thinking, feeling, perceiving, or behaving differently. This is also why people do things like drink coffee or alcohol, smoke cigarettes or cannabis, take ecstasy or shrooms, etc. The objective is to cause altered states that society, the prescriber, or the patient consider preferable to their unaltered state. This makes it simple to assess whether a drug is “working”. If the altered state is the one you were wanting, then the drug is working. If the altered state is not the one you were wanting, then the drug is not working. If you feel there are “no changes” you consider beneficial, then obviously the drug is not working. The only concept of “working” is tied to altered states. There aren’t any objective, medical, scientific measures of antidepressants “working”. The idea of the drug and the idea of using the drug just revolves around mental changes. What mental changes are considered desirable or undesirable depends on the individual person and the situation they’re in. Or, if the patient is depending on other people (marketing, doctors, family, whatever) to tell them what is desirable, the measure of a drug working depends on whatever goals and interests those other parties have.
