After a few weeks without any benefits at all, it is unlikely someone would find the same drug and dose adequate in the future. While it can be helpful to ‘make sure’ by giving a drug around 2 months at a dose hoped to be optimal, most desired effects would be apparent to some degree within the first several weeks for most patients. Only 2 weeks may not be enough time for some patients, but stretching into 3–4 is making it less and less likely there will be a turnaround in how useful a drug is. A prescriber will then consider whether to increase the dose again, suggest supplementary measures, or try a different drug instead. How long to give a drug will depend in part on what effects you are wanting to experience, as mentioned before. Some effects are more likely to take weeks instead of just hours to come on more fully. In any case, it is all up to you what “working” means and it is up to you to hold drugs accountable to that.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How long can it take to recover from bipolar disorder?
Answer: That depends on the person and what their “bipolar disorder” is. “Bipolar disorder” isn’t a cause of any experiences. It is just a label of convenience attached to any number of things that are occurring for any number of reasons. Clinicians, researchers, the press, and laypersons apply this label to a variety of things which don’t all function the same and don’t all have the same course. Given how it is a label which does not just refer to one kind of experience or cause or outcome, we can’t make proclamations about recovery based on the diagnosis itself. Individual experiences are not all the same and “recovery” can also mean different things to different people. Your question helps avoid the need to overgeneralize outcomes because it asks “can”. That could be taken as a range or as a maximum. In either case, it isn’t asking us to say what 100% of people experience on the basis of the label. Some people experience an episode of mania once and then never again, even if they don’t make radical changes in their life. For some lucky people, it is just a matter of weeks to “recover”. Usually, things are more complex than that. Many people will have enduring triggers, or patterns of cycling, or a greater susceptibility to stress in general. There can be depression, or psychosis, or not. There can be underlying psychological roots which need to be worked on, or ones which perhaps can only be responded to in the present but never fully ameliorated. While it seems likely a smallish subset of cases are a neurodevelopmental disorder instead of an independent psychological crisis, the diagnostic criteria are not designed to differentiate between patients experiencing a non-developmental psychological cause and patients experiencing a neurodevelopmental one. Marketing dogma, some of which you have heard repeated in this thread already, usually speaks on only the most intractable cases instead of the full spectrum of patient experiences. It speaks of a “bipolar disorder” which is not connected to the real world of how the diagnosis is used or what the diagnostic criteria entail. What “recovery” means is also important to piece out here. If someone discovers there is a key trigger and that everything is totally fine as long as they avoid that trigger, are they recovered? Almost all humans can be made manic with the right trigger, so the only distinction here is that some triggers are more common than others or harder to avoid than others. Or, on the other hand, some people continue to experience mania, depression, or cycling but consider themselves recovered because they are able to manage well and maintain a high quality of life and meet their personal goals. Of course, some fewer people continue to experience severe difficulties for the rest of their life and feel themselves quite unrecovered. As a range, “recovery” can take anywhere from days to a lifetime. It all depends on the person, the nature of their experiences, how they choose to respond to them, and what “recovery” is taken to mean here. There is no medical disorder we can monitor for change and then declare has been eliminated as part of recovery. It isn’t a medical recovery, it is a recovery only in other kinds of ways — psychological, social, existential. For some people, recovery means shedding the very label itself and the psychiatric way of thinking about their experiences. There is a rich and empowering conversation to have when defining “recovery” and what our individual goals, priorities, and limitations might be.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is there any evidence that antidepressants for MDD/anxiety do anything but sedate the nervous system? If there is not why are we making tired people more tired? You get someone with mildly less anxiety but too foggy and tired to be productive?
Answer: Yes. Pretty much every level of evidence we have about drugs marketed as “antidepressants” is that they do more than just sedate. Almost all of their actions are actions other than sedating actions. We don’t understand much of what is going on, but we do know they are all sedating, stimulating, and altering other aspects of functioning. The range of systems acted upon is quite wide — not just serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine are affected. For instance, we commonly see an impact on estrogen, sigma, and opioid receptors, histaminic effects, glutamatergic changes, and so forth. Whether or not any this has value to someone experiencing chronic depression or anxiety is a lot more complicated and variable. But what if these drugs were ‘mere sedatives’? Some people have trouble sleeping, some people have obsessive thinking which can be dumbed down, some people prefer feeling slowed to feeling normal. Are these drugs commonly impairing? Yes, and inappropriate prescribing and management feeds into an epidemic of iatrogenic disability. Effects like apathy syndrome, sedation, cognitive impairment, and movement disorders can interfere with everyday functioning and quality of life. However, being tired doesn’t always mean being totally unproductive, people aren’t always starting off already being particularly productive, and many of the mentally disruptive effects of these drugs that might be considered useful aren’t about sedation. There is no doubt that these drugs do more than sedate. Whether what they do is considered useful and whether they provide upsides which outweigh their risks and downsides when compared to alternatives is a bigger and more central question but also one which has to be answered on an individual level.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is their any way I can get on another mood stabilizer while tapering off Seroquel? So I won’t get the nasty side effects.
Answer: That’s not really how it works, unfortunately. There are three key factors to be aware of here: It is true that some patients find certain drugs (whether psychotropics or supplements) useful for preventing or alleviating some of the withdrawal symptoms of psychiatric drugs. There has even been limited talk of using psychedelics to ease off psychiatric drugs without a prolonged withdrawal period, though no systematic evidence-based protocols have been created for it, just as there aren’t even any systematic evidence-based protocols for tapering itself. But, the most powerful tool in your toolbox is the taper itself. Making less extreme reductions and making reductions less often are the main variables which can help you avoid or mitigate reduction-emergent symptoms. Doctors often try to rush patients off, or even cold turkey them, but that is needlessly harmful for many people. As you seem to be aware, withdrawal syndrome isn’t the only concern here, either. Other kinds of drug effects can surface or worsen, and trying to quit can be destabilizing regardless. People are going to be more susceptible to psychological crises and to struggling with managing anything that may have been going on before drug use ever began. It is wise to be inquiring about how to keep the situation more stable as you reduce and go off a neuroleptic. However, your question does not include any information suggesting that adding more drugs would be helpful or appropriate, and if you did add a psychiatric drug during your taper, the term “mood stabilizer” is not going to express whether or not that drug is a reasonable fit. Asking a prescriber is how to get more drugs, but if you were wondering if it is actually a good idea, that is a more complicated discussion. If your end goal is to be off all these drugs, it is also counterproductive to be adding drugs instead of subtracting them. A quetiapine (aka Seroquel) taper will take so long that you will become physically dependent upon whatever additional psychotropic you add in, moving you in the wrong direction overall. People will usually need to stay on a drug meant to help with discontinuation stability for at least a little while after their drop to zero, too, meaning you’d be on that additional drug during the taper and for a while after. Whether that means a total length of 6 months, 12 months, 18 months, or longer is more personal. That is also setting aside how you will have to spend many months tapering the drug you added in after that period. The value of other drugs can increase if someone isn’t able to properly taper, like an emergency cessation, but that doesn’t appear to be the case here. Your question does make it clear that you need more information before making a decision about how to handle your tapering of Seroquel, in addition to having some conversations with the professionals in charge of prescribing, managing, and dispensing your drugs. To help with that, there are several links below to content and websites which explain tapering concerns in greater detail. Most doctors screw this up, so you want to be armed with good information before trying to work out a reasonable tapering plan with whoever is prescribing. Remember that it is your own health and life on the line here, not theirs, so if they think you are being too cautious or moving too slowly, they risk nothing to tell you to go faster but you risk everything to trust their potentially baseless advice. Aside from looking through resources like the ones linked below, you can also ask your prescriber to use the Maudsley Desprescribing Guidelines, Volume 2 once it is released.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible to be in 2mg or 5mg of Aripripazol for an adult? I want to get off meds but I’m scared I will never be normal again. My first episode was at 38 and I’ve had two or three embarrassing moments.
Answer: What dose someone finds useful will vary. Whether someone finds any drug amount useful will vary. Most people find these kinds of drugs more harmful than helpful overall, particularly if they use a drug long-term. Much of the time, no particular dose changes that balance. These are harmful drugs and it is only exceptional cases where someone stays on them and live a much better life as a result. To confuse things further, trying to quit these drugs can cause entirely new problems for patients due to issues like physical dependence. Even though most people are probably best off staying away from drugs like neuroleptics, this does not mean someone is likely to succeed off of drugs if they quit drugs but don’t do anything to address the reasons for the episodes. (You don’t mention what these episodes are, but the same principles apply to depression, panic, mania, psychosis, etc.) Some causes are temporary and pass even if you don’t do anything. But, most causes require us to put in some work to understand what is going on and to change things in our lives so that we can prevent future episodes or so that we can respond to new episodes more constructively. Having episodes does not mean drug use will be helpful or that drug use is necessary. Using drugs also may not stop episodes from happening even if we find it helpful. But, if you have found drugging useful, it is important to evaluate whether that usefulness outweighs any downsides and risks, and whether fewer drugs or lower doses can still help you as much as you feel is justified by the risks involved. If you plan to reduce or discontinue drugs, it is also important to discover strategies that can help you meet your goals outside of drug use. Drugs are just one of many possible tools for changing how we feel and behave. They are an easy tool because they cause radical changes very quickly, but they don’t address the original causes of repeating episodes. Whether you can or should use any particular amount of aripiprazole is not about being 38, or having episodes. What matters here are your goals, your present and past responses to drugs, your support options, your willingness to invest a lot of time and energy into working on the causes of these experiences, and stuff like that. Is it possible for you to do great without drugging? Maybe. Many people can, but your question does not provide that information. Will drug use be better for you overall? We can’t know that from your question, either. Anyone “can” use a neurolpetic. What matters is whether it more responsible or more preferable to use one, and only you can decide that. Having these experiences can be difficult and confusing. Responding to them can be complicated and it can take a long time to better understand what works for us and where we want to be going. Most people have better options than drug use, but those options will not always be explained to them or provided through local institutions. Many people have to create their own path if they want to succeed, with or without drugs. There are books and communities and also some professionals who can help patients that want to do better, but each person will have unique needs and responses and will have to have an active role in life changes. Educating and finding resources which are relevant to you are vital steps in the process of rehabilitation.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is 75mg Effexor a good enough dose for severe depression and anxiety?
Answer: “Good enough” isn’t measured in milligrams. There are three fundamental considerations here: As others have partly mentioned, patients should usually be started below 75mg/day and will usually require more than 75mg/day for their ultimate maintenance dose if they are in the group of people finding venlafaxine adequately helpful, tolerable, and better than safer alternatives. It is on the lower side of clinical doses and higher doses will be causing a different ratio and potency of particular influences. Whether those influences lead to desirable alterations or undesirable ones depends on the patient and situation. Is it fair to see how someone feels on 75mg/day before escalating further? Sure.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I went from 15mg of Lexapro to 10mg in a week and now have anxiety. Is this normal?
Answer: Yes, that is very normal. There are three main reasons why patients very often experience anxiety when changing SSRI doses. The first is that these are neurodisruptive drugs and their influences will very commonly cause anxiety and other such effects when a new dose is started. Initiating a drug, increasing the dose, or reducing the dose can all be destabilizing. People usually adjust within days or weeks if this is the cause. If you notice things getting worse rather than better, it is more likely that either the anxiety is due to another drug cause or that it will not be resolving if you keep using the drug. Another primary reason for anxiety with a dose reduction is withdrawal syndrome. If someone has been using an SSRI continuously for several weeks or longer, withdrawal syndrome is to be expected and can sometimes happen even with a partial dose reduction instead of a full discontinuation of the drug. 15mg to 10mg is a significant drop and liable to cause withdrawal for many people. It may take weeks, months, or even longer to resolve, but reinstating the original dose will often help within a few days to a few weeks. Tapering more slowly may help reduce the intensity and longevity of the emergent anxiety. A third key reason why some patients experience anxiety with SSRI reduction or cessation is rebound syndrome. Though withdrawal will sometimes involve rebound symptoms, rebound can happen even if classic withdrawal does not. “Rebound” in this sense is not referring to a recurrence of previous psychological experiences, it is referring to supersensitivity in the nervous system caused by changes meant to be adaptations to drug actions. Essentially, the anxiety results from overcompensation following a dose reduction. It often takes months or years for the anxiety to fully fade.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does Lexapro dose go by your weight?
Answer: Not really. Though it is true that larger people sometimes need more of a drug for the same effect, and babies and children will usually need less, SSRI doses are not usually calibrated between adults based on weight. Firstly, because any dose is already so potent it will be acting very intensely. There is no expectation that someone 50 or even 100 pounds heavier would respond much less strongly to the same dose. And secondly, because commercial doses of SSRIs are not made to be calibrated to each patient. There are only a limited number of standard dose increments for pills and most prescribers will only tweak doses very roughly, if at all. Thirdly, because our metabolic capacities matter more than our weight, by far, when it comes to drugs like SSRIs. Most notably, our liver enzyme complement. Some people process these drugs much more quickly than others, and this can potentially impact both what dose someone is prescribed and how slowly a drug should be uptapered. It can become even more important if someone is using multiple drugs at the same time which rely on some of the same enzymes to be metabolized. So, CP450 testing, which tries to estimate some of your enzyme complements, will be more relevant to dose management than weighing a patient. Younger patients will usually be given lower-end doses, and it could be that an adult much larger than their peers will sometimes require a higher dose for a similar level of action. But since these drugs usually don’t provide the effects and outcomes desired, personal variability in reactions will be more important than weight as well. Higher doses are not far more likely to be useful than lower doses for any adults, regardless of weight — drugging usually fails either way — and even taller or bulkier people may find the lowest standard dose adequate or require a much higher dose to experience the maximum upsides they can with the drug.

Question: Why isn't drugging someone against their will considered a crime against humanity?
Answer: Probably professed intent and legality. I’m no lawyer, but reading from a UN source oriented around lay readers like myself, it seems that systematic involuntary drugging in the form of psychiatry is not likely to be considered a crime against humanity because it will be legally allowed and claimed to not intentionally harm. Criteria like “imprisonment or other severe deprivation of physical liberty in violation of fundamental rules of international law” are ducked for it being legal, criteria like “inhumane acts of a similar character intentionally causing great suffering, or serious injury to body or to mental or physical health” or “enforced sterilization” are ducked for it being stated as not intentional. I answered this within the context of other questions in your Quora history. Answers mentioning that drugging a single person would not, by very nature, qualify are also correct in saying so. United Nations Office on Genocide Prevention and the Responsibility to Protect

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why is it okay to lobotomize someone with antipsychotics?
Answer: That’s something only you can answer for yourself. What is or isn’t “okay” is totally arbitrary and personal. You can select any values you want and it could be that nobody else will fully agree. I don’t know why you think something is or isn’t, would or wouldn’t be okay. There are plenty of relevant facts about antipsychotics we could discuss, like their potential upsides, their risks, their typical outcomes, the social context for their use, why prescribing has been hyped up and ramped up. But, there’s no way any of us could tell you prescriptively that using these drugs is okay. Why do so many people feel it is okay to lobotomize people with antipsychotics? Pretty much all the same reasons as they felt it was okay to lobotomize people with psychosurgeries, for instance: The motivations behind promoting chemical lobotomization are varied and not everyone will support the idea or facilitate the actual drugging of patients for all the same reasons. Some will even not be okay with it but still remain complicit.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is bipolar disorder (Type 1 and Type 2) a degenerative/neurodegenerative brain disease if left uncured?
Answer: No. The answer is no for two overlapping reasons: (1) “bipolar disorder” is not a brain disease and is not defined in any way with relation to the brain, and (2) there is no medical “cure” for “bipolar disorder” because there is nothing going on to medically cure. That doesn’t mean things can’t worsen or that nobody needs help to live a better life, it just means we are talking about psychological and behavioral concerns instead of fixing problems in the brain. If someone is struggling with a brain disorder, that isn’t “bipolar disorder” and it requires appropriate assessment and assistance which psychiatry is not designed to provide and which psychiatric diagnoses offer no value in. Brain Disease? “Bipolar disorder” is a “psychiatric disorder” (sometimes called “mental disorder” or “mental illness”). “Psychiatric disorder” is a concept which was invented to a cover a variety of things which are not brain disorders, and the exact experiences covered changes from year to year. In fact, there is no inherent physical difference between so-called “mental illness” and the absence of “mental illness” because any kinds of physical traits and functional states can be labeled as being part of “mental illness” if we want. This is the opposite of brain diseases where there must be one or more specific physical differences which allow us to differentiate and label what is going on. “Psychiatric disorder” is about emotions, thoughts, and behaviors, not what is going on in the brain or the health of someone’s brain. And, more pointedly, if there is something wrong with the brain, that automatically makes the issue medical instead of psychiatric. Brain problems are usually, though not exclusively, the domain of neurology. Since brain disorders can be caused by many different kinds of issues, and involve many other systems of the body, it is not as simple as saying all brain stuff is about neurology, but there is innately a neurological component if we are talking about brain health and functioning. If someone finds out their mania or depression are due to a brain problem, “bipolar disorder” is not a compatible diagnosis. That’s how psychiatry has set things up. Cure? Since something being wrong in or with the brain means psychiatric diagnoses are disqualified, there is no way to “cure” these concerns in the literal, medical sense. There is nothing wrong with the body to treat or resolve. It is true that brain problems, even ones caused by psychiatry itself, commonly get misdiagnosed as “bipolar disorder”, so the diagnostic criteria clinicians are supposed to be using are often ignored to some extent in real life. Still, the concept itself, and what psychiatry says it is targeting is a collection of experiences with no underlying medical disorder and no physical distinction from the experiences non-psychiatric patients are having. In the broader, more metaphorical sense, perhaps you can say we can ‘treat’ or ‘cure’ things like depression, mania, psychosis, and cycling. But, it is not about improving brain health, it is about changing the factors which lead to those experiences in the first place, and about helping people respond constructively to them and their risks. You can’t medically treat or cure things like trauma, grief, or loneliness, but you can do things which help people navigate those difficult situations more capably and successfully. Psychiatric diagnoses don’t tell us anything about what someone’s needs are and how to help them, though. Neurodegenerative? Stress and trauma are not brain disorders but they can certainly have an adverse impact on our functioning and quality of life. The human body is a physical machine with physical needs and the stresses of living do take a toll, just like driving a car adds wear to the car even if it is working properly and you treat it well and aren’t crashing it or anything like that. The body has numerous processes and mechanisms it uses to try and address the wear accumulated throughout daily life, and to replace some of the stuff that wears out or gets broken. We are always in a state of self-repair and regeneration, from before we are both until the day we finally die. This is a consideration for all living organisms. When we are in more extreme states or when we are operating outside the ideal range of bodily stress continuously, this can be harder on our body. It doesn’t take a medical disorder for us to be adding extra wear. For instance, being a professional athlete or concert violinist or archer or forensic accountant or translator will all produce additional stresses and wear in particular ways. If someone has unresolved psychological struggles or they are having more physically stressful experiences episodically, like depression and mania, that can be harder on their brain. It can also lead to longer-term changes in the brain as it adapts to the demands of those experiences, just as we see with other chronic stresses.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible for someone to become dependent on their SSRI medication and unable to stop taking it?
Answer: That is the standard response to these drugs, though it happens in a matter of degrees. Clinically speaking, “dependence” refers to two different but sometimes complementary kinds of experiences: physical dependence and psychological dependence. That is to say, the body’s chemical dependence upon something and the mind’s emotional and behavioral dependence upon something. Both are an issue with drugs such as antidepressants, and both contribute to preventable harms, injuries, and deaths caused by drug use. There are constructive and mitigating ways to respond to the creation of physical and psychological dependencies upon SSRIs, but the bottom line is that most people can’t just quit when they want to and a small portion of people can’t quit at all, even if a drug is only causing undesirable effects and has no upsides for them. Though many nuances won’t fit into a summary, I can still briefly review some key aspects of the concerns below. Physical dependence is about how our body comes to rely upon a foreign stimulus, such as the actions of a drug, to maintain homeostasis. Basically, we need to use that drug for our body to be able to function properly. When drugs interfere with how our nervous system functions, it must adapt around that interference so that it can keep us alive despite the actions of the drug. This is obviously very helpful, but the consequence of adapting to the presence of a drug is that we have to adapt again if the drug is no longer present. Adjusting takes time (months to years, depending on the circumstances) and can produce uncomfortable, debilitating, or even life-threatening symptoms in the meantime. Most patients will experience withdrawal if they try to quit an SSRI after use lasting at least a couple of months, and quitting after years of use tends to be harder. Not all patients encounter severe symptoms, but studies suggest that severe difficulties are experienced by a majority of people who do notice withdrawal. Tapering slowly and in gradual increments can often reduce how severe withdrawal becomes, but most doctors try to taper patients more quickly than is best for them and there are still no systematic evidence-based protocols for antidepressant tapering even though these kinds of drugs have been prescribed to patients and causing physical dependence for more than 60 years. The result of physical dependence is that most patients can’t quit an SSRI when they want to. They will have to spend months or years still using the SSRI while trying to taper down the dose at a tolerable rate, enduring not just the toxic influences of ongoing use but also the potentially serious effects of trying to discontinue. Some people will keep on a drug simply because tapering off is too harmful or difficult, and a small subset of patients are unable to taper at any rate and end up stuck on the drug for life. So, most literally speaking, most people can eventually stop antidepressants if that is what they choose, but the feasibility of doing so depends on the situation and the cost involved will range from very low to very high. Psychological dependence is about how we come to reshape our thoughts, emotions, sense of wellbeing, and lifestyle around a stimulus, such as the altered states of a psychotropic drug, including psychotropics like SSRIs. Both conscious choices and the natural psychological pressures involved contribute to the changes made. This category is a lot broader and more hodgepodge than physical dependence because it is not about just one kind of interest or intention, it is about many. Jonesing and compulsive use are things we recognize in the mainstream as being expressions of psychological dependence, and SSRI use won’t necessarily look like that. But clinically, psychological dependence is often also characterized through things people are doing as a result of continuing drug use or to keep up their drug use that they would not normally do and have good reason to normally avoid doing. Things like missing important social events because of drug use, spending burdensome amounts of time in everyday life trying to get the drug or recover from the effects of the drug, losing control over how much of the drug is being used or whether the drug is used at all, putting up with unreasonable dangers just to obtain or use the drug, and so forth. Many of these will be the social telltale signs of what we more colloquially call “addiction”. Though they can sometimes be more subtle or framed differently with antidepressant use, many of the same basic problems of this nature faced by stereotypical drug addicts also impact a lot of SSRI patients. People won’t go around robbing to pay for SSRIs like they might for crack or heroin (though to be fair, SSRIs are just cents per daily pill), but there is still often an adverse lifestyle effect with ongoing use. It may be noticed or unnoticed, it may be excused or regretted. Many psychiatric drug users are also under the impression that drug use is providing benefits it actually is not. Some patients think a drug is or will be making them more functional, more whole, more real, more free even while it is doing the very opposite. Many are convinced the drugs provide a special medical benefit, but that is just a marketing lie to get people hooked on the idea as well as the drugs themselves. Just like the use of drugs on the street, for recreation and for coping, it is true that sometimes people prefer a drugged state to an undrugged one, for a variety of reasons. However, when someone overestimates the value of a drug or thinks they are doing better because of use even though the reality is that they are being impaired or acting in problematic ways they would not want to sober, this becomes a problem. As a pattern, it can be psychological dependence.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Medication (Lexapro) induced mania? Is it a clear sign of true bipolar disorder?
Answer: No. By very nature, mania from any cause cannot be “a clear sign of true bipolar disorder”. The concept of “bipolar disorder” is always in flux and no two professionals will necessarily agree on where to place the boundaries, but the bottom line is that diagnostic criteria explicitly exclude drug reactions and that there are many causes of mania or courses of mania other than what the mainstream “bipolar” diagnostic criteria cover. An SSRI-induced mania tells us nothing about the specific cause of someone’s mania. So, we need to always keep in mind that there could be a cause for mania which is not going to fit into the “bipolar disorder” idea, such as a medical disorder, and that there are additional requirements to the “bipolar disorder” diagnosis which an episode of drug-induced mania won’t usually meet. Context is also relevant here. Reacting to a pro-manic drug with mania does not suggest “bipolar” just as reacting to pro-apathy drugs like neuroleptics with apathy syndrome does not suggest “schizophrenia”. SSRIs are not neutral drugs which rarely cause mania, they are stimulating drugs which very commonly cause manic reactions. Hypomania or even mania are reactions which can be predicted on the basis of the mechanisms of SSRI drugs. We don’t need to study patients using a newly formulated SSRI to know that some people will be made manic by them because it is innate to the pharmacology of the drugs which do what these drugs do to the nervous system. Insofar as research has looked into it, most people who go manic from SSRIs never fit into the “bipolar disorder” patient profile per the standard diagnostic criteria. Not at the time, not later on. If we are speaking “true bipolar disorder” as if to say that many official diagnoses are not referring to a more serious and fundamental lifelong pattern of mania and depression from only a more narrow subset of causes, that disparity between antidepressant manias and “bipolar” diagnoses grows even more. It is also important to remember that patients with experiences meeting “bipolar disorder” criteria won’t necessarily go manic from using SSRIs anyhow. Some simply don’t find such drugs triggering, some only respond with mania to specific drugs or doses, and some may go manic but only if they are not also using other drugs at the same time. But since ‘signs’ can be hit or miss and thus won’t always be present, this is just supplementary information for your question. In summary:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible to get prescribed Ozapin for psychosis without schizophrenia?
Answer: Easily. Almost any doctor who is interested in prescribing olanzapine (aka Ozapin) for psychosis in “schizophrenia” diagnoses is also interested in prescribing olanzapine for psychosis in non-“schizophrenia” diagnoses or in emergency situations without any diagnosis. This is for three reasons. Firstly, so-called “antipsychotics” are prescribed to anyone. You don’t need any particular diagnosis to get a prescription, generally. Regional institutional and administrative policies can vary, but the basic fact is that these drugs are prescribed extremely loosely and I have never in my life heard of a patient who sought this kind of drug from doctors and found no way to get it prescribed just by honestly sharing their experiences. Secondly, there is no special value to neuroleptics in one diagnosis versus others, whether we are talking about patients experiencing psychosis or patients experiencing other things, like depression, anxiety, rage, tics, insomnia, homesickness, mood swings, dementia, etc. There would be no reason for prescribers to give a patient olanzapine or other neuroleptics if they have a “schizophrenia” diagnosis but not if they don’t. The vast majority of prescribing falls outside the uses ‘approved’ by regulatory agencies because regulatory agencies aren’t there to tell practitioners how to use drugs or when and there is no limitation placed on their ability to prescribe these drugs whenever they want to. Thirdly, what a patient wants or thinks or needs doesn’t generally matter. Most people will easily receive a prescription for a drug like this even if they don’t want one or it would be counterproductive for them. You don’t have to experience psychosis or be construed to be experiencing psychosis, you don’t have to be impaired or in danger or in distress, you don’t have to agree that anything is wrong or that drug use would be a good idea or reasonable measure. Doctors who prescribe antipsychotics but do so only sparingly and with great selectivity are a rarity, and there are always plenty of other doctors a patient can look to if their first doctor is one of those rare exceptions.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does stopping antipsychotic medication suddenly cause hypnic jerk?
Answer: It can, sure. The symptoms that can be caused by reducing or quitting an antipsychotic are numerous and potentially serious. The more quickly someone discontinues, the more likely they are to encounter more severe and longer-lasting drug symptoms. Hypnic jerks are not an unusual symptom to experience, especially in the earliest weeks after quitting, since sleep regulation and neuromuscular functioning will often be in disarray as a result of the changes caused by drug use. Exploding head syndrome, sleep paralysis, nightmares, insomnia, and lucid dreaming are some related symptoms patients commonly experiences after sudden discontinuation. It is unsafe to discontinue these kinds of drugs without an appropriate taper if a patient has been taking them for more than a few weeks. How slow to go will depend on the individual patient and the situation. Most doctors give bad tapering advice and recommend people quit more quickly than they can handle, so it is important to read about tapering risks and management before trying to reduce one’s dose. Some examples of places to learn about reducing and recovering from neuroleptics are linked below:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why are the same psychiatric labels that are designed to help people, also the same labels that one feels naturally inclined to reject because they clash with their beliefs about themselves?
Answer: There are no psychiatric labels “designed to help people”, if you are talking about patients. Psychiatric labels, whether official diagnoses or other terminology, are designed to help clinicians and other professionals — researchers, academics, politicians, people marketing and selling services and products. We can get into big trouble if we start evaluating these labels with the assumption that they are meant to help the people being labeled, as they very much are not. If the labels were accountable to what happened when they were actually used, they would be abolished. So, questions about why they can hurt people or restrict recovery progress or poison society or be hijacked by profiteers, bigots, and scaremongerers can arise from that misunderstanding about why they exist in the first place and how they are maintained. This same kind of misunderstanding applies to the proposed clash you mention. Psychiatric labels don’t tell us what to believe about ourselves, they are labels used by outsiders to refer to experiences we think differ from our own, or, if we are being sloppy, to people who differ from how we see ourselves. They are descriptive of our perspective, not prescriptive of what the things and persons being labeled are capable of, or why. We might find the beliefs or characterizations of someone else offensive or wrongheaded or dangerous, and that is fine. Neither the experiences of the labeler nor the experiences of the labeled are changed based on the label being retrospectively assigned. Again there is the separation between the ideas of one person and the experiences of another. I don’t think this necessarily answers the full scope of your question, though. Sometimes the ideas of others are more correct than our own idea, or would be more useful to us. But if we feel threatened by them, or by the people trying to change our beliefs, that can lead to conflict. The whole context and dynamic of the exchange can matter. Likewise, sometimes people think they have a better idea than us but they don’t, so their trying to force their idea upon us can lead us to be less receptive to anything they say. Because psychiatric labels are an influential tool integral to an entire system of oppression and abuse, if you say there is a natural inclination to reject them I would suggest there may be a natural inclination to reject being abused, when we recognize it as abuse.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does a psychiatrist's refusal to prescribe mood stabilizers for someone diagnosed with bipolar disorder indicate a lack of belief in the diagnosis?
Answer: We can’t assume anything. While the most reasonable assumption would simply be that the psychiatrist doesn’t think it is appropriate to prescribe the patient whatever you are labeling here as “mood stabilizers”, whether as the prescriber themselves or in general, even that assumption isn’t safe and there could be alternative explanations. Because whether a diagnosis was assigned according to popular diagnostic criteria at the time is irrelevant to whether a particular drug is a good idea for a patient, there should be no particular association between the psychiatrist not prescribing drugs like anticonvulsants and their stance on whether a previous clinician was following the standard diagnostic criteria when using the “bipolar” diagnosis. But, some people are morons and will base their prescribing on diagnosis instead of patient needs, so the lack of a logical connection doesn’t reliably tell us what this psychiatrist’s beliefs are. It is essential to always allow the possibility that a practitioner may be an idiot, miseducated, tending conflicts of interest, or plain malicious. There is one more complication here, which is what “belief in the diagnosis” is meant to convey. Belief that the diagnosis was applied according to the industry rules by the previous clinician? Belief that the experiences meeting the diagnostic criteria actually did occur? Belief that using the diagnosis is constructive or relevant? Belief that the diagnosis is as valid as other psychiatric diagnoses? Belief that psychiatric diagnoses are valid in the first place? The question reads differently depending on what you are asking. In any case, the diagnosis doesn’t really matter, as it only has administrative value instead of informational value to patients or prescribers. Psychiatric diagnoses are also provisional in perpetuity — a change in someone’s experiences can lead to a change in diagnosis because diagnoses are retrospective instead of deterministic and a diagnosis does not refer to why something happened or what will happen in the future. Whether these realities are integral to the decision of the psychiatrist is beyond what anyone on here could answer for you. They are the best source on their reasoning through this matter.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: My boyfriend has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder. He takes his drugs. Will my unborn children inherit from him because I don't have it myself?
Answer: The simplest thing to say is that “bipolar disorder” isn’t genetic. That is a complicated statement, though. There are indeed genes and collections of genes which may increase the likelihood of someone experiencing mania or depression. There are likewise epigenetic factors which can be inherited or otherwise passed along which can increase the likelihood of someone experiencing mania or depression. So, genes aren’t entirely irrelevant, although no particular genes are required for a “bipolar disorder” diagnosis and no genes are implied by one either. The association between genetics and psychiatric diagnoses is pretty vague and other factors matter more, like life stressors, trauma, and coping resources. Also remember that psychiatric diagnoses are not causes, they are labels for experiences with varied, unstated, non-medical causes. They have no physical identity, no genetic signature, and no universal underlying dynamics. The vagueness involved applies to multiple aspects of the association here. For instance, experiences of mania or depression aren’t themselves “bipolar disorder”. A psychiatric diagnosis like “bipolar disorder” will only circumscribe a subset of them based on whatever the popular criteria are at the time, meaning many experiences will not be labeled that way, and a diagnosis will only potentially come up if the experiences occur in the first place. Having a parent with a history of episodic mania/hypomania with or without depression should absolutely be taken into account when providing for a child’s health and psychological needs and preparing for future risks, but it does not mean they will have the same experiences. As I mentioned before, other factors matter more than genetics and someone’s genes can never tell us whether a psychiatric diagnosis will one day be handed out. There are medical conditions which can be genetic and can cause mania and depression as symptoms, but “bipolar disorder” excludes all medical conditions. So, if your boyfriend was misdiagnosed, which happens pretty commonly, it is possible there is an underlying heritable medical concern. Some are easily treatable, but on the other hand some are not even identified yet. Additionally, the use of psychiatric drugs can affect sperm and the resulting pregnancy and offspring, though the full scope of risks is not clear and the rate of drugs’ effects on sperm being a primary contributing factor to a child’s later mania or depression is not something we have good statistics on. It is incredibly difficult to measure for and you are much better off focusing on the things you can control in the present in facilitating a healthy pregnancy and good environment and skills for childrearing. Bringing this back around to genetics and psychiatric labels, it is also relevant to mention that you don’t really know what your genes are in terms of susceptibilities just by knowing you don’t have a history of bipolar depression. You might have genes which carry certain risks even if you are not suffering as a result, or you might have genetic material that will be passed on and involve risks in a child that weren’t present for you. We still don’t understand the whole process of sexual reproduction in humans and exactly how particular things are passed along and managed. Some basics may seem simple, but the details become a lot more complex and it isn’t a clean 50/50 split. Ultimately, anyone can have experiences which lead to a “bipolar disorder” diagnosis and we can’t know what your child will experience just by hearing one parent was given a psychiatric diagnosis.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can antidepressants cause psychiatric disorders?
Answer: That depends on your definitions. “Psychiatric disorders”, at the very least in the modern era, explicitly exclude all drug effects, so drugs can never cause them. Not in psychiatric patients, not in non-psychiatric patients, not in healthy trial volunteers. As soon as drugs, whether ones marketed as “antidepressants” or any other kinds, caused the experiences being diagnosed, those experiences are ineligible for psychiatric diagnoses (aka “psychiatric disorder” or “mental illness” diagnoses). But, what is psychiatric disorder? Anything we say it is. All it takes is a popular vote, which is the culmination of cultural biases, economic incentives, and philosophical inertia. Some of the things we used to label as “psychiatric disorder” are no longer labeled that way, and some of the things we did not used to label as “psychiatric disorder” are now labeled so. It is a completely open-ended characterization and tells us nothing about what is actually going on. The diagnostic criteria themselves, the checklist of things which are said to collectively qualify particular experiences for a psychiatric diagnosis, get a bit more specific. But, not specific as to the cause or nature of those experiences, just whether certain things are construed as happening at all. These criteria mostly refer to experiences like anxiety, dysphoria, hallucinations, delusions, anger, cognitive impairments, loss of control, social debilitation. So, we have to already identify concerns before applying the diagnostic criteria — we don’t learn someone has panic attacks or depression or a lack of empathy, we just plug in those already-acknowledged experiences to see what administrative label is being preferred in the mainstream industry at the moment. This is where the overlap with drug effects can be complete. The drugs marketed as “antidepressants” are a relatively varied assortment of psychotropics, all of which act on the nervous system to produce altered mental states. They act on many other things body as well, but their marketed purposes, including their namesake, are focused on their actions in the nervous system. Though individual drugs, or general types of drugs (like MAOIs, reuptake inhibitors, antagonists), can cause particular issues more often or less often than others, all the basic risks will be shared across all antidepressants. This is true especially of the neuropsychological effects — things like depression, insomnia, psychosis, apathy, mania, anxiety, panic, violence, suicidality, compulsivity, disinhibition, sedation, cognitive impairment, loss of libido, rage, social withdrawal, mood swings, and so forth. In fact, undesirable mental and behavioral effects are more common, more likely, and probably more intense on average than desirable ones. More to the point, all the diagnostic criteria for common psychiatric diagnoses can be met by drug effects except the criterion which excludes drug effects from being eligible. These drugs are very commonly causing clinically substantial, potentially long-lasting mental effects and destabilization that can lead to a psychiatric diagnosis if the clinician is so sloppy or exploitative as to ignore the diagnostic criterion excluding drug effects. The vast majority of patients experience one or more adverse neuropsychological effects from antidepressant use, usually multiple, and sometimes even single specific effects are so overwhelmingly common as to be experienced by a majority of users. On paper, there shouldn’t be a mass movement of clinicians labeling many of these drug reactions as “psychiatric disorder”, but in reality the diagnostic criteria don’t matter and patients are at very high risk of misdiagnosis and mistreatment.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can taking psychiatric medication have negative effects if the diagnosis is incorrect, such as prescribing anti-depressants for bipolar disorder?
Answer: Diagnosis is irrelevant; bad reactions are always possible. How someone reacts to a psychiatric drug is unrelated to diagnosis. No psychiatric diagnosis tells us how someone will or must react to any particular psychiatric drug. They aren’t that kind of concept, and actually tell us nothing at all about someone’s body or how it is functioning. All of these drugs have negative effects, and all patients who take them are affected negatively. The question we have to grapple with is whether any drug upsides outweigh the downsides (including any reactions going on right now and the risk of additional or worse ones in the future), particularly in comparison to other options someone has for addressing the concerns at hand. This is a decision which must be weighed on an individual basis, and reevaluated continuously if someone has elected to use drugs. Psychiatric drugs are fundamentally dangerous and harmful drugs and they can always have a seriously negative impact on a patient. It doesn’t depend on what someone’s diagnosis is, it doesn’t depend on someone receiving a diagnosis, and no diagnosis can protect someone from adverse drug effects, either. Diagnoses are just empty phrases we pack whatever criteria we want into, and the criteria packed into them in official diagnostic guidelines don’t include anything that determines drug reactions. Because these drugs are problematic for all patients and the factors shaping drug reactions are the same factors whether or not a psychiatric diagnosis was assigned or assigned per the criteria in vogue at the time, there is simply no realistic relevance to diagnosis here. What matters is the person and their unique qualities, their health, their environment, their experiences, their needs, and psychiatric diagnoses don’t communicate that stuff. A diagnosis being applied in accordance to the popular rules of the day does not suggest the drug or drugs prescribed will be helpful, or more helpful than harmful, and diagnoses can’t protect patients from the adverse effects of psychiatric drugs. A diagnosis being misapplied, not following the rules set by the trade bodies that create the guidelines, will not produce worse drug reactions or poorer drug management. These drugs have the same actions no matter the patient, no matter the diagnosis or how it was assigned. If a doctor is doing a bad job, relying on diagnoses for prescribing or management, they are already fucking things up whether or not diagnostic criteria were followed. Diagnoses provide no understanding to patients or clinicians. They are, by nature, an administrative tool rather than a medical or psychological tool. They are also a social tool in the sense of being used for political sanctioning and industrial marketing and stuff like that, but the important consideration here is that they don’t tell a patient what is going on in their lives or in their minds or why or what will help them or how they will feel in the future or what will happen if they use any particular psychiatric drugs. Whether or not someone finds a drug alteration useful is not about their diagnosis, and the same drug effects can occur no matter what someone’s diagnosis is or isn’t. This does not mean all people and all situations are the same, it just means that psychiatric diagnoses don’t convey any of the details which play a part in shaping drug reactions and outcomes.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is taking an SSRI a permanent solution for depression?
Answer: Only if it kills you. Most people don’t find SSRIs very useful in depression. Only a small portion of patients find SSRIs to lead to a remission of depression, and only a subset of those patients find that remission to last more than several months. There are indeed exceptional cases where someone takes an SSRI, feels much better as a result of drug use specifically, gets back to everything being fine, and then never experiences depression again even after going off the drug. These are very atypical, but there are definitely examples. After all, we are handing these drugs out to millions upon millions of people decade after decade, so we cover a significant range of outcomes. However, a catch is that SSRIs don’t somehow prevent depression from happening in the future. New instances of depression can occur for any number of reasons, and staying on the SSRI will not be an impenetrable shield blocking all causes of depression, or even any causes of depression. SSRIs don’t have any literally “anti-depressing” mechanism. The SSRI could even itself be the cause of depression, both with use and as a result of an attempt to discontinue. SSRIs are a tool some find useful in depression, but they are not a “permanent solution for depression”. For most, they aren’t even a temporary solution, and the majority of patients find them outright more harmful than helpful. The only people guaranteed to never again experience depression as a result of SSRI use are the people SSRIs killed. It’s a shitty and sobering thought, but efficiently cuts through the false marketing narrative questions like this are generally based upon.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible to experience a depressive episode while taking an SSRI medication?
Answer: Of course. There is basically no reason for someone to not experience a depressive episode while taking an SSRI. SSRIs don’t literally “antidepress” people, as if they are some sort of antidote to a poison or a magical incantation. They don’t have any special properties which specifically prevent depression or stop depression. They are just a handful of drugs among thousands of psychotropics which cause altered states that some people find useful in one or more ways in depression and many don’t. It is always possible to experience depression even if an SSRI is being taken. Reactions vary, and the reasons for depression as well as the underlying dynamics will vary, too. We are ultimately talking about a complex situation with many different variables influencing outcomes of use. However, most depression patients given an SSRI will not experience that SSRI to lastingly resolve their depression, so we are actually talking about the majority of depression patients here, not just a few exceptional cases. It is also worth mentioning that SSRIs can cause depression, and that they can worsen or prolong depression which was already happening. Is it possible for one specific person to experience SSRIs to reduce depression or even stave off future depressions? Sure, depending on the person — it is uncommon but not impossible. But, SSRIs are far more likely to not prevent depression, or to cause an entirely new depression (or what some call an ‘apathy syndrome’ or other clinical analogues). Reactions can change over time, as well, so a drug that starts off as helpful overall may turn into a net negative later, or someone can see little usefulness in early days or weeks of use but then report drug upsides after that initiation period.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can taking antipsychotics for life increase the risk of developing psychosis again in the future, specifically paranoid schizophrenia?
Answer: Yes. The use of neuropleptics always increases the risk of developing psychosis later on, especially in the months following dose reductions or discontinuation. This is true even for people with no history of psychosis before drug use began. The longer someone uses an antipsychotic, the higher the risk becomes. Other factors, like drug management quality, health, support systems, and patient education can also play into how risky drug use is in this respect. “Paranoid schizophrenia” is a concept which is patently unrelated to drugs. By definition, drugs cannot cause it, so drug use should not increase the likelihood of it. In reality, adverse drug effects and the long-term consequences of drug use on the body are commonly misconstrued as “schizophrenia” and using neuroleptics does increase the likelihood of someone’s having experiences that end up labeled by a clinician as “schizophrenia”. As for people with a history of paranoid psychosis actually meeting the official, if arbitrary, diagnostic criteria, continuous neuroleptic use tends to increase the risk of recurring episodes. However, research seldom tries to differentiate between adverse drug effects and adverse drug outcomes (issues which entailed a particular susceptibility and pre-existing dynamic, like someone being neurologically or psychologically overstressed). And in any case, individual reactions can vary.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I haven't been taking my antidepressant (Luvox) regularly due to my forgetfulness, and I'm scared to confront my doctor about it. What should I do?
Answer: Your doctor works for you, you don’t work for your doctor. Your doctor is not your parent, elementary school teacher, or commanding officer, they’re your employee. They work for you to help you with whatever you ask for their help with within their area of practice. I know it can be scary if a doctor has a bad attitude or is abusive or threatening, but ideally you are only hiring doctors who are reasonable and who are open to communicating with you. It is a very common thing to have trouble staying on a daily pill schedule. Your doctor will surely have heard this dozens or hundreds of times from their patients. It is a normal thing to struggle with and is something that basic logistical steps can be taken to help you with. It says nothing about your character or their doctoring. If your doctor gets frustrated, it is part of their duty as a clinician to not take it out on you. If you want to be taking drugs as dangerous as these, it is important to be prepared to have the difficult conversations — talking about things like suicidality, sexuality, being unimpressed with effectiveness, being unsure of management suggestions, etc. It can be uncomfortable to be direct about your concerns related to drugging, but there is no way to be properly addressing them if you don’t share them or if you don’t have a doctor that listens. Not everyone is lucky enough to have access to a good doctor, and that means sometimes patients have to take steps to protect themselves, like limiting information or not openly challenging things a prescriber says. But, if you are on good terms with the prescriber, this is something there should be no significant downside to reporting. If you want to be taking the drug every day, you need to learn how to make that happen, and your prescriber might help.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does depression medication from a psychiatrist actually work? If so, how long does it take?
Answer: Individual responses vary. Depression medication from a psychiatrist usually fails, so if we are looking at averages or looking at the net impact on society, we would say that the drugs don’t actually work. However, the situation isn’t quite so simple because what most people experience or what the average or net experience is does not describe every single case. Exceptional patients may find drug use very helpful, or even entirely sufficient. Sometimes right away, sometimes only over a longer course of time. This is not so common and can still involve serious risks or bad reactions, but it is important to acknowledge. So, most people given a psychiatric drug for depression will be better off not taking it, but this is not a universal experience. Someone’s health, history, alternatives, and past responses can all shape whether a drug trial is worth the risks involved, and less dangerous alternatives should generally first be exhausted. How long does drugging take to work? Well, that depends on what you mean by “work”. Just as individual responses to drugs can vary, so will what people are seeking from drug use in the first place. This is for several reasons, such as how “depression” (or even specific depression diagnoses in psychiatry, like “MDD”) will be a hodgepodge of multiple concerns with multiple typical experiences and causes, how the goals and priorities of patients can differ even if they are experiencing something very similar to each other, and how drug management can influence outcomes and different patients will receive different quality management and management styles. While these drugs are causing very significant alterations from within hours of the very first dose, what relevance those alterations have will depend on the patient and their interests in addition to the uniqueness of their reactions. For example, someone taking a stimulating drug for tiredness or a sedating drug for insomnia may often find it ‘working’ within the first day or three because those effects are acute-onset effects of these drugs whereas someone wanting a drug to numb dysphoria or impair their cognition to reduce ruminating may experience escalating ‘working’ from the drug over a period of weeks or even months as those drug effects tend to intensify with continuous use. But, there is some unpredictability involved still, as some patients experience an effect right away, like apathy syndrome or sexual dysfunction, that others didn’t experience for several weeks, or which others may not experience intensely in the first place. Psychiatric drugs have no special value in depression, as they are alterants just like other psychotropics whose usefulness comes down to what someone wants to alter and balancing of the risks of all available options.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is bipolar disorder a lifelong condition or can the symptoms eventually go away?
Answer: Neither. “Bipolar disorder” is a diagnosis whose criteria change from time to time and which is applied to a range of different concerns whose nature, courses, and underlying dynamics differ. It is not just one kind of experience, so it does not have just one kind of outcome. For some, these experiences or a vulnerability to having them will be lifelong. For some, the experiences or susceptibility will not be lifelong. The diagnosis does not try to distinguish between those two basic categories of cases and anyone insisting otherwise has not not educated themselves about the scope of what is going on. This is in addition to the complexity of how the way we respond to the experiences and causes can shape what happens on an individual basis. Can the symptoms eventually go away? Well, the first thing to address there is that these aren’t “symptoms” in the medical sense — they aren’t experiences resulting from an underlying medical condition. “Bipolar disorder” is not causing anything, it is the label some clinicians will use to refer to the experiences themselves. The cause is not commented on, and the so-called “disorder” is the experiences themselves rather than why they are happening. So, there is very much a reason for the experiences, but “bipolar disorder” neither is the reason nor does it explain the reason. It is essentially an industry shorthand for saying “those things the patient talked about with me”. The reason for these experiences will depend on the person and circumstances. “Bipolar disorder” can refer to any number of reasons. In theory, the diagnosis does not apply to experiences resulting from medical disorders or drug effects, but in reality practitioners will misdiagnose medical problems and drug reactions as “bipolar disorder” with great frequency so the diagnostic criteria and guidelines attached to them aren’t something we can rely on to describe the reality of practice. Either way, we are left with a heterogeneous collection of experiences and what is going on to cause them will usually be integral to whether and how they can be abated. Causes and how they express will shape what happens when we try to improve things. Sometimes, the underlying causes can be addressed. Other times, we can’t figure out what they are or don’t have a way to ameliorate them. In both kinds of situations, there can still potentially be strategies and interventions which reduce the intensity or frequency of the experiences under diagnosis, improve social functioning or quality of life, or provide relief in some personal manner. For some people, finding a good approach can help resolve current concerns and then entirely prevent new instances. For some people, new instances will still occur to some degree no matter what is tried. An absence of new instances does not mean vulnerabilities to recurrence are also absent, but occasionally that is the case.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why is there still so much research being done on depression when for most people taking anti-depressants helped cure it?
Answer: Three reasons: These concerns encompass far more than just patient wellbeing — they impact the costs to society of depression, disability, and adverse drug effects, they shape the way political power is formed and wielded, they respond to class warfare and other economic dynamics within societies, they influence our toxicity to the environment, and so forth. Also note that the majority of research into depression isn’t research into new drug products. The multi-industrial investment in depression research is much more variegated and expansive, and drug companies spend more on marketing current psychiatric drugs and profitable narratives than they spend on developing new psychiatric drugs anyway. So, in short, depression research is a significant convergence of economic and political factors and the everyday citizen has an emotional stake in the wellbeing of others even though those other factors are the real drivers.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible for taking Abilify to cause hearing voices and hallucinations? If so, what is the recommended treatment for this side effect?
Answer: Yes, and the treatment depends on the mechanisms involved. There are multiple means by which so-called “antipsychotics” can cause hallucinations or other ‘psychotic symptoms’: toxidromes, strokes, autoimmune and allergic reactions, psychosis and delirium, insomnia and disrupted dream architecture, withdrawal and rebound syndromes, and more. Some are more common and more likely than others. Generally, a key part of treatment is to reduce or discontinue the causal drug, in addition to any interventions for mitigating the symptoms themselves (where possible and necessary). However, because this can often be a reduction-emergent effect, like a supersensitivity syndrome, sometimes temporarily reinstating a higher dose of the drug is an important part of management — the very opposite strategy compared to most other kinds of cases.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can depression be so bad that taking anti-depressants have no effect?
Answer: That depends on what you mean by “no effect”. The drugs marketed as “antidepressants” usually fail no matter how severe a depression is, and many depressions are likely to be intractable because of the mechanisms involved — regardless of severity. Antidepressants don’t treat any underlying causes of depression, however the altering effects of antidepressants can still be useful to some patients in a subset of circumstances, whether stimulation in fatigue or sedation in insomnia or numbing in dysphoria or cognitive impairment in rumination or so forth. There is no inherent connection between the severity of a depression and how someone reacts to these drugs or how useful someone finds a particular drug. However, as a general trend, the people with the most severe depressions will be the most likely to benefit from only modest drug upsides, and the people in the worst situations will often be the least likely to report adverse effects as highly problematic since they are already disabled and may already be in constant physical pain and mental suffering. No depression is so severe that adverse drug effects can’t or won’t happen. How perceptible they are to a person and how problematic they are rated to be can be affected by pre-existing circumstances, but these drugs are causing dangerous dysfunction in the body no matter what was going on beforehand or how someone is feeling. They always have an effect, there are always negative consequences. What is not guaranteed is someone experiencing positive consequences, and that is a bit more subjective as well.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How can I significantly reduce withdrawal symptoms of marijuana?
Answer: Taper: reduce the dose gradually over time. Tapering is typically the very best way to reduce withdrawal from any psychotropic drug. Some people can taper so slowly that they never experience any substantial withdrawal symptoms, many can taper so slowly that withdrawal does not become severe. With cannabis, withdrawal is often on the mild to moderate side to begin with, so the vast majority of people should be able to taper at a pace which keeps symptoms from becoming severe. How gradually to reduce will depend on the details of each case and on someone’s personal reactions and history. Anecdotally, cannabis seems easier to taper than many psychotropics, for instance SSRIs, and should take a much shorter time to successfully discontinue — perhaps a few months, on average. But, individual cases will vary and some people struggle more than others. Other standard withdrawal management practices can also be helpful. That spans things like reducing stressors (both physical and psychological), maintaining a positive mental perspective, utilizing distractions, making sure your diet is good, sleeping and resting more than usual, drawing on your social support network for comfort and encouragement, and considering interventions for specific symptoms — things like supplements or breathing exercises or even just taking a walk in nature. Consulting with a professional and getting the input of withdrawal support groups can help you find strategies that are useful for you personally. Be sure to consider the complications any pre-existing factors, like medical disorders or health anxiety, can have on your attempt to quit weed and what management needs might be created by them. For people already in withdrawal, reinstating a partial dose of cannabis is the thing most likely to help, or reinstating a higher dose if someone is tapering rather than already totally off it. Strategies for managing symptoms during tapering apply just as much to symptoms persistent long after discontinuation, as well, so consulting with people who know about recovering from cannabis withdrawal is recommendable even if you skipped a taper. In all but the most severe cases, the body’s mechanisms of self-correction and self-healing should alleviate withdrawal symptoms when given enough time, particularly if someone is not doing things which hamper recovery (like adding more stress to the nervous system through additional drug use, inappropriate levels of exercise, etc). Some symptoms may linger for months longer than others in some patients, though, like anxiety or sleeping problems.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is some psychosis incurable?
Answer: All psychoses have causes, not all causes have clear solutions. There are two categories of psychosis to address: organic (expressions of medical problems) and inorganic (psychological causes). There is no ‘cure’ for inorganic psychosis because it is not the result of a physical disorder. Some instances can be resolved, whether by addressing the underlying psychological causes or by working through the psychosis itself. For some, this will also lead to a prevention of future episodes, and has a similar functional effect to curing a medical disorder. Overall, the outlook is pretty good on average for inorganic psychoses if someone has the right support and care, though this does not guarantee all cases can be resolved or adequately helped. Unfortunately, most patients do not have the right support and care, and mainstream practices tend to make things worse rather than better for many of these people. Organic psychoses are also case-dependent. We may or may not have a curative understanding of an organic psychosis, it depends on the details. In either case, we may often be capable of prevention and of mitigation if the situation is amenable, but some organic psychoses have no accessible cure because the cause is either too extreme for us to remedy (like many cases of brain damage) or too unclear for us to treat. To state these instances as ‘incurable’ is referring to the ability for specific methods and understandings, so in the future or in a different medical system it could be that cures would be available. Some prospective treatments may raise existential questions, though, regarding things like personhood — like if the person who is cured is the same person who was seeking treatment if we augment their brain with new tissue or implants. In summary, some psychosis is resolveable, some is curable, and some, to the best of our knowledge, seems not to be at present.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can you have hypomania with major depression without being bipolar?
Answer: That depends on what you mean by “being bipolar”. Plainly speaking “bipolar depression” just means depression with two poles: depression and mania. So, any depressions with both depression and mania, whether simultaneously or apart, would be bipolar depressions. However, if the depression and the mania are unrelated to each other, having differing causes and potentially different courses as well, that is not a bipolar depression. Someone might still say you are “being bipolar” though, because the poles are both there even if they aren’t related to each other. “Bipolar disorder” is a psychiatric diagnosis which only refers to a subset of these instances. It is applied both to related and to unrelated instances of depression and mania appearing at some point in someone’s history. It doesn’t distinguish between any causes for either the depression or the mania aside from ruling out all organic problems, like medical disorders and drug effects. But in actual practice, many clinicians ignore that essential diagnostic criterion and just apply “bipolar disorder” to anything. Many or most instances of someone experiencing hypomania as well as clinical depression (or even more specifically, an episode of depression in “major depressive disorder” if you want to narrow things further) will not meet the diagnostic criteria for “bipolar disorder”. Very often, there will be excluded causes for the hypomania, for instance psychiatric drugs. But, whether or not someone is regarded as “bipolar” is a much looser thing, so “being bipolar” is an arbitrary idea which will be used differently by different people and in different situations.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Will splitting the Zyprexia dose help decrease the sweet cravings at night?
Answer: Maybe, but probably not enough. Neuroleptics such as olanzapine (aka Zyprexa) cause radical hormonal and neurofunctional changes in the body which can lead to cravings. Lower doses can mean less likelihood of intense or sustained cravings, and splitting a dose between a morning and evening dose can potentially affect how intense our cravings are. Whether splitting a dose increases nighttime cravings, reduces them, or has no meaningful effect will depend on the patient and their situation so we can’t predict whether it would help. But, it is a consideration to try, especially if other measures have been inadequate. Typically, more direct approaches are required — changing your diet and lifestyle to work with some of the metabolic changes that are occurring, considering diabetes drugs, and minimizing, quitting, or switching away from olanzapine. Adjusting dose timing can be one part in a multi-variable plan to reduce difficult cravings and should not be ignored. Definitely discuss with your prescriber and pharmacist before making any changes, and be sure to research independently to learn about better drug management and non-drug options since professionals seldom provide patients all they need in these areas.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do bipolar disorder patients have to take daily medication?
Answer: Different people have different goals and needs. The first thing to clear up is that “bipolar disorder patients” are not interchangeable. Any answer claiming all these people are the same, or have the same needs or experiences, is bullshitting you. The reality is that “bipolar disorder” is a label applied to many different kinds of experiences with varying underlying causes, varying courses, and varying responses to interventions and lifestyle drugging. It is not just unreasonable but outright harmful to pretend otherwise, even aside from the high rate of misdiagnosing medical problems, including the effects of medications themselves, as “bipolar disorder”. There are two questions to answer, having established that. The first is why some people use drugs at all, and the second is why a large portion of those people use drugs daily.
