Though it is a dangerous lie that all of these people need to or should use drugs or that drugs will always help, it is true that many people find drugging useful in one or more ways. What motivates drug use and what goals someone has in using drugs will depend on the individual and their situation, including especially their level of education about options and the support resources available. People claiming psychiatric drugs treat an underlying disorder of the brain are either exploiting you or the victims of exploitation themselves. “Bipolar disorder” is, per the diagnostic guidelines used in clinical practice and to create standard research rubrics, not a brain disorder and there is no scientific validity to the marketing narrative that psychiatric drugs given to “bipolar disorder” patients medically treat any problems in the brain. It would be pretty hard to demonstrate medical efficacy in the total absence of demonstrating medical pathology anyhow. But, these drugs do cause potent changes in the brain, which can carry both upsides and downsides. They are pretty dangerous, but immediate changes may be desirable as well. Some people use drugs to curb an episode of something, like mania, depression, psychosis, others only find drugging useful in reducing the intensity of new episodes or certain aspects of these experiences. Some fewer people are lucky and find drug use to reduce how often episodes occur, or help them with everyday stability. There are always costs and downsides to this, so these are tradeoffs being made, and responses can differ between patients, drugs, and periods of time, as can what tradeoffs are considered worthwhile. Many people find some or all drugs intolerable, worsening, or at best unhelpful, and most people report more downsides than upsides. Your question can ultimately only have a very personal answer if you want to get detailed. The way these drugs affect our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors will be unique to each individual and circumstance of use and you are coupling that uniqueness with the variable goals and needs involved. But a general answer would be that people consider the tradeoff worth it in the moment, they are desperate to reduce or quit their drugs but don’t know of any adequate alternatives, or they aren’t benefiting (or aren’t substantially benefiting) from daily drugging but physical dependence or other adverse effects prevent them from discontinuing drugs or from using only drugs intermittently. Only a modest subset of people given a “bipolar disorder” label seem to be best off with daily drug use, but that doesn’t mean all the rest aren’t being targeted by psychiatry. Likewise, that doesn’t mean all the rest are receiving the education and support they would need to succeed, so using or rejecting drugs isn’t the only critical axis under discussion. It isn’t even the only critical axis shaping the outcomes of daily drug use. Many patients are tricked into believing drug use is essential or their only hope, and this fuels a lot of counterproductive use that has a net negative impact on things like health and quality of life. As such, a large portion of daily use is people who are worse off for it but are, for varying reasons, continuing forward.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I ran out of Venlafaxine, can I substitute with fluoxetine?
Answer: Learn and weigh your options. If you have been using venlafaxine for more than 1–2 months and you will not be having access to it or to other prescribing for at least another 1–2 months, it might be worth considering a cold swap to fluoxetine if the alternative is an unmitigated cold turkeying of SRIs in general. This carries its own risks and is something to discuss with a pharmacist if you’re not able to talk with your prescriber. However, if you’re just missing a couple of days between refills or plan to get a new prescription within the next week or two, adding fluoxetine may likely be more problematic than helpful, as it can be upsetting and also has a long half-life that can interfere with your reinstating venlafaxine when you have it again. There is no perfect or one-size-fits-all answer here and you have to consider the details of your situation, your history of drug reactions, and your access to resources. On one hand, venlafaxine and fluoxetine are actually a bit more cross-compatible than most SRI drugs and fluoxetine is the gold standard tapering SRI, but on the other hand, none of these drugs are truly interchangeable and whether or not you experience problems swapping them or starting a new drug in general is more personal and variable. There is also the concern of drug usefulness — my answer so far has focused on minimizing withdrawal phenomena, but a drug being helpful to you brings a whole different set of concerns. If you find venlafaxine useful, that does not necessarily mean you will find any other drug useful. If you’ve been on fluoxetine in the past, which may be the case if you have a stock around, that is a decent gauge of its potential but you may or may not respond in the same way when going back to it, especially if you just cold turkeying venlafaxine. If your question is just whether these two drugs are fair substitutes for one another, the answer is no. The pharmacology is a lot more complex than that, and even switching between release designs or manufacturers of the same drug can cause problems for some patients. Whether swapping for fluoxetine is your best risk-reducing measures in the moment, though, depends on more than just that. I strongly recommend getting in contact with your professionals to see what options they have in mind and what their recommendations are. Remember that professions can still give bad, harmful advice so you should research additionally before making a decision instead of following their advice blindly. And, as mentioned, if you can’t see your prescriber and can’t see another doctor, at least speak with a pharmacist, which is free and doesn’t require an appointment in places like the US.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible for people with schizophrenia to be convinced by others that their experiences are not real?
Answer: Most anyone can be gaslighted. You can convince people of anything with enough guile or psychological pressure. “Schizophrenia” is something prolific gaslighting revolves around. Many patients become convinced they have some sort of medical disorder/chemical imbalance, or that drugs are necessary to help fix their brain. It is socially expected to believe that patients should be drugged and that they can’t choose for themselves and may even be dangerous and violent in ways other people are not. What “reality” is and whether someone’s experiences are to be considered “real” is something often integrated into all that gaslighting. Telling a patient that their experiences being labeled as “schizophrenia”, especially psychosis itself, aren’t valid or don’t reflect anything meaningful is a common part of psychiatrizing them and gaining control over their behaviors. It is not a universal belief, but it is common and it goes hand in hand with the false, profit-producing narrative that “schizophrenia” patients have broken brains and need to rely on lobotomies and the claims of others if they are to live a better quality life. It can be observed in everyday life that people, whether “schizophrenia” patients or anyone else, can be convinced their experiences are not real or don’t matter.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why am I only now getting side effects, months into taking antidepressants?
Answer: Why not? While these drugs are bad for your body from the very first dose, extended exposure is worse for your body than brief exposure. Toxicity can escalate, progressive changes occur in response to the dysfunction-inducing mechanisms of the drugs, and someone is very likely to experience new adverse effects when using for months at a time rather than just days. Though drug initiation effects sometimes fade within the first several days or weeks of use, it is typical, not unusual, for someone to notice new problems after continuous use. Indeed, the fading of initiation effects is itself a delayed-onset alteration — drug tolerance resulting from ongoing exposure provoking functional changes in the body.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can taking antipsychotics prevent the reoccurrence of psychotic symptoms in patients with schizophrenia and/or bipolar disorder after they stop using them?
Answer: Long-term changes in reactions are possible, but usually in an adverse way. To start off with some context, so-called “antipsychotics” aren’t shown to prevent future psychoses as a blanket effect, they are prescribed to try and curb certain aspects of present ones. They are studied and approved on the basis of their short-term effects on psychosocial rubrics. In the long-term, they may or may not have any preventative value — that depends more on the patient and situation than the drug, and plenty of people find these drugs counterproductive or unhelpful even in the short run so longer-term prevention is out of the question for them. In short, neuroleptics can often interfere with experiences dubbed “psychosis”, but they don’t usually resolve or prevent psychoses. They are one tool among many which can cause changes in current experiences and in the direction and characteristics of future experiences. A second bit of context here is that these drugs do cause long-lasting changes in the body, most notably the brain. Whether use is brief or extended, these drugs cause alterations and damages which won’t disappear just by someone quitting the drug and letting it all exit their body. The nature of these changes is complex; they are far-reaching and impacting more than we currently understand. Everything from our body’s metabolism to our cells’ mitochondria to our neuronal sensitivity can remain affected by drug use long after cessation. These kinds of changes can potentially affect future psychological experiences, too, including whether or not psychosis occurs and what it looks like if it does. It is actually very common for drug use to be affecting someone’s propensity to experience psychosis after discontinuation. However, one of many problems here is that the influence is usually an adverse one: patients who use and then quit a neuroleptic are more likely to experience additional future psychoses, not less. This is probably for three central reasons: Of course, these factors are not the only things influencing patient outcomes, and not everyone responds to drug use in the same way. Not only that, not everyone has a bad psychiatrist or bad recovery environment or lack of education or support. The average patient is kinda fucked, but the exceptions may fare much better (or, by that same reasoning, much worse). Given all this variability, the previous use or discontinuation of drugs like neuroleptics don’t guarantee any particular outcome with respect to future psychoses. There is simply way more involved that is likely to generate new psychoses or stress someone’s vulnerabilities versus things that are likely to prevent future instances that would have otherwise occurred. In the end, it is all the more personal details of drug use which are more important. Things like tactical use and management quality, professional accountability, clear communication and education, resource networks.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does olive oil help alleviate some of the symptoms of bipolar disorder?
Answer: What does that mean? Can a diet higher in olive oil lead to better health and favorably changed mental experiences? For many people, yes, that is the case. Does it have any specific or universal benefits in patients with a “bipolar disorder” diagnosis? No, because “bipolar disorder” provides us no specific or universal details about the underlying causes of someone’s experiences. The diagnosis does not give us any understanding of what will help someone, and the reality is that the needs and responses of each person will vary a lot and the diagnois does nothing to enable us to understand what is happening, why, and how to help. Like any other adjustments to lifestyle, diet, or drug use, there can be both upsides and downsides to incorporating more olive oil. Learning about the upsides and downsides, how to manage them, and how to maximize the potential benefits involved should precede making significant changes. Some people will find a specific dietary regimen quite helpful, and in exceptional cases even sufficient unto itself (especially patients who had a medical condition which was misdiagnosed as “bipolar disorder” instead). But the average person probably won’t find adding more olive oil to their diet to make a huge difference on its own.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why has psychiatry been reduced to pill-pushing?
Answer: Insofar as that is true, it is actually more of an expansion than a reduction. While it is true that the clinical psychiatry which predominated before the psychopharmaceutical revolution in the mid 20th Century is different from the clinical psychiatry of today, and trends like psychoanalysis have become far smaller in the market, psychiatry as an industry has expanded immensely. Non-pharmaceutical psychiatry has become a shrinking minority share of the market, but the expansion of psychiatry and of psychiatric prescribing outside of the typical contexts of drug use in the earlier decades of psychiatry probably has a stronger influence on our perceived flood of prescription-only practitioners. We are dealing more with psychiatric expansion than psychiatric reduction. This is even more prominent in healthcare systems where prescribing is covered but other interventions and approaches often are not, or where prescribing has indefinite coverage but even the next-leading market option, psychotherapy, has very narrow coverage (like 10–12 appointments, or 3 months of service), and in healthcare systems where psychiatric practitioners sign on because they are prescribing-only. In those kinds of situations, exemplified in the US perhaps more than anywhere else, psychiatry outside of pill-peddling is basically no longer mainstream and is also no longer accessible to the average patient. Psychiatry is not a monolith, but the exceptions to industrialized psychiatry are far fewer, less visible, and outright unaffordable for many. The public face of psychiatry is a prescribing-focused one, and most of psychiatry and psychiatric marketing is funded by drug manufacturers and related profit-seeking bodies. The current version of psychiatry patients are walking into when seeing a practitioner is primarily a reflection of those vested interests and how they steer the philosophies, values, and practices of the field. Psychiatry is also more of a tool of government control and suppression than ever before, often having an exclusive arrangement and one which is more pervasive than ever before due to the aforementioned expanding of the marketplace into new social territories. This is about the governmental institutionalization of psychiatry in addition to the industrialization of psychiatry. Drugging ticks several boxes of relevance to industrialization: systemization (a standardized flow for diagnosing, prescribing, managing, charging/reimbursing), product mass manufacturing, government backing and integration, globalization. Psychiatry has built itself into the culture, the government, and the economy, and drugging in particular is a key to the success of that because of the industrial goals it meets. This is dangerously unaccountable to real-life patient outcomes and the needs and preferences of the everyday citizen, so the power of psychiatry in modern society and the incredible reach it has is not resulting from or even strictly related to patient outcomes. Psychiatry as an industry and drugging as a manifestation of that are revolving foremost around things other than patient wellbeing. Pharmaceutical psychiatry is most favored because it is good for people other than patients and their communities. However, there are also some cultural pressures outside of direct industrial investment. Many patients are in a hurry to be able to feel how culture says they should feel or work as much as culture says they should work, and some are desperate in general. Drugs are the most potent of outpatient options and cause immediate changes in someone’s health and mind. These are usually adverse and problematic, but the idea of immediacy is the highlight to a lot of people. Many are also unaware of all the potentially superior options, and how to make use of them, because drug-oriented marketing is the mainstream landscape and there is significant stigma against drug non-use.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible for someone without a diagnosed mental disorder to request an SSRI or other anti-depressant from their primary care physician?
Answer: Do whatever you want. Anyone can request any drug they want to. Whether their PCP is open to requests or suggestions or discussions is a person-by-person thing. There is very little suspicion around drugs people don’t have much fun with, but some doctors feel threatened or offended. With any drugs, it is usually more relevant to discuss context instead: what concerns you have, what you would consider helpful, and why you think certain interventions might be a good fit. No diagnosis, psychiatric or otherwise, suggests that drugs like SSRIs or other so-called ‘antidepressants’ are appropriate, so there is not really any relevance to diagnosis here. And, to note, around half of the prescriptions are for non-psychological concerns so it is not weird at all for someone to bring up the idea regardless of their history of experiences. That said, PCPs are almost never possessing the expertise to properly prescribe and manage these kinds of drugs. Your average psychiatrist already does a frightfully bad job, and PCPs will do worse in some areas, on average, though probably be less harmful than psychiatrists on average in other respects. A lot of doctors these days are basically like streetcorner drug dealers, primarily writing prescriptions and seldom suggesting anything else. Many lack education or proficiency or interest in other kinds of support, some are inundated by patients who just want a quick fix, some will be working in a system where anything other than drugging may not be covered. Most patients given antidepressants find them more harmful than helpful, so be sure to research enough to know whether pushing for them is in your best interest before sitting down with your doctor.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does antipsychotic medication cause laziness?
Answer: In a sense. Antipsychotics, aka neuroleptics, typically cause things like apathy, anhedonia, cognitive impairment, reduced self-awareness, fatigue, sleepiness, physical slowness, adverse metabolic and cardiovascular effects, loss of libido, impotence, poor sleep quality. Such effects can be mild, moderate, or quite severe. Higher doses and longer periods of use tend to increase how badly someone is affected. So, people are likely to be less active in nearly every sense: physically, mentally, socially, sexually, creatively, academically, vocationally. From the outside, this can make it look like someone is just lazy, a lethargic bum with few interests and probably an anemic social life. From the inside, it can feel like your brain is molasses and your body is 20 tons and there’s no reason to give a shit about anything anyhow, your passions now hollow and your thoughts dropping halfway to completion like pigeons shot midair. These drugs lobotomize, sedate, and impair. Some psychiatrists and psychologists who volunteer to try them are on record saying they are horrific to experience.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why is there a debate of effectiveness of the more refined SSRI’s when Iproniazid and Imipramine clearly worked in the 50s despite their side effects?
Answer: The assumptions built into your question provide us easy answers: SSRIs didn’t “clearly work” when given to severely depressed inpatients as we saw with early MAOI testing. If drugs like iproniazid and imipramine had good reporting from the trenches which spurred interest and further drug development, why would that imply SSRIs, which do not share that history, also “clearly work”? The contrast in origins and lack of proper comparability has only accelerated since the release of SSRIs, as well. Nowadays, SSRIs are primarily prescribed for concerns other than depression and, when in depression, primarily for depressions that are not as severe as was typical of the inpatients experimentally given MAOIs. (SSRIs are still pro-manic, just not as potently pro-manic as the MAOIs.) In short, SSRIs are differently acting drugs with different economic aspirations, testing procedures, and applications. Drugs like iproniazid and imipramine heralded a change in direction for the worldwide psychopharmaceutical machine, including that machine’s influence over mainstream psychiatry. SSRIs are perhaps “more refined” in terms of the logistics or sophistication of development, but obviously that refinement has not yielded a commensurate increase in drug effectiveness. You can find countless practitioners who saw the mainstream switchover from MAOIs, TCAs, and NaSSAs to SSRIs who will insist that SSRIs were the least helpful drugs yet. There is no reason to assume the development of SSRIs decades after the lucky chance pro-manic influence of MAOIs would make SSRIs more clinically powerful than MAOIs. And, to note, SSRIs primarily provided advantages in reducing certain drug risks, especially in overdose, rather than being introduced as more effective. Verily, SSRIs were rejected for being laughably shitty and it took things like bribery, fraud, and marketing lies to make SSRIs into blockbusters. In trial settings meant to resemble key demographics of real-life use for depression, placebo did as good as SSRIs or even better on average. That itself should draw debate, and has. “Refinement” can be the opposite of helpful. Leaving aside how SSRIs are in no way a refinement of MAOIs and focusing instead on selectivity of action versus TCAs, there is no reason to assume a stronger SRI action than NRI or DRI action would make SSRIs more effective. In fact, there is no innate value to SRI, NRI, or DRI in depression, nor are those the only mechanisms of potential relevance when patients respond positively to a reuptake inhibitor drug. The idea that serotonin is the most important focus is a marketing con, not a scientific theory. The proposition that selectivity is a superior direction for efficacy is baseless, and selectivity is foremost about decreasing or increasing particular risks. Fewer heart rhythm problems but more emotional numbing, for example. Newer drugs, more expensive drugs, more protractedly developed drugs have no advantage over other drugs just by those merits. Early drugs may have been more successful than SSRIs clinically specifically because of what they do that SSRIs don’t, or don’t do as potently. Definitions of “clearly work” have changed. How we define, measure for, and chart ‘efficacy’ is different than it was in the 50s and 60s. Some changes are counterproductive changes and ultimately impede any legitimate search for a useful drug. Characterizing efficacy through RCTs when populations are heterogeneous is stupid, for instance. Other changes facilitate a more accountable conceptualizing of drug outcomes and reflect that we are in an era where what matters to the patient and what the patient experiences hold a little more social weight than they did back in the day. While ratings scales have some serious and troubling weaknesses, some of the methodologies for assessing and denoting drug efficacy in the earlier decades were ridiculous and if you go back and read the medical journal articles you can see how idiotic some of these practitioners look. “Working” isn’t enough. If a drug is so harmful that someone prefers not to be on it despite any upsides it carries, it doesn’t matter if the drug is said to “clearly work”. It fails at the task patients want it for. Quality of life, social and cognitive and sexual and physical functioning, medical wellbeing are all negatively impacted by these drugs more often than not. In fact, the majority of patients discontinue an SSRI because it was either more harmful than helpful or simply unhelpful, and some of the patients who are happy with SSRIs up through discontinuation end up regretting ever having used them because of the adverse effects occurring after cessation. There is a strong argument to be made that we are massively overprescribing drugs like SSRIs, and that with a far more reasonable application, we could boost our success rate. But, that still leaves the question of how many patients would actually find SSRIs preferable. 1:10? 1:100? 1:1,000?

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can SSRI change my personality trait?
Answer: Drugs that change the brain change what arises from the brain. There is no universal agreement about what “personality” is, or whether traits are inborn or acquired or some mix of the two, or whether things must be permanent or must be fluid. But, something we do know is that, in a physical universe, the roots of personality are physical. The nervous system, our hormonal functioning, our cardiovascular functioning, and all the other things which contribute to what goes on in our minds are physical systems and drugs like SSRIs change what is going on in those systems. SSRIs change the brain itself. So, whatever we say personality is, there is the potential for SSRIs to alter it because SSRIs are altering the functioning and structure of the underlying physicality. Some drug changes are temporary, lasting only about as long as the drug is in our system. Some drug changes are transient, fading away even while we are still using the drug because of plasticity or other mechanisms in the body. Some drug changes are long-lasting, persisting well beyond drug discontinuation and potentially being lifelong. This includes both outright damages to the body, like the killing or damaging of cells, and changes which don’t require any destruction. Our thoughts, feelings, perceptions, choices, and behaviors will be affected to some degree when SSRIs are used. So, everything from our cognition to our sexuality to our preferences to our habits can be altered. This may be light and perhaps not even noticeable, it may be more moderate, and it can also be extreme. Persistence, likewise, varies. Many things not usually associated with personality, like muscle response times and taste and metabolic health and blood clotting and seizure threshold, can be impacted, too. The specific changes someone experiences will be personal and can depend on many factors. Some factors will be general, like the drug, dose, and duration of use, others will be more individual, like someone’s genes, health and drug history, and neurological uniqueness. While we can note red flags that may increase the rate of certain issues, reactions are relatively unpredictable, even giving many patients the same drugs at the same dose with the same management. So, the bottom line is that SSRI use will change you, in the brain and in the mind, and whether or not this is considered a ‘personality’ change will depend on the specific responses involved and what definitions you are choosing to use.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it true that SSRIs like fluoxetine can prevent many types of cancer?
Answer: No, but SSRIs modify cancer likelihoods, both positively and negatively. SSRIs are not really outright preventative of cancer in any direct way, though they can have chemotherapeutic properties, depending on the specific cancer, because they are toxic to many kinds of cells (in the body or otherwise, which is a bad thing except in these atypical circumstances where the cells are cancerous). However, SSRIs modify the risks involved in developing cancer or cancer being fatal because they modify how the body is functioning. Changes in our hormone ratios and metabolism, cardiovascular functioning, and immune system, for example, can all impact the development and spread of various cancers. SSRIs cause innumerable local and body-wide changes and these will inevitably interact with some cancers. This can be a favorable net interaction, leading to a lower incidence of some cancers, or the opposite, leading to a higher incidence of some cancers. There can also be changes to risk factors which are secondary to drug reactions, like lifestyle adjustments or long-term medical conditions caused by drug use that increase or decrease the likelihood of particular cancers developing. SSRIs, by their nature, cause a net loss in health in the body, but this will not have an adverse effect on the development of 100% of medical conditions. There are always trade-offs with these drugs, so the question is whether the trade-off is worth it and our best option to meet needs.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: It’s been two months since my last antipsychotic injection and I still don’t feel normal. How long does it take to wear off me?
Answer: You may or may not ever feel “normal” after months of antipsychotic use. Importantly, returning to normal and a drug being out of your system are two pretty different measures. A drug being gone from your body does not mean the alterations and damages it caused vanish, it just means the acute intoxication phase has ended. You should expect to experience a trailing off dose of a depot neuroleptic for at least several months after your last shot. The dosing period ford depot shots varies, as some are designed to last for a month, others closer to 3 months, or even 6 months more recently. After your last injection, it will still take a lot of time for the body to clear out almost all of the drug, and some may still hang around in your tissues even after that. But, this is not a timetable for drug effects themselves. The harms caused by antipsychotic injections are a much more complex thing to deal with. Some harms may easily reverse, others may take months or years, and some will never go away. It depends on the specific effect, patient, and situation. You may need at least 1–2 years before feeling “normal”. Longer for worse cases, shorter in uncommon instances, and potentially much, much longer if you’re more sensitive or spent years drugging. It is completely normal to still feel impaired after months of antipsychotic use even if two months have passed since your last dose, and if it was a typical monthly injection, that would mean you are only one month ‘off’ and are still excreting the drug. Add to the difficulties of recovering from drug harms the fact that withdrawal syndrome typically follows cessation of continuous antipsychotic use, especially if you don’t taper off gradually. Withdrawal and rebound syndrome symptoms are liable to be occurring for several months or longer after quitting, regardless of whether other effects (for instance apathy or anhedonia or sexual dysfunction or metabolic disorder) began during use and didn’t resolve just by quitting the causal drug. If you did not notice any discontinuation-emergent effects, that just means you are lucky and are probably only dealing with the consequences of use outside of those which create physical dependence. The bottom line is that you will probably notice incremental improvement over the next many months, but may not feel normal anytime soon (and may not feel fully normal for years, if ever). It is common for some symptoms to get worse before they get better, or for someone to experience oscillating symptoms, and how we manage our recovery can be an important factor in symptom severity and duration. There are things we can do to make our situation worse, which should be avoided if we want to promote recovery, and things we can add to our lives to help facilitate recovery. Most of recovery depends on the body’s natural healing mechanisms, but we have to provide the necessary space, materials, and time if we want the best chance at feeling back to normal again.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can Zoloft and antipsychotics change my brain and interrupt my thoughts even after taking them only for 2 months?
Answer: Of course. They can do so after taking them for only 1 day. These drugs fundamentally stop the brain from working correctly and change the brain. Anyone using them for one day or one month or one year will experience alterations as a consequence. Two months of use is a fairly long time and is liable to have a more severe and lasting impact than just a couple of days of use. Feeling like your thoughts are interrupted is a classic symptom of drug use, especially antipsychotic use, and the longer you use for, the more likely you are to experience escalating impairment and longer-lasting drug problems.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How long does it take for your brain to go back to normal after stopping SSRIs?
Answer: There is no good reason to think your brain ever fully gets back to normal. I. How Normal Is “Normal”? This is a somewhat vague and complicated question, though. What does “normal” mean, and how do we know if a brain is “normal” or “back to normal”? The brain is a plastic organ, and the nervous system is perhaps the most plastic system in the human body. It is expected to change over time, in response to everything we encounter and experience. Potent psychotropic drugs cause changes whose effects can ripple throughout our future. And more importantly, there can be changes caused by drug use which are never reversed, either because they cannot be or because the brain is always moving forward to a new arrangement or state of being and does not return to how it was before drugs even if it adapts away from some of the changes made by drug use once we quit. Change in the broadest sense is the brain’s normal. Are the changes caused by these drugs “normal”? Many of them clearly are not, as they are things the body cannot do to itself and can even be medically pathological. Some influences fall within the range of what we can anticipate from living life in general, and the brain has a natural capacity to adapt to stressors we experience in everyday life. But, some mechanisms and effects are different from and more extreme than everyday stressors and can leave a more lasting mark on the brain, or even damage it. SSRIs impair the brain, very literally, and prevent some of the nervous system’s natural mechanisms for adaptation from functioning. While discontinuing the drug, and waiting for it to leave our system, will remove some of those impairing mechanisms, the consequences of those impairments can still remain. The effects caused by drug use are also about the harms done to the brain and the changes caused during use, not just the acute intoxication of drug use. SSRIs cause abnormality in 100% of patient brains, as a result of their mechanisms. Some of this, like reuptake inhibition, can reasonably be assumed to dissipate in the weeks or months it takes for a drug to mostly leave our system. Some of it, like neuronal dematuration or mitochondrial damage, may take longer, like months or years, or may never actually go away. Indeed, some effects are, by their nature, not reversible, like the killing of brain cells. Surprisingly little study has been performed into the long-term and lifetime impact of SSRI use, and the mechanisms and actions of these drugs are all incompletely understood if understood at all. We don’t have a catalogue of all the changes, and certainly cannot say with competence that the changes all reverse or when they are all gone after discontinuation. Since most people experience drug symptoms long after quitting, the question of how we define normality also takes a back seat to the question of whether patients are being adversely impacted by whatever a drug has done to them during use. II. The Patient Experience I gather the patient experience is what this question is really focused on. What is going on in the brain on the subcellular level is a lot less relevant to patients than how they feel, and whether they can have the same experiences and health and abilities as they did before drug use. This is yet another facet of the complication, as individual reactions and recoveries vary widely. A rare few patients feel about as good as normal shortly after quitting, but most patients are experiencing obvious symptoms for months, years, or longer. Withdrawal syndrome itself typically lasts 2–3 months after continuous drug use, according to accumulating research, and that is only the first stage of drug recovery. All the changes and harms that aren’t tied to physical dependence will not be resolved by a cessation of withdrawal symptoms, and the end of withdrawal symptoms doesn’t mean that aspect of nervous system is back to normal anyhow — just that it is finally able to cope adequately with everyday stressors. High stress can provoke symptoms again until further recovery has taken place. Sometimes long-lasting symptoms will be pretty obvious, like tinnitus or tremor or an inability to orgasm. But, many persistent drug effects can be harder to discern, like mild to moderate cognitive impairment or changes in mood or behavior. It can be hard to exactly compare pre-drug and post-drug experiences when they occur over the course of years, especially since these drugs alter our perceptions. It can also be hard to feel confident that minor changes are due to drug use rather than other factors, in some cases. Because many professionals and other parties passing along marketing information instead of drug facts will often gaslight patients into thinking nothing is wrong or that drugs aren’t responsible, it is usually difficult to get a reasonable critical analysis from prescribers and other practitioners. Many symptoms end up being misdiagnosed as “mental illness” instead of drug effects, especially those related to cognition, emotion, and behavior — ironically and dangerously the very things psychotropic drugs such as SSRIs would be most expected to alter. Many variables are involved in shaping how someone reacts to an SSRI and what happens when they quit. There is a whole spectrum of drug problems and severity which won’t directly match up between different patients using the same drug at the same dose for the same amount of time. Many basic variables are known, like dose, duration of use, quality of management, pre-existing health, but some remain unclear. Identifying variables does not provide a perfect predictive understanding of drug outcomes anyhow, so there is no hard timeframe to quote anyone for their recovery. What effects are permanent for one patient may be short-term for another, what level of progress takes just two weeks for one patient may take 3 years for another. We don’t come to a better understanding of this variability by saying the brain is or is not normal during this struggle with drug symptoms, but I would hesitate to call the brain flat out “back to normal” while symptoms yet persist. III. Summary In short, there is no medically justifiable way to give a single, simple answer to your question. By many conventional definitions, the brain may never truly “get back to normal” after sustained use of an SSRI. We don’t understand all the changes well enough to say they all get left behind at some point after discontinuation, much less when that should happen on average. Averages only apply to a subset of patients, too, as plenty of experiences will involve more substantial changes or less substantial changes than average. Ignoring whether we characterize the brain as “back to normal” at some point, patients can expect to be changed. Sometimes this means symptoms lasting months, years, or a lifetime. Sometimes this means microscopic changes that influence our experiences more ambiguously. Sometimes it means changes in our overall trajectory, mentally or behaviorally. Nobody should use these drugs with the assumption they can magically do away with any changes or harms just by quitting or struggling through the withdrawal which usually follows discontinuation. Conversely, nobody should assume that symptoms remaining or newly arising after drug discontinuation are impossible to recover from just because the drug is out of their system. The plasticity of the nervous system is still profound, and some degree of recovery can be anticipated, at least for most kinds of drug effects. It is true there are irreversible harms for some patients, and maybe for most if we are also including the smaller-scale damages that may or may not lead to impairments in daily living. But, it is common for people to panic and fear the worst when they are suffering from months or years of drug effects, thinking they are doomed to permanent disability. The reality is that though our brains may never be exactly what they were before SSRI use, they will also not remain what they are in the times directly after use. When practitioners lie to patients about the expected duration of drug influences, they cause premature despair. The healing process is far more extended and extensive than shills and people outside their depth will tell you. Ultimately, I think “normal” and “recovery” should be understood as fuzzy stand-ins for the more distinctly tangible goals we have for our health and our lives. Just as our experiences vary, so do our priorities and values and what we want out of our lives and our post-discontinuation wellbeing. What symptoms it is most important to abate can differ between patients. Whether we are shooting for the fringe outskirts of “normal” or a dead-center average can depend on what specific aspects of our experiences we are considering. Getting more personal and more specific doesn’t mean we can conjure up a convenient number of months or years for when our goal will be met, but it does allow us to have more insight and better communication in tracking our progress and managing our recovery. There may be some psychological adaptation as well as physiological adaptation in our time after discontinuation, so the goals and priorities and values we have can change over time as a result of our experiences and troubles, and this can feed back into how we conceptualize our journey. So, the most useful form of the question at hand is something more like “How long would it often take for a person with History X, Drug Experiences Y, and Personal Traits Z to experience symptom remission after measures and responses L, M, N?”

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does paliperidone cause PSSD?
Answer: What is clearer to say is that all neuroleptics, including paliperidone, can cause long-term sexual dysfunction. These drugs can cause sexual problems during use, sexual problems which last indefinitely even after drug cessation, and sexual problems which newly arise as a result of reductions or discontinuation. Individual experiences and symptom courses can vary, and many factors influencing outcomes are still not known. Paliperidone and follow neuroleptics have that in common which pretty much all the other psychiatric drugs, including SRI drugs. But, the “PSSD” moniker is often more narrowly referring to a subset of sexual problems caused by a subset of drugs in a subset of contexts. It is primarily a term used when discussing drugs like SSRIs, SNRIs, and other serotonin reuptake inhibitors like TCAs or bupropion, rather than so-called ‘antipsychotics’. However, it is increasingly used, especially in internet groups, as a way to refer to most any lasting sexual dysfunction caused by psychiatric drugs without a limitation on the type or class of drug. Many more kinds of symptoms and problems are encompassed when the term is used so broadly. This expanded usage seems to occur largely because no more suitable or descriptive term has gained traction in the mainstream. But, you might cause confusion to use “PSSD” that broadly, for now. While it helps to have a recognizable blanket term for these problems, getting a bit more specific by adding a couple more words is perhaps the best middleground for the moment. Though neuroleptics and drugs such as SSRIs can largely cause the same basic problems when it comes to sexuality, from loss of libido to inability to orgasm to genital shrinkage, “PSSD” is typically used in the academic sphere to refer to a more selective subset of symptoms, often ones specifically thought to be related to SRI. You can read more here for a rundown with dozens of medical journal articles touching on the problem in the references section: Post-SSRI Sexual Dysfunction (PSSD) - RxISK It mentions there that non-sexual symptoms, like cognitive impairments, can accompany the sexual and genital symptoms diagnostic criteria revolve around. “PSSD” is not a wholly discrete concept or phenomenon, and the best way to express what you mean to include is to use a description instead of only a categorical label.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is some advice on a direct swap from 10mg Paxil to 10mg of Prozac?
Answer: The best advice is to not try it. Cross-tapering is generally the best way to swap SSRIs. A direct swap, or cold swap, does not really allow you much to adjust to make things turn out better for you. The standard tapering and discontinuation prep, like reducing stressors, eating right, getting extra rest, and having your support network primed, will still apply, but aside from education and preparation, tapering is the most relevant variable mediating discontinuation experiences. The question is a bit like asking how to not crash a car if you are always going to drive with your foot all the way down on the gas pedal. Sure, you can still steer some, but you’ll crash eventually unless you’re in a wide open area with no obstacles at all. Some people can manage a straight swap without any tapering, at least the first time they try it (maybe not all subsequent times, due to sensitization or other problems caused by this kind of rash maneuvering), but many will be hit with symptoms. Aside from withdrawal potentially becoming severe, or long-lasting, there is also the consideration of how upset from the change can disrupt your ability to trial or benefit from whatever drug is being switched to and make it difficult to know whether a bad reaction is due to quitting one drug, starting the other, or doing both. Most people have no good reason to skip a taper when moving between SSRIs, and there is always a significant chance of withdrawal or related complications when swapping.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do people with bipolar disorder take Zoloft?
Answer: Some do, some don’t. Some people find one or more SSRIs to be manic triggers, but some don’t. The “bipolar disorder” diagnosis does not differentiate, and will circumscribe some of each kinda of person. Some people find one or more SSRIs unbearable to use because of other adverse effects they cause. Most of those people will quit sertraline (Zoloft) sooner or later if it is so problematic. The bottom line is that someone with a history of mania should be extra-wary of pro-manic drugs such as SSRIs. If someone finds an SSRI to be a manic trigger, it is common but not at all guaranteed for someone to tolerate the SSRI without mania if they are not taking too high a dose and are on an anticonvulsant drug. But, whether anticonvulsants (including lithium) are relevant or helpful in the first place can vary. The causes of previous manias, the objectives with SSRI use, and someone’s reactions in general will all shape whether sertraline is something they choose to take. Extra caution should be used, tapering should be slower, and tools like CP450 testing can be even more useful in providing context for drug experimentation with SSRIs in patients with a history of mania.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I am so obsessed with trying to figure out what's wrong with me (mental health / diagnosis-wise). I think some of my symptoms are actually severe, but I could be exaggerating. How have you managed to get a decent perspective on your mental health?
Answer: Here’s the thing: YOU get to decide what matters. It isn’t about something being right with you or wrong with you, or difficulties being considered mild or severe, or something qualifying for one diagnosis or another or no diagnosis at all. None of that determines your own goals and priorities and whether you’d like one or more things in your life to be different. How common something is, whether other random strangers relate, what a clinician would say…those are all superficial in nature. What really matters is who you want to be and what you think matters. If there are things you’d like to be different, you can explore how to make changes or how to evaluate whether those downsides come with upsides you feel are a fair tradeoff. Psychiatric diagnoses are literally just bullshit. They don’t explain anything about what is going on with you, or what your needs might be, or how to constructively address anything going on. They aren’t a part of figuring anything out because they don’t bring any new information or insight to the table. Your experiences and beliefs and behaviors are the same no matter what label an industry applies to them, and applying a label does not provide anything to your understanding the experiences, beliefs, and behaviors themselves did not already. A decent perspective on these things is to embrace that your experiences matter, that psychiatric labeling is not a way to understand them or determine what your values are, and that if you are struggling, there are things which can be done to promote positive change. Honesty is important: being willing to confront our emotions, our needs, our behaviors, and the patterns in those things which require understanding for us to more capably create a better life for ourselves. Appropriately assigning causality is important: discerning what factors are producing the outcomes you desire, or the outcomes you wish to avoid, so you can respond to those factors constructively. Marketing mythology and industry acceptance is neither required nor necessarily even a helpful rather than counterproductive influence. It is normal to crave understanding, validation, agency, and to seek those things. But, some manners of seeking them will be more productive or less dangerous than others. I found it helpful to implement this in my own life, which I can resummarize in a few expanded bulletpoints:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why did my GP give me a different anti-psychotic medication knowing the previous one worked?
Answer: Yes, why did they? There are any number of possible explanations. Maybe your idea of ‘working’ and their idea of ‘working’ differ. Maybe the drug was causing too many harms to be acceptable to the prescriber. Maybe they wanted to try out a different drug to see if it’d be better in some way, like a better ratio of upsides to downsides. Maybe they have enrolled in a trial without you knowing. Maybe they were told to boost their prescribing numbers for this other drug. Maybe there is a temporary shortage or weird pricing going on. Maybe additional interventions conflict more with the previous drug than the new one. Maybe you’re being switched to a different drug source or brand, or being put on a combo drug. Etc. Ultimately, likely the only person to know this GP’s reasoning is them. You have to talk with them to find out what they are doing and why, or at the very least request your medical records with doctors notes intact if they refuse to explain or you can’t talk to them for a long while. It is not typical for a GP to have the expertise to responsibly manage neuroleptics in the first place, but a lot of psychiatrists do a bad job as well so you have to do your own homework either way and assess whether any individual provider is giving you reasonable advice. Also be aware that swapping antipsychotics is probably going to cause withdrawal syndrome and/or other drug symptoms.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can people recover from long-term depression without medication?
Answer: Some people can recover from some depressions. “Depression” is a wide open category of rather heterogeneous experiences, some of which can be recovered from and some of which, within our current means, probably cannot. This is true of shorter-lived and longer-lived depressions, and this is true whether or not we discuss drugs as an intervention. There are millions of people who can succeed in recovering from depression without drugs, and recovery without drugs is the default for some of the most common forms of depression — particularly for people who figure out how to approach their experiences constructively. There are many depressions which will respond better to strategies other than drug use, or which drug use will simply not be very helpful for. Drugs are not cover-all tools, they are highly limited tools which carry significant risks and downsides, especially psychotropics like psychiatric drugs. However, there can also be cases where drugs were instrumental (unto themselves or as an aid in promoting broader changes in someone’s life), or where drugs are the most relevant thing (like in treating underlying medical disorders, for the relatively few we can single out and targetedly treat with a drug, eg hypothyroidism or certain nutritional deficiencies). As such, there can be many factors which affect how relevant drug use is, and how readily someone can recovery from depression, whether with drugs or without them. The underlying cause of depression, someone’s resources and support network, and someone’s investment in recovery are all considerations. There is nothing about depression itself which makes drug use innately important or appropriate, but there can sometimes be causes of depression unlikely to be adequately addressed without drugs, or unlikely to be adequately addressed through any means at all. A noteworthy scenario to discuss further is where quitting drugs is the way to end a long-term depression. Whether runaway use of recreational drugs like alcohol or cannabis or continuous prescribed use of psychiatric drugs like SSRIs or neuroleptics, sometimes medication is the problem. This isn’t necessarily apparent until reducing or quitting resolves the depression or gives someone the opportunity to work on it more effectively, but it is a surprisingly common issue, especially with increased rates of prescribing and a refusal for the mainstream to acknowledge how often psychiatric prescribing is detrimental.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is there any evidence that long-term use of psychiatric medications can worsen mental illness?
Answer: Of course. There is every possible evidence. The evidence is so immediately apparent that drug manufacturers warn of this problem with even short-term use of their products due to catastrophes in their own clinical trials that were run to gain drug approval or improve their marketing position. It is a guaranteed risk of psychiatric drugs, a universal risk. We see this kind of problem occurring in industry-sponsored and independent clinical trials, in case studies, in systematic studies of medical records, in epidemiological studies, and even in animal studies. Aside from the patients and clinicians in question, we see it recorded by both drug companies and regulatory agencies as an issue drugging can cause. But, it would serve us to clarify what “worsen mental illness” even means. Theoretically, any drug alteration is mutually exclusive to “mental illness” — a drug effect is a medical concern, not a so-called “psychopathology”, even if the experience criteria totally overlap with psychiatric diagnoses other than the criterion about the cause of the experiences. Psychiatric diagnoses exclude all medical problems and drug effects, so calling a drug effect “mental illness” is a contradiction. The two concepts are traditionally incompatible, though it can be a gray area to talk about how earlier drug use created vulnerability to psychological stressors instead of directly causing experiences like anxiety, depression, mania, psychosis. Still, the industry largely ignores this vital distinction, both in how it performs research into drug outcomes and in how patients are diagnosed and talked about in everyday practice. Drug effects are routinely mislabeled as “mental illness”, whether “worsened” or “relapsed” (such as after a drug causes new or intensified anxiety, depression, dissociation, etc) or entirely new diagnoses (like “bipolar” after drug mania or “schizophrenia” after drug psychosis). Studies allegedly comparing the course of drug use to drug non-use will typically frame drug withdrawal syndromes as “mental illness” when there are study patients who discontinue drugs instead of staying on them indefinitely or never having begun use. Since all the same adverse psychological effects of these drugs can start right away, none being unique to longer-term use, it is not necessarily very useful to focus only on long-term use. However, there is some importance to looking at long-term outcomes. Firstly, because some effects (like apathy syndrome, physical dependence) are increasingly likely the longer someone stays on drugs. Secondly, because these drugs often interfere with self-assessment and longer periods without clear self-evaluation can facilitate poorer upkeep, including more harmful decisions about the drugs themselves. And thirdly, because it is essential to look at the long-term outcomes regardless of short-term gains or losses. This is one of the most critical deficits in standard drug research — the failure to ascertain whether any short-term upsides to drug use are maintained long-term, or contribute centrally to better long-term outcomes. Research usually shows a net worsening of patient outcomes with long-term drug use for tentpole psychiatric diagnoses like “major depressive disorder” and “schizophrenia”, particularly if we compare drug use to non-drug recovery strategies instead of doing nothing at all to support someone. Since drug use is always about trading away physical health or safety for aesthetic or practical gains, it is more useful to look at “outcomes” more broadly versus characterizing some drug influences as “mental illness” and some drug influences as not. We should be talking about the experiences and goals and priorities of the patient either way. The very concept of “mental illness” as used in the mainstream usually ignores any utilitarian lines of accountability or coherence, so whether or not we rate outcomes only in terms of “mental illness” becomes arbitrary anyhow. The bottom line is that psychiatric drug use can always worsen someone’s situation, and cause entirely new problems that psychiatric diagnostic criteria otherwise encompass, both in short-term use and in long-term use. Inappropriate prescribing and poor drug management, whether by the clinician or the patient, can exponentially increase the riskiness of drug use and greatly curb the rate of net positive outcomes with drugging. Longer drug exposure will involve worse outcomes overall as compared to shorter drug exposure, but how it works out for any specific individual is much more personal and situational.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do antidepressants, anxiolytics, benzodiazepines, and antipsychotics affect cognitive functions? And if so, is it a long-term damage?
Answer: Q1. Do antidepressants, anxiolytics, benzodiazepines, and antipsychotics affect cognitive functions? Yes. Like with other psychotropic effects of these somewhat variegated drugs, the manners in which they do so and the resulting experiences produced can vary by drug, dose, patient, situation of use, and drug management style. Individual experiences can differ, even to the same drug at the same dose used exclusively and for the same amount of time. There are many factors which can clearly make more severe cognitive effects more likely, for instance higher doses compared to lower doses, longer periods of exposure, combining multiple drugs, and failing to taper up or down. Q2. And if so, is it a long-term damage? Long-term damage from these drugs can involve cognitive problems as a symptom, but long-term damage will not always cause cognitive symptoms even if that damage is in the brain. Likewise, persistent changes or impairments after drug use does not require long-term damage, so someone experiencing cognitive problems as a result of using these drugs is not necessarily experiencing those problems because of damages instead of other kinds of drug changes. Long-term damage can cause adverse cognitive effects but we cannot know there is damage based only on symptoms.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can being diagnosed as mentally ill by a psychiatrist have long-term consequences? What happens if the diagnosis is incorrect or false, but the label remains?
Answer: Psychiatric diagnoses haunt you for life. The long-term consequences of psychiatric epithets are the same as the short-term consequences of psychiatric epithets: many people will treat you differently, regardless of the reality of your experiences, and this can have a severely negative impact on your life. This can interfere with relationships, with working, with receiving appropriate medical care, with protecting your family against outside parties, with social or political aspirations, and so forth. Detriment is baked right into mainstream psychiatric conceptualizing, including the diagnostic structures and how they are applied, and then broader society tends to be even more extreme in how they (mis)characterize and stereotype patients. All psychiatric diagnoses are “false” in the sense of being totally made up and not grounded in the real world or anything objective about someone’s body or self. They are just “bullshit” (a verbatim quote from a psychiatrist who was in charge of putting together the most relevant diagnostic manual of his day). But, diagnoses can be ‘correct’ or ‘incorrect’ in the sense of whether or not they follow whatever arbitrary rules are considered most popular at the time. The rules change year to year and their interpretation is incredibly loose and most clinicians don’t follow all the rules anyhow, though. “Correct” and “incorrect” diagnoses can be equally damaging, and equally persistent in haunting someone’s life and dreams. It is true that if someone receives a diagnosis and manages to keep that secret from everyone ever for the rest of their lives, negative consequences are far less likely to follow. But, that is not a very realistic outcome. Psychiatric diagnoses exist in large part for these things to be recorded, and nobody has full control over their psychiatric records. Simply being scheduled to see a psychologist or psychiatrist, or having been prescribed psychiatric drugs, even for non-psychiatric reasons, can also be stigmatizing. Due to the harmful nature of psychiatry and of mainstream perceptions about psychiatry, people are generally best off ignoring psychiatric diagnoses and preventing their spread.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do most people eventually recover from depression, or does it continue to affect them for the rest of their lives?
Answer: A majority of people probably recover forever. This is a somewhat sticky question to answer because there are so many different depressions with differing causes, courses, and possibilities and it is not very representative to lump them all together into a single statistic. We are adding together everything from extended grief to drug effects to inborn medical disorders to brain injuries to lifestyle problems to psychological trauma responses to work exhaustion and it isn’t particularly fair to equate them or imagine a statistic averaging outcomes will give us meaningful insight into depression as a whole or to any single category of experiences — especially since each category will still feature a lot of individual variation. It is very common for depressions, especially those without any medical disorder, to resolve forever after only a single episode, and still common for those depressions to recur up to a couple times but then be gone for good. But, plenty of people still struggle with depression their whole lives. This can pertain both to psychologically-oriented and biologically-oriented depressions, so it is not reasonable to say that one type of root cause is always totally resolvable, or never possible to recover from completely. The landscape is far more nuanced than that. Though the majority experience of depression is not a lifetime of depression, that shouldn’t diminish the fact or commonness of lifetime struggles. There is also complexity to the question because we face the prospect of degrees of recovery. For instance, someone could recover 99% and you’d still have to tally that remaining 1% as affecting them, and some people can be more susceptible to future depressions as a result of past ones, just as the opposite can also be true. Though your question was implicitly asking about impairments or struggles as being what it means to be affected by depression, it is also worth exploring the idea of constructive changes in reaction to these experiences. People will often carry lessons and growth from depression, including lifelong depression, so the effects of depression aren’t all adverse and can continue even if the depression itself did not.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: In the current state of psychiatric science, do you think DSM-V should assume a cautious, conservative posture or an assertive, transformative posture in making changes from DSM-IV?
Answer: It doesn’t matter. It does not matter what arbitrary lines are being drawn because there is no scientific rationale either way. The DSM is an industry tool serving industry interests. Patients have no direct stake in it. The influences which shape the revisions in DSM editions will be the influences most benefiting, and that means new editions are a reflection of their own concerns and considerations rather than a delineation of what we factually know or what works out best for psychiatry as a field or patients or society. This is not to say it there is no impact to patients or society when changes are made. But, the implementation of the guidelines is the key factor. Clinicians and academics don’t have to look at or talk about or use the DSM in only one particular way, so their mediating presence is integral to the effects of diagnostic concepts and guidelines on everything else going on. This, too, will be self-serving in nature, but there is at least the capacity for more altruistic intentions in some contexts.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are there any antidepressants that treat cognitive dysfunction caused by depression and anxiety?
Answer: That depends on what you mean by “treat”. Stimulant drugs, including the somewhat milder ones sold as “antidepressants”, can impact concerns like brain fog and difficulty thinking. Drugs like SSRIs are not literally treating anything in the brain in these instances, as they are not medically helping underlying causes and underlying causes may not involve any medical disorder in the first place. But, these drugs do all cause altered states, and someone may experience upsides as well as downsides cognitively as part of the drug alterations. There are drugs more likely to improve certain cognitive domains as compared to typical antidepressants, but cognitive impairments do not all work the same across situations nor do all patients react the same way to particular drugs. Whether drug use is a net positive for someone’s overall health and life is also a separate consideration, as even people who report cognitive upsides may experience downsides in other areas that make use more harmful than helpful and the risks involved are rather significant. Typically, if depression and anxiety are causing cognitive impairment, the most effective and risk-effective strategy is to reduce or resolve the depression and anxiety. Whether or not that is something drug use can help with, or antidepressant use more specifically, will depend on the patient and circumstances. If someone’s goal is just to temporarily use stimulants to improve certain aspects of cognition, there are more appropriate drugs to start with than antidepressants, including over-the-counter drugs.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does olanzapine cause emotional numbness? If I stop taking them, will my emotions return?
Answer: Q1. Does olanzapine cause emotional numbness? Very often, yes. This can happen in a matter of degrees, so some people will be more numbed or apathetic than others. Sometimes the degree depends on the particular drug, dose, or duration of use, sometimes it is more about someone’s personal sensitivity, health, or situation. Many factors go into drug reactions, and everyone is at risk of emotional numbing from neuroleptics (aka “antipsychotics”). Drugs like olanzapine are far more likely to cause undesirable emotional changes than to cause any desirable changes in our experiences, so this is not an unusual or exceptional kind of reaction. Q2. If I stop taking them, will my emotions return? Most people experience at least a partial recovery if given enough time. This, too, is something which comes in degrees. Some people feel to recover 100% of their emotional functioning while others report only incomplete recovery and a small minority feel like the numbness never improved at all. Physical and functional changes as well as outright damage can contribute to numbness and the speed and degree of recovery will depend on the ability for our body to rehabilitate by reversing or working around those drug problems. There are sometimes ways to support our recovery, but time is the most significant influence. Like with the onset of drug reactions, many factors go into our recovery experiences and the course they take. Some people will notice overnight change, or will start being less apathetic during the downtaper before the drug is even fully discontinued. Others struggle with emotional functioning for months or years after their last dose. In some cases, there is a simple, gradual restoration of emotional functioning while in other cases the numbness or other emotional effects can cycle in and out over time. There is no standard healing period after which we can predict you will feel like your old self again.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible for people to be misdiagnosed by psychiatrists if their symptoms do not fit into any specific category listed in the DSM-5?
Answer: Misdiagnosis is always a possibility no matter what. There will always be people who don’t follow the rules or don’t perform due diligence, and there will always be cases so complex that even a good practitioner might misunderstand, or screw up, or come to an errant conclusion. However, psychiatry works different from medicine as a whole because psychiatric diagnoses are never true or false, right or wrong, in any literal sense beyond the evaluator saying that diagnostic criteria are met. A psychiatric diagnosis does not tell us what is going on in someone’s body or mind and there is no way to use evidence to validate or discredit a diagnosis. The only concern is whether the popularity-based diagnostic criteria in use at the time are thought to be met. The whys and hows are irrelevant. “Misdiagnosis” just means someone didn’t apply the criteria as the industry expected. It doesn’t mean the earlier diagnosis was wrong or that a newer diagnosis is right in any sense other than adhering to those arbitrary criteria. It is not like someone getting misdiagnosed with cancer or a broken arm or Parkinson’s finding out the diagnosis was wrong. Nothing about a patient’s clinical situation or needs or experiences changes based on the psychiatric diagnosis applied. It doesn’t provide additional information, it doesn’t explain how to help someone, it doesn’t tell us what will happen in the future or how someone will respond to a therapeutic intervention. This is basically the opposite of how traditional medical diagnoses work. As for the second part of your question, there are many non-specific categories listed in the DSM for cases that don’t seem to fit into specific categories. They are usually subsets of the main diagnostic headings, “NOS” (not otherwise specified). However, you said “symptoms do not fit into any specific category”, and that is never the case. There is no such thing as an experience psychiatry frames as a “symptom” that doesn’t fit into multiple diagnostic categories. Psychiatric diagnoses overlap more than not, and applying a diagnosis is typically more about narrowing the set of potential diagnoses. There is substantial interpretive flexibility involved, so the same experience could potentially be construed as hypomania, depression, psychosis, anxiety, personality disorder based on the beliefs and biases of the practitioner.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can individuals without a bipolar diagnosis experience periods of mania? If so, what is the potential duration before it becomes dangerous?
Answer: Q1. Can individuals without a bipolar diagnosis experience periods of mania? Sure, pretty much anyone can experience mania. It is essentially a fundamental human capacity. The only difference between people is usually just what their threshold is for particular stressors causing mania. Some people are much more vulnerable to certain triggers. This can be neurological, psychological, or situational and may only be discovered when mania ends up getting provoked. A “bipolar disorder” diagnosis circumscribes only a minority subset of manic experiences. Most of the time people are experiencing mania, those experiences will not qualify for a “bipolar disorder” diagnosis. However, there is no innate difference between experiences which do and experiences which don’t. That is, the underlying causes and the mania itself and the course of things can all be shared and diagnostic boundaries are themselves arbitrary and are created based on industrial benefits. While psychiatric diagnoses exclude medical disorders, so all medical causes of mania are separate from ”bipolar disorder”, there are still psychological causes which can cause mania but not get labeled as “bipolar disorder”. Either way, there is no real relevance to the diagnosis here as it is not prescriptive or explanatory, it is just a retrospective label of convenience. Q2. What is the potential duration before it becomes dangerous? Dangerous in what respect? Thinking or behaving out of the ordinary for a society can always be dangerous, and can also cause issues if we would usually be thinking or acting differently from how we do in mania — pretty much a guarantee in one or more respects. Even just hours of mania can be dangerous in this sense. While we can sometimes become dangerous to ourselves or others, others always become more dangerous to us. This is especially true of powerful institutions like law enforcement or the psychiatric industry. Some people will undertake blatantly or situationally dangerous acts, like thrillseeking, risky sex, or trying something that the laws of physics won’t respond to kindly. Mania isn’t always grand beliefs and euphoric feelings, either — agitation, anger, depression, even suicidality can be involved (sometimes this is considered a “mixed state”, depending on the particular details). How dangerous mania is depends on what someone’s mania is like, and what their awareness and coping strategies are. There is also the concern of how mania is hard on the nervous system, and potentially the body as well. It is like putting a machine into overdrive for an extended period of time; parts will wear out faster, and things won’t always work as smoothly. The consequences of manic experiences, for instance reduced or absent sleep, can also take a toll. Danger in this sense tends to escalate over time.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can antidepressants stop you from emotionally eating?
Answer: Sure. Antidepressants can stop you from experiencing emotions (aka apathy), especially the reuptake inhibitors, so the consequences of experiencing those emotions can also be stopped. Antidepressants also frequently cause changes in our appetite, GI functioning, and related things. Nausea, reductions in appetite, metabolic problems, vomiting or diarrhea, and so forth can reduce eating in general, whether short-term or long-term. It would be misleading to characterize these disruptions as therapeutic for emotional eaters, but clinical trial rubrics aren’t about reality. Are these drugs a good option for people who are caught in a cycle of emotional eating? Not usually, no. They don’t address the underlying causes and may interfere with someone trying to understand and adjust those causes. Antidepressants can also amplify or exacerbate many of the adverse health influences of emotional eating. The risk profile overall is pretty unfavorable and use will not pay off for most patients prescribed these kinds of drugs. Only highly strategic use is likely to be more helpful than harmful.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is a good defense of Cannibalism?
Answer: Saying you value taste or novelty over safety from deadly prions. Spiritual powers. Profitability.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I have regular mood swings on half a day. Is this bipolar disorder?
Answer: By definition, no. The diagnostic criteria for psychiatric diagnoses such as “bipolar disorder” are based on industry input and a vote of popularity. None of those criteria are met by the information provided in the question. Also remember that “bipolar disorder” is not a type of mood swings or a cause of mood swings, it is just a shorthand label for a subset of experiences which may or may not involve mood swings. Psychiatric diagnoses are industrial classifications, not medical explanations or physical phenomena. What you know from experiencing regular mood swings is that you experience regular mood swings. It is worth doing some work to find out why. Psychiatric diagnosing has no part in that, as psychiatric diagnoses don’t add any information or actionable understanding. Your concern is causes and how to respond to whatever is going on.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can my parents force me to take antipsychotics if I don't want to? I'm 16.
Answer: Maybe. There are three kinds of ‘forcing’ you might be talking about: The first kind of forcing is something you can only work out by educating them, negotiating with them, or leaving them. The second kind of forcing is something you may be able to protect yourself against if you live somewhere that 16 is considered adulthood with regards to medical decisions or there is a process you can use to become ‘emancipated’ and have the right to make your own medical choices. The third kind of forcing is something nobody can be truly protected from, though there may be a psychiatric advance directive available to you which you could fill out and use to potentially prevent some instances of involuntary drugging. You can still be incarcerated even without forced drugging, though, and you can still be threatened with bad things if you decline to use drugs. So, if your parents are even remotely reasonable or open to dialogue, the first step is to research antipsychotics and to create an explanation for why you don’t think they are a good fit for you. Your goals, your priorities, your reactions, your needs are central here, though the fundamental risks and downsides of neuroleptics also play a role in characterizing responsible decisions about use or non-use.
