If there is no hope of finding common ground with your parents, you will have to be looking into what legal options are available to people of your age where you live. Keep in mind that if you take steps to protect yourself, this may have a negative impact on your relationship with them and your support network. But, if the relationship is threatening to seriously harm you, it may not be something feasible to maintain as-is.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do I become more depressed when I take mitrazapine at night but it is good for sleep but in the morning I wake up depressed?
Answer: Because those are often two different axes of effects. A drug can be sedating without causing low mood, dysphoria, or apathy, depending on its mechanisms, just as a drug can be sedating without causing hyperthymia, euphoria, or feelings of profundity. If you take a drug and feel more able to sleep but also feel more depressed, the conclusion to draw is that the drug makes you feel more able to sleep but also more depressed. The specific mechanisms are not necessarily going to be clear, and you don’t really explain what “more depressed” means — unmotivated, fatigued, dysphoric, suicidal, achy, cognitively impaired, something else? In short, there is no reason to expect mirtazapine to make you feel less depressed, many reasons why it might make you feel more depressed, and these can be independent of effects on sleep. Since the sedating influences of mirtazapine will actually interfere with healthy sleep structure and thus the mental and physical processes which depend on healthy sleep structure, feeling more able to sleep can still be connected to feeling worsened depression in some cases. Since you are reporting a significant downside with the mirtazapine, its use should be reassessed and you might find a lower dose, different drug, or entirely different approach more appropriate.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I want to stop my antidepressants but my psychiatrist doesn’t want me to. What should I do ? Quit myself or wait?
Answer: Neither. While it doesn’t matter what your psychiatrist wants, there are two important things you need to get straightened out before proceeding: That said, most people prescribed antidepressants are better off not taking them, so it is very likely that quitting is your best move if you already have reasons for wanting to stop, as you’ve said. How we discontinue can make a big difference in what happens when we do quit, though, as can what we do after quitting to address any ongoing concerns which led to drug use in the first place, if there are any remaining.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do SSRIs like Zoloft actually help with major depression or is it just something that is good for light to mild depression?
Answer: The more severe depression is, the more likely drug use might be considered helpful. There are three major factors consider here: Usually, drugs like SSRIs are least likely to be worthwhile for “light to mild depression”. This is both because they are unlikely to resolve the depression or offer substantial benefits and because they will usually involve far more downsides and serious risks than upsides and serious gains. Most prescribing in depression is not for severe depression and most prescribing for depression fails. Patients are not usually experiencing the upsides they wanted and will usually say that drug use was more harmful than helpful, especially once post-discontinuation effects are accounted for. Use in clinical trials even leads to a decrease in patient survival in standard trials such as those run for drug approval. That said, most studies are not of severely depressed patients, and most depressions are not severe. This doesn’t mean these drugs are a magic bullet when depression is severe, but patients experiencing severe depression are more likely to find the overall influence of drugs helpful or justifiable in net and are less likely to have less drastic options that can adequately address whatever is going on. SSRIs are potentially the group of drugs marketed as “antidepressants” which are least likely to be effective in severe depression, but other groups will not necessarily be far better. SSRIs mostly became popular due to marketing, expanded uses, and having less acute organ toxicity in use and especially in overdose compared to MAOIs and TCAs. When it comes to drug use, there is actually no reason to believe drugs marketed as “antidepressants” will be more helpful than drugs which are not. As others have mentioned, a primary variable here is why a depression is happening in the first place. There are many different causes of depressions, some medical and some psychological, and these will shape the experience and course of the depression. Since drugs such as SSRIs have no targeted medical relevance to any causes of depression, there is never a cause of depression which makes SSRIs uniquely suited to be helpful. But, there are some kinds of depressions where standard alternatives may be less likely to be adequate. Conversely, there are depressions where psychiatric drugs are highly unlikely to be appropriate, and where medical treatments or cures or psychological work or lifestyle changes may be extremely effective. This does not hinge on the severity of a depression.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: My Prozac dose was increased to the highest dose of 60mg then it gave me mania what is the cause of this?
Answer: SSRIs are pro-manic drugs and higher doses are more pro-manic than lower doses. Drugs like fluoxetine (aka Prozac) are fundamentally pro-manic. They cause mania in psychiatric patients, in non-psychiatric patients, and in healthy study volunteers. MAOIs causing mania in patients is how the whole concept of “antidepressants” was cooked up in the first place. While some people are more susceptible to this drug effect than others are, there are many situational factors which can increase the risk of a manic reaction. A high dose of the drug is one of those factors. Apparently your body was able to cope with the disruptive effects of doses lower than 60mg without going manic but 60mg/day overwhelmed it. This could be as simple as saying something like “I didn’t throw up after 4 beers but I threw up after 6” — it may just be a threshold was crossed. Or, the increase was too abrupt, or you were made vulnerable by a previous drug discontinuation or medical condition, or any number of other possibilities no information was provided to sort between. We aren’t entirely sure exactly how particular drugs and drug mechanisms cause mania, though a serotonergic influence is often involved, just as we don’t have a clear picture of how manias not caused by drugs work. Mania is defined and identified by psychosocial criteria, not by what is going on in the brain. Psychiatric drugs in general typically involve the risk of mania, though not necessarily for all the same reasons, and serotonergically stimulating drugs (including SSRIs) all the more. Some answers are trying to blame “bipolar disorder”, which doesn’t really make sense because “bipolar disorder” is not a cause, it is an effect — the description of the experiences caused by something else. “Bipolar disorder” also excludes any drug reactions, so a pro-manic drug causing mania is not a reason to diagnose someone and research thus far has shown that most people made manic by SSRIs never have experiences qualifying for a “bipolar disorder” label. It is a normal and very common drug reaction, but one which makes it clear something has to change for the patient’s safety and similar drugs may need to be avoided in the future.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do I feel like I'm getting worse and worse after 3 cold turkey months of taking Effexor for 13 and a half years when the first month I seemed to be almost cured?
Answer: Recovery is a process. While some patients experience an onset of post-discontinuation symptoms and then those symptoms all collectively fade over time, many patients experience new symptoms arising long after others first did, and many people experience symptoms that come and go in waves, sometimes over and over again for months or years. The bottom line is the recovery is a process rather than a simple forward progression away from symptoms. Some symptoms may newly appear or worsen over time, some may cycle on and off periodically, some may morph into something else. After more than a decade on drugs, you can anticipate there being more difficulties ahead, this is not something people can usually quit overnight and then feel recovered from within days or weeks or even a few months. The body is trying to restabilize and to address any underlying problems drug use had caused besides just physical dependence (deficiencies, damages, downregulation, and so forth). There is more to recovering from long-term psychiatric drug use than just getting through the withdrawal symptoms, and for some people all the other stuff involved can actually be more taxing or confusing than withdrawal itself. It is not unusual for someone to have months or even years of worsening symptoms after more than a few years of continuous drug use. More than a decade of use should be taken as a giant “caution” sign to take steps slowly. People with a history of severe stress on the nervous system, which you mention in your post, are also more likely to struggle with recovery as a result. Cold turkeying is bad news in general, and can potentially alter the course and severity of withdrawal. It can also make it more difficult for someone to transition away from daily drug use. Dysfunction, disorientation, and impairment are typical, not strange or uncommon. After use as long as you mention, patients often require specialized consultation so that they can properly prepare themselves for the journey and have the resources and support to work through the months or years of struggle. Skipping a gradual taper was likely a very bad idea, though it may be possible to reinstate a partial dose to see if it alleviates your symptoms at all. Read places like Surviving Antidepressants and discuss your options with your doctors: Important topics in the Tapering forum and FAQ

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I’ve been on Remeron (antidepressant) for 4 days. If I quit now, will I get withdrawal symptoms?
Answer: You shouldn’t. It usually takes several weeks to a few months for someone to become appreciably physically dependent upon an antidepressant. Different people have different levels of sensitivity to use and quitting, and different rates of becoming physically dependent, but 4 days of use should not cause withdrawal. Even 2 or 3 times that duration of use should still be something a patient can quit without withdrawal, and a rapid taper of reducing incrementally for several days before full discontinuation can be tried if there is a concern about abruptness. If someone thinks they’re in withdrawal, reinstatement of a low dose of the drug can also potentially restabilize them and is an option if jumping off the drug caused problems. However, an exception is when people switched to their current drug from a previous drug and were physically dependent upon that previous drug. Though swapping drugs often still produces some degree of withdrawal anyway, even if they are in the same basic class (like NaSSAs in this case, or reuptake inhibitors for drugs like SSRIs and SNRIs), if someone was lucky enough to avoid withdrawal through the actions of the new drug, dropping the new drug will take away that support and withdrawal symptoms can develop. Someone may also find the road a bit rockier for swapping drugs and then quitting them back to back, as that is multiple major stress events for the nervous system. There not usually being withdrawal after 4 days does not mean someone will feel totally fine after quitting — effects caused by use or the transition on or off the drug may still cause symptoms that take a while to fade away. Also, if someone experienced a more serious drug reaction, they may be working through that for a while if it is something they recover from eventually. For people concerned about physical dependence with short-term use, keeping doses low can reduce the risk of more serious withdrawal reactions. Since this can also affect the actions of a drug like mirtazapine (aka Remeron), management can be more complex than just using less of a drug.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why does OCD feel so real?
Answer: What happens in our mind is real. Our perception of ‘realness’ depends on our mind and happens in our mind. It is not about what is going on objectively or in an outside world. When things are going on which affect our mind, they consequently affect our perceptions of what is real. We don’t evaluate obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors using different physical or psychological machinery from the machinery we use to evaluate all our other experiences, and we experience these things through the same physical and psychological apparatuses as well. So, when things are going on in the brain or going on with us psychologically which impact what we are experiencing and how we are perceiving, what we are thinking before those factors change our reality works the same as what we are thinking after those factors change our reality. Our mental perceptions are incredibly flexible, moldable, and largely lacking in self-awareness. We can feel and experience things pluralistically — multiple different or seemingly conflicting things being true at the same time. All sorts of mental processes are going on at all times to facilitate being alive. We aren’t constantly consciously reality-checking our assumptions or how we are connecting ideas or our emotional states to see if they match what other people are believing or experiencing. Even if we tried to reality-check things in that way, the machinery we use to do so is subjective rather than objective, meaning we can’t self-assess in a way which works around all influences on our experiences and perceptions. When thoughts and feelings are occurring organically, the natural tendency is to take them at face value. There is no universal understanding of “OCD” because the label is applied to a variety of differing physical and psychological phenomena. We can’t say that the brain rewires in way X and that results in experience Y or stuff like that because it is not so singular or simple. But, the bottom line is that anxiety is a real experience with evolutionary and everyday value and when we aren’t listening to or properly understanding anxiety cues or those cues get attached to things we no longer want them attached to, it can cause distortions in how we respond to situations. In a sense, humans are anxiety machines and we sometimes need to consciously tweak how our anxiety response is working — what we consider threatening, what the repercussions are thought to be, what physical state to get into when a trigger is perceived, and all that.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I’ve been on olanzapine for two years and want to stop taking it as I do not have any medication condition that the medication was intended to treat. How long will this take?
Answer: Several months to a few years. Tapering after two years may take anywhere from several months for the luckiest patients to a few years for the most sensitive patients. Many people will be able to find a pace somewhere in between those two which works best for them. The rate of discontinuation is something that needs to be personalized, and some reductions will be easier to make than others. For many, the final leg of tapering is the hardest while the first drop may be the easiest. How quickly and how often to reduce needs to be calibrated in response to how a patient feels after their previous reductions, and someone’s goals and priorities in discontinuation need to be accounted for. Because of how harmful antipsychotics are, people in a stable and healthy place before starting their taper are usually better served by quitting at a less conservative rate whenever possible. Also keep in mind that tapering and withdrawal is only the first stage of recovery and someone may spend years or even decades of their life rehabilitating from the lingering effects of continuous antipsychotic use. Whether there are lasting impairments or noticeable symptoms will vary from patient to patient, even if we compare the same drugs used at the same doses for the same lengths of time. Individual experiences vary, so how complicated or difficult discontinuation is and how long it takes for someone to feel recovered will differ, as will whether someone ever fully recovers at all. Before talking with your provider to discuss how to most appropriately taper off, check out some previous discussions of neuroleptic tapering, discontinuation, and recovery in threads like the ones linked below, and mine the posts for off-site resources that can help you formulate a plan with your prescriber and respond to challenges which may arise. And as a note on the framing of your question, the reasons for prescribing an antipsychotic have no bearing on whether or not a patient can or should quit, or what they must do to quit responsibly. What a drug is approved to be marketed for is irrelevant. Most uses of psychiatric drugs, including most prescriptions for these drugs, are not evaluated or approved by regulatory bodies and regulatory approval for marketing does not suggest a drug ought to be prescribed or that it will turn out good for patients or for society as a whole. The lack of an official prescribing indication is not a reason to avoid or discontinue a drug just as the presence of an official prescribing indication is not a reason to use or continue a drug. These drugs don’t really have real ‘intentions’ — manufacturers are happy to sell them to anyone buying and part of marketing is getting prescribers and policymakers on board as well.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can quitting both of olanzapine and mirtazapine cold-turkey be fatal?
Answer: It is unlikely but still possible. These kinds of drugs can cause a very serious physical dependence as well as other issues with the body that present substantial discontinuation risks after continuous use. After a month or two, someone needs to strongly consider the ramifications of quitting, with or without a taper. Withdrawal syndrome, supersensitivity syndrome, and the intense disorientation that can result from going off neuroleptics and NaSSAs can be dangerous. Though potentially life-threatening symptoms are not uncommon, the good news is that they are usually survived — especially if someone is lucky enough to get proper medical help. There are factors which can make life-threatening risks more dangerous, like old age, concurrent medical conditions, poor lifestyle support for recovery, being overstressed before quitting, cold-turkeying instead of tapering, quitting multiple drugs at the same time instead of one drug at a time. A lack of education about discontinuation risks and a failure to properly manage a discontinuation can be key factors in worst case scenario outcomes. In the few withdrawal deaths from these drugs that make it into medical journal articles, there will pretty much always be at least one really stupid medical decision involved. Olanzapine and mirtazapine can each cause death when used or discontinued alone, and going off both at the same time without any tapering is asking for trouble all the more. Nevertheless, most patients will survive that even if they receive no medical intervention whatsoever. The suffering, harm, and potentially lasting consequences should cause anyone to think twice about quitting so carelessly, though. If given the option, tapering, even self-tapering, can potentially make a big difference in the risk profile. Even careful discontinuation carries heavy risks and can be quite difficult for many people, but some of the most concerning life-threatening risks are reduced more steeply by tapering than many other risks.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does taking antidepressants and getting natural sunlight at the same time have any weird effect on serotonin or mood?
Answer: Antidepressants do, natural sunlight shouldn’t add to the weirdness. Some people are sensitive to the level of sunlight they take in, especially in areas far from the equator and in particular months of the year. So, it is possible that changes in sunlight exposure hours can impact someone’s mood, and seasonal depression or hyperthymia is not particularly unusual in many regions. But, someone not normally thrown off by changes in sunlight exposure is unlikely to find it becoming a dramatic factor when using drugs marketed as “antidepressants”. They can indeed change how we react to stimuli, and can mess up all sorts of stuff in our brain and with our hormones that could alter our level of responsiveness to sunlight, but usually any changes in mood will be due to the drug itself, not the drug + sunlight. Antidepressants are the major culprit here. They stop the nervous system from working correctly and are prescribed specifically to prevent normal functioning. Most patients will notice mood changes, whether modest or intense, whether short-lived or throughout their entire period of use. Such drugs are far more likely to cause undesired psychological effects than desired ones, and many of the most serious adverse effect warnings are neuropsychological: mania, psychosis, depression, violence, suicide, and so forth. Apathy syndrome is extremely common, especially with reuptake inhibitor drugs such as SSRIs. Feeling ‘weird’ is par for the course when using these drugs, and some people will feel even weirder after drug initiation or cessation, or after dose changes up or down.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Antidepressant gave me mania does this mean I’m bi polar?
Answer: No, plain and simple. Anyone can experience mania as a result of using or trying to quit antidepressants, as they carry that risk fundamentally. Some people will be more likely to experience it than others, and some drugs and situations of use will be riskier than others. At least in what research has been performed, most people experiencing a manic reaction to antidepressants never receive have experiences meeting the criteria for “bipolar disorder”. Add to that how drug-induced mania is the opposite of “bipolar disorder” — a diagnosis which excludes all drug reactions, medical disorders, and injuries. None of this makes your reaction irrelevant, though. Your reaction makes it clear that future manic reactions may be possible and you need to be careful with similar drugs and other stressors commonly experienced to cause mania. Some patients whose experiences do meet the diagnostic criteria for “bipolar disorder” find certain drugs, for instance most drugs marketed as “antidepressants”, to be manic triggers for them. Some don’t. The diagnosis does not tell us what someone’s triggers or vulnerabilities are, or how they will react to any particular drugs, and no psychiatric diagnosis can ever be reasoned on the basis of a drug reaction. With that laid out, the presence of absence of a diagnosis like “bipolar” doesn’t matter anyhow. Psychiatric diagnoses do nothing for a patient unto themselves — they add no information or insight, they provide no game plan for rehabilitation or support for understanding how to respond to any difficulties or disturbances. Your experiences are whatever they are regardless of how a clinician might choose to label them, so your priority should be the experiences themselves and how to work towards your goals and protect yourself while keeping in mind there is at least one realized manic risk out there for you.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why are 70% of Americans on SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) when decades of medical studies are showing serotonin levels have nothing to do with depression?
Answer: They aren’t, but the reasons for use are still relevant. Stats It is surprisingly difficult to nail down a reliable statistic for SSRI use, whether in a calendar year or lifetime exposure, but research suggests that the rate is closer to 10% of all Americans using an SSRI in the past year. The rate will be higher if we focus only on adults, as relatively few babies and young children are taking SSRIs. We can figure it is somewhere around three times that rate for lifetime exposure, and higher if we include all drugs marketed as “antidepressants” rather than just SSRIs in particular. The rate of use in the past year will be much higher if we lump all psychiatric drugs together, though not all uses will be psychiatric just as is the case for SSRIs more specifically. But, even that will probably be closer to 40%-60% rather than 70%, higher if we expand our window beyond just the past 12 months. So, asking about some 70% overall rate of SSRI use is blatantly misleading. However, 10% is itself an incredible level of use which requires some serious justification and it is still important to address just why the hell prescribing rates are so high. Industrialization The single greatest factor behind psychiatric drug prescribing rates is the industrialization of psychiatry. Industrialization has been the greatest driving force behind the pharmaceutical-centric model which consumed almost all of mainstream psychiatry and behind the disease paradigm which goes hand-in-hand with that model. Systemization of products and services can be exceptionally profitable, and getting the government and mainstream organizations on board creates an unstoppable industrial paradise. Because these motivations were never accountable to things like therapeutic efficacy or patient outcomes, industrialization can freely conflict with the needs of patients without that conflict challenging the power industrial psychiatry or society’s ideological, emotional, and institutional investment in it. Marketing, institutionalization of marketed concepts, legislating, and funding all strengthen industrialization and, in doing so, increase prescribing rates. Targeting Competition Industrialization is an innately competitive trend in psychiatry and psychology, including research and academia, policymaking, institutional and outpatient services and programs, and every other facet. The consequence of this is that a rise in popularity for industrial psychiatry means reduced popularity of alternatives, no matter how useful or superior they might be. Attention, research, funding, political and governmental support, and marketshares are all sapped away from otherwise successful alternatives to psychiatry when industrialization is the engine of psychiatric popularity. As such, a meaningful part of the ever-increasing use of psychiatric drugs is a global dismantling of or industrializing of all the other ways people previously received support, or could receive support in the future. Clients are finite, so this is a zero sum game for industry parties. Desperation With or without the industrialization of psychiatry, people as individuals and society as a whole can be quite desperate. The reasons for this desperation are manifold, like a failure to prioritize wellbeing and quality of life, a lack of enculturated support systems, lifestyle pressures, heterogeneity of experiences and difficulties, a poor understanding of what depression can be and how to help people going through it, and even the negative effects of psychiatry itself and its products’ adverse influence on health and wellbeing. Desperate people often do desperate things, even if they are unlikely to work out, even if the risks are not justified. Industrial psychiatry takes full advantage of this human vulnerability and perpetuates the psychology behind feelings of helplessness and brokenness which so many patients were already experiencing beforehand to some extent. In short, a lot of prescribing is predatory, even if professionals say they personally are well-meaning. The Serotonin Myth While no “chemical imbalance” narrative has any substantive evidence behind it, and general hypotheses like monoamine deficiencies in psychiatric diagnoses were abandoned by serious researchers more than half a century ago, these narratives have never been a legitimate justification for prescribing. They are absolutely a compelling marketing tool, and plenty of professionals buy into the marketing themselves and imagine themselves to be doing good by spreading the myths and prescribing drugs like SSRIs, but their function has never been as a true medical rationale for prescribing. The mainstream dissemination of these narratives has been to serve industrial needs rather than patient needs. Because ‘the serotonin myth’ was never more than a myth, debunking it does not necessarily disrupt how compelling it is as a marketing narrative or curb prescribing. These marketing lies have been referred to as ‘zombies’ because they are unkillable through standard means. That said, serotonin levels can be important in depression. Medical disorders like those impairing serotonin synthesis can cause depression, for instance, and even the serotonergic mechanisms of SSRIs themselves can cause depression because of the changes in the nervous system caused by stranding serotonin between synapses. The distinction to draw here is that psychiatry is all about the depressions which aren’t medical disorders. Diagnoses like “major depressive disorder” (and all other psychiatric diagnoses) explicitly exclude depressions which are the result of medical problems or drug effects, though clinicians can ignore this criterion and misdiagnosis is extremely common — particularly when psychiatrists are misdiagnosing the adverse effects of the drugs they or their peers have prescribed. Though most SSRI prescribing these days is not even for depression, typical prescribing in depression is for depressions with no underlying medical disorder.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is Kratom just as good as an SSRI for major depression?
Answer: “Just as good” as placebo? SSRIs and other drugs marketed as “antidepressants” don’t best placebo in standard clinical trials. That doesn’t mean nobody finds them helpful, just that the bar here is extremely low and SSRIs are simply a bad fit for most people experiencing major depression. I think it is fair to say the same thing about kratom: it will be a great option for a subset of individuals but a bad fit for most people. What works is what works, but what works is highly individual. Ideally, someone can resolve a depression without drugs at all, but that isn’t always the case and kratom does have a place in psychiatric prescribing. Like other psychotropics, it should not be blanket prescribed on the basis of diagnosis and there are a range of factors to account for when prescribing and managing it. Experimenting alone is less likely to be successful versus getting appropriate professional consultation. There are also some additional considerations. Kratom comes in many varieties and products which are not interchangeable. It is basically a whole group of drugs and drug products and someone won’t necessarily know what they are getting when they make a purchase, and may have special needs regarding strain or potency. Of course, the regulation of psychiatric drug manufacturing is startlingly poor and a lot goes wrong with that so buying a prescription drug at the pharmacy doesn’t ensure quality. But, substances regulated as supplements have even less oversight and even more quality variation in the US. Like with SSRIs, the differences between kratom strains can make a difference in both drug upsides and drug downsides, and thus our concept of efficacy or ‘goodness’. Preparation and dose are relevant, too. Is kratom at least as good as placebo? Sure, but that doesn’t mean it should be used without selectivity.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I have tried 2 SSRI's, Lexapro and Sertraline. I had really bad reactions psychologically to these. Should I try a different SSRI?
Answer: Probably not. Though most people find any SSRI more harmful than helpful, there are a minority of people who find at least one SSRI more helpful than harmful. The more bad SSRI reactions you have, the less likely you are to be one of those uncommon people. If you are completely set on using drugs, two really bad SSRI reactions usually means it is time to try a different kind of drug instead of a third SSRI. Possibly something other than a reuptake inhibitor, and maybe even something non-psychiatric. There are many factors to consider when navigating these choices, like what you want a drug to do, whether there are any underlying medical conditions to address, whether there are any lingering drug effects from past regimens, what your CP450 test says about your metabolic abilities with respect to these kinds of drugs, what kind of services and drugs you can afford, and so forth. Management is also an important element, as sometimes bad reactions are the result of poor tapering practices or giving someone too high of a dose. The specific reactions you had to the escitalopram and sertraline and the reasons behind them are worth considering when deciding where to go from here, but the bottom line is that most patients with this history will do best on a drug other than an SSRI if they insist on using drugs, and most patients will be best off without using any of these drugs at all if they are open to that possibility and have the support to make proper use of non-drug strategies. You need to be learning about your options and discussing with your clinicians.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do antidepressants make your body weaker and more prone to death?
Answer: Basically, but nothing is quite that simple. The drugs marketed as “antidepressants” have a wide range of actions, none of which are universal to all drugs in the marketing class. Even focusing on subsets, like reuptake inhibitors, will still yield variation between drugs. Keeping this in mind, all these drugs do stop the body from working correctly and possess toxic mechanisms and this can have an adverse effect on overall health and on susceptibility to many medical concerns. They can also cause directly life-threatening effects. These drugs alter everything from our hormonal regulation to our immune functioning to our sleep and can be toxic to many vital organs. But, by the same basic means, they also make some health conditions less likely to happen. Changing how the body works and what can colonize it will impact what health conditions we can be less susceptible to. Some of these drugs have even been studied as medical treatments for dangerous health conditions like cancer because of their toxicity. So, yes, these are harmful drugs which cause problems in the body and make us more vulnerable to many problems and even to death, however it is not a strictly unidirectional influence — even toxic drug mechanisms can involve a protective factor against some health threats. They will not be providing a net health benefit, but it is important to recognize the complexity of how altering the body’s functioning can affect health, both in the short term and longer term.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can taking an antidepressant like Prozac for an extended period of time have negative effects if one does not have a history of depression or anxiety?
Answer: These drugs are bad for the brain, period. These drugs are toxic and disruptive and innately have a bad effect on the nervous system. They are bad for us, this is not avoidable. Longer uses are worse for us than shorter uses, higher doses worse than lower doses. Individual reactions vary, of course. Someone’s reason for using drugs does not make them any more or less toxic, and having no reason to use drugs at all does not remove their risks. There are factors which can increase susceptibility to certain drug mechanisms or effects, but simply having no history of depression or anxiety does not confer any protection from the harmful effects of drugs like SSRIs.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can psychiatrists be wrong when diagnosing someone with depression or bipolar disorder? How do they determine if the symptoms are not caused by a physical issue?
Answer: Psychiatric diagnoses aren’t right or wrong in that sense. No Right Or Wrong Unlike standard medical diagnoses, which usually state a specific physical problem or pathology which we can then either prove or disprove is correct, psychiatric diagnoses can’t be right or wrong. They aren’t making statements about physical reality, like something going on in the patient’s body or there being a pathology there. We have no way to physically validate or invalidate them, as they make no physical claims. Psychiatric diagnoses are just labels of convenience, like saying “those experiences there” instead of specifying why the experiences are happening or how they are happening in any physical sense. The nature and function of psychiatric diagnoses are thus very different from standard medical diagnoses. Indeed, we can know nothing about a patient’s current experiences or what kind of help they might need or how they will react to interventions on the basis of their diagnosis. This is opposite how diagnoses usually work — usually, the point of a diagnosis is to supply at least some of that information so clinical decisions can be made effectively and documented efficiently. Psychiatry invents their own set of rules for how diagnoses are supposed to be applied, so there is still the possibility of misdiagnosis in the sense of a clinician not properly following those (ever-changing) rules. But, it is actually not expected that they follow the rules — most don’t, not in full and in earnest, and nobody is going to get in trouble for not following the rules. To the contrary, psychiatry gets a lot more business and pharmaceutical manufacturers make a lot more money when psychiatric diagnoses are applied sloppily and without proper qualification. If psychiatrists were actually performing due diligence to rule out physical issues, a huge amount of patients would be shifted out of the psychiatric system and there would be incredible demand for physicians who treat the most commonly misdiagnosed issue: psychiatric drug effects. As it stands right now, no doctors typically specialize in or more generally diagnose and treat psychiatric drug effects. Non-psychiatrists will usually point you back to psychiatrists, who caused the problem in the first place and were trying to claim it’s “mental illness”. Differential Diagnosing How should clinicians distinguish psychological concerns from medical problems? Psychiatric diagnoses are what are known as “diagnoses of exclusion”, which means other possibilities first need to be thought up, tested for, and ruled out. There are countless dozens of medical conditions which can cause any or all of the experiences meeting the diagnostic criteria for psychiatric diagnoses. A physician or other practitioner has to systematically review those possibilities and find a way of ruling them in or out. This involves things like a physical and psychological evaluation, including an exam, a basic neurological assessment, compiling a patient history and limited family history, plus broad as well as narrow testing (like a blood panel looking for common endocrinological and infectious issues associated with the experiences reported). It is a process which will require multiple appointments, a lot of questions, and tracking down leads and abnormalities. Injuries, congenital conditions, nutritional deficiencies, drug effects, infections, and acquired medical disorders all must be ruled out. Note that “depression” is an inclusive clinical term and applies both to many medical conditions and to many psychological designations. “Depression” is a diagnosis of inclusion rather than exclusion, so someone’s experiences meeting the criteria and there not being a more appropriate way to categorize those experiences (such as based on additional criteria being met for another issue) will mean the label is appropriate no matter the cause. A medical or psychological cause does not need to be established for us to know someone is experiencing depression. “Bipolar disorder”, on the other hand, is a very specific subset of psychiatric diagnoses. Some bipolar depressions are included in those diagnoses, some are not. Manias without depression can also be included, so there are not necessarily two poles to speak of despite the name of the diagnosis. Like with other psychiatric diagnoses, “bipolar disorder” is only an acceptable diagnosis per the rules if all medical causes have already been properly ruled out. Tails I Win, Heads You Lose The tricky thing about psychiatry is that no physical findings can actually disprove a psychiatric diagnosis. Even if a clinician uncovers a medical problem that would perfectly explain a patient’s symptoms, a psychiatrist can still insist that there is a “psychiatric disorder” instead and that the medical problem is unrelated. So, not only can psychiatrists ignore the key criterion of first ruling out medical problems before applying a psychiatric diagnosis, they can also disregard any medical findings that come in later. If a patient isn’t going to stand up and say “fuck you, your ideas are stupid”, there is no real counter to the psychiatrist’s mindgame. They will continue to label and drug and shock and do whatever else to a patient so long as the patient allows it, and they may also try to get the government to lock a patient up or commit them to forced ‘treatment’ if the patient decides their psychiatrist is the problem and they find other medical professionals more convincing. This is a special privilege of psychiatrists which other kinds of doctors cannot do. What if a psychiatrist was wrong to apply a diagnosis because they didn’t follow psychiatry’s rules for diagnosing? Nothing, but if they aren’t willing to adjust their thinking or their labeling and you aren’t finding them helpful, it is your responsibility to leave them. There are still phrenologists out there who will happily take your money, after all. What if a psychiatrist said there wasn’t a medical disorder but there ended up being one, whether because the psychiatrist didn’t bother to look properly or because new evidence came to light later? Again, it is the responsibility of the patient to seek the most qualified professional they can and to decide whose process they find most reasonable or helpful. A psychiatrist may or may not admit the truth of someone’s situation, and may or may not make appropriate recommendations for how to proceed. Many people think there is a level of accountability to psychiatric claims and behaviors that is simply not there. We are the front line protection against abuses and lies. While some bad behavior may be reportable, the psychiatric system itself is built foremost on grifting and trickery, so patients who want better help will usually have to take that step independently.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do I find professional help in withdrawing from antidepressants?
Answer: Search for doctors experienced patients already endorse. The vast majority of clinicians are not educated and experienced enough with antidepressant withdrawal management that they would be worth hiring. They could very easily give you bad advice which puts you in danger or sets back your recovery from antidepressants. Almost everyone you encounter going to a hospital, getting referrals within your networks, or taking names from insurance company rosters will be lacking the kind of expertise required to properly help patients going off and withdrawing from antidepressants or other psychiatric drugs. Research-based standards aren’t in place, educational programs are rare and optional, and clinicians are fed a steady stream of false information and bad advice by drug companies and other special interest parties. It is an important and very understandable question that you ask and something relevant to all patients ever prescribed a psychiatric drug, even for non-psychiatric reasons. Both because most doctors would be inappropriate to see and because experts are often more visible than their peers, the best way to get good quality support for antidepressant withdrawal is databases created by patients and personal recommendations from patients. Your prescriber or GP is very unlikely to have a good recommendation for you, though that doesn’t mean to not bother asking at all. Also keep in mind that the needs and reactions of individual patients will vary, so advice which is bad enough to put one patient in the hospital may still not cause much of an issue for another — shitty physician management doesn’t always end in disaster, so even an idiot may not totally derail your recovery. Not all clinicians who are good or expert will be personally or philosophically compatible, either, meaning we have to have more parameters for selecting than just “knows what they’re talking about”, sometimes. Three examples of provider directories that I’m aware of are linked below. The most organic and relevant is the first link, taken from the world class antidepressant withdrawal support forum Surviving Antidepressants. None of these directories are anything close to complete and comprehensive, and sometimes there will be clinicians which may not provide the expertise or bedside manner needed. Nevertheless, I’ve never seen a more helpful listing of providers myself, and I have performed a systematic review of resources available in my own area, covering hundreds of psychiatrists and psychiatric facilities and networks, multiple insurance provider networks, all United Way materials I could obtain, and asking all sources I contact if they can recommend any other leads to check out. Good help remains difficult to find, and potentially impossible to pay for if you’re in a country like the US. Still, awareness is increasing over time and patients themselves are more attuned than before to some of the dangers involved.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does lithium "stabilize" mood by making people feel dull, flat and depressed?
Answer: Kinda, sure. “Stabilize” in this context means restricting the brain from operating normally in ways which can also limit our emotional range and responsiveness. Drugs like lithium aren’t fixing the brain or tweaking our functioning in a way that only affects experiences like mania or hypomania. All psychiatric drugs are causing altered states 24/7 and have actions which are not selective to particular experiences or particular processes in the brain. They are all globally acting and can affect all our experiences. Individual reactions to psychotropic drugs are variable and unique. For many patients, this restrictive influence on aspects of neurological functioning can lead to a very obvious dulling effect, or even be depressive. There is no “free lunch”, pharmacologically speaking. What that means is that if we want to restrict what someone can experience, the mechanisms we use to impose that restriction will impact their everyday experiences and can involve any number of undesirable downsides. Not all adverse drug effects will be caused by the same actions as we are relying on for hoped drug upsides, but there will always be undesirable effects caused by the drug mechanisms which can also produce desirable effects. The type of lithium used, the dose and dosing schedule, and other adjustable aspects of a lithium regimen may affect how someone feels while using it. Chronic use is also liable to change how someone is feeling on it, as some drug changes are progressive.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the difference between depression caused by a chemical imbalance and mental issues?
Answer: Your question states the only difference. There are many different kinds of and causes of depression. Some causes are medical, others are psychological. Though it is a deliberately ambiguous concept usually employed in pseudoscientific marketing instead of legitimate medical discussions, “chemical imbalance” may be a fair description of a certain subset of medical causes, like drug toxicity, problems with neurotransmitter synthesis, various seizure disorders, many endocrinological disorders, and so forth. Though some very specific causes can have dimensional traits that make them easier to identify based on the experiences reported by patients, there are no distinctions between so-called “chemical imbalance” depressions and psychologically driven depressions which would allow us to distinguish between them on the basis of the experiences reported. Both refer to a whole range of varying experiences which are not distinct as depressions. Specifying a cause is the only causally-related distinction here.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the relationship between antidepressants and herbs for depression?
Answer: The relationship is that some drugs are herbs and some drugs are not. “Antidepressants” is a marketing class of drugs containing an unbounded variety of drugs with differing pharmacological actions. Any drugs can be added to this category at any time, including herbal drugs. None of the countless actions these drugs have are what make any of these drugs “antidepressants”, and the same actions are found in herbal drugs as well as synthetic ones. The most relevant difference between herbs and synthetics is that synthetics typically have just one main active chemical and then a uniformized delivery vehicle whereas herbs are prepared for use to maintain appropriate dosing and contents but can contain any number of pharmacologically important chemicals. This is an artifact of how the mainstream economy works, not what is more effective, less dangerous, or providing better outcomes overall. The range of herbal drugs, and their respective sets of mechanisms, used for depression far exceed the much narrower collection of drugs currently marketed as “antidepressants”. So, in that respect there is very little overlap despite there being an enormous overlap in drug activities (like reuptake inhibition, reuptake enhancement, agonism, antagonism, releasing, monoamine oxidase inhibition, and so forth). A key distinction holding to date is that “antidepressants” as typically defined only contains psychotropic drugs whereas herbal drugs for depression may or may not be psychotropic. Nutritional supplementation, for example, is an herbal therapy for depression (most notably depressions with a medical root) which can be highly effective but has no analogue in antidepressants. Synthetic supplements are their non-herbal counterpart.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do people really experience an improvement in their mood when they start to take anti-depressant medications?
Answer: Some people do, most people don’t. Numbing is more common, particularly with reuptake inhibitors. There are a few caveats to address here, though. Most people don’t find antidepressants to be particularly mood-lifting, and some mood-lifting effects are actually adverse reactions, like euphoria or hypomania. However, most people using these drugs aren’t looking for improved mood anyhow — they are taking drugs for any number of other reasons, like anxiety, tics, neuropathic pain, migraines, sleep problems, etc. If we looked only at depression patients, we still see that the average person does not experience any mood improvements from antidepressants not also occurring with placebo, though. But, this partly also depends on what we consider “an improvement in mood”. Some people consider emotional flattening, as is typical with antidepressants, to be an improvement. Some people experience a better mood just by curbing overwhelming anxiety, or getting more sleep. Antidepressants aren’t really “mood improving” agents, but there are means by which they can indeed lead to improvements in mood, whether in the earliest days of use or after weeks of continuous use. Adverse mood reactions are more likely, like mood swings, apathy, suicidality, etc, but individual experiences vary a lot.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are there any pros and cons to taking medication for mood disorders like depression or bipolar disorder?
Answer: There are pros and cons to all drug use. As this is just a shitty spam question meant to increase ad revenue, there isn’t much else to say. All drug use involves potential upsides and downsides. That applies to psychotropic drugs, and to psychiatric drugs more specifically. That applies to all people, not just patients and not just patients experiencing unipolar or bipolar depressions. No drugs offer benefits without risks, and no drugs feature only downsides and no upsides. Deciding what matters and how to manage the dangers involved is the real trick and is part of how we separate ‘drugs’/‘medications’ from plain everyday chemicals in the first place.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How can you differentiate between a mental illness and actual existence when someone is experiencing hallucinations?
Answer: There is no such distinction. If someone is experiencing hallucinations, there is nothing you can do to ascertain whether that person has received a psychiatric diagnosis. There is nothing about hallucinations which would be able to tell you that, and “mental illness” doesn’t cause hallucinations. What you say is an hallucination versus a shared reality depends on your definitions, and you can apply those definitions to come to a conclusion about whether you are thinking there is hallucinating going on at all, but that is already implied by your question.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can people keep getting prescribed antidepressants indefinitely by going back and forth between different psychiatrists?
Answer: That is typically unnecessary. Most psychiatrists a patient could see would happily prescribe them antidepressants forever. No need to duck out and see a second or third prescriber, much less maintain some sort of secrecy about it all. The main reason people don’t stick with the same prescriber for antidepressants over time is because the system is so fucked they can’t keep seeing the same doctor — they either can’t get an appointment or can’t afford an appointment. A lot of prescribing falls onto GPs and other less-suited clinicians, not that the average psychiatrist does a great job of prescribing and managing these drugs in the first place. It is an atypical psychiatrist who would tell a patient to quit their antidepressant, and saying they will flat out cut the patient off sooner or later would be even more unusual. People wanting to use antidepressants for the rest of their lives should have little to no trouble finding a single psychiatrist to supply them. Some psychiatric places are so swamped patients don’t even see a psychiatrist and get their prescription from a PharmD or NP or other practitioner. Many of these folks will be more interested in maintaining the status quo of prescribing than suggesting drug cessation when appropriate. But, can someone bounce around between multiple prescribers simultaneously or in sequence to maintain a supply of drugs just one prescriber would not provide? Of course, people do that all the time, usually to obtain more recreationally viable drugs like benzodiazepines or stimulants. Antidepressants have very little value or street value once generic, as most of them are, and someone lucky (or unlucky) can potentially find a hookup that lets them have free pills for life, even, via clinician sample packs.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it necessary to have a bipolar diagnosis if you do not experience any symptoms?
Answer: What? Diagnoses are never ‘necessary’ unless there is something someone wants to accomplish which requires a diagnosis. Things like insurance reimbursement, drug trial participation, or certain social support programs may require a diagnosis, likely a specific one, but aside from those kinds of situations, there is no value to having a diagnosis. It is never necessary, and tells us nothing about what someone is experiencing or why.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How long does it take for an SSRI to become effective after the consumption of alcohol stops?
Answer: Drugs don’t become effective. That is to say, SSRIs are doing whatever they do, period. Whether someone is drinking or not, whether someone is depressed or not, whether someone is taking them for a day, a week, or a month, SSRIs have the same actions and influences. Our responses can vary, depending on a whole slew of factors, and combining psychotropic drugs will usually lead to a different outcome as compared to using only one drug by itself, but the relationship between this as what someone considers “effectiveness” is a lot less defined. What we consider “drug efficacy” is totally open-ended — it can be anything we want it to be, and will be something different to each patient. Whether or not someone’s idea of effectiveness is reasonable will vary, and most people are never able to meet their clinical goals using SSRIs because SSRIs too seldom cause the changes people are hoping for. In that sense you could consider most ideas of efficacy unreasonable, or you could just figure SSRIs are usually a failure so expectations must be tempered even if the goals are reasonable. Someone quitting alcohol and using SSRIs will likely notice immediate changes in their experiences, whether subtle or substantial, because quitting alcohol is usually noticeable and using SSRIs is usually noticeable. Whether any of the changes are something someone actually wants is more personal. SSRIs are always just doing whatever they do, but the more we change our circumstances of use, and the more we continue to take a drug which causes progressive alterations in our brains, the more likely we are to see alterations, whether desired or undesired.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the chemical process behind the effectiveness of antidepressants?
Answer: There is no such thing, Mr Spambot. “Effectiveness of antidepressants” is a variably and subjectively defined idea with no particular underlying process. Clinically speaking, “effective” just means causing changes in how someone is thinking, feeling, or behaving that society, the prescriber, or the patient were wanting. There are innumerable ‘hows’ as to the way these changes can be brought about, and the very same changes can be desirable in one patient but adverse reactions in another. The whole idea of “antidepressant efficacy” as a measurable and uniform phenomenon is a marketing myth, not a pharmacological reality. It exists as a concept to facilitate the drug and psychiatric industries but has no scientific basis. We know scientifically that these drugs are doing all sorts of things in the nervous system and the rest of the body which can alter experiences, but none of them constitute “the effectiveness of antidepressants”. Even when we specify parameters for alterations we want to consider effectiveness in a particular situation, the underlying mechanisms involved tend to be incompletely understood, or lacking much outline at all. Since mechanisms are an integral part of marketing messages, drug companies opted to just invent some appealing lies in order to sell drugs better, and that decision is one of the most successful and profitable decisions ever made in the history of mankind.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it common for SSRIs to initially worsen symptoms?
Answer: The most common thing is for SSRIs to make someone feel worse but not better. Given that these drugs stop the brain from working correctly, adverse reactions are exceedingly more common than desirable reactions. This is not just an initial thing. Most adverse drug effects stick around or get worse, they aren’t just transient symptoms arising during drug initiation. But, there are symptoms more likely to fade than not (such as nausea, for instance), which can make the earliest weeks or months harder to tolerate or impossible to tolerate, particularly when someone is not properly tapered. Whether or not those are what you consider to “worsen” someone’s situation is more complex. These drugs typically cause anxiety or nervousness for at least a while, but that is only worsening pre-existing anxiety concerns if there are pre-existing anxiety concerns. Most patients aren’t taking these drugs for any one concern, like depression or anxiety. So, whether things like mood swings, apathy, sedation, impotence, or fatigue are grouped as “worsening” instead of entirely new drug problems depends on the variable context. In short, ‘bad’ effects are almost guaranteed to occur, ‘good’ effects are less common, but the uses of these drugs are very broad-ranging so the expectations involved will vary a lot. If someone reacts badly to a drug, they may or may not feel less bad later on, instead of just as bad or more bad. Someone reacting badly at first does not suggest they will experience desirable drug effects later on. They may or may not. No matter how long of a chance someone gives SSRIs, they are usually more harmful than helpful.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do antidepressants work? Do they only affect brain chemistry or do they also help with dealing with problems and improving overall well-being?
Answer: “Antidepressants” work by radically altering what is going on in the body. “Work” in this context just means a drug is causing altered states. There is no specific mechanism of efficacy, as people want these drugs to do any range of things, even contradictory things. Drugs like antidepressants don’t just affect brain chemistry, they affect the chemistry of the entire body. Every organ system is affected to some degree. Exactly what a drug does depends on the specific drug, as “antidepressant” provides no pharmacological specificity and is just a marketing class. Do these drugs “help with dealing with problems”? Inasmuch as any drug does. Someone feeling tired enough to sleep after drinking alcohol is receiving “help dealing with problems”, for instance. What about “improving overall well-being”? That is a subjective thing to assess, whether an experience is ‘better’ or ‘worse’. People can feel pretty great on heroin, but is that improving their well-being or just making them feel different for a short time? People get to decide that for themselves. What is considered desirable, good, or worth the tradeoff is ultimately a personal call.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is there a risk of developing depression from long-term use of anti-depressants?
Answer: Antidepressants are ‘depressogenic’. There are a variety of mechanisms to these drugs which can cause new, worsened, or prolonged depression. These mechanisms are a concern no matter who a patient is or why they were using drugs, or what their personal or family history has been. Non-psychiatric patients need to be just as cautious about these kinds of effects, and people with no history of depression can still be depressed by drug use. Drugs are pretty equal-opportunity when it comes to neurological dysfunction and adverse mental effects. These drugs are fundamentally pro-depressing in some key ways, and this will inevitably mean that some patients are made to be depressed by using them. It can be a reaction which comes on pretty early in use, but sometimes it is something that develops over a period of months or longer. In some cases, it is a reduction-emergent effect, such as part of a withdrawal syndrome. Some drugs and doses will be higher risk than others, but reactions are still somewhat unpredictable and occur across a spectrum. Because “depression” is itself a wide range of experiences with differing underlying physical and psychological dynamics, it is also relevant to emphasize that we aren’t talking about a singular kind of experience or drug reaction here. Some instances will be an apathy syndrome, others will involve things like low mood or dysphoria and fatigue, some people will experience anxiety or dread or dissociation as part of their drug symptoms while others won’t. The addling of the brain with antidepressants can cause a rich variety of adverse neuropsychological experiences with dimensions and nuances that can be as unique as each individual and situation.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do antidepressants work in managing negative thoughts and mood swings? Is blocking bad chemicals in the brain a possible alternative to taking antidepressants?
Answer: Q1. How do antidepressants work in managing negative thoughts and mood swings? Nobody knows. Now, we know for sure that these drugs stop the brain from working correctly, disrupting any number of processes and forcing the brain to rewire itself to keep us alive. This can have an enormous effect on things like cognition, memory, mood, awareness, wakefulness, dreaming, sexuality, etc. So, the broad answer to your question is just that these drugs disrupt brain functioning and lead to new functional states which may be experienced as different from how things were before. This is a bad thing, healthwise, and the effects are almost always considered deleterious, but there can also sometimes be ways to take advantage of them. Someone struggling with insomnia may appreciate sedation, for example, and someone with obsessive thinking might feel that cognitive impairment is a bit of a rest. It would be a mistake to think that any effects some patients report as desirable occur due to the same drug mechanism, or that the same mechanism will produce the same experiences in all patients. Q2. Is blocking bad chemicals in the brain a possible alternative to taking antidepressants? Antidepressants have nothing to do with “bad chemicals in the brain”, aside from how they are a bad chemical in the brain, when used. All the neurotransmitters and other things antidepressants act on, directly and indirectly, are good. All the hormones and other chemicals involved in thought, mood, insight, behavior. They are a part of the body’s natural functioning and their numerous roles are key to our wellbeing and our body’s daily operations. “Bad chemicals” would be things that get into the brain but which we don’t want there because they are causing issues, harming the brain. Psychotropic drugs such as antidepressants, toxic heavy metals, poisons, etc. If someone has a problem with these kinds of chemicals, whether symptoms include ‘negative thoughts and mood swings’, something generally needs to be done to keep them out of the brain, or remove them from the brain. That’s a medical concern, not a psychiatric one. As for the idea of ‘blocking’, antidepressants are already chemical blockers. They stop the brain from using chemicals like it is designed to, and this is the main way in which they exert a psychotropic effect. There are many different drug mechanisms, and each drug has its own unique collection of them, but the bottom line is that these drugs operate by interfering with our management of ‘good chemicals’. In fact, all methods of affecting our thoughts and feelings work by altering what is going on with our ‘good chemicals’.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What are the consequences of refusing medication for bipolar and schizophrenic patients?
Answer: Aside from the risk of psychiatric violence, there are no innate consequences. It is true that psychiatric drugs are extremely potent alterants and there will usually be a difference in someone’s life if they take them. This might be a good difference, a bad difference, or a mixed outcome. Adverse effects are far more common than desired ones, bad outcomes more common than good ones, and disability and death are usually elevated rather than decreased with the current use of these drugs. But, someone saying no to all the risks and potential upsides of drug use doesn’t create for them a life path. Anything can happen in the future, saying no to drugs doesn’t tell us what kind of life someone will have, much less what they will be doing to respond to whatever experiences they have. All the other factors involved are going to have to be considered if we want to know how a decision turns out. Given the framing of the question, it is hard to say stuff like “having emotions” and “not dying” are the kinds of consequences you were meaning to ask about. Plus, not everyone would experience the exact same adverse effects, so there are relatively few things we can say for sure someone was able to avoid by saying no to drugs. The simplest and most useful thing to know is just that neither the diagnoses you mention nor refusing psychiatric drugs will determine someone’s future, quality of life, or options for working towards their goals. Psychiatric labels aren’t psychic crystals, and they do more to convince people to be and seek to be impaired than not. Saying no to psychiatric drugs puts you in the crosshairs, though. Many will argue than anyone saying no to psychiatry must need psychiatry, anyone saying no to drugs must need drugs. There is no substance to these kinds of religious beliefs, but since the psychiatric religion shapes government policy, we are all under threat of psychiatric violence no matter how moronic the reasoning ends up being.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do people stop taking medication when they feel better, i.e., antidepressants or anti-anxiety medicines? Some don’t even bother to talk to their doctor first.
Answer: Because it seems logical. If someone takes a drug to accomplish a goal and then they accomplish that goal, why would they still keep taking that drug? If you are gambling your life savings to try and get together $1.5 million dollars to help your friend with serious medical bills, for example, you will stop at $1.5 million dollars in winnings instead of potentially losing everything just to continue gambling. You’ve done what you set out to do. Psychiatric drugs are dangerous and things turn out bad rather than good for the majority of patients. If someone feels better after use and wants to quit now that they do, that is the most reasonable and responsible conclusion to come to. The complication here is that psychotropic drugging isn’t that simple. Most notably, we don’t have the freedom to quit whenever we want because our bodies become physically dependent. Trying to go off a drug can be a pretty tricky thing, and someone can encounter severe adverse effects when quitting, or experience destabilization from the attempt. This is dangerous unto itself but also puts someone in the crosshairs of misdiagnosis, mistreatment, and pressure to keep using drugs forever even if that is the worst thing for them. Because most professionals are not honest or knowledgeable about these risks, most patients never know until it is too late either. Another complication is that we don’t always feel the same way forever, and if we aren’t taking into account our ability to sustainably respond to stressors, our goal of feeling a certain way by using drugs may not continue to be met into the future. This is the case even for patients who don’t quit drugs, but it is something to consider when the topic of when and how to transition off drugs is being discussed. Patients may often find an adjustment period necessary, as well, even aside from any withdrawal they might face, especially if they were using drugs for more than just a few weeks to a few months. Put most basically: indefinitely drug use is not the default, it must be carefully justified. Patients and prescribers need to provide very substantial and persuasive evidence that continuing drug use is the best possible option. That’s how evidence-based practice works, maintaining accountability, but it is also seldom that indefinite drug use is someone’s best option, as well. If we were to put no thought into the decisionmaking and simply treat all cases one way or another, the best net result would be if we eliminated indefinite prescribing. Luckily, we don’t have to throw anyone under the bus by ignoring the ability to reason with evidence whether continuing a drug is a good idea. Why do so many people quit without first talking to their doctor? That is perhaps an even more complex question with a variety of potential answers, such as:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it harder for antipsychotics to treat the negative symptoms over the positive types?
Answer: Harder? I don’t know if that is the best way to put it, no. The problem isn’t how “hard” or “easy” it is for antipsychotics to do something, the problem is that antipsychotics have particular mechanisms and that’s that. If those mechanisms bring about changes we are considering favorable, then great, success. If not, then we are using the wrong tool. Cars don’t have a harder time driving across the ocean, cars are, for the most part, simply not fucking boats. Your premise is that we are focused on an intended use. The marketing mythonarrative about antipsychotic use and the concept of “schizophrenia” involves the lie that these drugs medically treat something. That helps sell drugs, services, policies, and research but has no reality to it. These drugs are not treating some things and then failing to treat others, there is literally nothing to be treating and any effects experienced are the simple result of drug actions with no special medical relevance. Intentions for use must follow from the reality of mechanisms and reactions. Neuroleptics are great at impairing the brain, disrupting our ability to think, to remember, to emote, to even stay awake at all. This can have an obvious acute impact on experiences like psychosis, or insomnia. But, on the other hand, wanting an anhedonia-inducing drug to help someone not be anhedonic is asking to drive a car across the ocean. Antipsychotics are impairing, they’re sedating, but their mechanisms actively work against things like motivation, pleasure, verbalizing. We can’t chastise the drugs for not doing well enough, not trying hard enough. We are just fucking idiots if we think we can use them for things they have no pharmacological reason to reliably do. The marketing name “antipsychotic” misleads people into believing these drugs have a special place in “schizophrenia” and related diagnoses and intense marketing and social pressure push them on everyone as a failed coverall. If we are being honest, though, they’re simply one of numerous tools and have a narrow range of usefulness.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: When does antipsychotic induced akathisia from withdrawal go away?
Answer: There is no particular timeline. The dynamics behind an instance of akathisia can vary depending on the individual, their regimen, the situation of use and discontinuation, and all the medical and psychological factors which influence drug reactions. Lucky people get relief in just days, but it is not uncommon to have weeks of akathisia to one extent or another — hopefully low-grade, because high-grade is potentially literally unbearable. Months to years is less typical, but still something some patients struggle with. It is also variable whether someone is experiencing akathisia all the time or only some of the time, and how often it reoccurs across a longer scope of time. Akathisia brought on by drug cessation may or may not end when the core withdrawal symptoms fade away, which will usually take at least several months but can sometimes take far, far longer. Someone may also notice themselves more sensitive in the future to experiencing akathisia as a reaction to stressors, most notably drugs that cause akathsia, even if symptoms have fully abated. Proper management of discontinuation and potentially seeking medical and psychological intervention for emergent akathisia may help curb symptom severity and duration. People in the throes of akathisia are recommended to seek personal support, even just as a palliative measure.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I was on an SSRI for 8 years. Is my brain damaged?
Answer: Yes, but it is important not to be hasty in deciding what that means. These drugs are fundamentally toxic to the brain, so 8 years of use would damage anyone’s brain. That’s par for the course. But, the level and extent of damage to expect and whether that produces noticeable symptoms or vulnerabilities to stressors is a much more complicated matter. We know these drugs are not friendly to the nervous system, and will be harming cell parts and even killing cells, but, alongside that influence, the brain is constantly rewiring and adapting as well, attempting to mitigate the harmful effects of SSRIs and adjusting around anything else going on in someone’s life as well. So, changes are guaranteed, damages are guaranteed, but how does someone actually feel? After 8 years, someone will probably never feel and function exactly like they did before SSRI use. Too much has been changed, reworked, or lost. But, this is not primarily a concern over brain damage, as the most common forms of damage from these drugs will be very smallscale rather than the loss of huge portions of tissue like you might see after a stroke or TBI. There are more extreme situations where more severe brain damage occurs, often as a result of drug reactions like toxidromes, hemorrhage, stroke, or even accidents like falls. But without an extreme drug reaction, one would anticipate only a modest loss off tissue, if any obvious loss at all. And this doesn’t get very precisely into symptoms, still. The wide array of potentially lasting drug symptoms following SSRI use are increasingly documented, but it remains unclear which are definitively a result of damages and which are more about disorder and deleterious brain changes caused by drugging. Many people associate experiences like cognitive impairment, memory loss, apathy, etc with brain damage because they involve the brain, but SSRIs are perfectly capable of causing these kinds of harms, even indefinitely, without damage. If a patient has no particular complaints about drug effects after a thorough and educated review, the question of damages is somewhat secondary — the practical concerns of daily functioning and quality of life take precedent. It is great to avoid damages when possible (though living life in general wears on the brain to an extent), and it is great to avoid SSRI use when possible, and to keep doses as low and brief as possible if drug use is to occur. But, the presence or absence of damages also does not determine whether someone is feeling okay or not. If this question was meant to communicate that there are symptoms which are causing problems after years of SSRI use, those symptoms need to be addressed on their own terms, especially since we may not understand their exact mechanisms still and even if we saw there was damage at their root that wouldn’t necessarily tell us someone’s prognosis or options for recovery.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I’m going into my 11th-grade year of high school, and I want to be someone underclassmen can trust, rely on, and feel safe with. Does anyone have any advice on ways I could make younger students more comfortable around me?
Answer: It is as much about what you don’t do as what you do. The obvious stuff, like being honest, straightforward, thoughtful, even-tempered, and empathetic, is a given. I think there are some boundaries or aspirations which will be more informative, like: Conversely, there are also some “do” things besides just having decent character, such as:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I’m 14. I have snorted molly for the past 2 days and I feel really depressed today. When will my serotonin rise again?
Answer: Hopefully you will start feeling better in days to weeks.
