The problem isn’t a fall in serotonin per se, but ignoring that, MDMA can be rather exhausting on the brain, and all the more if you try to make it hit harder by snorting it. The harder you party with a drug like molly, the more likely you are to have an intense and prolonged period of recovery. Some experienced partiers start having rules about how often to roll, including not taking molly two days in a row. This becomes all the more important as we get older or we stress our system with years of drug use and other stresses (like staying up all night, potentially without adequate food or water, for instance). If you really are 14 and are asking this question, it suggests you’re not in a position to be doing molly. Aside from it being inadvisable at that age regardless, if you don’t have a good education about the effects, risks, comedown, and management of molly then you should not be taking it in the first place. If you don’t have good online resources or helpful communitymembers locally, start building up your knowledge before continuing with experimentation. It is much easier to prevent a housefire than try and save your house after it is half burned down. It is typical, though not universal, to get the blues as part of coming down from molly. The nervous system needs time to readjust to a different way of functioning and we can feel dysphoric, apathetic, fatigued in the meantime. Different people bounce back at different rates, and this bounce back tends to slow as we get older and older. Though sometimes there are preventative steps to take which can reduce the intensity of length of the comedown period, there is no avoiding the possibility that a rehabilitation period is necessary. Ideally, it is just a day or three of feeling low, but some people are hit harder and require a week or longer to get back to normal. Dosing and sensitivity, along with health and a variety of other factors, can impact what happens. Whether someone sees immediate progress in this symptom or only a slow and gradual improvement is variable and, like with any drugs, we have to learn our own responses and respect our body. Like with most drugs that hype you up, solid aftercare can help with the intensity and uncomfortableness of comedown symptoms.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: My doctor put me on Prozac for depression, anxiety, and an eating disorder. 8 consider myself an emotional person. If Prozac emotionally numbs me, will I ever be able to go back to the way I was before?
Answer: Emotional numbing from SSRIs is typically partially or even fully reversible. Individual reactions vary, and the course of recovery can vary across patients and situations, but the bottom line is that emotional numbing is usually reversible to some degree. Some patients may never be quite as sharp and responsive as they were before drug use, some may feel good as new, and a small minority remain highly numbed indefinitely, long after everyone else has seen progress in their condition. The specific mechanisms involved and someone’s health and history may play a role in their susceptibility to this drug effect and their ability to recover from it if it occurs. If you are concerned about this effect, or it being lasting, that emphasizes the need to start ‘low and slow’ on any SSRI. Avoiding unnecessarily high doses and keeping the tapering stresses lower can reduce the riskiness or help someone detect this problem earlier so it can be responded to immediately. It is also worth mentioning that how we approach recovery can potentially impact the receding of symptoms, as there can be factors which interfere with recovery or end up being counterproductive. Just quitting the causal drug is not all we can do to promote recovery from that drug, and the use of other drugs can complicate things.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why am I experiencing severe memory loss, derealization, confusion, coldness, nervousness, and feeling outside of myself with pressure in the brain? My doctor switched me from Xanax 1.5 to cymbalta 60 mgs but it is causing extreme fatigue.
Answer: The best and most likely explanation at a glance is benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome. Going off a benzodiazepine, such as Xanax, is liable to cause any number of symptoms like these, particularly for patients who have been taking it for at least 1–2 weeks straight. A personalized taper, slow and gradual, is often necessary to reasonably transition off the drug, whether or not it is being replaced by another drug. This is all the more important if the drug being switched to doesn’t have the same basic actions. Cymbalta is not a benzodiazepine. But, just because a reaction to reducing or discontinuation the Xanax is the most obvious and most likely explanation here, it is not the only possibility and there is no way anyone on Quora could do all the doctory stuff that needs to be done to sort out which possibility is the right one in this case. There is no escaping the necessity of seeking professional support to properly rule in or out explanations and manage your discontinuation more appropriately. It could be your current doctor is not adequate, but not enough information is provided.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it true that ECT can cause retrograde amnesia and make you forget many years of the past?
Answer: Yes, sadly. ECT, like other significant seizures, can have a broad-ranging negative effect on memory. Short-term and long-term memory can both be affected. Things like names, learned skills, and languages can be affected, it isn’t just ‘episodic memories’ (the stuff we play back kind of like a movie to review events in our life and how we felt or thought during them). Sometimes people feel to lose chunks of time, sometimes what is lost is spotty. The specific type of and calibrating settings for the ECT and the number of sessions can affect how likely particular losses are. ECT can temporarily or permanently take away memories and can also interfere with the formation of new memories in the future. It is not just past experiences to be concerned about. The degree of loss, type of loss, scope of loss, and permanence of loss will all vary by patient and situation. All persons considering ECT need to be advised about how commonly amnesia occurs and how it is also very common for losses to be partially or fully irreversible. The bottom line is that inducing seizures isn’t good for the brain and we will always pay a price in brain health and functioning when causing them.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Has there been a "dumbing down" of mental illnesses, such that a person of the general population is now casually prescribed Abilify or Seroquel under the assumption they're part of a "psych-population" distant from the prescribing nurse's origin?
Answer: Well, here are some facts, but they require context: These two facts do have some overlap, but the primary culprits are not the ones stated in those two facts. The industrialization of psychiatric prescribing is a big factor here, both in the volume and range of prescribing and also in how diagnoses are defined and applied and what the clinical dogma is about responding to them. Our cultural situation, in terms of how we view suffering, psychiatry, psychiatric drugging, social acceptance, emotional wellbeing, and agency, is pretty fucked. We have built a world where psychiatric predation is an extremely profitable enterprise and has social and political goals tied into it, not just industrial goals. So, on one hand, yes, the idea of “mental illness” has been increasingly broadened and also increasingly leveraged for financial gain. But on the other hand, psychiatric drug prescribing was never hinging on that — prescribing is its own concern. The more accusations of “mental illness” there are floating around and the more people that can be convinced to believe marketing lies about when and how to use drugs, the more prescribing balloons, but prescribing is on the rise regardless. A ton of psychiatric drug prescribing is to non-psychiatric patients or for non-psychiatric purposes, and diagnoses aren’t the gateway to psychiatric drugging, prescribers are. Overall, the distinction between so-called “mental illness” and so-called “non-psychiatric population” has melted away more than ever before. This is especially with the popularity of considering psychiatric diagnoses “forever diagnoses” and coupling that with the statement that most people or everyone will qualify for at least one diagnosis sooner or later. The industry has effectively given the impression that drugs are the primary or even exclusive tool for social and personal betterment and that everyone should be considered a viable target. This has been very deliberate but also comes with a momentum of its own, facilitated in part by the broader social context I mentioned. “Mental illness” is an accusation leveled more widely, more freely, and more incoherently than any time previous, but the parties involved would happily continue the ever-increased drugging of the world’s population even if diagnoses were thrown into the trashbin overnight. The agendas support each other, but are not determining of each other.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is depersonalization and derealization a side effect of Lexapro?
Answer: Dissociation is a risk of all drugs like escitalopram, yes. SSRIs, including Lexapro, and most any other psychiatric drugs can cause dissociation, both as an effect of actively using the drug and as a reduction-emergent effect. This includes depersonalization, derealization, and other forms of dissociation. Some kinds of reactions will be more common than others, and how often dissociation happens can also depend on factors like the dose, duration of use, management strategies (most importantly tapering speed), someone’s health, any other drugs being used, someone’s propensity to dissociate, and so on. Patients with a history of dissociation should be cautious with psychotropic drugs in general, but since there are differing causes for dissociation, stressors that are triggers for one person may not be so for another, or may even reduce the incidence of dissociation (for instance if strong emotions are a trigger for someone and a drug is emotionally blunting). No special medical or psychological history is required to experience dissociation with an SSRI, nor is any predisposition implied by that kind of reaction. It is not a rare effect of drug use or drug discontinuation, but is not guaranteed to happen by any stretch, either, even if someone is more susceptible.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it credible that after a mental trauma a person got mild hallucinations and delusions, got better without meds and then got a serious worsening of symptoms? (see my comment below for important details of this question)
Answer: It would make sense for trauma-oriented hallucinations or delusions to continue to be responsive to psychological stressors. When psychological stress becomes so overwhelming that we experience what some regard as psychosis, that has implications for our future experiences. It means perhaps we will be more vulnerable to stresses for a while, or that how we respond to that initial instance or episode can shape how we respond to stressors in the future. If these experiences are oriented around trauma, it would make sense for them to get better with an improvement in circumstances and some self-care and then reappear or worsen if there are stressors introduced or ramped up. The initial cause of these experiences is also not the limit of what can stress us, so some people may find additional stressors to still be relevant (like psychotropic drugs, inadequate sleep, poor nutrition, excessive exercise).

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are Olanzapine withdrawals life-threatening?
Answer: Olanzapine withdrawals are very commonly severe but not usually outright life-threatening. As with any neuroleptics, olanzapine innately has some fatal risks. These can involve a variety of organ systems and encompass many different mechanisms, when mechanisms are known at all. Reduction-emergent drug effects share this general pool of life-threatening risks, and some will be more common with discontinuation than with general use while others will be less common with discontinuation than ongoing use. Most withdrawal effects are not going to be life-threatening and most patients will not be on the verge of death even if they unwisely cold turkey olanzapine. But, life-threatening risks are usually less of a concern here than serious effects which are not necessarily immediately threatening someone’s life. For example, disability, long-term harm, personal and social losses, and exposure to misdiagnosing and mismanaging are key dangers that are far more commonly experienced. In antipsychotic withdrawal, some of the most common ways in which drug effects may threaten someone’s life include things like heart rhythm problems, akathisia (which is a major suicide risk), neuropsychological crisis (psychosis, mania, etc which may result in dangerous behavior), seizures, and accidents or falls from disorienting drug effects like sleep deprivation, dizziness, blood pressure issues, cognitive impairment.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is sweating a byproduct of taking lexapro. No other antidepressant does this. What is it about lexapro?
Answer: Excessive sweating is a risk of all these kinds of drugs. Sweating (sweating more than usual, sweating in areas of the body you didn’t before, night sweats, etc) is actually one of the most common reactions to drugs like escitalopram (aka Lexapro). But, as you say, not everyone will respond to every drug with the same reaction even though it is a risk with all of them. It is not always clear why this reaction happens at all, so it is potentially even less scrutable why some patients avoid it when switching to a different drug which has the same basic actions, like moving between various SSRIs or SNRIs. If someone finds a particular drug to be triggering but not other drugs with shared actions, I would look at their medical history and current circumstances, any other drugs they might be taking, what their diet is, their dose and dosing schedule, and get a CP450 test run to see what their metabolic management of the drug might be like. It is possible that minor differences between drugs are enough to cause this problem, whether alone or in combination with other risks factors that would be revealed through assessing factors like the ones I just mentioned.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: On what point will a psychologist tell you to get antidepressants?
Answer: Any point. Psychologists hold any number of views about when antidepressant use is appropriate or to be brought up or recommended. Some will think it should never be a recommendation, others think nearly everyone who sees them should take one. Most will fall between those two extremes. There are a lot of personal value judgements involved, as well as differences and nuances based on education and past experiences, plus what kind of clientele they serve. This all applies to actual antidepressant prescribers, too. Keep in mind that a psychologist’s ability to provide aid should be separate from when they recommend antidepressants. Someone might be needing support or intervention that a practitioner is unable to provide, but that does not suggest drug use is the logical next step. Conversely, some psychologists work extensively with patients who are on drugs and will make adjustments to their practice to accommodate this or maximize the upsides of drug use. Antidepressants have pretty intense limitations. They usually fail, as typically used, some of their downsides are pretty risky, and they can be counterproductive instead of just being either helpful or neutral. They provide no medical remedy to experiences like depression, and have no special relevance. They can impede psychotherapy for many patients, though they can make it more possible for others. Sometimes, people never even need to see a psychologist until they experience adverse drug effects. But, when will a psychologist tell their patient to get antidepressants? That depends entirely upon the psychologist.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can I be denied ADHD meds for too much THC?
Answer: That is up to each prescriber. Prescribers are the ones deciding when to prescribe and will be responsible for their prescribing, insofar as anyone is. It is a question of individual preference. Some prescribers don’t want to work with patients who use cannabinoid products, some are okay with it, some will only be okay with it in certain situations. There is no way to know beforehand what any specific doctor will be okay with, and you may be told one thing one day and then a totally different thing later on so be aware that what you share and who you trust can impact and maybe threaten the reliable management of anything you get prescribed. If your doctor wants to drug test you before prescribing Adderall, as your post says, that may or may not even involve a test for THC, and if it does, it will not likely report a specific concentration. Preliminary drug testing is generally pass/fail, and fails are supposed to be tested with more precise methods which can confirm a positive result or expose it as a false positive. Testing for THC concentration is a more complicated thing and has no particular value to a prescriber in these circumstances. Plus, blood or urine concentration will depend on more than just how much cannabis or cannabinoid products were used. Because responsible drug prescribing and management would have to take into account cannabinoid usage, I would foremost recommend finding a prescriber who can work with you as you are instead of someone demanding you to change things you already feel are working for you or who you cannot share vital details with because it might derail your ability to get professional consultation at all. If you aren’t sure where this new guy stands, research your ability to see a different provider and then, if there are alternatives, be frank with him about your concerns and switch to someone else if they shit the bed.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If I am switching from Fluoxetine to Mirtazapine, how quickly can I increase the Mirtzapine dose?
Answer: There is no single answer or equation to provide. There are three factors to account for, though: The same basic principles apply to cross-tapering as to normal tapering, though. Each individual has their own tolerable rate which may differ from what other patients can handle, circumstances can impact how tolerable or appropriate at rate is, and there is a need to distinguish between reduction-emergent adverse effects (such as withdrawal syndrome) and other influence (such as the initiation effects of a different drug, in this case). If someone is struggling with a particular rate of crossing over, the plan should be retooled. A minimum of a few months of cross-tapering should be anticipated, and some patients will require more time than that; sometimes much more time. Since responses vary, some patients can do a cold swap without symptoms while most will struggle to some extent and need to find a rate of reducing and uptapering which suits their own responses. Much depends on a combination of caution and adjusting to the responses of each individual as the taper proceeds. Someone’s history of drug responses, in addition to factors like health and psychological stability, should inform how much caution to use and how to interpret particular responses. In short, this is a risky but entirely common and reasonable maneuver which someone should seek informed professional support for. A Quora post can’t cut it, and there are logistic details to get into like how to even create the necessary doses. Someone being a prescriber doesn’t mean they must know how to taper well, and a lot of prescribers screw this up, but supplementing professional consultation with research online can improve your chances of successful swapping.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it true or untrue that if a person have voices inside his head but he doesn't hear them with the ears but with "the mind", they are still classified as hallucinations?
Answer: Perceiving voices without the expected accompanying external stimulus is usually considered hallucinating, yes. There is a tricky aspect to this, which is that all experiences are hallucinated in the sense that they are all made up in the mind and there is no direct importing of external phenomena to our internal perception. Anything we perceive through our senses is translated by our body and constructed into an improvised narrative in our brain. Being awake and dreaming while asleep operate pretty similarly, as we are generating our own perceptions in either case. We are always introducing things which are not directly derived from the outside world, and a lot of context and interpretation is required before we can perceive as we do and maintain a coherent consciousness. So if someone is speaking aloud, we don’t hear the soundwaves, we hear a phantasmagoric imagining. Basically, what goes on in our mind is always imaginary, whether or not there are specific external cues. If we are perceiving music, whether our ears are involved or not doesn’t change the fact that it is still relying on our imagination to be perceived. But, by saying hallucinations are perceptions which lack an expected external correlate, we are still stating a relationship which can have practicality. If you are hearing music and someone sitting next to you isn’t hearing that music, that is a helpful distinction. Whether you’re wearing headphones, or making up a song in your head, or are remembering music you’ve heard, your experience is different from theirs and acknowledging that difference can be helpful. If someone’s perception of voices seems to them like hearing outside sound or like a different kind of aural perception doesn’t necessarily change whether something is considered hallucinating. It can be a relevant detail, but ‘hearing voices’ is essentially referring to something similar to sensory perception by default. All the more since locative attribution of senses is somewhat cultural — not everyone perceives themselves as hearing from their ears, for instance. How we abstractly define our interactions with external and internal stimuli is very open to interpretation and to social influence. Whether a particular experience is considered hallucinating will depend on who is doing the defining and evaluating. A general answer is of no use, ultimately, since the specific application is what will make the determination.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do SSRIs have the potential to cause nerve damage?
Answer: Of course. SSRIs are neurotoxins at clinically prescribed doses, and below, so SSRIs cause neurotoxic effects. Not everyone will experience the same damages, severity or scope of damages, or symptoms as a result of damages, but these drugs have a very clear potential to cause nerve damage. Even in the information about drugs like SSRIs that pharmaceutical companies supply to the public in their pamphlets, nerve damage is usually mentioned very specifically, usually in the form of neuropathy and related terms. This is on top of the damages which can occur as a consequence of more sweeping adverse effects typically also warned about, like seizures, toxidromes, brain bleeds, or rarer effects like rhabdomyolysis, SJS/TEN. It is baffling that so many posters claiming to be professionals or knowledgeable about psychiatry are so totally oblivious to this established risk and sometimes even go so far as to try and explain it away as being the fault of patients if problems do occur. Given that the drug manufacturers themselves warn about effects which can cause nerve damage or effects which indicate nerve damage, there is no way to honestly defend SSRIs as being free of this risk. Such answers might as well be claiming that SSRIs also don’t cause impotence or apathy or serotonin syndrome either. It is ludicrous, and a scary showing of the dangerous quality of mainstream information on these drugs. There is plenty of room to debate how pervasive or how serious certain toxic influences are, or how often particular outcomes happen. Even whether particular symptoms are the result of damage rather than other drug alterations. There is a lot we still don’t know, and the mechanisms and prevalence of what we do see occurring are themselves still often at least partially unknown. In short, most of what we need studied is not given much attention and there is not much funding invested into clarifying these things because most research is oriented around marketing drugs more profitably. However, the issue of whether these drugs can cause nerve damage has been definitively settled and anyone claiming otherwise is dramatically unqualified to answer this question.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I have been taking Olanzapine (Zyprexa), Carbamazepine, Artane, and Amitriptyline for over 2 years. I now have trouble recalling people's names. Is this normal?
Answer: Sadly, yes it is normal. The bad news is that all of those drugs are known to cause memory problems, especially with protracted use and with higher doses. The good news is that with such a clusterfuck of drugs, you might see a cognitive improvement by reducing one or more of the drugs even if you stay on them all. Ideally, this many drugs will not be taken in the first place, much less for years at a time, but sometimes people are medicating many things at the same time and options are limited. If these are all drugs you consider essential, it may be difficult to discover which is responsible, if it is only one of them causing the problem, since you cannot experimentally remove it to see what happens (which would require a period of tapering as well). Some of these drugs are more likely to cause that particular kind of memory problem, recalling names, but the truth is that it could be any of them or any combination of them, or it may even be for something that led to drug use in the first place, like seizures. Cognitive impairment, and memory problems more specifically, are par for the course with these kinds of drugs, most especially if you are using several at once and are staying on them long term. In any case, though, this is something to discuss with your prescribers and you should particularly note if this is progressively worsening, as it often does and can end up obscuring more and more of your memory. Discuss your options, discuss drug optimization, and discuss alternatives which can reduce your drug load.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What are the risks of not being honest with a psychiatrist about your mental health issues?
Answer: If you want something, you may not get it. Good advice depends on good information. If a practitioner is not provided good, accurate, adequately detailed information, their input and management can suffer greatly as a result, even if they are a good psychiatrist. This question can read a bit like asking what the risks are of screwing up the guidance system for an intercontinental nuclear missile. Psychiatry is already dangerous enough when everyone is honest and acting aboveboard. That said, most psychiatrists are not very good psychiatrists and will either rather often do a poor job even with good information or will use correct information against you instead of for you. Being selective about what you share is essential when dealing with medical professionals, because your wellbeing and your life are at risk from them, but sharing too little or lying when correct and complete information is necessary for you to get what you want from the consultation can be pointless at best or deadly at worst. The ideal is to find a practitioner who earns your trust and accountably acts in your interest. There is such a thing as a doctor who helps, including some psychiatrists. Patients who don’t have that luxury are stuck with deciding what to share, how, and when in order to both protect themselves from bad physician behavior and ideas and to still work on what they want to with their clinician. Before making these kinds of decisions, I strongly recommend educating about psychiatry, psychiatric dogma, and patient outcomes.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do you stop feeling numb and empty on antidepressants?
Answer: There’s usually only three options: Feeling numbed, apathetic, unmotivated, anhedonic, uncreative, empty, slowed, withdrawn, sexless, or other such things is extremely common with the use of antidepressants, and there is not usually any great solution to these kinds of effects other than getting off the drug which is causing them. There can be exceptions, and someone can easily trial a lower dose of the same drug even just as part of the natural tapering off, but the basic things to understand are that this is very common and that measures like supplementation, dose changes, exercise, etc are unlikely to make the drug effects disappear outright.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can you switch from an SNRI to an SSRI without complications?
Answer: Maybe, maybe not. No two drugs, even if they are both SRIs (or even lower-NRI SRIs like most SSRIs), are totally interchangeable so switching can always cause complications. Some people will experience complications, some won’t. It can depend on many factors, like the specific person and specific drugs, someone’s medical and drug history, the dose and duration of use of the specific drug being discontinued, and so forth. Some drugs will be easier to switch between than others, on average, but responses also vary so much that the worst outcomes and best outcomes can both happen in the least likely circumstances. A guiding principle in drug management is ‘risk reduction’ — understanding and addressing the risks involved, since we can’t know for sure what will happen or what someone’s reactions will be or how to best protect them and ensure the preferred outcomes. Far more people suffer, or even die, from being too cavalier with these drugs than from being too cautious with them. A carefully calculated cross-taper between SNRIs and SSRIs can work out for many patients, with the specific speed of taper depending on factors like the ones mentioned above. But even with professional support, not everyone will have a smooth ride.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do you have to wean off one SSRI before starting another, if the first one is not working anymore?
Answer: Typically. The bottom line is that physical dependence occurs regardless of whether someone finds a drug helpful or tolerable. With continuous use, the need to taper appropriately when quitting emerges and this is regardless of whether the drug was considered useful in the past or is considered to still be useful. The speed and depth of physical dependence can vary between individuals, and between drugs and situations, and someone’s sensitivity to making reductions can also vary. As such, tapering is foremost a precaution — we know for sure some people will need it, but we can’t tell who will need it or how much they will need it beforehand but the consequences of rushing off can be severe. When switching between similar drugs, such as from one SSRI to another, it is usually possible to cross-taper, though, which speeds up the process of moving between them because you are reducing one drug while increasing the other. A key downside to that is that it can sometimes obscure whether a bad reaction is due to reducing the old drug or starting the new drug, especially because the most common drug initiation effects and the most common drug cessation effects with SSRIs usually overlap very significantly. A limitation of cross-tapering is that no two antidepressants, even if they are both in the same general class, will be fully interchangeable so the nervous system must still adjust to differences in things like half-life and binding affinities.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can you be prescribed an SSRI if you don't have depression and never had it before?
Answer: Of course. In capitalism, drugs are for everyone! Anyone can be given an SSRI prescription. Most prescriptions are off-label, most prescriptions are inappropriate, but anyone can be given an SSRI prescription. There are no prerequisites to meet as to someone’s needs or what they have experienced or tried in the past, and the majority of prescriptions aren’t for depression at all. There are plenty of situations in which SSRI use could be extra-dangerous, due to someone’s medical state or current drug regimen or sensitivities, but prescribers may or may not take those factors into account when scribbling a script. “Antidepressants” is just a marketing name, it is not a comment on the actual actions, efficacy, or appropriateness of the drugs. There is nothing special about them setting them apart from other psychotropics or limiting their use to a select group of people.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible to not notice one’s overstimulation?
Answer: Absolutely. “Overstimulation” is a narrative — it isn’t just facts, it is a story explaining how those facts relate to one another. Being in an experience does not necessarily yield the narrative to us. Sometimes we don’t yet recognize what an experience is, whether because it is new or because it has overwhelmed us or because we haven’t had much training in recognizing how overstimulation works. The better we learn ourselves and our reactions and the more aware we can be of our tolerances and limitations, the more likely we are to recognize overstimulation when it is starting to happen and to know how to respond. Many people are not given much support in working all that out and may not figure out the narrative itself until adulthood, or later. There is also less practical pressure to recognize it until the stakes or severity are raised.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can it be possible that the Zoloft medication could be working because social media does not make that person as nervous anymore?
Answer: “Working” is whatever you want it to mean. SSRIs (such as the sertraline you mention) are used just like any other psychotropic drugs, such as alcohol, caffeine, cannabis, ecstasy, cocaine. That is, people take them to experience certain effects. Not everyone wants to experience the same effects, and not everyone reacts to particular drugs or doses in the same way, but everyone has goal-oriented use in mind and the goals involved are personal. People use drugs like Zoloft to change their feelings or experiences in one or more ways. If those changes happen, they say the drug is working. If not, they say the drug is not working. In either case, the drug is still acting on their brain in the same basic ways. In that sense, the drug is always “working” mechanically; it just becomes a question of whether someone finds the outcome preferable. There is no physical pathology the Zoloft is medically alleviating, as if you are taking an antibiotic or insulin or something to prevent seizures. There is no physical or objective measure of success, it is whatever you define it to be. That does not mean all goals are equally reasonable, or that a drug is equally likely to help someone in all ways. Some outcomes are far more likely than others, and some reactions may mean a drug should be changed in dose or changed out entirely. If you are asking whether a particular change is indicative of other changes, that really depends on what changes you are measuring for. If someone is less nervous in one context because drugs have numbed their anxiety response, it is likely they will also feel less nervous in many other contexts, for example. But if someone feels less nervous in one context, that does not necessarily mean they will no longer have nightmares, for another example — perhaps the relationship is more complex.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can more than one antidepressant be prescribed at a time for treating major depressive disorder (MDD)?
Answer: The average psychiatrist will pile on about as much as you will let them. There are three separate questions integrated into this bot question which are worth unpacking individually: 1. Is it common for professionals to prescribe multiple drugs marketed as “antidepressants” in depression, and in “MDD” cases more specifically? Yes, it is extremely common, for several reasons. The primary and most notable reason is that one drug is usually ineffective. Multiple drugs seldom makes things much better, but when your only or your primary tool is prescribing drugs, more prescribing is the natural reaction to those tools failing, even though simply using better tools instead would be a better idea. Perhaps the secondmost common reason is that a lot of new prescribing goes on to cover over the adverse effects of existing prescribing. These drugs are not easily tolerated, sometimes with trial dropout rates being between 70% and 90% in the worse examples. Adding more drugs because the drugs already being used are too harmful can also have a snowballing effect on drug intolerability and the level of impairment a patient experiences. This is referred to by some as “the drug merry-go-round” because a patient is subjected to an increasing number of drugs at increasing doses and for increasing durations of time as their state worsens due to the poor prescribing itself. Many prescribers, including many psychiatrists, lack the education, awareness, or drive to prescribe more efficiently and keep patients off the drug merry-go-round. Since there is no such thing as an “antidepressing” mechanism, drugs are also usually relied upon for select influences and patients are often wanting an assortment of influences no one single drug will provide. The marketing name “antidepressant” suggests to patients these drugs are a one stop shop to feeling better, but that is just a highly profitable mythology, not any sort of pharmacological characterization. This need for specialization is aside from how standard clinical goals in depression are usually unachievable through drug use regardless. It is easy to use uppers and downers and numbing agents and anxiolytics to affect those dimensions of our experiences, but depression is a complex and highly variable psychosocial state which has no single functional dynamic and no single cause or course. 2. Is it a good idea to do this? Not usually, but there can be exceptions. Most single-drug prescribing is already off-track and causing more harm than good, and most prescribing fails in “MDD” patients even when additional drugs are added. Put another way, most patients quit these drugs because their are unhelpful or are more harmful than helpful, and some patients who found drug use helpful still regret use after discontinuation, usually because of effects that happened later on or only became apparent after discontinuation (like severe withdrawal syndrome or semi-permanent sexual dysfunction). So, the context for prescribing here is that we can expect failure in the majority of cases and that adding more drugs is not going to vastly change the rate of successes. However, the whole reason psychiatry exists, besides making boatloads of cash and being a tool of social control convenient for governments and special interest groups, is the exceptions — the atypically great outcomes, the psychiatric successes. Occasionally, one drug is rather helpful in key ways, or one drug is inadequate but two drugs is much better. This is not the most common outcome, but there are still exceptional patients who find this strategy, or psychiatry more generally, worth their time and money and worth the dangers involved. If the average prescriber is going to keep suggesting new drugs and more drugs until a patient finds success, turns drugs down, or is killed by them, the gravity of prescribing is to keep loading on more drugs no matter the actual odds of success, no matter the harm being done in the aggregate. Conversely, clearing away risk factors can improve the likelihood of drug use or drug combinations being someone’s best option, or at least a more reasonable one. Talking about how standard prescribing practices and management quality are poor is important, but the corollary to that is also important: if someone can make the best use of less dangerous options, and get top notch professional consultation, and educate themselves about how to navigate the choices and risks involved, they will suffer far fewer preventable harms and preventable therapeutic failures. So, how good of an idea it is to use multiple drugs, ‘antidepressants’ or otherwise, is not just about the drugs, it is also about the patient and their situation and resources. 3. Are there special considerations when combining multiple antidepressants? Yes, with the specific considerations depending on the particular drugs, doses, and patient. Drugs with overlapping mechanisms, like prescribing multiple reuptake inhibitors, and drugs with interacting mechanisms, which is pretty much all antidepressants, will create net influences and effects which differ from using each drug independently. These drugs all act globally and will all impact the effects of each other. This will increase some risks, and will usually increase the net danger, but can also potentially decrease other risks depending on what effects we are looking at. There are other kinds of interference to be aware of, as well, like when drugs are competing for metabolism in the body and adding two drugs together ends up increasing the amount of circulating doses beyond what was intended or anticipated for. Like the rest of the complications, this doesn’t depend on whether a drug is pitched as an “antidepressant”, or even a psychiatric drug at all. Someone’s medical health, history of drug reactions, current clinical goals and priorities, access to education and support (particularly for if things go badly), and other details can play a part in properly managing the possibility of combining multiple drugs, just as they need to be looked at when deciding about prescribing any drugs at all, or making choices about how to taper on and off them. In short, combining drugs always increases some risks while potentially decreasing others, and creates a more complicated environment for proper management, troubleshooting, and eventual discontinuation. Some drugs are riskier to combine than others, and combining higher doses is more dangerous than combining lower doses. This is not actually specific to what is considered an “antidepressant” versus other psychotropics. Situational details matter, too, and drug decisions need to be patient-oriented rather than chemical-oriented.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: When do weird dreams when coming off sertraline/Zoloft stop?
Answer: Experiences vary, but somewhere within the first 2–3 months off on average. While some lucky people either skip this symptom entirely or only have a few days or weeks of it, typical antidepressant withdrawal syndromes last at least 2–3 months and this is one of the effects which is often prevalent throughout instead of only occurring in the earliest days. As I said, experiences do vary so there is no hard line to draw and the range of time people report is wide. It is common to see this fade within the first couple months, but a minority of patients will have symptoms for a lot longer, and weird dreams can often be a part of that — many months, a few years, or occasionally even longer periods of time. Though tapering can often help mitigate the severity of withdrawal symptoms, sleep and dreaming are usually one of the first things affected by psychotropic drug use or discontinuation and will be one of the things most sensitive to reductions. That means tapering is more likely to completely prevent some drug effects, for instance hypomania or seizures, than completely prevent sleep-related effects like weird dreams. Patients should also consider that withdrawal symptoms may indicate their taper was too fast and that slowing down their taper or stepping back up to a higher dose to stabilize before reducing again might be beneficial. A final thing to mention is that sometimes changes in our dreaming are not so much about withdrawal even if they are related to drug discontinuation. Chronic use of drugs like SSRIs can cause pretty radical changes in how the brain is working, which can in turn affect everything from our emotions to our memory to our beliefs to our personality to our sexuality. When someone goes off of psychiatric drugs, especially after using them for years (and most especially if they began before adulthood), there may be a lot of adjusting going on in the brain and our dreamlife can reflect some of the changes going on. This is for both functional and psychological reasons.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Has anyone tapered off sertraline/zoloft due to chronic sleepiness? I’ve been tapering from 125 by 12.5 every 10 days & currently at 25. I want to go to 12.5. Would the sleepiness indicate I just don’t need it?
Answer: Q1. Has anyone tapered off sertraline/zoloft due to chronic sleepiness? Sedation is one of the most common effects of sertraline and one of the more common reasons for people to quit, particularly in the earliest weeks of use. Some people develop a drug tolerance which largely reduces the sedating effects experienced, some don’t. Q2. I’ve been tapering from 125 by 12.5 every 10 days & currently at 25. I want to go to 12.5. Would the sleepiness indicate I just don’t need it? If taking sertraline makes you sleepy, the only thing we can really know is that taking sertraline makes you sleepy. (Assuming, of course, you aren’t on multiple drugs, which can complicate what might be responsible and how sertraline plays a part.) Feeling sleepy on sertraline doesn’t tell us whether or not you are physically dependent or whether or not you are finding the drug more helpful than harmful. If a main priority or point of taking sertraline is to not feel sleepy, then that makes sertraline something you don’t need by definition, though. If you were meaning whether to ask if your tapering plan is appropriate, that depends in part on how long you were taking sertraline before trying to quit. You can still be physically dependent even if use still makes you sleepy like it did when you first began using sertraline.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can someone off schizophrenia medication be forcibly committed by a GP just like that, even when not showing any symptoms?
Answer: Probably. There are three key things to consider: How the process works differs from place to place, and what kinds of fraud or blackmail work in one situation may not work in another. But, someone labeled as “schizophrenic” who has elected to not use drugs is considered by many professionals to automatically be eligible for psychiatric violence. Their reasoning is that experiences diagnosed as “schizophrenia” always require drugs therefore no one in their right mind would refuse drugs and being undrugged is innately dangerous, ergo all necessary steps should be considered acceptable to pressure or capture and subdue such individuals. Reality doesn’t matter, alternatives don’t matter. Exactly who is in charge of doing particular aspects of the committing or paperwork will depend on the facility and circumstances, so people might pick apart your verbiage there a bit, but the bottom line is that a GP can get you nabbed, yes. Even if you are “not showing any symptoms”, yes. It is going to potentially be harder and more legally demanding to keep such a patient locked up indefinitely instead of for a temporary hold, but if there is money to be made or a political point to drive home, someone might go through the bother. Keep in mind that these mechanisms are not designed to produce the best patient outcomes, much less ethically.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the difference between the brain and the mind in regard to mental illness?
Answer: “Mental illness” refers to the mind and not the brain. It says right in the term, “mental” rather than “physical”. Of course, just what is ‘the mind’ or ‘mental’? In typical psychiatric and psychological discussions, how someone thinks, feels, perceives, believes, chooses, and acts will usually be circumscribed under “mental” to some degree. Not all experiences must be only mental or only physical, or the same mixture of each in every instance. For example, when we talk about anxiety, we often discuss both the mental experience and physical signs like clenching, racing heartbeat, or blood pressure changes. Additionally, many or most people embracing psychiatry or psychology figure that everything mental is also physical, based on the belief that all the things we experience, in our minds or otherwise, are produced by goings on in our physical bodies. This is loosely called medical materialism in philosophical parlance. In this respect, all mental experiences are also physical experiences. The catch is that we don’t define things physically in the same ways as we define them mentally even if we are talking about the very same experiences in each case, and concepts like “mental illness” are focused on mental definitions rather than physical ones. For instance, sadness or dysphoria is not defined physically, it is defined emotionally and behaviorally. We have physical definitions for things like diabetes or seizures or arrhythmia or cancer, but not for “mental illness”. The idea of “mental illness” has no physical underpinnings, no physical distinctiveness, no physicality at all. Indeed, we can choose to call anything “mental illness” we want regardless of what is going on physically. This doesn’t mean any experiences we label somehow have no physicality, just that the labels don’t draw any physical lines about how those experiences work or what they mean. The most-used functional definitions of “mental illness”, and the specific psychiatric diagnoses found in mainstream guidelines like the American Psychiatric Association’s DSM and the World Health Organization’s ICD, patently exclude medical disorders, as well as other physically defined things like drug effects and injuries. That is the only physical line drawn, so everything else and all the reasons for those experiences to happen will still be eligible for psychiatric diagnosing. Specific psychiatric labels inevitably get applied to a multiplicity of underlying physical phenomena, as the labels aren’t designed to be physically specific or physically accountable. It is valuable to look at how the brain works, and how the body works more broadly, if we want to understand psychology and mental experiences because there is a clear and undeniable interplay. However, an understanding of the physics and chemistry involved in the human body will not provide a full understanding of how it feels to have experiences and how to be a more robustly mentally adaptive human. It doesn’t tell us about things like social expectations, quality of life, or having a meaningful existence. There is a lot which will never have a physical definition, and “mental illness” is one of those things because that is what kind of idea we have decided for it to be. There is an importance in understanding both how to address the non-physical stuff and how to support doing so with knowledge of what is going on in the body itself. It is useful to remember how things like nutrition and social environment both play into mental wellbeing, for instance. We also need to be able to discern when there is a specific medical cause of someone’s experiences which will require special intervention. If we went around calling everything “mental illness” instead of first ruling out literal medical illnesses, countless patients would not be getting vital care. Though, on the other hand, calling something “mental illness” can give a false impression of what it is and what we know about how to help people. The bottom line is this: brain problems are a medical issue whereas “mental illness” refers to mental experiences judged by a society to be abnormal or unacceptable with no regard for what is going on in the brain. Though medical problems are supposed to be ruled out before a psychiatric diagnosis is used, this rather significant criterion is very often ignored or paid only half-hearted lip service. So in theory “mental illness” excludes all medically pathological experiences and causes of experiences, but in reality anyone can be labeled as “mentally ill” for any reason and a medical explanation can be ignored or refused because mainstream psychiatry is not accountable to physical reality.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How difficult is it to get accepted by a psychiatrist for treatment, especially if you have no insurance?
Answer: It should be easier than being accepted by any other kind of doctor, usually. Most psychiatrists don’t accept insurance, and those who do will not generally require it. As long as you pay, they are unlikely to care what goes on after they’ve got their fee. The main obstacle here is not someone being a psychiatrist, or whether you plan to seek reimbursement, it is overbooking. A lot of medical professionals have full schedules and full patient loads and plenty are not open to taking on new patients. However, there are usually still going to be local or localish options with openings. On one hand, many of these practitioners may still have wait lists or say they are unable to schedule you for a month or three, or potentially further out if they are also juggling clients who pay with insurance. It is not unusual for a patient needing insured coverage to be waiting 3-6 months or more, even in areas with many doctors and facilities. On the other hand, most psychiatrists will take on most any patient as long as there is no legal concern involved, and will happily drug you out of your gourd if that’s what you’re looking for. I almost never hear of an available psychiatrist not accepting a paying patient. Aside from people accused of recreational interest in the drugs or the rare specialist who focuses only on a small subset of concerns not usually met (like a narrow slice of anxieties, for instance, or only Asian immigrants with difficulty adjusting culturally), it is extremely unlikely a psychiatrist with an opening would say no to your money. Whether or not you end up being compatible is a subsequent issue to address, but incompatibilities would have to be pretty wild for the average psychiatrist to tell a patient to stop giving them money. I’m not trying to imply psychiatrists are, almost by nature, money-grubbing. The point is that most won’t give half an ass whether they’re getting you where you want to go or not — if you’re paying them, it’s all about their worldview and their plan and if you don’t like it, go hire someone else instead. Of course, if you tell them you’ve found someone better and won’t be returning, some will be jealous and resentful. There’s always a flood of new patient prospects, though, so a patient moving on is not usually a financial loss. So, to reiterate: most patients would have zero trouble whatsoever being accepted as a patient by most psychiatrists, and paying out of pocket is usually a bonus to them rather than a problem. If you’re asking whether you’d have an easy time finding free or low-cost psychiatrists, the answer is no, probably not. Though some areas have government programs to facilitate that, there is often going to be a wait list involved, may still be copays involved, and especially for people not considered by the system to be in a serious crisis, there may not be any support at all.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why does Wellbutrin give an amphetamine-like high when snorted even though it is an antidepressant?
Answer: It is a stimulating drug, so it stimulates. Amphetamines are only one of many kinds of stimulants. Bupropion has things in common with amphetamine and also some of the other stimulants, and is a stimulant itself, though milder than many that people use recreationally aside from alcohol and nicotine. Crushing and snorting bupropion basically augments and intensifies the effects experienced with typical oral dosing by changing the manner in which and how rapidly particular amounts of it are hitting your brain. The harder we make the come-on of antidepressants with significant stimulant properties, the more likely someone is to find it recreationally useful or similar to drugs with popular recreational followings beyond the mild end of things. Be aware that this can increase the dangers involved, too, or create entirely new kinds of risks. That angle covered, there is nothing which makes an antidepressant an “antidepressant” except marketing. There are no pharmacological traits required, or suggested, or anything which physically sets antidepressants apart from other drugs. So, the actions or reactions involved are not specified or divided by the “antidepressant” label. It doesn’t matter at all here that bupropion is sometimes marketed as an antidepressant, just as it doesn’t matter that amphetamine was sometimes marketed for depression in previous decades and is still used far more exceptionally for depression in the present day. Any psychotropic drug can impact experiences of depression, and being called an “antidepressant” doesn’t mean there is anything special or extra-helpful about a drug for people experiencing depression.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why does blocking dopamine D2 receptors reduce agitation and irritability in autism?
Answer: Reducing brain functioning reduces brain functioning. Dopamine antagonists like neuroleptics were introduced to psychiatry as chemical lobotomies and are used for the same purposes as the surgical lobotomies they were prescribed alongside. When we take drugs that stop the brain from working correctly and impair communication between areas of the brain, this is liable to affect our experiences. Dopamine antagonism is not necessarily the only relevant mechanism to discuss in this context, and these drugs can just as easily cause new or increased agitation or irritability, but the basic explanation behind changes in emotions and behavior is an impairing of brain functioning. This is not at all specific to autism, though children with autism are a juicy target for marketing for three reasons. Firstly, desperate parents. Secondly, because kids usually have less of a say in what they take and less of an ability to explain how a drug is impacting their lives in a way adults will understand and listen to. Thirdly, because autism can commonly compound one or both of those difficulties. Neuroleptics (later rebranded as “antipsychotics” to sell better, like the mythical “antidepressants” and “mood stabilizers”) tend to dampen all emotions and a range of normal behaviors and responses. At an extreme, this becomes total apathy, amotivation, and anhedonia, but the influence ultimately comes in degrees. There is a threefold effect to impairments caused by these drugs. There is the direct reducing of mental functioning, and on top of that there is a reducing of how people express their own inner experiences (which can give the impression to outsiders of things being or working better than they actually are). Additionally, there is ‘anosognosia’, where our ability to evaluate our own health, wellbeing, and functioning is itself impaired so we may think we are fine and very functional even if we are in bad shape and suffering.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Has anyone heard of the new antidepressant EXXUA coming in 2024? What makes this medication different from the other antidepressants?
Answer: How different? While it is not a particularly unique drug when looking at individual actions alone, and has also been around since the 80s, the main thing usually setting these drugs apart from one another is the specific assortment of actions and the potency involved. Gepirone more resembles buspirone and some of the more recent antidepressants (SMS drugs) and antipsychotics (such as aripiprazole and similar drugs) than SSRIs in key ways, and is being pushed as a partial agonist rather than a reuptake inhibitor. Selective partial agonism is notable because typical reuptake inhibitors are non-selective (indirect) serotonin agonists and that means mucking up more than directly agonizing only a subset of neurons. The mechanism and scope is different, which means the impact on the nervous system is different in ways. The same goes for the antagonist influences of reuptake inhibition versus gepirone’s partial agonism. That doesn’t necessarily make it good for depression or likely to be helpful, but it means someone will usually feel at least a little different on gepirone versus a reuptake inhibitor like SSRIs and TCAs. Due in large part to still acting heavily on the serotonin system, many of the most common effects will be those we typically see with other well-known antidepressants as well, for instance nausea, dizziness, headache. But, there is likely to be a difference in the rate of certain other effects which will be more common in certain other drugs, like some kinds of sexual dysfunction, whether due to the mechanisms gepirone prominently features or the mechanisms it largely lacks. How this plays out in everyday use is yet to be seen in the US, and preliminary clinical trials usually provide us a somewhat poor picture of the reality of millions of patients taking the drug, especially if they are not designed to give us a good picture. Another difference which is a little interesting is that it was rejected by the FDA more times than most other antidepressants despite trial results being pretty shitty both with drugs like SSRIs and gepirone. There is going to be a specific financial motivation behind continuing to pursue US approval for gepirone, though I don’t follow pharma news so I can’t tell you what it is. Something we can count on is that the impression or narrative of gepirone being different is going to very profitably outpace the practical value of those differences and what improvements patients experience by psychiatry incorporating gepirone into its armamentarium. As with other psychiatric drugs, the earliest years of marketing will be filled with claims about how gepirone helps with things it doesn’t actually help with or lacks risks it actually possesses. We are still doing battle with the marketing myths that propelled SSRIs into global blockbusters decades ago. Will someone who didn’t find other antidepressants helpful find gepirone helpful? Probably not, but there is a small chance. Every time we add a new drug to the formulary, there is a chance that at least a couple patients who were not finding drug use successful will find the new addition much better than the previous options. There may also be patients who prefer gepirone to drugs which they have already tried or have remained on due to the adverse effect profile experienced. But gepirone is not opening a new pharmacological door, as we have a variety of partial serotonin agonists around already, and is not a magic bullet for depression either way. It is just one more tool in a large toolshed where no single tool is a great fit for most patients. The more interesting research will be the research suggesting who is the best candidate for trialing gepirone versus other drugs.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do the effects of antidepressants (SSRIs) build up over time?
Answer: I guess that depends on what you mean. The actions of SSRIs are immediate — they are the same on the first day as they are after weeks or months or years of use. They are performing their namesake reuptake inhibition within hours of taking the very first dose, as well as their hundreds of other actions. But, the changes don’t stop there. The nervous system is plastic, and changes over time with or without drug use going on. It changes in response to everything we encounter in our daily lives: foods and climates and social environments and tasks and ideas and feelings. The nervous system, including the brain, is changeable by design, and psychotropic drugs will continue to prompt changes when taken continuously. As such, the brain will not look the same after one day of use as it looks after one year of use, or one decade of use. Alterations caused by drug use become more prominent, more ingrained, more extensive, and the normal course of development and upkeep will become increasingly distant as drug use is preventing it. The rate of these changes, and their depth, and the way they feel will vary across patients and situations, but the bottom line is that ongoing use of a dysfunction-inducing drug will cause ongoing changes in the nervous system. If we are talking about “effects” as in the way we feel or act or function when using these drugs, the ongoing changes being caused by continuous exposure can indeed influence our experience of drugged states (and our experiences after quitting). This is not because there is more of the drug in our body or because the drug is somehow acting more potently over time, it is because the body is fundamentally changeable and drugs like SSRIs are a potent force of prompting change because they infiltrate places they are not supposed to and break functioning in ways we have no proper defenses against. Only indirect adjustments can be attempted to work around some of the problems caused by drug mechanisms, and though we can establish a new balance of drug actions and functional adjustments, continuous exposure still pushes some changes further over time. They are not a neutral or static force in this sense, they are a progressively disruptive force. The body responds to input, so continuous actions by drugs yield continuous responses. There is also the consideration of changes or harms which are not focused around plasticity. Damaging or killing cells in the body, for instance, and causing medical problems by preventing healthy functioning (in everything from our blood to our liver to our jaws, not just our brains). This can have a snowballing effect on our experiences — an adverse drug influence can lead to a systemic problem which has its own set of symptoms and concerns. Everything from numbing our genitals to changing our scent to interfering with maturation to changing our gastrointestinal functioning can have repercussions reaching beyond just those drug effects. These effects of SSRIs tend to accumulate over time (“build up”), so long-term use will lead to more of them than brief use.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do any psychiatric medicines cure psychosis, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, etc. permanently?
Answer: No, that’s not how psychiatric diagnoses work. There is no literal illness so there is no literal cure. Anything considered “mentally ill” cannot be cured because there is nothing medically wrong to fix or remove or alleviate. Psychosis is a broader label and, unlike psychiatric diagnoses, it can have a medical underpinning in non-psychiatric cases. But, it is not itself a medical disorder and it cannot be medically treated. Treating the underlying medical problem in such cases may lead to a cure of the underlying medical problem, but the psychosis resolving is not guaranteed and not what is being cured even if it does resolve. For psychiatric diagnoses, whatever a clinician or patient considers improvement may or may not last beyond the period of drug use which was said to be responsible. The same goes for non-drug interventions — some people might find it lastingly useful, others may find it only a short-term help. It depends on all the details your question does not mention. The labels you cite don’t contain that information, and the use of a drug or of a specific drug does not explain. When improvements occur, what they are and why they happened will be what to look at in trying to figure whether they will last indefinitely. The natural course of someone’s experiences are a big factor here. Some things will naturally happen once and then not recur, or will only recur if certain extreme stresses are applied. There are often things people can do to make themselves more capable of handling stresses, or to avoid unnecessary stresses. On the other hand, some experiences have a naturally cyclical or ongoing nature and that can require a partially different set of skills or approaches if lasting resolution is the goal. Whether drugs fit into successful intervention or lifestyle adjustments is variable, and personal. Drugs quite often make things worse, or more prolonged, but this is not universal.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do antidepressants work if depression is caused by a chemical imbalance in the brain?
Answer: There is no correct answer to this question. If you say “antidepressants work” and “depression is caused by a chemical imbalance in the brain” and then ask us to connect those two ideas with a causal explanation, there can only be a correct explanation if those underlying assumptions are correct. Put most simply, they are not correct, so all answers will be incorrect in one or more ways. That also means we could write anything we want, since we aren’t bound by what is right or wrong anymore. It becomes a free for all of nonsense. It is better to focus on facts rather than hypotheticals: Because depression is many things and these drugs have many actions and patient experiences and preferences vary, what is considered “working” and why someone might say a drug “worked” is not possible to refine into a single statement. There are many different actions and outcomes that might be relevant, depending on the person and situation. While we can state more directly that drug use usually fails to meet someone’s goals, and is usually more harmful than helpful, individual reactions do still vary. But in all cases, these drugs “work” by disrupting what was already going on, not by normalizing brain functioning or restoring brain health.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is there any way to stop using antidepressants without going through withdrawal effects? How can you taper off them safely while avoiding withdrawal symptoms?
Answer: Q1. Is there any way to stop using antidepressants without going through withdrawal effects? Maybe, maybe not. It depends on the person. While many people would be able to reduce so slowly that withdrawal effects would not happen or would be so mild as to largely be imperceptible, the rate at which reductions would have to occur to best assure this would be impractical. Patients are usually stuck choosing between going at a reasonable speed which kicks up some symptoms or staying on a drug for many months or years longer than they ever wanted to. For some people, there is a happy medium where they can reduce and rest and reduce and rest and avoid severe withdrawal. For some people, even a cold turkey cessation would feel alright, though this is less common and is also still going to strain the nervous system and set someone up for adverse drug reactions later on in life. For some people, even tapering very slowly is still a rough time and moving at a pace which is just a fraction of the ‘happy medium’ folks is still very uncomfortable. Many factors can affect what rate of tapering is tolerable, what approach to reducing works out best, and what symptoms occur in the first place. The best way to avoid withdrawal is to avoid the drugs that cause it or to only use those drugs for a very brief time which is too short for a deeper physical dependence to develop. As soon as you are physically dependent, there is not necessarily any shortcut to being off and feeling normalish again. Not everyone has more severe or long-lasting withdrawal problems, but they are, sadly, very common. Q2. How can you taper off them safely while avoiding withdrawal symptoms? Well, that is kind of a tautology. If someone is tapering, that means they are gradually reducing the dose to give the body time to adjust to each drop. If someone is tapering so fast that withdrawal symptoms are being caused, then tapering more slowly is how to avoid those symptoms, by definition. Speed has a number of variables, like what increments someone is reducing by, how often reductions are being made, and what other changes are being managed at the same time (like other drugs, or diet, or lifestyle). A total absence of withdrawal symptoms is usually an unrealistic goal. But, severe symptoms almost certainly indicate someone is moving too quickly and may be making their long-term situation worse as well. Someone should be looking for a balance between health, day-to-day functioning, and quality of life. Unnecessary drug use is bad, but quitting too slow or too fast can also carry costs. Finding the right strategies and right tapering plan requires research and personalization; there is no one plan which is the best fit for everyone that I could share here.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are the withdrawal effects from Pristiq not worth taking the medication? There's no easy way to get off it.
Answer: While they are a good thing to factor in, most use is unjustifiable more generally. It is true that SNRI withdrawal is one of the most common and most commonly severe effects of using such drugs, and the consequences can be far greater than many people expect — loss of health, loss of relationships, loss of the ability to work, and so forth, in the more serious instances. While there are steps that can be taken to mitigate withdrawal severity, and maybe even withdrawal duration, there are no guarantees to be had and a lot more comes down to personal sensitivity and other pretty individual variables. Perfect use can still cause massive problems and horribly managed use can still be escaped without much harm; it really depends on the specific person and situation. But, I think it might be unfair to suggest drugs like desvenlafaxine (aka Pristiq) are by default otherwise a good option aside from the risk of serious or intolerable withdrawal problems. These drugs are actually usually a bad choice even if we neglected to factor in the withdrawal risks (the logistical demands of tapering, the medical and psychological difficulties of tapering and quitting, the lack of proper professional support for most patients, etc). This lack of appropriateness is due both to poor average efficacy and significant dangers. Most people won’t find these drugs useful enough to warrant the risks involved, and most people will have more of a bad experience than a good one regardless. There are certainly some drugs which are even more dangerous or even less likely to help, but drugs like SNRIs typically strike a poor risk/benefits ratio for the average patient. They are drugs most suited to a rather select subset of circumstances and require specialized expertise and management to properly employ. The vast bulk of prescribing is ill-fitted or worse, and patients pay the price. While occasionally there are people who felt an SNRI was a great fit until withdrawal turned the whole experience into a net negative, most people didn’t feel SNRI use was a great success even before withdrawal and there are a lot of concerning risks beyond just withdrawal. In short, SNRIs being a good first-line tool is usually a fallacy, and one which patients need to inform themselves about because their aspiring prescriber often won’t. It is great that there is increasing awareness of the withdrawal risks of these kinds of drugs and the terrible suffering some patients experience, both as a result of standard use and, at least as often, as a result of bad professional practices. But, the extreme commonness of withdrawal difficulties is not the central deciding factor to look to in weighing the appropriateness of an SNRI, and the scales usually tip against use before the various aspects of physical dependence are even added in.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it normal to get used to an antidepressant?
Answer: Like most psychotropics, antidepressants cause significant drug tolerance with ongoing use. Pharmaceuticals marketed as “antidepressants” are psychotropic, which means they cause altered mental states by acting on the nervous system. Because these drugs have mechanisms that interfere with the normal functioning of the nervous system, the nervous system responds to those mechanisms by making adjustments to try and lessen their overall influence. Without this ability to adjust, psychotropic drugs would easily kill us. While these adaptations cannot fully neutralize the effects of a drug on the neuronal level, they can greatly curb some of the mental effects we experience from using them. Effects like sedation and stimulation are some good examples of drug initiation effects patients will often feel reduce over time if they continue to use the drug every day, though it isn’t the case for all patients. This can be a good thing if someone found an effect undesirable, but an inconvenient thing if they were taking the drug specifically to cause that effect. The adaptations revolving around continuous exposure to dysfunction-inducing drugs like antidepressants can also lead to new, later-onset effects, usually ones considered problematic, like apathy syndrome or movement disorders. Being on a drug like antidepressants can also impair our ability to perceive how altered we have become as a result of taking them, so sometimes ‘getting used to an antidepressant’ refers to becoming unaware of changes (often bad ones, but potentially desirable ones as well) that are being caused. Someone might insist they aren’t different at all, or not notice that they are experiencing substantial changes in how they are feeling or behaving which are rather obvious to outsiders. This is sometimes called ‘anosognosia’. It does not necessarily take long-term use to happen, but the longer someone spends on a psychotropic drug, the harder it may be to remember what it was like to not be altered.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What do you think about psychiatry or neurology not treating problems like psychopathy and sociopathy that harm others' lives but "supposedly" treating "so called" mental problems that are caused by things like traumas or social isolation?
Answer: That’s not particularly accurate. In cases where psychopathy is considered neurologically treatable or in some manner amenable to psychotherapeutic support, there are professionals offering their services. Not only that, but psychiatrists in general will happily prescribe to most anyone for most any reason. Tell them you shit every day but you took two shits on Thursday and you’ll have your choice of three different classes of drug. Whether or not you consider psychopathy/sociopathy “problems”, there are definitely people ready to ‘treat’. It would be underestimating psychiatry to say they are unscrupulous but that they have highly refined targeting in who they aim to swindle. And, on the other hand, stuff psychiatry also labels as “mental illness” but which are caused by things like traumas and social isolation can still harm others. Depression, for example, can hurt everyone in a relationship with the patient, it is not a burden wholly independent to the individual experiencing it. Mental crises can lead to uncharacteristic decisions, compulsive behaviors, or even violence, depending on what is going on and how it is being handled. Disruptions to relationships and communities are nearly guaranteed on some level. This isn’t ultimately how psychiatry decides what should or shouldn’t be labeled, ostracized, or suppressed, but it can play a part.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is my brain already permanently damaged from Zyprexa since I was on it for over 36 weeks?
