Answer: We wouldn’t be able to know that. While it is guaranteed that your brain has been harmed by this use and that damages on some level are possible and perhaps even standard, permanence is a different matter. It is quite possible your brain will never fully be the same, even if you feel very recovered overall after a while of being off the olanzapine, but this may or may not have to do with damage. Most drug changes are not the damaging or killing of neurons and other cells, and likewise most persistent symptoms people commonly report are not centered around damage to tissue rather than adverse functional changes and impairments. That said, microscopic damages (to things like cells, mitochondria, and even DNA) seem to be an integral part of drug use, so it is likely that after weeks on the drug, there are various kinds of damage to cells in your brain and other parts of your body. Whether or not these smaller-scale damages cause symptoms or health conditions is a more complicated thing to figure out, and we simply lack a great understanding of all the implications involved. It is a risk worth considering when weighing drug use itself, but is not something we can given an armchair prognosis about for people wanting to recover from use. Unless you experienced a severe drug reaction which is known to cause more profound brain damage, like toxidromes or a stroke or something like that, your best measure of recovery will be your actual symptoms. The use of a neuroleptic or experiencing symptoms after discontinuing it does not really tell us too much about whether your brain has been damaged and whether those damages are things which can be repaired over time. It is simpler to focus on symptoms themselves — symptoms usually improve to one degree or another, by whatever means, as a natural part of healing from drug use. Supportive lifestyle choices can encourage this.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do Wellbutrin or ziprazedone cause emotional numbness?
Answer: Emotional numbness is a risk of bupropion, ziprasidone, and taking both at the same time, too. Particular doses and durations of use can be more likely to cause emotional numbness, and some people may find one of these two drugs to cause emotional numbness even if the other did not, but both of these drugs involve a significant risk of emotional numbness. It would be less common but still possible for someone to find neither of these drugs to cause emotional numbness on its own but the combination to newly cause it. Notably, the drug mechanisms behind this influence likely differ between bupropion (Wellbutrin) and ziprasidone (Geodon), and the actual experience of emotional numbness may feel different from one drug to the other, depending on the patient. Also worth mentioning is that reducing or discontinuing one or both of these drugs can also cause emotional numbness, due to changes caused during use that change how we are feeling when less of the drug is around. Likewise, even in the absence of concerns like physical dependence, there can be long-lasting emotional numbness which proceeds for weeks, months, or years after the drug which caused them has been discontinued. The changes caused by drug use will not necessarily be reversed just by going off the drug, and sometimes there can be damages which perpetuate adverse effects as well. All of these risks apply to all patients, but not all patients are equally susceptible to all drug harms or causes. Some patients are also made more vulnerable through situational factors, like their health or other drugs they are using or past drug responses. The bottom line is that if someone notices a new or increasing emotional numbness, drugs like bupropion and ziprasidone should be key suspects in evaluating contributing causes. Using one or both of these drugs will not guarantee a severe emotional numbness, but there is still guaranteed to be some degree of emotional disruptiveness to them because you can’t cause dysfunction in the brain in the way these drugs do without it affecting our mental states.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the difference between neuroleptic and antipsychotic drugs? Can they be used interchangeably?
Answer: Right now, they are entirely the same drugs. “Neuroleptic” is a description of a particular drug mechanism which is shared by all drugs currently marketed as “antipsychotics” but is not necessarily the mechanism which is behind a reduction in whatever is being called “psychosis” in any given patient and it is a mechanism found in drugs not marketed as “antipsychotics” as well. The degree of neurolepsis will be related to the dose of the drug, and most specifically the level of dopamine blocking going on in certain areas of the brain, but the degree of neurolepsis has only a partial relationship to the degree of psychosis being reduced. Neurolepsis does not stop psychosis itself as a wider idea, it only prevents the brain from functioning correctly and this disruptiveness will affect whether some experiences can continue or how intensely they continue. How relevant that is to a particular patient will depend on the nature of their experiences. “Antipsychotic” is strictly a marketing term and does not specify any particular mechanism. It was adopted so that referring to the drugs at all will already be increasing the profitability of the products. The name is part of an institutional and industrial agenda relating to power and money and its popularity reflects the success of that agenda. As we already discussed with neurolepsis, there is no “antipsychosing” mechanism to antipsychotics, nor even a universal “antipsychosing” effect overall. These are drugs which disable the nervous system, yes, but they are not a targeted intervention which disrupts or prevents psychosis. After all, “psychosis” refers to a pretty inclusive and heterogeneous group of experiences whose underlying physical and psychological dynamics are not always shared, in part or in full. The idea of an “antipsychotic” drug makes no literal sense, it is just a highly effective marketing metaphor. The same goes for related psychiatric marketing terms, like “antidepressant” or “mood stabilizer”. To date, the body of drugs marketed in the mainstream as “antipsychotics” are all neuroleptics, but this may not always be the case. Drugs which are not dopamine antagonists, directly or indirectly, may soon be sold as “antipsychotics” as well, and tentative research has been in progress for decades, primarily because of how incredibly lucrative and overprescribed these kinds of drugs are. The poor average efficacy and serious dangers involved with current drugs are a driver but not the primary driver, especially since the risks are so routinely mismanaged that we are already passing up most opportunities to do better with what we already have on hand. There are also plenty of drugs which some people find useful in psychosis which are not marketed as “antipsychotics” even when prescribed to the same patients for the same reasons as antipsychotics, highlighting that the marketing term is about the social and industrial agenda rather than a description of application or effectiveness. It is fair to say that some antipsychotics will be more potently neuroleptic at average doses than others. But, this does not seem to impact the average efficacy of the drugs in psychosis patients. Sometimes “antipsychotic” is used to refer more colloquially to the neuroleptic or dopamine antagonizing influence of drugs, so we could also in that sense say some drugs are more antipsychotic than others. However, as a marketing class this is not usually an intended accommodation and it is pretty binary whether a drug is said to be an antipsychotic. Exactly where someone draws the line is not always the same, though. Being approved for use in “schizophrenia”, for example, isn’t necessarily the only or the main qualifying criterion, just as being useful in psychosis never has been. Conversely, neurolepsis is a more pharmacological rather than sociological distinction and the only debate to have is what intensity of dopamine blocking at what receptors should be said to qualify a drug as neuroleptic. For more, you can browse my related answers on this topic linked below or check out books about the history of psychopharmacology like those by Dr David Healy.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does Caplyta work better for psychosis than abilify?
Answer: There is no evidence suggesting that. Successful use of neuroleptics for psychosis depends far more on the individual patient, the type of psychosis, the causes involved, and the various factors relating to quality of life and access to support. In many or most cases, if we are pooling by that huge umbrella category “psychosis”, the specific drug is almost an afterthought, or someone’s success a fluke of statistics. In a largescale blind test, we would not expect any of the drugs marketed as “antipsychotics” to substantially outperform the rest. That is also to say that we have not improved the average usefulness of these drugs since they first entered into psychiatry more than half a century ago. If we monitor patients for more than just several weeks, we can also anticipate many aspects of outcomes will be better in placebo or other non-drug groups. As typically prescribed, antipsychotics cause more harm than good and can impair long-term progress for a lot of patients. The point of focus here is that antipsychotics are not usually going to provide the desired outcome and no one drug is going to be uniformly superior to the others when it comes to such a broad application. It is the relative risk levels of particular adverse effects which better set these drugs apart. Some are far more likely to cause diabetes than others, for instance, or are more likely to cause seizures. Since reactions occur across a wide range no matter the drug, statistics only tell us about likelihood rather than predicting for sure what a specific patient will experience.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are there any examples of people getting better while being prescribed psychiatric meds like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and antipsychotics as opposed to tapering off of them under a doctor’s care?
Answer: Of course. It is the exception at this point, but there are examples, sure. Even most of the psychiatrists highly critical of the psychiatric industry and the preventable harms being done and the overuse and misuse of psychiatric drugs will endorse the idea that at least some patients find drug use worthwhile and at least some of those patients find drugging dramatically useful. The problem is not that nobody ever finds these drugs even remotely helpful. The problem is that the relatively few people who find them to be overwhelmingly useful can’t justify the far greater scope of harms, disability, and death being caused supposedly in their name. We shouldn’t have to maim, torture, and kill unthinkable numbers of patients just to get a good result here and there. There are many ways in which we can adjust how drugs are studied, manufactured, regulated, marketed, discussed, prescribed, and managed that would increase the proportion of successes to failures, good outcomes to bad ones. So in that sense, that are actually many problems and many ways to work towards solutions. However, the apparatus of prescribing — the intersection of politics, social pressures, industrial investment, and institutional self-interest — is moving away from solutions more than it is moving towards them. That is to say, a big part of the reason why psychiatry is doing such a bad job in net with psychiatric drugs is that it is designed to. Not wholly on purpose, though there are some nefarious and blatantly undermining choices involved, but as a consequence of the various interests in play and how patient wellbeing and patient rights are being mediated. It is possible to find at least a couple people who found drug use revelatory. You can also find people singing the praises of other drugs, from cannabis to alcohol to heroin. This applies both to situational use and to lifestyle use. There are some very serious, very concerning reasons why this kind of outcome is not the standard, though. You can also consider this answer a tidy QED for the clueless trolls and shitgoblins roaming Quora insisting I am definitively anti-drug or a Scientologist or some other equally ridiculous thing just because I think preventably hurting and demeaning patients is bad and am willing to stand up and say so. Of course, since facts were never the crux of the matter with such individuals, there is no expected efficacy here and the goal is just to lay things out for the readers who are genuinely interested.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why don't people who are on antipsychotics get better even though they take their meds religiously?
Answer: You already know the answer to that. There is no reason to assume drug use will be the defining factor in someone’s recovery, and no reason to assume antipsychotics will even be a positive overall force. If people don’t “get better” despite drug use, clearly drugs are not what can or will resolve whatever is going on. There is also a very large difference between taking drugs religiously and taking drugs successfully. Neither zealous adherence to prescribed regimens nor faith in psychiatry or psychiatric drugs is a magic process which ensures success. Most often, drug use is not very successful. Not 100% of the time — there are drug successes, they are just less common and are usually the beneficiary of a consolidation of positive factors (like proper exclusion of medical causation, tactical prescribing at minimal doses for minimal durations, informed consent, and so forth). The more people that are given drugs in bad ways and bad situations for bad reasons, the more we drown out successes with avoidable harms and failures. Faithful use is no protection against such factors. Inconsistent use can cause problems of its own, most notably withdrawal syndrome and other drug crises rather than a simple failure of drug success, but the vast majority of problems contributing to the perception that antipsychotics aren’t sufficient are unrelated to how closely a patient follows their prescribed regimen. All the more since withdrawal syndrome, supersensitivity syndrome, and other effects commonly conflated with “worsening” or “relapse” in the psychiatric sense are quite often the result of a patient faithfully following their prescriber’s directions. In short, antipsychotics are not usually the right tool for the job at hand, and they have much more potential to cause harm than good. One should not expect consistent antipsychotic use to make them “get better”, and even the most faithful use will usually fail to provide that outcome. The reasons for drugs failing to provide what we want can be rather plural, but what is always shared in common is that something is being done wrong which must be changed in order to improve what is being experienced.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are antipsychotics chemical lobotomies?
Answer: Dopamine antagonists marketed as “antipsychotics” are chemical lobotomies, yes. This is not an exaggeration or a misleading metaphor, it is a literal statement about what the traditional surgeries and pharmaceuticals have in common, which is disrupting communication between certain areas of the brain in order to produce key mental and behavioral deficits in patients considered by some in society to be beneficial or more acceptable. This vital connection and shared application is what led to neuroleptics being introduced as “chemical lobotomies” when they arrived on the psychiatric scene already filled with surgical lobotomy procedures in many regions, and it is why antipsychotics are still used today for pretty much all the things surgical lobotomies were used for in the past. Drugs gobbled up the surgical marketshare and then expanded far beyond it. They are among the most financially successful drugs ever created. Surgical and chemical lobotomies are not alike in all ways, but this is also true if comparing different surgical lobotomies to other surgical lobotomies or different antipsychotics to other antipsychotics. There is overlap in all cases, but there is also contrast, so the exact states produced and the outcomes involved can vary. Basically, the word “lobotomy” does not actually impart a singular experience and outcome or refer to just one kind of intervention. To add to the complexity, antipsychotics are not the only drugs discussed as being chemical lobotomies in the medical literature, and chemical lobotomization is not always about getting the drug into someone’s bloodstream. Whether we are looking at surgeries, drugs, or both, lobotomizing is a whole variegated collection of methods and outcomes. People insisting otherwise stand in dispute with history rather than terminology. It has become rather unpopular (and even under vociferous attack) to refer to antipsychotics as “chemical lobotomies”, primarily because it turns patients on to the fact that antipsychotics do indeed lobotomize. Billions of dollars have been spent to change the public perception and professional management of neuroleptics and being more straightforward about their actions, risks, and seriousness undermines profitability as well as increasing skepticism about psychiatry itself. It is fair to say that there are meaningful differences between typical surgical lobotomies and typical use of neuroleptic drugs, some favorable and some not favorable, but it would be misleading to say that neuroleptics are fundamentally non-lobotomizing or that we explain them better and more honestly to deny that lobotomizing influence which was originally more of a sales point rather than a criticism. Marketing actively tries to make you think backwards about these things. These drugs have a literally lobotomizing effect but they are marketed as “antipsychotics” (or even “antidepressants”, “mood stabilizers”) despite those kinds of characterizations being purely metaphorical. There are no literally antipsychosing or antidepressing or mood stabilizing drug mechanisms, and the very ideas of psychosis and depression and mood are metaphysical rather than physical. What is important is the story being told about drugs and drug use, and whether patients and the public are captured by that story. Marketing isn’t about the truth of what goes on, or about promoting the most responsible, educated use of drugs and the best outcomes of drug use or non-use. Capturing people so well that they reject more direct and honest explanations of drugging is powerful and highly lucrative.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: When I forgot to take Prozac/fluoxetine a day, I literally sleep all day like I can't even open my eyes. Is this normal?
Answer: Yes. Whether this is a hard comedown from the stimulant effects of the drug, a withdrawal syndrome, or some other drug effect, it is not at all an unusual way to feel when missing a dose. Because fluoxetine is such a long-acting drug, patients are more likely to experience issues with a single missed dose of other SSRIs than with fluoxetine, but some people still very much notice a single missed fluoxetine dose. The physical dependence these drugs produce is significant and patients should take the steps they need to in order to ensure they aren’t skipping doses. Setting alarms, having a backup stash, or other strategies can be helpful.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Will sertraline make me want to leave my bed and socialize again?
Answer: Probably not, but it is possible in some cases. There are any number of reasons which might keep someone confined to their bed most of the time and uninterested in socializing, or unable to socialize. Sertraline treats none of them, but the altered states produced by sertraline may interfere with a handful of them in a way that some patients can find useful. The question as stated is so broad as to be unhelpful to you because no broad answer would be very actionable and no one, not even your prescriber, could know for sure how you will react beforehand. How to handle the option of drug use depends on all the factors which went unstated. The most obvious situation associated with what you mention and the use of SSRIs is depression, but you never say whether that is what is going on here. If this is depression, the cause is still the most relevant factor, and personal reactions are the second-most relevant. These rate ahead of the specific concerns you have, as those are a lot more general. Most people won’t find sertraline to be far more effective than placebo in these matters, but a small subset of patients can find sertraline or another particular drug very useful. It can even be substantially useful right away sometimes, if you’re in that luckiest group. Statistically speaking, sertraline is more likely to be net harmful rather than net helpful, and is unlikely to be useful enough to bother taking. Figuring out whether you might be one of the exceptions to that overall trend requires a lot more specificity, and should also involve first exhausting the less dangerous or more targeted therapeutic options and getting tested for medical problems which might be treatable. A solid professional recommendation about drug use comes at the end of a long process of interviewing, investigating, and trialing rather than at the beginning. And even then, outcomes can be unpredictable.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is an empty mind after taking antipsychotics a sign you've been lobotomized?
Answer: Probably. While the adverse neurocognitive effects of antipsychotics are caused by a range of mechanisms, preventing normal communication with the frontal lobe appears to be a key mechanism contributing to problems like the sense of having an empty mind or lack of internal monologue. It has not been clarified just how much of the these effects come down to that drug influence, and it may vary from patient to patient as well as between doses and drugs. Not everyone perceives or describes the deficits produced by drug use in the same way, either, so the phrase “empty mind” is not a singular concept understood by everyone to be the same thing. In short, the lobotomizing influence of neuroleptics is a likely suspect here, but is not necessarily the only possible explanation or contributing factor.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If I deliberately stop taking Klonopin to induce a withdrawal until the point I'm shaking and then take a pill, would the effect increase?
Answer: Reducing tolerance is not about inducing withdrawal. Reducing tolerance is about reducing how much of the drug you are exposed to so that the adaptations around use are diminished in degree. If you use a lower dose for a while and then move back to your usual dose, you will probably notice a difference, though it will typically be short-lived. Putting yourself into withdrawal does not reset tolerance, and can actually cause a whole new set of problems and make it harder for your nervous system to respond normally to the use of psychotropics in general. You may feel more relief if you beat back withdrawal symptoms with a dose, and some people may find a day or two of drug non-use to reduce their tolerance slightly, but this is simply not a feasible or reasonably safe way to try and address benzodiazepine tolerance. There’s pretty much no upside to this kind of scheme and I would not ever recommend trying it. If benzodiazepine tolerance is a problem for you, you need to be discussing your options with qualified professionals and looking into alternatives.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does stopping antipsychotics, make you stop feeling depressed and sucidal?
Answer: It is a common experience. Many people find antipsychotics to cause depression, suicidality, or sometimes-related constellations of effects like apathy, loss of motivation, anhedonia, low libido, fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleeping and dreaming problems, dysphoria. Indeed, such effects are more commonly experienced than desirable drug effects and much more commonly experienced than drug successes. For people made depressed or suicidal by antipsychotics, getting away from the drug is usually going to fix that problem. If the depression and suicidality are not being caused by or perpetuated by drug use, quitting may not turn things around, though it can be part of an overall pattern of positive change and rehabilitation. There are two complications to mention here. The first is that recovery won’t necessarily happen overnight. Just going off the drug may not be enough to undo all the adverse changes caused by drug use, and someone may need to spend months or years recovering. Some people notice positive changes even before they have completely stopped, others require longer and recovery is not always 100%. The second complication is that continuous use will usually produce physical dependence and other changes which can cause new symptoms (withdrawal, supersensitivity, etc) for patients reducing doses or going off drugs. Both drug use and drug changes, including full discontinuation, warrant serious and informed professional consultation so people can learn the risks involved, the strategies and resources available for managing them, and create a plan which meets their own goals and priorities. Sometimes quitting is a simple thing and an easy fix, but sometimes quitting gets very difficult or precipitates a crisis and there is no guarantee that drug effects will quickly resolve after discontinuation. Be sure to research independently to supplement consultation, as most prescribers are not going to be very correct or helpful with their input regarding antipsychotic recovery and you may even have to find an entirely new provider to help you.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do some people not respond to antidepressants that work on monoamines?
Answer: There’s no reason for them to. All experiences that lead to someone using drugs marketed as “antidepressants” (everything from anxiety, depression, or insomnia to migraines, tics, bruxism) have causes, and those causes will seldom or never be “treated” by these drugs. The drugs have no medically beneficial mechanism in that sense, so from the very start, there is limited relevance to them. But, like any psychotropics, these drugs do cause altered states, and those alterations can impact the experiences which led to use. Whether alterations are preferable or not depends on the individual and situation, and the very same alterations can be a desired effect to one person but an intolerable adverse effect to another. People who don’t find antidepressants useful generally have no reason to find one useful. That is, the drugs offer no medical benefits and offer no or inadequate desirable alterations. While these drugs are marketed and prescribed as if they are typically effective and comfortably safe enough to be used by hundreds of millions of people in the current manners, the reality of the situation is that they usually fail and that they are more harmful than helpful in net. The standard or average response is to find antidepressants more harmful than helpful, so the better and more specific question here is why some patients do find antidepressants helpful enough to bother taking. Those are the exceptions. The answer to that will depend on the specific patient and circumstance each time — no two people will necessarily find the same drug or kind of drug useful for the same reasons or in the same ways. These are very broadly and variably acting drugs and they affect many aspects of our everyday functioning and experiencing. There is no single and efficient pharmacological answer to the question of why some people prefer drug use, and in cases where someone finds a drug very helpful it is often unclear why. Most uses of these drugs are in situations where there is not a physical understanding of someone’s experiences in the first place, so how a drug causes desirable changes will likewise remain unknown. All that said, “work on monoamines” is a very large net to cast. One might argue that pretty near any drugs acting on the brain are ‘working on monoamines’, since even drugs that are not directly binding to monoaminergic neurons are still going to have an affect on monoaminergic functioning. The nervous system is highly interdependent and interregulatory, so changes caused by a drug in one system or one area will inevitably impact others. This is necessary for our survival and will be even more pronounced with drugs which have many actions on many things. Common drugs best known for their actions on other systems, for instance opioids or cannabinoids, still have a marked effect on monoaminergic functioning, and plenty of drugs have both direct and indirect influences. It is true that the particular kinds of effects or influences and where and how strongly they are happening will shape what it feels like to experience the alterations of a drug. But, this is not particularly tied to most antidepressant applications. The direct monoaminergic actions of antidepressants may or may not be what someone finds most relevant if they find a drug useful, and the monoaminergic influences of antidepressants do not offer any advantage over the monoaminergic influences of other drugs. We know that acting on neurotransmitter systems like serotonin and dopamine is a quick way to radically change our experiences, but psychiatric drugs don’t do so in a cause-targeted, medically healthy, or particularly unique way.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do antipsychotic injections cause emotional blunting that is enduring even when you're off of them?
Answer: Antipsychotics cause long-lasting changes. While many of the things patients experience are the result of the drug actively impairing the nervous system or causing problems in other parts of the body, the effects of these drugs are not limited to those mechanics. Antipsychotics, like any psychiatric psychotropics, cause complex, long-term changes in the nervous system which will affect how it is functioning into the indefinite future. Some symptoms may be lifelong, others may take months or years to fade away. Some of this is about neuroplastic adaptation to the dysfunction-inducing influences of drugs, some of it can be the result of toxic damages. The nervous system is designed to be so changeable, so that we can adapt to the stresses in our environment and what they demand of our body. Homeostatic regulation is there to maintain conditions inside our body which facilitate our survival and proper functioning, and many things can be changed inside our bodies to promote adaptation to whatever our situation may be. Drugs are a more potent and direct stressor than most of the things the nervous system is designed to adapt to, so the adaptations produced with drug use tend to be more extreme and longer-lasting, and there are some drug actions which we have evolved no direct counter to. If our bodies did not respond adaptively to drugs like neuroleptics, we would be killed by using them. However, our ability to adapt can only take us so far, and drug impairments are still inevitable because the seriousness of what these drugs do to our bodies is beyond our natural ability to completely prevent or work around. Some drug effects are temporary, and our plasticity can overcome them after discontinuation, but some drug effects are not so easy to reverse. Some, especially more severe toxicity, may not be possible to reverse in many cases. The result of all this is that symptoms typically last beyond the period of drug use. This is a very general answer, as the exact mechanics behind emotional blunting, anhedonia, apathy, and amotivation are not clarified and may actually differ at least partly between patients and situations. So, we can know the drugs have caused changes by the presence of symptoms and by looking at what is going on in the brain but we don’t know precisely what changes have caused these particular effects. Dopamine and serotonin are usually involved, but may not be the full picture. Additionally, it can take months for a drug to more completely leave a patient’s system, so some effects may relate to residual drug binding even if it is less profound than during active use.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Starting on 40mg of Prozac, is this a high starting dose?
Answer: It is unnecessarily high. Whether or not the dose is appropriate for ongoing use, and whether or not someone can tolerate it at all, will vary. But, it is unnecessarily high specifically as a starting dose, as that is independent of the patient or their reactions and reasons for use. Starting lower and then tapering up can reduce some of the risks involved with drug initiation and can also make it more likely someone will find use tolerable to begin. Not only that, but we cannot know if 40mg is even necessary without first seeing whether a lower dose is adequate. It would be needlessly harmful to use a higher dose of a drug for the sake of prescribing convenience instead of patient wellbeing. Most patients don’t find any dose adequate, but the focus here is optimization. So, some people can do fine starting at 40mg/day, but many will be better served by starting at a much lower dose and then only escalating over time. Jumping on at 40mg will bite some patients in the ass while others will not notice any significant problems as a result. Additional risk-reducing measures can also be explored here, like properly informed consent, making sure the clinician has taken a thorough personal and family medical and psychological history, testing for medical conditions, and liver enzyme testing to see if someone might likely require a lower-than-average or higher-than-average amount of fluoxetine to experience the intended dosage.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do people commonly have bad dreams while taking olanzapine/Zyprexa?
Answer: Yes, nightmares and similar dreaming issues are very common with all neuroleptics. Individual experiences vary, and higher doses as well as longer uses tend to increase the risk of these kinds of dreaming problems. They are very common, they are normal, and they indicate drug use is having an adverse physical and/or psychological impact. It is important to discuss all drug reactions and one’s personal goals and priorities with the prescriber when using these drugs so that people can mitigate adverse effects and demand a change if drug effects are not tolerable.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does your intelligence return after taking Seroquel (quetiapine)?
Answer: Some recovery is very likely to occur after quitting a neuroleptic. The body, including and especially the nervous system, has all sorts of wonderful mechanisms for promoting health and helping with healing. One of the benefits of these abilities is for people to go through recovery after quitting impairing and toxic drugs like quetiapine. These abilities are not miraculous in that they won’t always be able to reverse, work around, or otherwise overcome problems that had been caused by drug use. But, they work diligently and progressively to try improving our health and functioning, and this will usually mean a restoration of intellectual functioning as well. Nearly 100% of patients should anticipate some degree of cognitive recovery after antipsychotic use and discontinuation. How much recovery ultimately happens, and how long it takes, is a much more complex discussion and is not something we have a great understanding of. Means of recovery and rewiring are always there, but some patients experience far degrees of restoration than others do, even after longer periods of time. Many factors can impact recovery from these drugs, like genes, health, lifestyle, environment, and history of exposure. There is also an unpredictability to it. Someone who experienced marked cognitive impairment as a result of antipsychotics can reasonably hope for significant amounts of recovery in the years following discontinuation, and many will notice improvements even during their downtaper and in the earliest months of being drug-free. There can also be complications, like withdrawal syndrome and supersensitivity, and those can lead to new or continuing cognitive problems, but given enough time we see progress in moving through them. However, for patients suffering from cognitive impairment caused by more catastrophic drug effects like severe toxidromes or stroke, the long-term prognosis will usually be negatively impacted. In short, expect some recovery but don’t take a full restoration for granted — it may never come. Some factors can make a full recovery less likely or more delayed.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are schizophrenic people just abused, or traumatized autistic people?
Answer: You are referring to two incompletely overlapping groups. There are people who are abused or traumatized. There are people diagnosed as “autistic”. There are people diagnosed as “schizophrenic”. All three of these groups partially overlap but no one group completely overlaps with any other. It is relevant to point out that autistic folks are more liable to be abused or traumatized than the average patient, and that abuse or trauma can fuel many experiences that ultimately get labeled as “schizophrenia”, but that doesn’t suggest all people have the same experiences for the same reasons.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How common is it for Schizophrenic delusions to be true after years of substantiated claims by the Schizophrenic with empirically substantiated proof to be proven true? Does the government suppress such truths as a function of torturing people?
Answer: The wording here is somewhat self-contradictory. A ‘delusion’ can happen to coincide with ‘reality’, so someone can ‘delusionally’ believe something which is actually also true to other people. But, if you are asking about “substantiated claims…empirically substantiated proof”, that isn’t a ‘delusion’. People can argue about whether the facts are adequately substantiating, but if there is evidence, it becomes a discussion of evidence rather than independent perspective. That is not to say viewpoints aren’t psychiatrized all the time. Certainly, someone’s feelings or beliefs or concerns can be labeled as a ‘delusion’ by the psychiatric system or by critics or by the government regardless of whether they are evidence-based or logically formulated. Usually, this is part of a larger plan of suppression, not a single incidence of sadism unrelated to the way people are being treated more widely. Government suppresses truths for its own ends. Things like torture are primarily a means to an end, not an end itself, so aside from specific members of government who can enjoy torture for its own sake, government disinformation, denial, conspiracy, and harming people to enforce untrue belief systems is not about the torture, it is about what is gained through those behaviors. Most paranoias about the government in “schizophrenia” are probably off the mark, in part because they are often a lot more personal. The government is spying on everyone, but not necessarily paying extra attention to you. The government is oppressing everyone, but not necessarily possessing a unique agenda against you as an individual. Sometimes it is very personal with the government, and this can get people feeling paranoid as well. The US government has had torture programs and psych experiments and such, and still does have some. It is essentially baked into the mandate for a political power that large. I don’t think most people feeling like the government is torturing them are being targeted by those kinds of efforts, but that kind of government torture has produced people like the Unabomber. Lies and denial generally go hand-in-hand with government torture, but it doesn’t so much matter what someone believes is true beforehand.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can antipsychotics cause depression?
Answer: Sure, but that means many different things. Antipsychotics can cause the entire collection of experiences which qualify for a ‘clinical depression’ diagnosis, so in the fullest sense of the term, these drugs can cause depression. But, less inclusive uses of the term can also apply. Antipsychotics can cause depressed mood, or dysphoria, for instance. They can also cause individual symptoms or a range of symptoms often labeled as depression, like apathy syndrome, social withdrawal, cognitive impairment, fatigue, suicidal thoughts or urges, compulsive behaviors like drinking or gambling, sleeping and dreaming problems, metabolic disorders, etc. Antipsychotics are literally depressing in the neurofunctional sense, too — they dampen or prevent (‘depress’) certain kinds of functioning in the brain.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it possible to stop psychosis from schizophrenia without antipsychotics?
Answer: Sometimes. Sometimes it is not possible to stop psychosis even with antipsychotics. The basic fact is this: the experiences labeled by some as “psychosis” happen for a reason, and if we adjust that underlying reason or the physical and mental processes which result from it, we can change someone’s experiences. Psychotropic drugs are not, by far, the only things which change underlying reasons or how they play out. What kind of approach will mitigate, resolve, or prevent psychosis is a highly personal detail which a psychiatric diagnosis tells us nothing about. It is also useful to remember here that “schizophrenia” is not a cause of psychosis, it is a diagnostic label applied to some instances of psychosis. The actual cause of those experiences is not being commented on. The diagnostic criteria are supposed to exclude all medical disorders and drug effects, but the criterion specifying that often goes ignored or unpursued by clinicians. How someone reacts to drug use, or to other interventions, is not established or explained by a “schizophrenia” diagnosis. It is common for patients continuously taking antipsychotics to still experience psychosis sometimes. Whether someone finds them preventative varies, as does whether someone finds drug use to curb a psychosis which has already begun. Because of how potently brain-impairing antipsychotics are, it is typical for someone to notice a difference when taking them, but they have no fundamentally ‘anti-psychotic’ mechanisms which can be relied upon to cause specific mental and behavioral changes. In acute psychosis, it is relevant to be thinking about stabilization — finding a way to prevent the present experience from being a runaway crisis which is not moving someone in the direction they wanted to be headed. Short-term neurolepsis is not the only way to promote stabilization. But, you can anticipate a pronounced and disabling effect to neuroleptic drugs if they are given, particularly in medium to high doses. Whether we consider that a good thing or just a convenient or face-saving thing is a more complicated discussion.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What in your personal belief is the most effective medication combination for treatment resistant depression?
Answer: There is no such thing. There are absolutely some less common options individual patients find groundbreaking (like adding or using amphetamines, benzodiazepines, lithium, cannabis, supplements, psilocybin, ketamine, etc), but there is no blanket recommendable option. “Depression” is any number of things, and “treatment resistant depression” is basically a meaningless term. Most depressions will not be resolved with use of standard marketed drugs like SSRIs. That itself underscores how essential it is to have a personalized approach, to depression and to drugs. When we start lumping together stuff which is not the same and should not be expected to react the same, we are undermining our own ability to have insight into proper intervention and support. Factory-line psychiatry is self-defeating for patients to pursue.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I have 20 pills of Fluoxetine 20MG capsules. How much money can I get for selling them?
Answer: Probably $0. There is no good reason to think you’d be able to get money for them. You might have to pay someone to take them from you. Fluoxetine is dirt cheap at the pharmacy and anyone who actually wants it can probably get it for free by seeing any doctor at any time. There are countless thousands of unused pills from discontinued prescriptions floating around in people’s drawers and closets. Do SSRIs have street value? Yes, sure, you might get $1 to $5 a pill, or more if you’re lucky. But, SSRIs have very little street interest. Finding someone who would pay you money would be difficult and likely impossible. If you’re asking this question instead of flipping the fluoxetine already, that suggests you are not networked or experienced and are unlikely to unload it. That said, there’s no reason to take on any sort of legal risk to do so, and you also don’t want someone’s health in your hands. There is no upside. You would make more money more quickly asking random people in a crowd for a handout or sitting at a bus stop with a change cup in front of you. Better yet, you could sell (‘donate’) some plasma, banking far more. This is not likely a serious question, but for the people who legitimately wonder, you have received a serious answer.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I had an antipsychotics withdrawal for a month, went back on it, but still have mood swings. Is it a withdrawal?
Answer: Possibly. There are three key points to cover. Firstly, reinstatement reducing some withdrawal symptoms does not guarantee all will be reduced. So, it is not unusual for some symptoms to carry on even after others have been diminished or completely resolved. Secondly, the timeframe can matter, so maybe these mood swings will disappear eventually but it will take weeks or longer beyond the resolution of other symptoms you noticed. And thirdly, there are aspects to antipsychotic discontinuation which can cause mood swings even if they aren’t withdrawal. Destabilization is a concern and doesn’t require physical dependence or withdrawal syndrome to be causing changes in how you are feeling or functioning. Aside from those caveats, it could be there are other factors involved which are causing these mood swings. But, if they first arose with the original discontinuation and you didn’t make any changes in your life besides quitting the antipsychotic when all these symptoms began, it is most likely connected to your month off the drug. Because a proper, personalized answer requires professional insight gained from reviewing your drug and medical history, interviewing you about your experiences, and perhaps even doing some basic testing, nobody on Quora can tell you for sure what is going on. But withdrawal or other drug effects are clearly a possibility her and you should pursue an answer with your clinicians.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do antipsychotic medications worsen psychosis in people who are not psychotic?
Answer: Antipsychotics cause psychosis in some patients, including some patients with no history of psychosis. As you are a bot, it is fair to point out that your question is somewhat illiterate — “worsen psychosis” implies the presence of psychosis. Getting past that flub, yes, antipsychotics sometimes cause psychosis. This is a risk for all patients, both those with a history of psychosis and those without, both psychiatric and non-psychiatric patients. The mechanisms and effects of neuroleptics are the same either way, after all. There are multiple means by which these drugs sometimes cause psychosis, but the most common and best known type of antipsychotic-induced psychosis is ‘supersensitivity psychosis’, aka ‘rebound psychosis’. This is the result of neuroplastic changes caused by continuous drug exposure which lead to psychosis usually after a drug is reduced or discontinued. Patients experiencing these changes due to drug use can experience drug-induced psychosis even if they had never before experienced psychosis. There is great relevance here particularly since most antipsychotic prescriptions aren’t for psychosis patients in the first place, so the majority of use revolves around patients who can only experience new psychosis, not worsened psychosis. And for patients who were already experiencing psychosis, neuroleptics can deepen, prolong, or cause an increased recurrence of psychosis.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What is the difference between clinical depression and major depressive disorder? Can both conditions exist simultaneously?
Answer: “Major Depressive Disorder” is one of many “clinical depression” diagnoses. “Clinical depression” basically just means that a depression is said to be distinct enough to qualify for an official diagnosis. Not all depressions are necessarily going to meet that threshold, as some may be too atypical or mild or otherwise outside the norm for diagnosing. Clinical depression can have any number of causes — trauma, diseases, injury, intoxication, etc. “Major Depressive Disorder” is a psychiatric diagnosis which is used to label a modest subset of clinical depressions. It has more stringent criteria and excludes most types and causes of clinical depression. It is still a very broad and heterogeneous category, but most clinical depressions don’t fit the diagnostic criteria for one or more reasons. Since ‘MDD’ is a “clinical depression”, that answers your question. But, it may be useful to note here that multiple differing clinical depressions can indeed occur simultaneously. This is particularly something to look out for when at least one depression is medical rather than psychological in nature, like an endocrinological disorder or drug causing a new or additional depression in someone who was already depressed for a different reason. The characteristics of the depression will differ in at least one way, even if that way is just about the duration of the depression. Usually, other dimensions are also affected, like mood, sleep, sexual functioning, cognition, energy levels, bodily health. Sometimes the depressions will seem pretty similar, other times they can be a contrast to each other. In psychiatry, many mood diagnoses are exclusive, so patients can be moved from one diagnosis to the next when new criteria are satisfied but won’t be given both diagnoses at the same time. However, there are exceptions to this, including with depression, and someone can have an episode of depression said to qualify for ‘MDD’ on top of some pre-existing depression diagnoses, like dysthymia. That is sometimes called “double depression”. But, as mentioned, most overlapping depressions involve at least one depression with an organic cause rather than two unique psychological conditions. This is both because some organic depressions are extremely common (especially those caused by doctors themselves) and because of how selective many psychiatric diagnoses are.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do anti-psychotics worsen schizophrenia long-term?
Answer: What does “worsen” mean? There are some basic facts we do know: How those build into an answer to your question is more complicated. What we are calling “schizophrenia” in the first place, what we are measuring as something which can improve or worsen, and what we say qualifies as “worsening” are all interpretive lenses which filter the information we have, and how we gather information in research and in clinical interviews. The simplest thing to say is that there are many patients whose quality of life will be worsened, whose level of ability will be diminished, and whose clinical course will be adversely impacted by antipsychotic use, especially protracted use. Exactly how many, and how to sort those patients from the rest, is more complex.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do psychiatrists avoid giving mood stabilizers or antipsychotics?
Answer: Most avoid not giving anticonvulsants or antipsychotics. There are at least a few scrupulous prescribers out there who prescribe minimally and tactically, and even fewer who seldom or never prescribe at all, but the general trend is to shovel out anticonvulsants and antipsychotics about as readily as antidepressants. They avoid it like rich people avoid tax breaks. Barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and amphetamines all have a political agenda against them which has curbed prescribing in comparison but anticonvulsants and antipsychotics are prescribed more often than ever before to more people than ever before. A lack of regulation and accountability, illegal marketing and risk whitewashing, consumer desperation and vulnerability, runaway off-label prescribing, and other influences all contribute to the trend. I get the impression anticonvulsants are not being pushed quite as hard as antipsychotics, but this is probably partly because anticonvulsants had a larger pre-established off-label and non-psychiatric market whereas a lot of money has been more recently invested in bolstering the use of antipsychotics in those areas. Notably, antipsychotics have been increasingly recommended to patients as “mood stabilizers”. In short, it is no harder to walk out of your very first psychiatric appointment with an SSRI, antipsychotic, or anticonvulsant — they all flow like water from a tap and you can readily access them even if your experiences don’t meet the diagnostic criteria for any psychiatric label. It may not be the same in all countries, but that is how it works in the United States and many other countries with a dominating psychiatric industry. Maybe practitioners posting in here will claim that they prescribe very sparingly personally, but the reality of the situation is bigger than that even if we took them at their word.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why is there a shortage of psychiatrists in the US?
Answer: There isn’t. There is a misapplication of psychiatrists in the US. Many psychiatrists are fully booked, no longer open to new patients, or otherwise swamped with requests, that is true. But, this isn’t because we have too few psychiatrists. Indeed, given the trends in what society relies on psychiatrists for and what psychiatrists themselves are doing with their patients, an increase in how many psychiatrists we have would likely increase the net demand for psychiatrists rather than reduce it. There are many factors which can limit how many people become psychiatrists, like the cost of education, the greater appeal or pay in other areas of practice or research, the length of time it takes to become a clinician, the strenuous work involved in good practice, the hostile industrial and administrative environment which threaten quality of care, and so forth. These are valid concerns to address and can even promote psychiatrists leaving practice. They are not, however, the reason why there is claimed to be a shortage of psychiatrists in the US. That so-called ‘shortage’ is foremost the relying on psychiatrists to do work or help with things they shouldn’t be involved with. Psychiatric intervention is usually failing patients while non-psychiatric alternatives are typically lacking in support and access, and may even be pushed out of the area by psychiatry. Prevention and social education are lacking or absent. Countless patients are diverted to psychiatry instead of more appropriate or helpful forms of professional assistance, and psychiatrists are often misdiagnosing medical issues as psychiatric ones — especially the ones they are creating themselves through mismanagement and ignorance. Overreach and poor practice compound the problem already founded on a lack of social and governmental support for superior alternatives, a failure to invest in prevention, and deceptive psychiatric marketing. At pretty much every step along the way of designing a system of support and care, we are making bad decisions as a country. This is usually because the dynamics involved are influenced by parties who benefit from influencing them in their own favor. We don’t have a patient-oriented model of care, or even a results-oriented model of care. Psychiatry in its mainstream form has been thoroughly industrialized and works as an industry. Our goals, priorities, and methodologies are all fucked. This is a self-perpetuating problem, as well, because poor psychiatric conditions will be an attrition against good practitioners and good practice, which will in turn lead to fewer good practitioners, more bad outcomes (increasing the burden on doctors, psychiatry, ERs), and an increase in practitioners who are allowed to persist in incompetence or who are looking to take advantage of the terrible state of the system. A few policy changes, or incentivizing people to become psychiatrists, won’t fix what is wrong. Most psychiatric patients should probably have never been psychiatric patients, at least as psychiatry is practiced today. Current infrastructure would be sufficient to help at least some of them better, but there is a lack of education about and support for alternatives in addition to the systemic neglect to spend in ways most efficient and effective for patients. So, we could be doing better, and getting better results, even with the current funding levels and such, but a more radical restructuring of our infrastructure is what we need the most as a society.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do all depressed people try therapy first before they resort to prescription antidepressants?
Answer: Of course not. Probably most don’t. There are three main reasons why this is: This is in addition to how psychotherapy isn’t necessarily going to be useful or a good fit anyhow, and many practitioners will be inadequate. Neither drugs nor psychotherapies are things we can make the best use of in a factory-line fashion, but navigating the complexities of selection and quality differences can be difficult and confusing. Most people are not being equipped to most capably and responsibly respond to depression, and the institutional approach to these collective concerns tends to be counterproductive as well.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I’ve tried many antipsychotics over the past 2 years and they all make my OCD worse. Why do Antipsychotics make my OCD worse?
Answer: Why not? There are some nuances to address, though. First, “OCD” is not one kind of experience with one kind of cause or underlying functioning. By mentioning a psychiatric diagnosis, you are not actually communicating what is going on — what exists to be affected by drugs, and how drug mechanisms are likely to interact with whatever is going on. A variety of things can end up being labeled as “OCD” and they don’t all work in the same way, so what we can anticipate as a drug reaction with regards to the underlying dynamics depends on what is being labeled rather than the label being used. Second, anxiety and compulsivity usually involve serotonergic and dopaminergic functioning to some extent, and antipsychotics are highly disruptive of that functioning. Whether the outcomes experienced are considered desirable or undesirable can depend on the person and situation as well as what was going on beforehand. It is typical for someone to feel different, but the exact ways they feel different and how intense those differences are will be more personal. Since breaking the brain is usually going to have an undesirable effect on how we are feeling and thinking, it should be unsurprising that you report worsening. Third, continuous use of a drug or attempts to discontinue can produce experiences that may differ from how it first felt to be using the drug. The changes caused by psychiatric drugs such as antipsychotics are progressive and cumulative. It is not like flipping a lightswitch, it is a bit more like digging a hole deeper and deeper. If a drug feels helpful at first, it may become the opposite when used continuously. This is especially common with anxiety concerns. And if someone found a drug useful or neutral, they may feel worsened by the drug if they try to go off of it, due to physical dependence and other changes caused by use. You are left with a few truths to think on: (1) antipsychotics are probably not a solution here, (2) changing how you approach these experiences is likely necessary if you want to see better outcomes, and (3) it may be there are underlying causes which need to be addressed if you want to experience relief, whether those causes are medical in nature or psychological in nature.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is 2.5 mg of olanzepine enough for schizophrenia?
Answer: That’s not how psychiatric drugging works. A psychiatric diagnosis does not tell us whether to use drugs, which drugs to use, or what doses to use. The purposes of using drugs will also very between patients, practitioners, and situations — not everyone shares the same goals or priorities. There is no objective or universal line about what “enough” would be, and people typically find neuroleptic drug use either unhelpful or more harmful than helpful anyway. In that sense, no dose of olanzapine is usually “enough”. Drug use is not ultimately “for schizophrenia”, it is for whatever specific alterations in thinking or feeling or behaving a particular prescriber decides. The feasibility of those goals and whether a particular dose of a particular drug can or will meet those goals is very personal and somewhat unpredictable.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is there any way to make an Olanzapine 5 mg pill only 4 mg? I have no cutter.
Answer: Making a liquid suspension is probably your best option, then. If professional compounding is not an option for you and you don’t feel able to cut a tablet, making a liquid suspension is probably the way to go. Using a straight razor or knife to get a 4mg pill out of a 5mg one may be too difficult to do with sufficient accuracy anyway, particularly without a scale, so a liquid suspension is the most reasonable way to calculate a correct partial pill dose if you aren’t having a professional compound a drug for you. There is information online about how to do this at home and what liquids to use: Tips for tapering off Zyprexa (olanzapine) However, you should not try it without first consulting with your pharmacist and prescriber to make sure it is okay to do this with your specific product and to help you figure out how to do it correctly. Patients rely on this method every day for getting the doses they need for tapering, but it does take some expertise.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I’m a teenager and I’m on my 2nd day of taking Fluoxetine (Prozac) and I feel su! C! Dal, is this normal?
Answer: It is a common and well-known effect of drugs like SSRIs, including fluoxetine. This effect has been known since before the drugs were even on the market, and warnings about it have been issued by regulatory bodies primarily based on the clinical trials which were run by drug companies to get their products approved in the first place. While most people don’t become suicidal as a result of taking fluoxetine, to the best of our knowledge, plenty of them do. This can be an effect unto itself, like suicidal thoughts or feelings or images or urges coming into someone’s mind, or it can be a response to other drug effects, like akathisia, depression, long-term loss of sexual functioning, severe withdrawal, etc. Though we can’t know from your question alone whether this is a drug effect or the result of other factors, suicidality as an SSRI initiation effect is not unusual and may or may not fade away with continued use. The prescriber and pharmacist should be notified right away and the patient needs to ask what to do to address the risk of it continuing or worsening. In some cases, the drug should be completely discontinued and stayed away from. Education and monitoring are called for. If nobody even talked with you beforehand about this drug risk, that further emphasizes the need for additional action to be taken. Many people recognize that a drug is making them feel this way and are able to challenge the feelings and stay away from self-destructive actions, but it isn’t always easy and that isn’t always how things work. This should be considered an emergency even if you have no plans on following through with these feelings. Be wary of being told that all you need is a higher dose, as that commonly worsens someone’s situation instead of helping. Advocate for your own needs and hold recommendations accountable to what you experience. Someone being a professional doesn’t necessarily mean they are right or helping.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How does psychiatry address concerns regarding the reliability and validity of psychiatric diagnoses?
Answer: Magic wands. Reliability is measured subjectively and doesn’t too much matter because it doesn’t matter to patients how often doctors select the same diagnosis for the same patient and circumstances. If there is to be any benefit for the patient, the practitioner needs to address the patient rather than the diagnosis. The diagnosis itself is immaterial to the patients in the clinical context, so how popular one selection is compared to the others is meaningless unto itself. Validity is a non-starter. Psychiatry addresses the lack of validity to psychiatric diagnoses by saying psychiatric diagnoses lack validity. Well, in private, or in academic literature, or in blogs and letters that industry marketing will paper over, anyway. Even in diagnostic manuals, if sometimes in roundabout manners. Diagnoses being stated outright as invalid is no obstacle because the marketing and the clinicians will often claim the opposite. Everyone wins, except patients. Magic wands are so valuable to psychiatrists because they help bridge psychiatric claims and reality. Anything is true or correct or helpful if you wave a magic wand which makes it so in your own mind. Reality doesn’t matter except as a jumping-off point for bamboozling people. Psychiatry is not needing to address concerns, it is only needing to wave magic wands. If there were some sort of objective accountability involved, psychiatry would already be dead in the water.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Could someone with a mental illness/disorder/condition (e.g. schizophrenia) be saying something completely nonsensical but still make sense to them?
Answer: Is it possible for you to not understand what someone means? Sure. Different people think different ways. Sometimes we ourselves think differently from one time to the next, as well. Someone meaning something when they say it is separate from someone else understanding what they mean from what they say. The more different someone’s thinking is, the more there tends to be a gap between what is said and meant and what is understood by others. This is true whether you use a psychiatric slur against them or not.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is psychiatry a threat to society considering how damaging it is?
Answer: What society? Psychiatry is an extension of society, a tool used by society to express, organize, and police itself. Any society producing or facilitating psychiatry is within that psychiatry. Psychiatry is a threat to many important things within a society, surely. But, it would be paradoxical to equate those things to society itself, since it is society which is manifesting psychiatry in the first place. The damage you highlight is society. So, psychiatry is absolutely a threat, but it is a threat by society against ideas and persons within that society. In the event society takes a new direction, as it inevitably does over time, psychiatry will be superficially retooled (given a new paint job, at best) to reflect this. Eventually, psychiatry will be considered outmoded as a mainstream tool of society, but that will likely take decades, if not a bit longer.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do antidepressants make you feel better after a few days, even if they're not working yet?
Answer: That is essentially self-contradictory. People use antidepressants to ‘feel better’, whatever that means to them — fewer headaches, less anxiety, no neuropathic pain, less dysphoria, etc. Feeling better is feeling better. Whether or not a drug is ‘working’ is based entirely upon that. Antidepressants are not given to patients to cause any specific physical changes or medical benefits, they are given to patients to change how they feel. Drug efficacy in the clinical trials run for drug approval will measure how people are feeling, not what a drug is actually doing in the body. It doesn’t much matter how a drug is changing someone’s experiences, it matters that people feel different. It is a common misconception that antidepressants aren’t working very potently immediately after they are begun. Substantial neurofunctional changes are occurring within the first couple hours of ingesting the very first dose of an antidepressant. Some people will feel differently within minutes. Because these drugs cause cumulative and progressive changes, in part because they stop the nervous system from working correctly and force it to undergo a lot of adaptation to keep someone alive, how someone feels after one dose will usually differ from how they feel after 50 doses or 100 doses. That can mean certain desirable changes only come on later, or disappear later. Some changes are more likely to start as soon as someone is on the drug, others are more likely to gradually increase over time. Likewise, some changes are ones our body will often nullify through drug tolerance while others are more likely to become more intense or encompassing over time. It is not at all unusual or unexpected for someone to feel different within a few days of drug use. Whether that is different in a good way or a bad way depends on the person and situation. Can placebo thinking also affect our experience? Sure, but drug actions are also in play from the very start.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why is there such a big push to replace illegal drugs with antidepressants?
Answer: Psychiatrists will sell you drugs, priests will sell you prayers, manufacturers will sell you consumption. The drug trade is lucrative, and there are more potential drug consumers on the planet than any other time in history. That means sweeping drug policies are more valuable than ever. If the choice is for a company to either have a piece of the action or not have a piece of the action, that’s a no brainer. Antidepressant manufacturers also have a lot of influence in governmental policymaking and drug regulation, and spend more on marketing their products than they spend on developing them. Marketing is what makes the biggest difference in when and how antidepressants are used, and manufacturers are even willing to take hits for tens or hundreds of millions of dollars to illegally market psychiatric drugs to augment the sales they get through legal marketing. The marketing is that damn powerful. Antidepressants are a juggernaut product and are the posterchild for psychiatric drugs in general. Pushing antidepressants is usually pushing psychiatry, too, and that benefits countless people to the tune of trillions of dollars. Psychiatry is an industrial institution, not just a philosophy. Pushing antidepressants isn’t just about replacing other drugs, it is about replacing the whole approach to drugs people have and societies. Drugs like meth, coke, e, and weed don’t require much marketing because people widely already know they can have significant upsides and anyone who tries them can typically see with the first dose whether it is something they fancy continuing with. Antidepressants don’t work that way — their upsides are usually only known through marketing permeation and trying a single dose is unlikely to demonstrate whether there are any benefits at all for someone. Most people are not a fan after giving them a try, either. Lifestyle drugging with antidepressants requires reprogramming what psychotropic drug use people think of as beneficial or acceptable or worthwhile. The ongoing push to swap illicit drugs or illicit drug use for antidepressants is a very shrewd move for drug manufacturers because there’s a ‘War On Drugs’, which means marketshares are being opened up and and drug companies can stand back and allow the government to literally gun down their competitors and then push their own products for them. Sweet fucking deal! For decades, psychiatry has been pitching drug use as the superior alternative to drug use. They have studied and sold their drugs (not just antidepressants) for addiction and for drug cessation. Not only that, but antidepressants are a big benefiter of the War On Drugs’ attacking of licit drugs and licit drug use, as patients previously given benzodiazepines, opioids, or even more peripheral drugs like gabapentinoids are increasingly forcibly switched to antidepressants instead due to political deprescribing of ‘funner’ drugs. The psychiatrist saying “that’s not a thing that’s happening” is coming off like a Flat Earther. Prescribing for addiction and for use-related concerns (difficulty quitting, difficulty staying off) is widespread and increasing, and drug companies are eager to get their drugs in the running for recommended use in addiction. Plus, drivers of illicit use and addiction, like trauma, anxiety, and depression, are already part of the antidepressant marketing core. We can see this discussed everywhere from medical journals to World Health Organization guidelines to the American Psychiatric Association website. Such denial likewise seems out of touch as you yourself say you’re asking this question specifically because you experienced this push firsthand. But the details you post about your own experiences do merit additional comment and explanation. For one clarification, meth is not an illegal drug, though your use was illicit, and psychiatrists are among the most common prescribers of it. Other stimulants are preferred in most cases, but it is still a legal drug and has a range of accepted uses. For another bit of context, the ‘rehab’ industry intersects with psychiatry but is not a perfect stand-in for psychiatry itself. As an analogy, you can think of psychiatrists as used car salesmen and rehab practitioners as used home appliance salesmen. I’m not trying to say that 100% of practitioners are bad people or people with bad ideas, but the industries themselves are awash with bullshit and if you are relying on faith instead of facts you are playing with fire and you are marking yourself as tasty prey. Doctors will generally say that drugs like SSRIs are less dangerous than meth, and that is true in some ways but is an incomplete story — many key risks are higher with SSRIs and other such drugs, and it is up to you to decide what risks and downsides are more worth the tradeoff involved. Doctors will also usually propose to you that using an antidepressant as a lifestyle drug is not the same as using a “recreational drug” addictively, even if the personal and functional goals for you are ultimately the same. The distinctions may largely be superficial for you. The legal ramifications for copping, holding, and using meth differ distinctly. In the end, psychiatrists and other medical professionals aren’t there to help you figure out the best way to use drugs as a lifestyle, they are there to sell you the particular services and products they specialize in using the ideology they are paid to represent. What you mention is the kind of input you’re paying to receive from workaday psychiatrists and GPs, just like priests would generally tell you that the way to salvation and a good life is through faith and prayer. It is what the average practitioner in their position is going to be taught, going to believe, going to say. They could also get in trouble for prescribing you meth instead, and likely have little interest in doing so. If you take their antidepressants, they have patient and a purpose and a mission. You become one of their faithful flock. If you say you prefer self-dosing methamphetamine, they get nothing from you unless they lock you up against your will or get a hold of you if something goes wrong with the meth use. Mainstream psychiatry is a tool of the government, not a challenge to it, so the enforcement of cultural mores and political agendas is also typically going to be worked into psychiatric services.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do psychiatrists broaden the definition of mental illness to sell drugs, but not broaden the definition of mental illness to include their side effects?
Answer: That premise isn’t true. There are two kinds of answers to this, one more technical than the other. The first answer is that diagnostic criteria don’t need to be changed if drugs are causing experiences that already meet those criteria. If you want to scoop up more patients, you have to expand the diagnostic criteria or the collection of diagnoses because drug effects are already routinely misdiagnosed as “mental illness”. Though the diagnostic criteria traditionally say that drug effects and other medical disorders causing the experiences would mean a psychiatric diagnosis must be off the table, practitioners and researchers can ignore this about as much as they want. The dividing line is purely theoretical and does not get applied very strictly in the real world. The practical definition of “mental illness” already includes drug effects. I think it would be short-sighted to say this is all about selling more drugs, however, as there are other industrial and philosophical motivations involved as well. The second, more technical answer is that psychiatrists have, albeit moderately, been expanding diagnostic criteria to include drug effects. Since there is the hypothetical distinction between medical problems and so-called ‘mental disorder’, these expansions targeting drug-addled patients are usually going to encompass those situations implicitly rather than explicitly, though. For example, antidepressant-induced mania was ushered in as a shoe-in diagnostic criterion for “bipolar” despite drug effects theoretically being ineligible for psychiatric diagnoses. The DSM-5 says: “A full manic episode that emerges during antidepressant treatment but persists at a fully syndromal level beyond the physiological effect of that treatment is sufficient evidence for a manic episode and, therefore, a bipolar I diagnosis”. Why is this implicit rather than explicit? Literally, they are saying that anything caused by the drug — “the physiological effect” — is not eligible. But, the implicit and rather brilliant part is this: the physiological effect of the drug can last indefinitely because drug effects aren’t just about active binding to receptors, the guidelines offer no timeline stating when a diagnostician can be confident the mania is not a drug effect anymore, and it is well-known that clinicians are very often going to label these kinds of experiences as “mental illness” no matter the actual role of the drug involved. Basically what this expansion provides is an official go-ahead for the misdiagnosis already commonly occurring. Putting it into the manual should increase the rate of diagnoses, which also means increasing service utilization, drug sales, and then the need for more even services and drugs to respond to the additional adverse effects created.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Could taking one single pill of 5mg olanzapine cause dependence or withdrawal symptoms, in the absence of any other medication?
Answer: I don’t see how that would be possible. One single pill of olanzapine can certainly cause significant adverse effects, including effects that last a long time in some patients.
