Some people have a catastrophic reaction to use, as well, which can lead to secondary symptoms that can last well beyond the period of use. Toxic damages can be done, but many persistent symptoms may be more about neuroplastic changes than the outright death of neurons. The persistence of symptoms does not suggest or require withdrawal, and most adverse reactions (including most long-lasting effects) are not about physical dependence. It is common for doctors to only admit to movement disorders being long-term problems with neuroleptics, but that is only one of numerous concerns. Withdrawal is a much more narrow subset of symptoms. Physical dependence is about the continuous use of a drug which produces changes in the body that create a homeostatic adaptation to the presence of the drug. In adapting around the drug, out body comes to rely on it being there so that our functioning is properly calibrated. Removing it means we need to recalibrate in order to function well again, and symptoms can result from the destabilization we experience in the meantime. If there is not continuous use, physical dependence does not develop. Some drugs can promote dependence more quickly or profoundly than others, but a single daily dose of any neuroleptic should never cause physical dependence and subsequent withdrawal symptoms. A single depot shot is a different matter, as those can be acting for months or even half a year and are very liable to cause physical dependence when used for more than a few weeks. Only a few neuroleptics come in depot form, and not all products are equally long-lasting. It is also common for patients to be given a ‘loading dose’ which lasts less time than the follow-up longer-term maintenance dose, so someone given multiple doses isn’t necessarily given the same dose each time. You asked about a 5mg pill, though, so depots are not the focus. In the absence of any psychotropic history other than the single pill, I don’t see how physical dependence could develop. That says nothing about whether there are drug symptoms still occurring after discontinuation, though.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why do psychiatrists think that lobotomizing people is a form of treatment?
Answer: Because “psychiatric treatment” is basically anything said to entail change. There doesn’t even have to actually be change, just the imagining of change in the mind of the evaluating party. Of course, psychiatric criteria divide up the kinds of changes being looked for, so it is fair to say that some domains of change are being prioritized or focused on. However, the convenient thing about psychiatric criteria is that a clinician can use any amount of imagination they desire to fit experiences or remarks into those criteria. The process of characterizing, diagnosing, and treating “psychopathology” is completely open-ended and is as amenable to freestyling as a practitioner is prone to. There’s no science to it, there’s no objective accountability, there’s just the beliefs and biases and motivations of individual practitioners and of bodies put in positions of power over practice. Anything can be “mental illness” and anything can be “treatment”; what is accepted or marketed in the mainstream is a function of popularity and profitability. So, some ideas and interventions can rise in popularity or fall out of favor from one time to another, and surgical lobotomy is a prime example. What is enduring is the open-ended and socionormative nature of psychiatry itself. How we decide to call something “treatment” hasn’t changed. Unfortunately, you’ve received a lot of half-baked or outright shitty responses. Some people have straight up told lies about when and how surgical lobotomies were used, to make it seem like they were never a psychiatrically oriented intervention or that they were only used for very severe cases or violent patients. Almost all have overlooked the fact that lobotomies are currently bigger than ever, in the form of chemical lobotomies. For a while, chemical and surgical lobotomies were both in vogue, but now chemical lobotomies have overtaken their surgical counterparts and are globally dominant. Surgical and chemical lobotomies were always used for the same basic reasons: they cause change, and psychiatrists can say that change is a good change, a marketable change, and socially positive change. Surgical and chemical lobotomies were historically used for pretty much all of the same purposes, and chemical lobotomies are used for more applications today and in more patients today than ever before. It is only the rare psychiatrist who will tell you that neuroleptics are not “a form of psychiatric treatment”, and those psychiatrists are usually disowned by their peers for not adhering to industry dogma. The bottom line is this: psychopathology is the expression “we don’t like this”, whether that “we” is a social bloc, political party, family member, or the practitioner themself, and “treatment” is therefore anything said to have a desirable impact on whatever is being deemed psychopathological. This is entirely divorced from medical health, psychological wellbeing, evolutionary adaptation, personal agency. It is a strictly social judgement and the differentiation of “treatment” from “not treatment” is strictly subjective and transient. An intervention being harmful, dangerous, unethical, abusive, or otherwise terrible has no bearing except as those kinds of traits can impact popular opinion.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does escitalopram usually cause weight loss instead of weight gain like most selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)?
Answer: No. Like other SSRIs, escitalopram is known for net weight gains in patient populations if we are looking at continuous use, especially use for many months to years instead of just several weeks. How this pans out on an individual level can vary, since each person may gain weight, lose weight, or get fatter even if their weight stays the same, but the most common effects leading to weight loss tend to be passing effects or intolerable effects, meaning a lot of the patients who do lose weight early on will not maintain that loss or cannot stay on the drug regardless. Escitalopram is not the worst offender of all SSRIs when it comes to putting on weight, but patients should anticipate likely gaining at least a few pounds, and potentially much more. A net gain of 5–12 pounds is probably the most common range, with some patients not gaining that much and some gaining 15–20 pounds or more. As mentioned earlier, it is also possible to experience increases in fatty tissue with or without a net change in weight, so changes in appearance or size can happen either way. The only SSRI with a meaningfully different track record is fluoxetine, but even that causes gains in plenty of patients and the long-term losses due to psychostimulation may or may not be held. The specific doses being used, and whether someone is taking any other drugs or dealing with a medical condition, can affect how likely weight gain is and how much a patient gains. Many factors which can play a role in weight (like sleep, metabolism, mitochondrial health) are adversely impacted by SSRI drug mechanisms, so the problem does not come down to just one drug influence or effect.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Of the 9 criteria of BPD, is there any one of these symptoms that are always present with a diagnosis?
Answer: No, by definition. The framing of the diagnosis is the “always present” part — “a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, and marked impulsivity beginning by early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts”, as stated in the DSM-5, for example. Whenever there are optional criteria, they are optional. The DSM-5 says to be shooting for at least 5/9 criteria. Some diagnoses have mandatory criteria, but this one does not in that area. There are certainly statistics which can be appreciated here, like some experiences being more common or being more commonly construed as “BPD” by clinicians. But, if the diagnosis leaves open the possibility of being used in the absence of any one criterion, it will be used that way at least some of the time. And that is being a bit generous, as many clinicians routinely ignore or massage away diagnostic criteria, even mandatory ones. Diagnoses can be used variably, and with more than a little sloppiness. Keep in mind we are talking only about institutional responses. We aren’t talking about things caused by a diagnosis, because the diagnosis is not a cause, and we aren’t talking about what “BPD” ‘is’ outside of a diagnostic context, because the diagnostic concept is what diagnosing is concerned with. The experiences themselves aren’t what create labeling boundaries, and the labeling boundaries seldom refer to how those experiences work and how they are formed. So, we are talking about culture, not what any one individual is experiencing.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it ok to take SSRI once in 4-5 days only whenever you feel down? I am doing it and I enjoy it that day. Is it okay to continue like that?
Answer: What works is what works. If that is what works for you, and balances the risks and downsides properly, it may well be your best option. Your prescriber needs to be aware of this and account for it, and you need to be educated about the upsides and downsides involved, but there is nothing inherently harmful about intermittent use ‘as needed’ versus daily/bidaily use. I figure most patients would feel better on a very occasional dose than on a daily dose, with respect to the undesirable drug effects. But for people that have bad nausea or insomnia or other initiation symptoms, this might be unfeasible. SSRIs can still do things like curb anxiety, sedate, or stimulate with a single dose, and there is no reason to assume your days will all be better overall if you use an SSRI on all the days you never felt you needed it in addition to the few days you feel it would be a good idea to take. Avoiding daily use is a great way to reduce the most common harms of SSRIs, though it doesn’t address all of them and can be rough on some patients. Additionally, some SSRIs are so long-lived that taking them once or twice a week is more like taking other, shorter-lived drugs every day than it is like taking those other drugs once or twice a week. The standard daily dosing of SSRIs is more about convention and convenience and profitability than what works best for each individual patient. Though, to be fair, most SSRI patients are better off never dosing at all, so we are already focused on discussing just a modest subset of people given prescriptions. It would be unreasonable to say all patients will benefit the most from daily dosing rather than more personalized regimens. It is atypical but not unusual for someone to want to use SSRIs occasionally instead of maintaining a daily dose. The proof of the pudding is in the eating, as the old saying goes. But, it may be that a different intermittent strategy would be even more fitting here.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Has sertraline made any changes in my brain? I’ve been taking it for only 3 days but I experienced huge memory issues and dizziness.
Answer: Changes in our mental experience requires changes in our brain. Drugs like sertraline are causing substantial changes in our brain from the very first dose. It is why they are typically prescribed. The more we use them, the more profound those changes will become, so 3 days will not produce the same average depth and scope of changes as 3 months or 3 years, but 3 days of use still causes alterations which are visible on imaging and can produce symptoms for a long time after. We won’t always notice symptoms as a result of these changes, but any psychotropic drug effects are, by definition, resulting from brain changes. This includes things like changes in memory and cognition. The dizziness may be a psychotropic effect or it may relate to other drug actions, like blood pressure changes. What does this mean moving forward? A lot of changes in the brain can be reversed or grown away from, so there being changes is not seriously problematic unto itself. Remember that the brain is designed to be changeable, so everything from learning new skills to making friends to living in a new place will change our brain in ways that impact everything we experience later on as well. More unpleasant stressors, like trauma and loss, also impact the brain. A concern with drugs such as sertraline is that the changes they produce are often not benign changes — many of the drug effects are actually toxic or otherwise disruptive to the brain. Breaking the brain is a more specific kind of changing the brain. Will effects like amnesia or dizziness go away if someone stops the causal drug after 3 days of use? Probably, particularly if the effects were not secondary symptoms — that is to say, caused by drug effects like stroke, seizure, or serotonin syndrome instead of just being the result of a drug’s direct actions on the nervous system. But, that doesn’t mean the effects will fade completely, or that they will disappear as soon as the drug is stopped. A recovery period can be expected, with the length of that period depending on the person and situation, and sometimes people don’t experience a full restoration after drug use, even brief drug use. We shouldn’t jump to conclusions, and need to give our body time, and support resources, to recover.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I have taken 200mg of Seroquel (Quetiapine) daily for 6 weeks. Will my brain return to normal? I feel extremely dumb and tired.
Answer: It may be your brain will never be quite how it was before, but some degree of recovery should be expected. There are three basic facts to keep in mind: Variables like what steps we take to recover, how we reacted to drug use in the first place, age, health, and duration of use can play a part in recovery outcomes. Getting through the withdrawal syndrome stage of discontinuation can also be complicated and difficult and we won’t have a clear read on what drug problems are still around until after making it through that period of upset. Not everyone struggles greatly to largely recover from psychiatric drugs, but plenty of people face serious consequences which last years or a lifetime. Having a recovery-oriented attitude and taking the appropriate steps to facilitate rehabilitation should be priorities for patients wishing to experience better outcomes after psychiatric drugging.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is it okay for me to only take my antidepressants on the week and not on the weekends?
Answer: Not usually. Though occasionally patients will prefer to use antidepressants “as needed”, once a week or less, continuous use means physical dependence will develop and it is not safe to take weekend drug vacations while still using the drug all the weekdays. People will often find inconsistent dosing destabilizing, too, though it can depend on why they are using drugs in the first place — what effects they are desiring and how susceptible they are to destabilization from drug changes. Some drugs are so long-acting that skipping 2 days every week won’t necessarily make a huge difference, fluoxetine (aka Prozac) mainly. In fact, there are even established protocols for prescribing fluoxetine just once or twice a week as routine. But, that is still inconsistent use which can undermine how stable someone is and whether they experience the alterations they are wanting to. Some people are most interested in desensitization and other drug effects which become most pronounced after weeks of daily use. If your grandma is telling you one thing but the actual prescription says another, the question is whether your grandma is qualified to be managing your drug use. It is almost 100% certain she is not. Talk to your pharmacist, talk to your prescriber, read the prescribing information packet which is supposed to come with your drugs. The standard professionals won’t always be right or give you the correct information, so independent research can be instrumental as well, but this is a pretty straightforward issue.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can psychiatrists or psychologists write prescriptions for patients who are not mentally ill but just want medication?
Answer: Prescribers can prescribe for any reasons they want. There are laws regulating justifiable prescribing, but that doesn’t mean unjustifiable prescribing will necessarily be challenged or punished, or even brought to the attention of reviews. Generally, people who “just want drugs” are considered recreational users and the law does not look kindly on people enjoying prescriptions. Doctors can get in trouble for running ‘pill mills’, but the War On Drugs has already curbed prescribing of sought after psychiatric drugs across the board. Most of those patients are told to use other psychiatric drugs instead, nowadays, despite the majority of them not seeking recreation. People who have non-recreational motivations don’t require a diagnosis or to be considered “mentally ill” to get a prescription the government will approve of. This is particularly since industry is primarily concerned with the money involved, and you can be given psychiatric drugs for simple things like a runny nose, a bit of trouble sleeping, or nervousness adjusting to a new school or job. There is no minimum justification, there is just the matter of paperwork. There is as much non-psychiatric prescribing of these drugs as there is psychiatric prescribing, too, so psychiatric diagnoses are often immaterial even in the realm of paperwork. The bottom line is that prescribers can prescribe however they want, but some kinds of prescribing can end up landing them in trouble, including losing their license or going to jail. Most psychologists are non-prescribing unless they are also an additional kind of medical professional, like a doctor, nurse, or pharmacist, but some regions have provisional privileges for qualifying psychologists which cover a lot of psychiatric drugs. Who can prescribe, and what they can prescribe, and what limitations are put on things like reimbursement and the paperwork involved will vary by jurisdiction. On one hand, it is a bad idea to give someone drugs ‘just because they want them’, but on the other hand, that is what much of psychiatric prescribing ends up being. Rationalizations prescribers make to themselves are manifold and require nothing of reality or factuality. The distinction here is just whether the government or other mainstream parties consider use ‘fun’. Not detrimental, not therapeutically unjustifiable, really, just whether they think someone is having a good time. It isn’t the same in all countries, but that is an attitude endemic to the United States at least.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Can you see a psychiatrist without taking medication?
Answer: If you’re paying out of pocket and they’re willing to see you, sure. If you want your healthcare plan to cover seeing the psychiatrist, it is possible they will require drug use or require you to see only doctors who will require drug use. But if you’re free to see who want, you’re free to select someone that works with patients outside of prescribing drugs. There are some psychiatrists who prefer non-drug approaches, or who don’t prescribe at all. They are very uncommon, but they do exist. There are also psychiatrists who specialize in one or more non-drug therapies, like particular psychotherapies or more serious interventions like ECT. So, basically there are three components here: (1) what do you want, (2) what do they provide, and (3) how is this transaction facilitated.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If our GP refuses to prescribe a medication, can we ask for another one?
Answer: Ask who? If you are paying for your GP out of pocket, you can select any GP willing to have you. If there are limitations on what GP you can see, such as due to health insurance plans you are relying on, that complicates things. In most cases, you can still move to change doctors, following the steps required by any limiting administration. If you need to change doctors in order to obtain a prescription, be sure to do research as to how to select a doctor and consult with them in a way that helps your case.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do psychiatric hospitals force patients to take medication?
Answer: That is one of their core purposes. Subjugating targeted people is the primary role of psychiatric hospitals. The tools they use for this are ranged, and drugs are one of the most obvious and best known. There are two kinds of situations usually associated with involuntary drugging: (1) acute intervention (making a patient comply with a specific demand on a per-case basis) and (2) ongoing drugging (usually marketed as “treatment” to “help” them). The first kind of involuntary drugging is usually blanket protected by law within particular boundaries, and whether there is anyone to meaningfully enforce those boundaries can vary by region, hospital, and situation. A patient has no say in the evaluation of whether this kind of drugging is considered justifiable. The second kind of involuntary drugging comes in two main types. The first type is a hard legal obligation where the designated administrative apparatus dictates that drug use must occur. This can be ordered of patients not trapped in a hospital, too. Patients will usually have no real defense against this, though sometimes lawyers and other help may be available so that people can fight for their freedom. The second type of continuous involuntary drugging is extortion, where a patient is told they will be kept imprisoned or treated badly unless they use drugs they don’t want to use. In most countries, this second type of involuntary drugging is much more common than the first, in part because it has even fewer legal stipulations. Extortion likewise also occurs outside of psychiatric hospitals. Where you are, what hospital you are at, what kind of legal situation you are in, your medical and psychological history, and other factors can influence whether you, as a specific individual, are forcibly drugged while psychiatrically incarcerated. Much of this is not about the hospitals themselves, as the politics behind psychiatric violence and the industrial stakes in forcing psychiatry upon patients are what lead to the policies and practices under discussion. Some hospitals, due to their staff or the attitudes behind their design, are worse than others, but patients should always consider themselves at risk of involuntary drugging if they are in a psychiatric hospital, or are seeing a psychiatrist at all.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If a person takes more of a psychiatric medication than prescribed (Such as Lithium) in an attempt to hurt themself, will the psychiatrist refuse to allow the patient to continue taking that medication and no longer refill it?
Answer: A prescriber can always decline to continue a prescription, for any reason. While there is vaguely the expectation that a prescriber refusing to prescribe a drug any longer will either make efforts to hand a patient off to someone who can prescribe, if they aren’t opposed to ongoing use, or help a patient with the consequences of their deprescribing otherwise, this doesn’t usually play out favorably for patients in the real world. Sometimes a professional deciding to take a patient off a drug means the patient is screwed, and potentially put in life-threatening danger (such as a severe withdrawal syndrome), unless they independently seek out an alternative. There is no justification required, but fear of misuse is a factor which can be involved. The risks involved in deliberate overdoses are a factor any reasonable prescriber will consider when deciding on which drugs and doses to use in the first place, too. This has impacted the popularity and commonness of certain psychiatric drugs, like SSRIs versus TCAs. Accidental overdoses (of the patient or if someone else takes the drug) are also a consideration, but not as central to drug selection as whether a patient is considered at risk of purposeful overdose and what that can mean for outcomes. Due to the War On Drugs ideology, patients who plan to overdose on a drug recreationally are probably even more likely to be cut off than patients who are suicidal. Put simply, prescribers are never obligated to prescribe psychiatric drugs. They are just paid consultants and make their own decisions about when to use drugs and which drugs to use and in what amounts. They aren’t necessarily making good decisions, and they shouldn’t be trusted, but they basically have every right to withhold drugs, especially when they think it is too dangerous to continue prescribing them. Patients who think they have been mistreated, or that their deprescribing was mishandled, can report this to medical bodies, though it won’t necessarily do any good. Patients who think they should remain on a drug, have the option to seek additional prescribers, or to bargain with their current one. Edited the first sentence because the question was edited to asking “will the psychiatrist” from the original “can the psychiatrist”.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How will I focus more on my studies while I’m taking antidepressants and antipsychotics? How will I make good grades?
Answer: Maximize drug upsides, mitigate drug downsides. Daily drug use as a lifestyle choice always comes with upsides and downsides. In addressing academic performance, just like any goal, you will have to find ways to maximize any upsides experienced from drug use while acknowledging and working to minimize the downsides. Sometimes this has to do with the drugs in a very direct manner, like staying on the lowest necessary dose you can, changing off overly-disruptive drugs, or taking drugs at a particular time of day if that mitigates effects that interfere with your schooling. Ideally, there is no daily drug use at all and drugs are only resorted to in emergencies. Sometimes it relates to how you approach the tasks related to studying, like designating particular times for homework that coincide with your greatest level of alertness or prioritizing schoolwork over other things because it may take more time to do it compared to your undrugged self. There are also situational factors that can be adjusted, like what kinds of courses you take in the first place (and how many, and at what times), making the most of non-drug approaches so that you can use drugs as sparingly as possible, and, if appropriate, discussing your medical and psychological circumstances with school administration so that you can potentially get lenience with some of your academic obligations. In some countries, you can get accommodations with class attendance, tests, or other aspects, but that can carry risks and biases as well. Ultimately, this kind of question is as much about everything that led to drugging and the situation you are in as it is about the drugs themselves and their impairing influences. Not all academic goals are necessarily realistic if you find psychiatric drugs highly impairing, and you might be forced to choose between academic pursuits and lifestyle. All that said, your question is ambiguous and can also be read a different way. Instead of asking how you will be able to succeed academically while drugs are holding you back, maybe you are asking the opposite — how drugs can potentially enhance academic performance. Just because drugs are impairing does not mean they are always impairing things we wanted to work normally. For example, impairing our anxiety response or our ability to feel dysphoric can potentially affect concentration or performance in a net positive way, sometimes. For another example, stimulants are well-known as aids in spending extra time or effort doing schoolwork, though performance itself will not always benefit. If someone is telling you that drugs will help you academically, the validity of their reasoning will depend on your situation and how you react to the drugs.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Should I stop taking Xanax if I feel like I’m depending on it, but I only have motivation and energy when I am on it?
Answer: Are the costs and risks worth it and have you exhausted alternatives? To whatever degree, the use of psychotropic drugs is oriented around ‘depending’ on them to cause states we weren’t already experiencing. It is their objective to open doors or facilitate experiences that would not otherwise be happening. Sometimes the difference is moderate, sometimes it is radical. The more we rely on a drug to provide an experience, and the more encompassing the changes are, the more likely we are to have an ongoing physical and psychological dependence even if our objectives change and we no longer find drugging particularly useful or important. This carries consequences beyond just the everyday ability to function without drug use in the present, and quitting can be complicated and a potentially grueling long-term task. If you are relying on a drug for motivation and energy, it brings up the questions of why that is (why are your energy and motivation so low in general?) and what else might be useful (what other than a benzodiazepine might help you meet your goals but without the same risks or downsides?). There are many reasons why someone might find Xanax to help with motivation and energy, most obviously including chronic anxiety and depression, and it is not an inappropriate tool across all circumstances. But, if there are downsides you’re not okay with or it is threatening to become a net negative influence rather than a net positive influence, something needs to change. How to pursue change will depend on the details of your situation. Your goals, priorities, resources, and options need to be evaluated.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I was on Symbyax 6/25. I missed two doses of it at the first week. Now it is not working for bipolar. Why?
Answer: It sounds like you are saying it was never ‘working’. If it was already not doing what you wanted it to in the first week and it still isn’t doing what you want now, it was never ‘working’. This is not unusual, as most patients will find a prescription in bipolar to be more harmful than helpful, whether right away or over time. Though dose or drug changes can increase the likelihood of finding something that does ‘work’ for you, there is also a significant limit to what drug use can offer and people are often relying on drugs for changes they aren’t liable to provide. Most of management comes down to lifestyle choices, not drug use, and it is still the norm to find drugs a more negative than positive influence even after optimizing the regimen. These difficulties need to be discussed with the prescriber, and patients should always research alternatives, additional options, and how to properly manage prescriptions because their prescriber likely won’t be providing all the essential information on those topics. If by “at the first week” you meant the first two days of a week which was actually long after you had been taking the drug daily, there are two main possibilities. The first is that you aren’t experiencing a continuation of the same bipolar depression in the wake of the drug skipping, but rather a drug withdrawal syndrome. Once your system restabilizes on the reinitiated dose, these symptoms should gradually fade away, particularly if you reduce stressors during your recovery period. Consult with professionals for more support. The second possibility is that you experienced a more general decompensation as a result of the stresses of dose skipping, which withdrawal syndrome or rebound syndrome are not required for but can still happen alongside. Drug use, dose skipping, missing nights of sleep, overworking your body, and other stresses can threaten stability in people prone to mania, depression, or both. In any case, it sounds like you’re saying whatever you’re doing right now isn’t adequate, so changes need to be explored.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do antidepressants work? Why do people take them if they don't?
Answer: Q1. Do antidepressants work? That depends entirely upon what you mean by “work”. Psychotropic drugs cause psychotropic effects, though the exact effects can vary by person and situation, dose and drug management, as well as other factors involved. What regulatory standards consider ‘drug efficacy’, what a clinician considers ‘working’, and what a patient considers ‘working’ can all differ. The goals and priorities of each individual patient will also commonly differ. Indeed, the very same drug effect might be counterproductive or intolerable for one patient but desired or the entire purpose of use for another patient. Some drug changes or outcomes are reasonable to hope for, others may be quite unlikely. It is common for people to be expecting drugs to provide benefits they generally won’t, due to marketing or cultural beliefs. Increasing the complexity involved, most drug effects a patient might be wanting to experience are not reliably occurring in all people taking that drug, how someone reacts will usually change in noticeable ways over time as the nervous system and other parts of the body are progressively altered by exposure, and the objectives involved are experiential or psychosocial rather than medical so ‘working’ is a lot more subjective and personal than something we can clearly test for and measure or something we can use the body to figure out. The bottom line is that most patients given antidepressants quit them because they aren’t ‘working’, aren’t ‘working’ enough, or are too harmful regardless. However, exactly what ‘working’ means to someone, and why or how a drug is said to be ‘working’, is still very personal. It is not meaningful to claim “antidepressants work” or “antidepressants don’t work” unless we explain what that is really saying. Q2. Why do people take them if they don't? There are three main reasons why this happens: There are other, less common reasons, too. Some people are legally forced to use these drugs, even if they are not helpful or are being more harmful than helpful. There are many minors given these drugs who may not know better or who are forced to use them even if they report serious downsides. Some people stick with drug use because they are never told they are taking antidepressants and this plays into how comfortable they are continuing on what they are prescribed, especially if there are no appreciable gains in the meanwhile. Some people mistakenly believe there are upsides which are actually either not really happening or are being misattributed to the drugs. Improvements during drug use aren’t always the result of drug effects, and sometimes we think we are doing a lot better than we really are but drug use or social pressures related to use diminish our ability to evaluate our situation more realistically. Some people are so incapacitated by use that they can’t even manage a proper self-check and make the call to go off a drug that is dragging them down.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Will the bad dreams caused by fluoxetine subside if I reduce my dose from 60mg per day down to 20mg?
Answer: It is possible, but I wouldn’t bank on it. In some cases, there is a dose threshold after which patients experience SSRI nightmares. In most cases I’ve seen (in literature, in anecdotes), any dose a patient considers useful still comes with the nightmares if that was a problem that stuck around after drug initiation. Other factors, like someone’s health, regimen beyond the SSRI, and environment, may be worth looking into if there is the wish to stick with fluoxetine but reduce the nightmares. Management tweaks regarding things like dose timing and taking the drug with or without food can also be explored. As others have brought up, you should also keep in mind that it is not safe to quickly reduce from 60mg/day to 20mg/day. Reducing doses quickly can actually potentially cause new or worsened issues with sleep and dreaming. It will likely take months or longer to most comfortably transition down, but there are some things in your favor here. The first is that fluoxetine is extremely long-acting, making smooth tapering easier than with any other antidepressant. The second is that you may still be able to tolerate a large initial cut to get your taper off to a running start. Be sure to research proper tapering and to discuss with the prescriber before making any reductions. In short, some patients may find reducing to 20mg/day useful with respect to eliminating nightmares or other kinds of bad dreams, and you won’t know whether you are in that group unless you try. There’s no way to predict with certainty, and no guarantee it will help. If you’re taking other drugs as well, be sure to account for how they may be contributing, to your sleep and also to the dose of fluoxetine you experience. Have a talk with your prescriber and pharmacist about your concerns and your goals and priorities and make sure to supplement with additional resources if you plan to reduce.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do psychiatrists really know what is wrong with their patients, or are they guessing most of the time?
Answer: Psychiatry isn’t about “what is wrong”. The rare empathetic, insightful, educated, dedicated psychiatrist is absolutely concerned about what is going on, what might be wrong, and how to correct it. Most of their time is spent on understanding and helping a patient, not figuring out a diagnosis or managing drugs. Most of their tools fall outside the typical psychiatric armamentarium, and a whole lot of it comes down to listening, with another significant amount of cases cracked by sussing out medical problems other professionals were too incompetent, uncaring, or biased to identify and sort out. More than a few spend much of their time cleaning up messes created by their peers, both patients who already knew they’d been screwed and patients who didn’t. But, psychiatry as a field of practice and as an ideological institution is absolutely not about what is going on, what might be wrong, and how to correct it. Psychiatric diagnosing is the literal opposite of ‘really knowing what is wrong’, and standard/best-selling psychiatric interventions like drugging, electrical disruption of the brain, and inducing seizures are likewise the opposite of correcting something that is wrong — they are concertedly causing entirely new problems and preventing normal functioning. Ultimately, what is ‘right’ or ‘wrong’ doesn’t matter to psychiatry. That isn’t how psychiatric diagnoses or prescriptions work, it isn’t the nature of ‘psychopathology’ as a philosophy. That’s not saying all psychiatrists are heartless, just that psychiatry itself is not focused on what is right or wrong in the medical or psychological or even social or environmental respects. Psychiatry is more about political agendas, like what sort of beliefs and behaviors should be considered acceptable and what sort of people need to be suppressed, and equally about how to fleece consumers most effectively. Psychiatry, as an industry, spends more on marketing in all of its varied forms than on actually getting results. Industrial concerns like profitability and capturing demographics are more of a driver than patient needs, and nothing has to be ‘wrong’ in the first place. The average psychiatrist has little to no stake in what, if anything, is ‘wrong’, and assigning a diagnosis or prescribing drugs isn’t about what is ‘wrong’. The average psychiatrist has one kind of tool, and it is blunt, often ineffective, and usually going to be causing more harm than help. If their priority was understanding what is going on or achieving the best results, their entire behavior and practice would be radically transformed. That isn’t the kind of profession they are in. As I said, there can be exceptions, but they can be difficult to find and even more difficult to pay for (particularly in countries like the United States where most psychiatrists don’t accept insurance anyhow and the best psychiatrists are even less likely to).

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If a psychiatrist is prescribing two medications and one of them is known to cause depression, is it safe for the patient?
Answer: Psychiatric drugs are unsafe. While it is true that some drug combinations and drug doses and durations of use and styles of management can make these drugs even more unsafe, they are fundamentally unsafe even when prescribed as scrupulously as possible. The questions faced by responsible patients are: whether the dangers are outweighed by the upsides, whether the dangers are being managed appropriately, and whether less dangerous approaches may be a better fit. Even under ideal conditions, psychiatric drugs are innately harmful and can cause a wide range of unintended harms, or at worst, lifelong disability or death. The vast majority of prescribing is not occurring under ideal conditions, as misprescribing and mismanagement are the norm. Most patients are given one or more drugs they should not be taking. However, this is not just about prescribers, as the superior alternatives which would better serve patients are often unavailable or inaccessible. Many psychiatric drugs are known to cause depression in at least some patients. This kind of danger is par for the course; using these drugs always carries a significant element of risk. It would also be quite dangerous to think that a psychiatrist is making a good call just because they are a psychiatrist, and to fail to look into viable alternatives to drug use before agreeing to take psychiatric drugs. Getting properly evaluated for treatable medical problems is another key risk-reducing step that is often overlooked.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do people stop taking their medication if it makes them feel bad?
Answer: Sure, billions of people do. Though some drugs used as medications have recreational uses and occasionally even a strong recreational following, the bottom line is that medication is usually harmful and commonly producing adverse effects. In most cases, the objective is to use the harmful aspects of drugs to produce net medical benefits. Drugs which harm infectious pathogens or cancer cells or parasites, for instance, also harm the human body. Drugs which impair or create hyperactivity in normal bodily processes will be causing harm even if there are upsides to doing so. How likely someone is to feel bad from drug use and whether what they experience is considered to outweigh the upsides of drug use will vary a lot based on the specific kind of drug and someone’s situation and priorities. Factors like drug management and patient education can also play a role. Sometimes it is essential to quit a drug that is making you feel bad. The harms may escalate or can be life-threatening, or may simply not be worth taking on. On the other hand, sometimes quitting a drug is itself the worst possibility even if taking it is unpleasant, and someone might be maimed or killed by whatever the drug was being prescribed to help with, for instance a serious infection. Balancing the upsides and downsides, the potential benefits and the risks, of drug use is a central part of responsible decisionmaking. Generally, patients require both information and professional consultation to come to the most constructive conclusions about their drug options. Sometimes additional drugs are prescribed to make use more tolerable. In many areas of medicine, drugs are overprescribed and can even cause more harm than good in overall populations, so sometimes refusing drugs in the first place is best.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How can someone with schizophrenia be forced to take medication if they refuse and are not violent?
Answer: Laws are laws. Forced chemical lobotomies work just like forced sterilization and forced ghetto relocation and forced euthanasia: some politicians give it the okay and boom. What criteria are set, and what criteria are actually followed, will vary. Sometimes practice precedes official policy, as well. There is also the possibility of covert or illegal dosing, like people hiding drugs in food and drink or giving a patients something they don’t know is a psychiatric drug under pretenses (like ‘vitamins’). This can be done by parents or other caretakers or by actual healthcare workers.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do I need medication if I don't have much enjoyment in life anymore, getting angry much more easily, don't feel happy at all, is it depression?
Answer: That’s not really how drug evaluations work. Are you experiencing depression? Maybe, maybe not. We can’t tell from your question, and it doesn’t really matter to how we answer your question anyhow. What matters is the things you mentioned and how you would want them to change. Whether or not certain diagnostic criteria are met and what particular label is slapped on the experiences doesn’t affect what your goals are or whether drugs are appropriate. This is life, a highly personal set of variables, not some magical A + B = Use Drugs formula. The first step in answering your question would be to consider what about your life you’d like to be different. The next step is to get a thorough medical evaluation to make sure there’s nothing going wrong physically which might be contributing. Then you research and discuss how to make changes in your life to bring about better outcomes. If nothing seems to be useful, months later, drug use may be an option to start weighing the upsides and downsides of. And if there are medical problems going on, addressing those is also important.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does a psychiatrist prescribing sleeping medication need to take the blood of a patient? If so, do they have to tell the parent if they find nicotine in a 14-year-old?
Answer: Blood pressure is good to check when managing drugs, and reporting requirements are regional. “Sleeping medication” can mean just about anything, including a whole bunch of stuff with a direct effect on the heart and on blood pressure. It is wise and most responsible to check someone’s blood pressure before prescribing, and throughout use. Taking down basic information like blood pressure at visits is a standard part of doctors appointments in some parts of the world, though psychiatrists in particular often choose to fly blind. In most cases, a doctor either won’t be troubled by the blood pressure or would prescribe drugs anyway, but it is still a useful risk-reducing strategy. As for mandatory reporting, what must be reported and to who depends on the laws and habits of the region. If you aren’t sure what the professional you are seeing has to report, ask them. Keep in mind they might lie to you, though. In some countries, a 14-year-old should be able to sign papers preventing any unauthorized medical disclosures to their parents, including test results and any private medical information shared during appointments. It is totally standard paperwork and should be asked about at your visit if you want to make sure your medical professionals are not sharing information you don’t want them to. They can still break the law, but it is a step I recommend.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does starting an SSRI antidepressant medication usually make a person's depression worse before it gets better?
Answer: Usually, people feel worse and experience worse health but the SSRI does not eventually improve their depression. Average depression patients simply don’t benefit, or don’t benefit appreciably, from SSRIs. Most patients quit SSRIs because the drugs were too harmful or because they were not helpful enough or not helpful at all. In the body of clinical trials which were run to get these drugs approved in the first place, the drugs did not even outperform placebo in terms of efficacy but caused a lot more adverse effects and even more deaths than placebo. This does not mean they are never useful to anyone, but statistically speaking, the most usual outcome is that people find the drugs intolerable or wholly unremarkable in effectiveness. As for the potential for worsened depression, things get messy because what we are calling “depression” can be very wide open. For example, if a drug is causing insomnia, or nightmares, or anxiety, that can cause an increase in their ‘depression score’ on commonly used rubrics, but addressing those specific concerns, such as by reducing or quitting the drug, doesn’t necessarily improve the depression itself. But, on the other hand, there is no independent process or set of experiences distinct from all others that we can point to as being “depression”. It is, in reality, an inclusive category with lots of overlap. So, it is simplest to say that most patients experience adverse effects when starting and also when continuing on SSRIs. How we say those effects relate to depression can vary, and those effects can involve entirely new instances of depression as well. Because these are potent psychotropic drugs, many of the most commonly experienced undesirable effects are psychological (cognitive, emotional, behavioral, psychosexual). Some of the non-psychological effects can still end up having mental symptoms, as well. Drug effects can lessen, intensify, or increase in number with ongoing use, and the specific effect and situation can be variables in what ends up happening. Some people do feel worse overall, regarding their depression, when starting an SSRI or other psychiatric drug. This may be temporary or it may last as long as the drug is taken. Sometimes other management decisions can impact this reaction, like dose, taper rate, what other drugs are used, or even just the story told about why drugs are being taken at all. While it is true that worsened depression in the earliest weeks does not guarantee lastingly worsened depression, most patients never find an SSRI to dramatically reduce their depression regardless; it is not the most usual reaction for someone’s depression to ‘get better’ due to these drugs.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What would be a better revenge against the medical complex? To massively promote alternative treatments to depression and anxiety, or to wage a propaganda war against psychiatric medication?
Answer: I think the best revenge is to do the opposite of what they are doing. That is to say: Methodology and outcomes are key. Promoting better alternatives can be a part of that. Waging a propaganda war may or may not fit in there. But, I think the core focus is the real concern: the motivations and the priorities involved. The medical complex is not harmful to all people in all ways, and a constructive, sustainable response needs to address individual differences in goals, responses, and situations. It will not be a strictly responsive strategy with respect to the harmful forces out there, it will be a self-propelled fight for betterment. When we have a proper focus and seek out the right tools and collaboration, there should be a natural gravity towards effective and legitimate aid. While I don’t think revenge is the best consideration to found a strategy on, regret, hurt, and compassion can still play a valuable role in motivating change and the processes which can bring about change. Just remember to put the needs of others before your own emotional satisfaction if there is a conflict in your advocating. If we are wearing the ‘helper hat’, our behaviors and priorities should match it. Conversely, people wanting revenge have an agenda which must be dealt with on a personal level. Advocacy work cannot properly be the arena in which they focus on their own betterment instead of the betterment of those they are advocating for. People who have been abused by the medical complex need to do a lot of self-work in order to be more fully capable of helping others avoid the same fate (or rehabilitate in the face of harms). Taking care of ourselves has to go hand-in-hand with helping others; a balance must be maintained if we are to meet our own needs and help others, too.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: What should I do about starting my antidepressants? I go on holiday in a month and I know the first month or so is the hardest part. Do I wait to get back or just take them?
Answer: That depends on your priorities and reactions. So far as the timeline is concerned, you should probably feel better after 1 month than after 1 week, with respect to drug initiation effects. There can be exceptions, and individual reactions vary a lot and can be unpredictable, but that trend is pretty common. If you are feeling so bad after 2–3 weeks that you can’t bear it or feel it would interfere with your holiday, you can taper off and try again after holiday, or try a different drug after holiday. Keep in mind that these drugs should be tapered onto, as well, so you are more likely to have a bad reaction if you start more abruptly and at a higher dose. Gradualness makes it easier to adjust to their dysfunction-inducing mechanisms and some people can find a gradual taper tolerable who would have found standard drug initiation intolerable. However, drug initiation effects are not the only reaction to account for here. There is the risk of drug effects which are more serious or more persistent that could interfere with your enjoying holiday. It is easier to have a read on how you will feel in the near future after 2–3 months of use rather than just 2–3 weeks, so there is a bit of a gamble involved here. There can also be specific drug risks to accommodate, like the potential for photosensitivity or temperature intolerance, for some examples with commonly prescribed antidepressants. In order to decide on when to start, you also have to consider whether the purposes of use outweigh these risks — if the reasons for going on drugs in the first place are more likely to interfere or demand more immediate intervention. Part of finding a balance will include whether you have exhausted or are currently exploring helpful strategies other than drug use, and whether you have a history of difficult drug reactions. Additional information about your own life and your goals and history are required to offer personalized drug support. Ideally, your prescriber has solicited this information and can give you tailored advice. Of course, many don’t or will not know what to do with that information, or simply don’t have the time, interest, or competence to give proper support. Calling up a pharmacy is another way to get some professional input. You should explain more about your situation beforehand, but it can be a useful way to augment your decisionmaking regarding drug management.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do small amounts of alcohol bring some self-awareness to overthinkers?
Answer: Anxiolytics reduce anxiety. If anxiety is interfering with self-awareness and a drug reduces that anxiety, it is possible that self-awareness can be bolstered by a period of reduced anxiety via drug use. Some people have realizations in new social or chemical contexts that were not occurring during life-as-usual. Alcohol is no more or less valid a psychotropic aid than other commonly drugs commonly used in depression, anxiety, etc. Which is also to underscore how selectively appropriate it can be and how easily it can become counterproductive. Are there situations in which some people may function better in some respects if they’ve had a drink or perhaps two? Sure. But there are limitations to that, there are downsides to that, and if it becomes a daily thing, that probably indicates drug use is not the answer. Since not all overthinking is due to the same underlying psychological or neurological dynamics, the impact of alcohol will be more personal than generalizable by that trait alone. In any case, it is likely there are still ways to gain insight other than drug use.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do I deal with a hypomanic husband who refuses to take his meds?
Answer: I’d recommend at least three things: So, asking how to work with a situation in a marriage is very much a partnered activity to go about answering, as one would gather from it being a partnership. I recommend explaining some of what you can and cannot do, can and cannot live with, in the marriage and asking him the same. Start with a focus on personal and relational needs instead of by saying one person or one behavior is the root of all problems. There has to be context for understanding the way dynamics work. If your husband endorses you having a more active role in responding to the hypomania, you can also use questions to find out why he doesn’t want to use those drugs, what he thinks works out best for him in life with respect to these experiences, and what goals he has that he feels drug use is not properly helping him meet even though he would like to accomplish them. There is liable to be far more common ground in goals than not, and finding strategies which work for both of you in meeting them would be ideal.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Should psychiatric medications be outlawed from prescribing to children until they are an adult?
Answer: No, we could instead outlaw bad prescribing. While most prescribing is inappropriate and/or mismanaged, I don’t think we could safely say that pediatric prescribing is universally bad in all ways. Occasionally, it may be a reasonable option, particularly short-term emergency intervention, though there are certainly significant risks. I think we can do better for society than a blanket ban. There are also two concerns with legality. First is that prohibition is a demonstrably failed paradigm for regulating drug use, especially the use of extremely popular drugs. Some harms will be reduced, but some will be increased under prohibition. And second is that barring prescribing doesn’t deal with the real roots of the problem. Quite the opposite — barring pediatric prescribing would sidestep the entire issue of bad prescribing more widely and would not put in place a framework that would facilitate good prescribing once children age in. Regulating prescribing itself would be complicated and imperfect, but would at least provide better outcomes. Even modest changes could yield massive gains in health and functional outcomes. At least half of good regulation would happen before prescribing decisions are ever made, though. Improving the quality of research and educational materials, improving the implementation of informed consent, improving support for superior, non-drug alternatives, and so forth. How psychiatric drugs are marketed and managed is as harmful as the drugs themselves can be. In short, bad pediatric prescribing is a symptom of psychiatric failure and eliminating the symptom by eliminating prescribing outright would not address the underlying failure. Further, information and alternatives (for everyday citizens, loved ones, practitioners, politicians) are generally the most effective antidote to systemic psychiatric abuses. Prohibition can seem an appealing option to some, but the problem runs deeper.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: All psychiatry has for schizophrenia is neurotoxic bioweapons and they just call it a day? How much do pharma terrorists pay the government to uphold these eugenic tools?
Answer: Q1. All psychiatry has for schizophrenia is neurotoxic bioweapons and they just call it a day? Basically, no. Practically, more or less. In reality, “psychiatry” is much broader than neuroleptic drugging (and other such drugging), with respect to “schizophrenia” diagnoses. But just because additional approaches exist does not mean they receive the same marketing and same support and same level of implementation as neuroleptics. So, for some patients, it is true that neuroleptics are the only thing psychiatry is offering. This is not universal, but it is a common marketing refrain that neuroleptics are all that would even be appropriate even when other options are available. Some psychiatrists do more than prescribe, and a few don’t prescribe at all or only prescribe maintenance or tapering regimens. It is interesting you lambast the toxic and misprioritized application of these drugs but don’t mention how the idea of “schizophrenia” is integral to abusive prescribing. The mainstream concept of “schizophrenia” is a big part of why drugs have become the near-exclusive clinical, industrial, and political response. We can’t adequately analyze and critique the misuse of drugs without looking at the fundamentally enabling definitions of “mental illness”, “efficacy”, “treatment”, etc. What we say we do or don’t ‘have for schizophrenia’ is contingent upon the formulation and implementation of “schizophrenia” as a social judgement, and the idea itself creates problems even in the absence of drugging. Settling for something shitty instead of investing in something better is a fair criticism of mainstream psychiatry. Most money is spent keeping things going the way they have been instead of providing superior alternatives. There are many strategies and ideas we have in the present, and have had for a long time, which would provide for better outcomes. But, they are not as industrially profitable or politically advantageous. Psychiatry is not in a mad dash for better tools and better, more therapeutic concepts. To the contrary, it continually doubles down in an entrenched refusal to become more relevant, more informed, or more accountable. In this respect, mainstream psychiatry isn’t settling for failure, it is actively and knowingly choosing a worse approach over a better one. Q2. How much do pharma terrorists pay the government to uphold these eugenic tools? I would posit that pharma goons, in their official roles, have no substantial political agenda beyond industrial interests (which can certainly mean weaving a more intrinsically political narrative for the sake of profits) and that it is government itself which uses the drugs in a way which would otherwise be considered terrorism were it undertaken by a party other than the government. By definition, legal and most especially state-sponsored actions are not usually considered terrorism. It is more convenient that way for the people in charge, naturally. It is important to keep in mind that government relies on psychiatry as a tool of its own power, it is not an otherwise benign actor somehow corrupted by industry. How much money is spent on ensuring governments forward the interests of pharmaceutical companies, and the worldwide misuse of neuroleptics more particularly? Trillions of USD on an ongoing basis, but exactly how it is all divvied up depends on what you are focused on. While there are a substantial amount of direct payments to government bodies and their related groups (campaign funding, for instance), a lot is spent on secondary and tertiary manners of influence and pressure (like lobbying and bogus research, respectively). Direct funding is only the more visible tip of the iceberg. To tackle that last past, are neuroleptics and related psychiatric drugs eugenic tools? According to mainstream psychiatry’s narrative, that would be a fair assessment. Part of the marketing facade is that there are fundamental physical, including genetic, differences in patients labeled as “schizophrenic”. Targeting those individuals for abuse, incarceration, and reproduction-impairing interventions sounds pretty eugenic to me. But, it seems to be a byproduct rather than a driver of modern psychiatric thinking, and is rationalized differently from psychiatric sterilization and execution programs which have largely gone out of vogue.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How can I get off of Rexulti .25? It was an add-on to antidepressants (which I am off) it is making my Vyvanse less effective. My doctor has tried tappering but horrible withdrawal.
Answer: Tapering more slowly. There are three main concerns to consider: Aside from adjusting the tapering plan, some people also find certain drugs useful on a symptomatic basis, whether because they help supplement particular actions of the drug they are going off or because they mitigate some of the impact of reducing the intensity of those actions. For example, an antihistamine may help someone with histamine-related symptoms when tapering a neuroleptic without forcing them to endure additional dopamine antagonism. Or, when the exact mechanism is not the focus, an example would be valerian root for withdrawal/rebound difficulties like insomnia. Nutritional supplementation may also be beneficial, in addition to eating a diet appropriate to the undertaking at each stage. As with reduction plans, the appropriateness of any of this must be personalized and adjusted along the way. Perhaps even more important are all the other strategies employed in withdrawal management and drug recovery which help someone prevent or cope with symptoms and improve their quality of life during the difficult transitional period. This can be everything from meditation to psychotherapy to bedrest to spending more time in nature to peer support groups to creating art. These strategies can also aid in helping with longer-term stability for patients who are quitting drugs but are still working through some pre-existing concerns. It is advisable to begin exploring some management strategies before making the first drug reduction, both so someone can learn more about what is useful to them and to have a support net in place before symptoms are provoked. So, I would suggest becoming more educated about your options in all of these respects and then having some planning sessions with your prescriber and pharmacist. Some places to learn more about tapering and withdrawal management are linked below, though these are not the full range of resources you might find helpful. If your prescriber is unwilling to work with you on this, it might be best to search out a new and more knowledgeable professional to help you with the final discontinuation. While there are more uneducated prescribers than educated ones when it comes to proper withdrawal management, there are still options to choose from in consulting with experts. However, not all countries have as many professionals to choose from, if any are noted in directories at all, and most will not accept insurance in the United States. Here are some starting places for learning more before proceeding:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Does Effexor (venlafaxine) cause emotional numbness and is this side effect more pronounced at high doses eg 300mg?
Answer: Emotional numbnness is a very common effect of SRI drugs, including venlafaxine. It tends to be even more likely with higher doses, yes. Emotional numbing or flattening, apathy, a loss of motivation, a reduced ability to feel pleasure, disinterest in usual hobbies, activities, or relationships, a loss of libido, and other drug effects related to our feelings, motivations, and level of satisfaction in life are typical with the ongoing use of SRI drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, even TCAs). These drugs prevent the brain from functioning normally and this interferes with processes essential for the regulating of experiences like emotion, perception, creating, socializing. Numbing and other diminishing effects on our experiences can also apply to physical sensations, taste, smell, etc. These drug effects do not depend on the reasons for someone to be taking the drug in the first place. They even happen in healthy volunteers in clinical trials designed to study what happens when people who have no psychological or medical reason to be using the drugs are taking them. The effects also do not depend on whether someone was finding the drug helpful or not. The same problems can occur whether someone finds a drug highly helpful, barely helpful, or completely unhelpful. Of course, they are often considered counterproductive effects, so they can factor into how helpful a drug ultimately feels to be using. Longer durations of use and higher doses usually correlate to a higher likelihood and greater intensity of these emotional effects. Though they can begin right away, with the first dose, it is common for them to escalate some over time as the dysfunction induced by drug use leads to more persistent global changes in brain functioning meant to accommodate or work around the dysfunction. Not everyone reacts to any given drug or dose the same way, though. Sometimes a lower dose of the same drug will not produce this problem for a patient, but oftentimes any clinically useful dose of the drug will still cause it if someone notices it happening. To learn a bit more about drugs like venlafaxine, I recommend doing some additional reading, for example at free resource pages like these:

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Do hallucinations start to appear gradually? Or all at once? It's just that there's been some things that I think are weird and I think are too subtle to be hallucinations?
Answer: Anything goes. “Hallucinations” are generally just anything you actively perceive that other people around you don’t. They aren’t ‘real’ or ‘fake’, per se. All perceptions are imaginary, and the main question here is to what extent other people are sharing particular imaginings. Experiences regarded as hallucinations can be subtle or dramatic, gradual or sudden, everyday stuff or very unusual stuff. Anything we can perceive or think or dream is being experienced through the same basic apparatuses, so the only limits of hallucinations will be the limits of those apparatuses. Hallucination is basically about how those apparatuses are being used. There are many different reasons for perceptions to differ between people. Which is to say, hallucinations can happen for many different reasons. The ways in which they happen, and reasons for which they happen, can impact their characteristics. Everything from meditating to laying down to fall asleep to using drugs to spiritual ecstasy to sensory deprivation to droning sounds to electrical stimulation of the brain to strong emotions can lead to hallucinating, as can many medical conditions, injuries, and fever or hypothermia. Essentially, anything which influences the brain significantly can play a part.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Are SSRI destroying receptors?
Answer: Yes. The only question is how often and to what extent this happens in patients. There are a variety of mechanisms observed by which SSRIs can destroy neurons directly or facilitate their death indirectly, plus the known prospect of catastrophic drug effects with an acutely toxic or otherwise damaging effect (toxidromes, seizure, stroke, brain bleed, etc). There are plenty of other means by which they damage neurons in ways which will not necessarily lead to neuronal death. However, no research is able to characterize how many neurons the average patient loses, detail with precision how dose and duration of exposure impact the destructive burden, or explain all the variables which may lead to much worse outcomes in some patients than others under similar circumstances of use. So far, it appears that other kinds of harms to neurons and the brain may be more responsible for poor outcomes, generally speaking. It is worth noting that not all SSRIs exert all the same toxic influences, or all the same toxic influences to the same extent, so the drugs are not fully interchangeable in these kinds of discussions. Also of interest is that research data used to hypothesize that SSRIs may spur neurogenesis in select areas of the brain may be looking at the aftermath of SSRI neurotoxicity rather than a healthy or independently restorative process. If your question is meaning to ask whether how someone feels on or after an SSRI is the result of receptors being destroyed, we don’t have a great answer to that so far. While many of the common effects, even serious or impairing ones, do not require or suggest brain damage, some drug harms do involve damage to neurons or other cells, and suspicion increases with effects lasting many years after drug discontinuation.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: St. John’s Wort makes me awfully tired and unfocused. I have elevated renin which means more angiotensin 2 which raises serotonin, which induces glutamate excess. Is it the wrong medication as an SSRI?
Answer: Right/wrong is based on how you feel. The downstream effects of particular influences can be useful in some instances of troubleshooting, but none of that explains someone’s response to a drug with respect to ideas like depression because they are broad and encompassing psychosocial concepts with no specific or discrete physical underpinnings. There are no physical details you could share which would tell us whether a particular drug will feel alleviatory unless you whittle things down to specific symptoms. If feeling tired means a more stimulating drug would be appreciated, for example, that is more feasible to tailor drug use around. But that, too, is based on how you’re feeling, not things like extrapolations about glutamate. What works is what works. So, the thing to consider here is whether St John’s Wort is doing what you want it to, and whether what you want it to do is something reasonable to expect of drug use in general. If there are downsides you don’t feel worth it or there aren’t the upsides you are depending on a drug to provide, clearly it either isn’t the drug for you or is being managed inadequately. (With herbal supplements, there is also the elevated need to consider the consistency of the source — the ingredient ratio, purity, uniformity, etc.) If St John’s Wort isn’t working out for you, then maybe something else would. Maybe not, but either way, you’d have your answer as to whether this specific regimen is fitting. Dealing with whatever is causing your elevated plasma renin may be essential here, though, and make suggestions about what drugs to use. You never mention what your symptoms or treatment goals are, so what potential relevance hypericum perforatum might have is unclear. But, since PRA changes are associated with a range of medical conditions and the nature of those conditions can influence what kinds of concerns you might have and how they respond to drug use, I recommend looking at the bigger picture with your consulting clinicians in order to decipher what kind of drugging might be appropriate. It isn’t unusual for someone to find reuptake inhibitors to cause tiredness or poor focus, but whatever is going on medically needs to be accounted for as well.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Let's say that I have a certain level of serotonin in the brain. I take serotonin for, let's say, a year. After stopping the SSRI, do the serotonin levels fall below these from before taking SSRI?
Answer: Unfortunately, the question is incoherent. The aim of the question is coherent, so I will build towards addressing that aim by dismantling the myths and misunderstandings which were incorporated into it. The TLDR is that someone should have roughly the same amount of serotonin around before, during, and after SSRI use and that what these drugs change is how the serotonin is put to use. The brain works differently before SSRI use than it does after SSRI use, and adjustments are made which will have to be adapted away from after drug discontinuation. Though SSRIs can also damage the machinery of the nervous system and make it harder to regain our health and functioning, the focus of this answer is reversible changes. The first thing to say is that SSRIs are not serotonin. SSRIs have an affect on the serotonin system, and also affect serotonin outside the nervous system in many ways. But, SSRIs are not serotonin or substitutes for serotonin. What SSRIs primarily do with regards to serotonin is impair mechanisms by which the body manages serotonin and, more directly, impair what serotonin can do. The main interest is in how this causes dysfunction in the brain which leads to altered states, but the effects outside the nervous system can also be clinically important and affect everything from blood clotting to our microbiome. So, the relevant thing here is that SSRIs do change what is going on with serotonin in the body, but they aren’t radically changing how much serotonin is around, including how much is being produced or available to be put to use. Thus, neither using nor quitting SSRIs will cause a big drop in how much serotonin is in our brain or in our body or available for the body to use. Use may impact serotonin synthesis or other aspects of serotonin availability, but the main concern is how the nervous system is disabled by and rewired by chronic use and that this will require time to adjust away from after use in addition to potentially causing serious symptoms during and following drug exposure. On the flip side, consuming serotonin is not usually relevant to any of this. If we take serotonin orally, it is going to be digested like food. In fact, much of the food we eat has serotonin in it, as serotonin is a vital component of regulation for many living things, both animals and plants, and is typically still in the parts of those things we consume on a regular basis. When we eat serotonin, it doesn’t get added to our stores of serotonin or float around in our brains to cause psychotropic reactions. Serotonin is synthesized in our own bodies and we take materials and energy from what we eat in order to keep our internal serotonin synthesis going. Serotonin also does not cross the blood-brain barrier, meaning the serotonin found in other parts of the body can’t hop a ride into the brain and start stimulating neurons there. Infusing serotonin directly into our bloodstream will cause effects, usually undesirable ones but sometimes medically useful ones, but that serotonin would not travel into our brain to be used like the serotonin synthesized by our brain’s own cells. Though your question asks about the brain, serotonin plays many, many different roles in the body, and is found in many places performing a variety of tasks. Even in the brain itself it does more than just one thing, and this multitasking increases the impact and complications of using serotonin-affecting drugs. This brings us to the idea of homeostasis which is the widesweeping set of processes by which the body maintains health and functioning. Conditions have to be just right in order for life to survive, and for our cells and systems to function properly. There are mechanisms in the body always working to make sure that the conditions are closer to ideal for our survival and for the functioning of all our parts. Every second, adjustments are being made throughout our body to facilitate adaptation to whatever is going on — the temperature of our environment, our state of nutrition, our wakefulness, any movement going on, psychological stresses, etc. Part of maintaining homeostasis is making sure serotonin is being put to proper use and is available where needed. In light of that, it is true that there are ‘levels’ of serotonin — levels of ongoing production, amounts held in store for neurons to use when prompted, concentrations floating around in our blood to fulfill tasks there, and so forth. Serotonin is in tons of places and part of homeostasis is making sure we have the right amounts doing the right stuff at the right times, second by second. SSRIs come in and mess a lot of that up, and the body has to use its mechanisms of adaptation to counteract, work around, or at least take into account the disruptions and impairments caused by drug use. Drugs are adjusted to just like other factors that work against our ideal conditions for survival.
