But, this doesn’t cause a massive increase or drop in the overall amount of serotonin around, in the brain or elsewhere. It causes a change in how serotonin is being put to use and in our abilities to manage serotonin and to use it to fulfill particular tasks. We don’t meaningfully lose serotonin or gain serotonin, the problems arise from the mechanisms managing serotonin and its uses being interfered with. And because the body has to adjust to this interference in order to keep us alive and to keep our body functioning as well as it can manage to under the circumstances, widescale changes occur with ongoing SSRI use. These changes start within minutes to hours of our first dose and continue progressively the longer we take the drug. These changes are an adaptation to the presence of the drug and the way it prevents the body from working normally. If the drug is removed from the situation, those adaptations are no longer appropriate and must be changed again for our homeostasis to be served. Quitting an SSRI involves a period in which the body is moving towards a new balance of functioning. Again, we don’t have too much or too little serotonin in this period, but the alterations to how serotonin is put to work will not be fitting to our new circumstances and our homeostasis can falter. We can experience symptoms and even more serious health problems until we can more completely maintain the conditions our body requires for thriving without the interference of drugs.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How is Caplyta different than other antipsychotics? My doctor just prescribed it for a mood disorder I have.
Answer: Any number of ways, and not much at all. Every drug has its own unique nuances, but the drugs marketed as “antipsychotics” are all more similar than dissimilar and lumateperone (aka Caplyta) is no exception. Since it has been far less researched and reviewed than most other drugs in its class, there is less solidified about it versus the other drugs. However, there are some meaningful differences worth noting in the current data, for instance: Like with any of these drugs, a patient may find lumateperone far better or far worse than another drug in the same class. As with the other antipsychotics, it is a toxic, lobotomizing drug and one whose approval is based on clinical trials that were never properly designed to support prescribing practices or even drug efficacy. If you find it helpful, great! There is no reason to figure this drug will cause more good than harm overall, in step with other antipsychotics, but individual reactions vary just as individual goals and priorities do. The net statistics aren’t the only thing that matter, after all. There are differences to each drug and whether any particular ones are relevant to your experience is not generalizable. Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Is brain mapping effective in getting a BPD diagnosis? Can a psychiatrist look at the results and find a correlation with the symptoms you experience?
Answer: Q1. Is brain mapping effective in getting a BPD diagnosis? Basically, no. There are no physical parameters which match to, suggest, or justify any psychiatric diagnosis. The diagnoses are not physically distinct, physically unique, or physically defined. No imaging results can justify or indicate or exclude a “BPD” diagnosis. What matters in applying a diagnosis is the diagnostic criteria. Now, clinicians can make all sorts of totally unscientific claims about imaging results supporting a “BPD” diagnosis, but there is no accountability involved so they can say anything they want. Since having a diagnosis provides no insight, no therapeutic options, no information whatsoever to what someone already possesses, there is little value in receiving a diagnosis in the first place unless you simply need a label as a passkey to access services. And if that is the case, the diagnosis may not matter, and its accuracy to diagnostic criteria may not matter. It depends on what is being accessed. Likewise, whether ‘brain mapping’ is considered a legitimately supportive aspect of diagnosing depends on who is making the rules. Administrative shit. Q2. Can a psychiatrist look at the results and find a correlation with the symptoms you experience? Well, you could say that about anyone. It isn’t particular to psychiatric diagnoses. What is going on in the brain will always correlate to our experiences, and the trick is just to look at things with patterns we can understand. It isn’t necessarily going to be very incisive or explanatory, but there are surely correlations to be viewed. Note that, as your question phrased it, we are talking about correlations to experiences rather than to diagnoses, as the underlying patterns of functioning or underlying structural traits can vary across patients even if they are given the same diagnosis. Because many different techniques fall under the broad umbrella of “brain mapping”, how useful and how specific and how legitimate a strategy is can vary, as can how relevant it is for each patient. Most of what we hear about ‘brain mapping’ is just marketing bullshit. Additionally, whether or not a psychiatrist can make use of ‘brain maps’ will depend on the psychiatrist, their training, their familiarity with particular procedures and results documents, and their perspectives about how to apply the results to clinical situations. Should we bother with ‘brain mapping’? If you have the money to burn and can separate fact from fantasy, I don’t see a big reason why not. Like palm reading, tarot, divination, personality tests, and other such tools, brain mapping used conscientiously can be a conduit to better self-understanding, confidence, and wellbeing (or a tool for grifting, exploitation, and control). A lot rides on what we are bringing to the table and our assumptions about how something works. Drink responsibly, as the saying goes.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: If someone with bipolar disorder stops taking their medication, what are the chances of them going into remission and not having bipolar anymore?
Answer: “Bipolar” isn’t something people can have or not have. There is nothing physical a person has or which is inside them to cause experiences labeled by clinicians as “bipolar disorder”. It doesn’t come or go, it isn’t there or absent, there just is no such thing. The focus here is the experiences themselves. Do someone’s experiences meet the diagnostic criteria? Did they in the past? A psychiatric diagnosis is not a crystal ball that magically predicts the future. Since it is not magic and there is no physical reality to it, the only conclusion can be that the diagnosis is unable to tell us what someone will experience in the future. The question asserts there were experiences in the past which met diagnostic criteria, if we generously assume the criteria were applied correctly. Will those experiences continue or recur? The diagnosis doesn’t tell us that, and outcomes vary. This is the case regardless of whether someone keeps using drugs. “Bipolar” is not a cause of anything, it is the term used for experiences already occurring for any number of reasons. The reasons for the experiences to happen will often play a very significant role in whether they continue or recur. That, how someone chooses to respond to them, and the steps taking in going off drugs are key variables to be considering: Also keep in mind “remission” is not the same as “not having bipolar anymore” — “remission” is explicitly saying the diagnosis still applies. People, many doctors and many laypersons, will often say that diagnoses are ‘forever’ and that there is no “cure”. The thing is, we define those however we choose to. If there is no medical pathology, there is nothing we can point to as objectively being illness or treated or cured. Our definition of someone being “mentally ill” is totally arbitrary and so how long we say that “mental illness” lasts is likewise arbitrary. If we keep using a label which describes experiences that happened in the past and then never happened again, I question the usefulness of that label. So, the answer to your question has no honest, representative statistic. It is not honest or representative to group patients and patient outcomes by superficial psychiatric diagnoses like “bipolar disorder”, and the reasons for experiences like depression or mania to recur in the future depend on factors that diagnoses don’t communicate to us. Experiencing “remission” or a resolution of underlying causes and patterns isn’t a matter of chance or odds, it is a matter of details and effort and compatibility. We are not all the same, our situations and experiences and concerns are not all the same, and staying on or going off drugs can both be catastrophic depending on those details and situations.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: How do antipsychotics cause damage to the brain?
Answer: Generally speaking, it may be simplest to organize by scale: Like most psychiatric drugs, antipsychotics are toxic to various parts of cells in the brain, like mitochondria, cytoplasm, and DNA itself. Not all drugs are equally toxic in all ways, but all drugs are nevertheless toxic. Since some of these damages can potentially be repaired or recovered from, not everyone would consider them “brain damage”. Their impact on someone’s day to day experience is also not necessarily going to be clear, but naturally this is all bad for the body and bad for the health of the brain even more specifically. It is not established how pervasive these damages are in individual patients given antipsychotics, and it can be a very difficult thing to measure. Again in line with what we often see with psychiatric drugs, antipsychotics cause cellular death, including the death of neurons. There can be multiple mechanisms through which this happens, and there is variation between specific drugs and also the doses being used and durations of exposure. Obvious symptoms may or may not result, but the more critical the connections are which are being compromised or the more loss of tissue there is, the more we can anticipate an adverse impact on health and quality of life. Problematically, even seriously disabling damage may not be readily visible to doctors using standard methods of investigation, such as brain imaging. Stroke, seizure, falls, infections, chronic sleep deprivation, toxidromes, autoimmune reactions, and other drug effects can cause brain damage. The means and mechanisms will differ based on the specific kind of drug effect and situation, but this is the most concerning category overall and is the category most likely to involve catastrophic damage occurring in a short period leading to lasting impairments or worse. In contrast to the smaller-scale toxic influences mentioned, this kind of damage is reasonably likely to show up on imaging or other testing, depending on the circumstances and sometimes the severity of the precipitating event. In essence, antipsychotics interfere with the normal functioning of the body, and can cause harm to the physical and chemical forms and structures of the body’s parts in addition to interfering with the processes necessary for maintaining health. Sometimes there are mechanisms discovered which are responsible for certain kinds of harms, but sometimes we don’t yet understand why particular problems happen. The paths to brain damage are somewhat diverse with these drugs due to how many things they interfere with and the complexity and interdependence of the body’s homeostatic mechanisms and broader functioning. Notably, not all symptom-producing interference will indicate brain damage. Even persistent symptoms can revolve around drug-induced dysfunction or other alterations which don’t necessitate damage to tissues, cells, or cell parts. It may be that typical cases with symptoms lasting years or longer comprise a combination of damage and non-damage changes, but not a lot of research is being done and measuring brain health and the factors contributing to it is a monumental task and one whose understanding is somewhat beyond our level of medical knowledge in the first place. Also worth mentioning is that sometimes there can be relief from symptoms even if damage remains, as neuroplastic adaptation can still be helpful despite. Not all drug recovery is about replacing or repairing damaged parts, and a lot of brain damage may be fundamentally irreparable in conventional medicine. Mitochondria can potentially be replaced, but someone with significant tissue loss will never be the same, for example. The body, thankfully, has many ways of improving functioning even if damage remains, and rehabilitation can often involve rewiring and retraining, not just a return of overall health or brain health.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: Why don’t psychiatric drugs work within 24 hours like alcohol? Why is there no treatment resistance with alcohol?
Answer: Drugs are drugs. Drugs marketed as “psychiatric drugs” are working within 24 hours just like alcohol. But, there are two caveats. First, not all drug have equally obvious effects. People can usually tell whether they have taken an amphetamine or benzodiazepine but may or may not notice an SSRI or buspirone, for example. This depends a lot on the specific mechanisms of the drug, but different people also react uniquely and the situation of use can impact how a drug feels. Second, the effects of a drug after one dose can differ from how it feels to be on that drug continuously. This is not different from alcohol, as having a few beers one day is usually going to feel different from drinking beers all day every day for weeks on end. Some psychiatric drugs tend to feel significantly different in some ways after continuous use, but plenty don’t feel so drastically different. Given individual variability and circumstances, people can still feel more or less the same way from day one onward with any of these drugs, from Adderall to Prozac to Xanax to Seroquel. As for “treatment resistance”, there is plenty of “treatment resistance” with alcohol and its low suitability played a part in it being phased out as a go-to psychiatric drug. There are again two complications to note here. First, the idea of “treatment resistance” is typically a way to blame patients or their situations for drug failure. Saying you’re using the wrong tool for the job is more honest. Alcohol is usually the wrong tool for the job if the aim is clinical intervention. The same applies to modern psychiatric drugs. Second, drug tolerance, lack of effectiveness, and adverse effects outweighing desired ones are entirely common with alcohol, particularly with continuous use. It is not at all distinct from standard psychiatric drugs in that respect. Like those other drugs, there are some things it usually does more often than not no matter how long someone has been using it. Sedation, stimulation, cognitive impairment, emotional blunting, and other psychotropic effects usually carry forward, though drug tolerance can develop to some.

Question: Why are no psychiatric drugs available over the counter in low dosage? Are they that inherently unsafe, or is there a systemic bias at play?
Answer: The premise is false, but the question in general is valid. There are a variety of psychiatric drugs available over-the-counter, though the exact ones around will depend on where you are buying. There are no mechanisms which make a drug a ‘psychiatric drug’ rather than any other kind of psychotropic, and also no mechanisms to psychiatric drugs which prevent them from being sold over-the-counter. The main focus here is regulation and how the regulatory process works, especially in light of how any drug can be or become a “psychiatric drug”. Standard psychiatric drugs are too dangerous and also too difficult to self-manage for them to be responsibly sold over-the-counter for the purposes they are normally prescription-only. The average consumer also cannot reasonably psychiatrically self-diagnose, though most psychiatric prescribing is off-label anyway so approval for marketing versus endorsement of use is an example of the kind of administrative line being drawn which is not necessarily a practical one. This is in addition to how the actual effectiveness of most psychiatric drugs tends to be very low and thus we would have drugs already inappropriate for most patients given prescriptions to use being bought up by even more patients that should not be taking them and will not manage them properly. The prospect of responsible, effective average use is basically absent, and is already lacking in prescribed use (which the FDA doesn’t really care about as it isn’t their responsibility). While regulatory agencies like the FDA also prefer that drugs “have a low potential for misuse and abuse” to be approved for over-the-counter marketing, exactly what that means is not always clear or coherent. Physical dependence, for instance, usually gets a free pass — it is drugs considered fun to take which are mostly being targeted. So, drugs like amphetamines and barbiturates won’t be acceptable, versus drugs like reuptake inhibitors and antagonists. There are some additional loopholes. Drugs that aren’t approved to be marketed regionally can sometimes still be bought, so drugs that are prescribed psychiatrically (or approved for psychiatric uses in other countries) can still potentially be available over-the-counter. This isn’t the case in all countries, but applies to the US. Drugs that have approved over-the-counter uses which differ from psychiatric uses can make a drug available for purchase for people planning to take it psychiatrically, too. Supplements with the same actions as prescription-only psychiatric drugs are also usually fine to sell over-the-counter. The regulatory process here treats supplements differently from everyday prescription drugs, and there is a lot more leeway for what their actions and effects can be, particularly when marketing claims are not violating policies. The main obstacle for psychotropic supplements in the US is the DEA, not the FDA. The DEA is concerned with the political side of drugs, not the clinical or pharmacological sides, so benefits, wellbeing, and safety aren’t their focus. As for dosages, it would make no sense to have a lower over-the-counter dosage available but higher prescription-only dosages. Firstly, because people should not be taking more than the minimal amount of these drugs anyhow. If a lower dose is enough to accomplish the goal, higher doses shouldn’t be prescribed. Secondly, because taking higher doses would just be a matter of buying multiple OTC packs and combining them. Thirdly, because lower doses are not much safer than higher doses, within the clinical range, and would not mitigate the dangers involved. Given that regulatory approval is an administrative process, there are costs involved. Research, paperwork, lobbying, and other investments are integral to getting new drugs and drug indications approved. For drug companies, there needs to be a financial benefit to gaining more approval for their products, and sometimes the financial incentive is inadequate. Most prescribing going on was never researched and approved, and there is no financial incentive to do the research or try to get it approved because it’s already going on and a failure to be approved could be counterproductive. Since most psychiatric drugs can be accessed by consumers with the snap of a finger and have very cheap generic formulations on the market, the fact that many are prescription-only is a pretty small hurdle. In theory, drug manufacturers would love for people to scoop up their products OTC by the armful even if they died as a result. But, the current balance brought in uncritical, free-flowing prescribing is still extremely profitable and empowering and there are some protections companies enjoy when products are prescription-only. It is more profitable to illegally market these drugs than to try and make them available OTC.
